articles.title: Qualcomm lâche une bombe : les rois de l'IA planchent bien sur leurs propres smartphones
articles.text:
Depuis le printemps, OpenAI se voit prêter un projet de smartphone piloté par des agents IA, sans confirmation de l’entreprise. Dans un entretien diffusé la semaine dernière, le PDG de Qualcomm, Cristiano Amon, a glissé sans citer de noms : « Eh bien, les entreprises d’IA commencent à faire des téléphones ». Certaines d’entre elles, parmi les plus en pointe du secteur, préviennent Qualcomm qu’il leur faudra, d’ici 2028, faire tourner en permanence un modèle d’au moins 100 milliards de paramètres sur un téléphone.
OpenAI en tête des candidats, ByteDance déjà passé à l’acte
En mai, Cristiano Amon assurait travailler avec « à peu près toutes » les entreprises d’IA sur des appareils tenus secrets, parmi lesquelles OpenAI et Meta. Il prédisait alors la fin d’un monde organisé autour du smartphone, que Qualcomm a lui-même contribué à bâtir, au profit d’objets à porter sur soi, des lunettes aux pendentifs. Au Snapdragon Summit de septembre, Qualcomm a surtout expliqué pourquoi le smartphone ne serait pas remplacé, et son patron assure désormais que les téléphones « ne vont aller nulle part ».
Fin avril, l’analyste Ming-Chi Kuo, réputé pour ses prédictions sur les produits Apple, affirmait qu’OpenAI préparait un smartphone conçu autour de ses agents IA. Qualcomm et MediaTek en codévelopperaient les puces, et Luxshare, un sous-traitant d’Apple, se chargerait de la fabrication. Début mai, l’analyste avançait la production de masse au premier semestre 2027, contre 2028 auparavant, et jugeait MediaTek mieux placé pour fournir seul le processeur, une version sur mesure de sa puce Dimensity 9600. Si tout se passe comme prévu, il table sur environ 30 millions d’exemplaires en 2027 et 2028 cumulés, soit à peu près la moitié de ce qu’Apple ou Samsung écoulent chacun en un trimestre.
Sur Android, les assistants concurrents de Gemini n’ont aujourd’hui qu’un accès restreint aux fonctions clés du système, auxquelles l’assistant de Google accède pleinement. Ming-Chi Kuo y voit la raison d’être du projet d’OpenAI : « Ce n’est qu’en contrôlant entièrement à la fois le système d’exploitation et le matériel qu’OpenAI peut fournir un service d’agent IA complet ». En juillet, la Commission européenne a imposé à Google d’ouvrir une douzaine de ces fonctions aux assistants concurrents, la plupart dès l’été 2027.
En Chine, ByteDance a tenté l’expérience dès décembre 2025 avec le Nubia M153, un smartphone conçu avec ZTE et piloté par son assistant Doubao. Les quelque 30 000 exemplaires de cette série limitée, vendue 3 499 yuans (près de 500 dollars), sont partis dès le premier jour. En quelques jours, WeChat, Taobao, Alipay et plusieurs applications bancaires ont pourtant bloqué ou déconnecté les comptes pilotés par l’agent, et ByteDance a fini par suspendre les fonctions de paiement, de banque et de jeu.
100 milliards de paramètres dans un téléphone, est-ce seulement réaliste ?
Les paramètres sont les réglages qu’un modèle d’IA ajuste pendant son entraînement : plus il en compte, plus il est généralement capable, et plus il réclame de mémoire. Présenté le 22 septembre, le Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, la puce pour smartphones la plus puissante de Qualcomm, fait tourner en local un modèle de 30 milliards de paramètres. Ce type de modèle repose sur une architecture dite de « mélange d’experts », qui fonctionne comme une rédaction où seuls les spécialistes du sujet prennent la plume. Sur ces 30 milliards de paramètres, environ 3 milliards seulement s’activent pour chaque fragment de texte produit. Apple a présenté en juin son propre modèle local bâti sur ce principe, avec 20 milliards de paramètres.
Même compressé à 4 bits par paramètre, un format pris en charge par les puces mobiles récentes, un modèle de 100 milliards de paramètres occupe à lui seul environ 50 Go de mémoire vive. Les smartphones actuels dépassent rarement 16 Go, et les modèles Android à 24 Go lancés il y a un an se raréfient depuis que la pénurie de composants liée au boom de l’IA fait flamber les prix. En février, Cristiano Amon imputait d’ailleurs les prévisions décevantes de Qualcomm à un problème « à 100 % lié à la mémoire ». Pour contourner l’obstacle, Qualcomm charge déjà une partie des modèles depuis la mémoire de stockage, plus spacieuse, et confie à un circuit dédié de petits modèles, de 200 millions de paramètres au plus, qui tournent en permanence. La mémoire de stockage reste toutefois nettement plus lente que la mémoire vive, et la qualité d’un modèle se dégrade fortement quand on le compresse en dessous de 4 bits.
Qualcomm, qui voit Apple remplacer progressivement ses modems par des puces maison, a tout intérêt à voir les laboratoires d’IA concevoir leurs propres téléphones, même si le premier smartphone d’OpenAI pourrait lui échapper.

articles.title: Apple annonce une nouvelle Apple TV 4K ultra puissante, mais gâche la fête en Europe
articles.text:
Apple annonce une nouvelle Apple TV 4K ultra puissante, mais gâche la fête en Europe
Apple vient de dévoiler sa nouvelle Apple TV 4K, avec une puce A19 plus puissante, de nouvelles possibilités audio et un Siri dopé à l'intelligence artificielle. Malheureusement, cette dernière nouveauté ne sera pas disponible en Europe…
Après quelques rumeurs persistantes, la firme de Cupertino renouvelle enfin son Apple TV 4K, dont la précédente génération remontait à 2022. Quatre ans plus tard, le fabricant présente un nouveau boîtier multimédia qui mise sur davantage de puissance, une expérience home cinéma améliorée et surtout une toute nouvelle version de Siri dopée à Apple Intelligence, mais pas pour tout le monde.
Face aux Google TV Streamer, Nvidia Shield TV et autres boîtiers TV, Apple continue de miser sur son écosystème et une interface particulièrement fluide. Si les nouveautés annoncées sont sympathiques, il y a malheureusement une mauvaise nouvelle pour les utilisateurs européens : Siri AI, la principale innovation de cette génération, ne sera pas disponible en Europe au lancement.
Apple TV 4K (4e génération)
Siri AI transforme les recherches à la voix, mais pas chez nous pour le moment...
C'était clairement la nouveauté mise en avant par Apple pour cette quatrième génération d'Apple TV 4K. Le fabricant intègre Siri AI, une nouvelle version de son assistant vocal qui s'appuie sur Apple Intelligence pour comprendre des demandes beaucoup plus complexes et proposer une bien meilleure expérience conversationnelle.
Plutôt que de rechercher un film par son titre ou le nom d'un acteur, on peut ainsi poser des questions à Siri comme on le ferait à un Gemini ou un Chat GPT. Siri AI pourra également répondre à des questions pendant la lecture d'un contenu, par exemple pour connaître le lieu de tournage d'une série. Les réponses apparaîtront dans une petite fenêtre afin de ne pas trop perturber le visionnage.
Malheureusement, toutes ces nouveautés seront absentes de la version européenne au lancement. Apple ne précise pas quand Siri AI pourrait être déployé chez nous, et il faudra donc se contenter des fonctions classiques de l'assistant vocal. C'est assez regrettable puisque l'intelligence artificielle est justement le principal argument de cette nouvelle génération.
Une puce A19 jusqu'à deux fois plus rapide pour l'Apple TV 4K
Sur le plan technique, Apple remplace l'ancienne puce A15 Bionic par une A19 nettement plus performante. Le fabricant annonce jusqu'à 50 % de performances supplémentaires pour le processeur et un GPU jusqu'à deux fois plus rapide.
De quoi rendre l'interface tvOS encore plus fluide, accélérer le lancement des applications et améliorer les performances dans les jeux Apple Arcade. La précédente Apple TV 4K était déjà particulièrement réactive, mais cette nouvelle puce devrait offrir davantage de marge pour les années à venir.
Apple ajoute également un décodeur matériel AV1, un codec vidéo de plus en plus utilisé par les plateformes de streaming, notamment YouTube et Netflix. Il permet de diffuser des vidéos de haute qualité tout en consommant moins de bande passante, un ajout appréciable.
Trois microphones pour contrôler l'Apple TV sans télécommande
Autre changement bienvenu, Apple intègre trois microphones longue portée dans son nouveau boîtier. Jusqu'à présent, il fallait utiliser la télécommande Siri Remote ou un autre appareil Apple pour interagir avec l'assistant vocal.
Désormais, le boîtier pourra capter directement les commandes vocales grâce à un système de réduction du bruit capable d'isoler la voix de l'utilisateur, même lorsque le téléviseur diffuse un film ou de la musique.
Cette nouveauté matérielle équipe déjà de nombreux téléviseurs et peut s'avérer intéressante, mais son intérêt sera forcément plus limité en Europe sans les nouvelles capacités conversationnelles de Siri AI. Il faudra également vérifier quelles commandes vocales seront effectivement proposées sur les modèles commercialisés chez nous.
La télécommande évolue elle aussi, mais conserve son design habituel. Elle profite désormais d'une localisation précise grâce à l'application Localiser et pourra émettre un son pour être retrouvée plus facilement. Pratique lorsqu'elle finit entre deux coussins du canapé.
Jusqu'à quatre HomePod pour un véritable système surround
Apple veut aussi améliorer l'expérience home cinéma avec une nouveauté plutôt intéressante pour ceux qui sont déjà pleinement dans l’écosystème de la pomme : la possibilité d'associer quatre enceintes HomePod à l'Apple TV 4K.
Jusqu'à présent, on pouvait déjà utiliser deux HomePod pour profiter d'un système stéréo avec spatialisation audio. La nouvelle génération va plus loin en permettant d'installer deux enceintes à l'avant et deux à l'arrière pour créer un véritable système surround.
Cette configuration sera compatible avec les nouveaux HomePod mini 2, mais aussi avec les HomePod de deuxième génération. Apple précise toutefois que les enceintes devront être associées par paires identiques à l'avant et à l'arrière.
Il faudra aussi voir ce que cette configuration vaut face à une véritable installation home cinéma ou aux barres de son haut de gamme accompagnées d'enceintes surround que nous testons régulièrement.
Prix et disponibilité de la nouvelle Apple TV 4K 2026
La nouvelle Apple TV 4K est disponible en précommande dès ce 13 octobre 2026, avec une commercialisation prévue le 13 novembre 2026. Elle s'affiche à un tarif de 350 €, quand on trouve l’Apple TV 4K de 2022 autour des 250 € aujourd’hui.
Cette nouvelle version apporte donc quelques améliorations intéressantes, notamment avec sa puce A19 et la possibilité de créer un système surround avec quatre HomePod. L'absence de Siri AI en Europe enlève toutefois une bonne partie de l'intérêt de cette nouvelle génération, du moins pour le moment. Pour les possesseurs d'une Apple TV 4K de 2022, le passage à ce nouveau modèle ne semble en tout cas pas vraiment indispensable.

articles.title: Nvidia says DLSS 5 is now twice as fast and uses 20% less VRAM
articles.text:
In brief: Nvidia DLSS 5 slashed NBA 2K27's frame rates by at least 60% when it launched in September. An update scheduled for this week aims to substantially reduce the neural rendering feature's performance and VRAM overhead. Later this year, DLSS 5 will also support RTX Spark-equipped PCs, Hogwarts Legacy, Where Winds Meet, and classic games through RTX Remix.
NBA 2K27 will receive an update this Friday that aims to make DLSS 5 twice as fast, increasing overall frame rates by up to 40% while maintaining similar visual quality. Future titles that receive official DLSS 5 support, starting later this year, will use the new, faster model by default.
Nvidia claims to have doubled rendering performance and reduced VRAM usage at 4K by 20% through neural model refinements and system-level pipeline optimizations.
In early September tests, maintaining 60 frames per second in NBA 2K27 at maximum settings with DLSS 5 neural rendering enabled essentially required an RTX 5090. An RTX 5070 could just about achieve the same feat at 1440p, while upscaling offered little improvement. The update, arriving on October 16, could make smooth performance more achievable on mid-range and upper-mid-range GPUs.
Hogwarts Legacy will support DLSS 5 with the new model starting November 5. Screenshot comparisons indicate that developer Avalanche Software has significantly scaled back the neural renderer's impact on the game's visuals compared with the initial March demonstration, which drew sharp criticism for altering skin textures and potentially hallucinating new details. The new version appears to modify lighting and shadows while leaving characters' faces untouched.
Where Winds Meet will receive a more dramatic visual overhaul through DLSS 5 as well.
Official neural rendering support is also coming to classic games through RTX Remix starting October 23. Screenshot comparisons show changes to reflections, lighting, shadows, and ambient occlusion in Fallout 4 and the original Mirror's Edge.
Meanwhile, a beta update to the Nvidia app, available today, adds a new frame generation preset designed to improve performance at the expense of a slight reduction in visual quality. The new "Preset C" introduces a lighter version of one of the algorithms used to analyze in-game elements.
Nvidia claims the new performance mode is up to 35% faster on an RTX 5060. To try it, opt into beta features after updating the Nvidia app, then navigate to Graphics > Global Settings (or select an individual supported game) > Driver Settings > DLSS Override – Model Presets > Custom > Frame Generation > Preset C.

articles.title: Industrial Next wants factory robots to switch tasks in minutes, not weeks | TechCrunch
articles.text:
In most factories, automation is fixed: robots and machines are programmed for one specific task and product. Changing a line means reprogramming and physical retooling, or swapping out equipment, which can take weeks or months. San Francisco-based Industrial Next says it’s changing that.
The startup, which presented today on the Startup Battlefield stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, builds AI-driven, self-contained robotic stations powered by proprietary foundation models that connect vision, task context and motion. The company says this lets a production line be retooled in minutes rather than weeks without traditional programming. The goal is to let manufacturers automate complex and delicate tasks that traditionally require human labor.
The company announced on stage that it’s partnering with BMW Group Technology Office to evaluate Industrial Next’s AI-powered dexterous manipulation for manufacturing.
Industrial Next was founded in 2021 by Lukas Pankau and Allen Pan, both of whom previously worked at Tesla. Pankau served as a lead electrical architect at Tesla before moving on to Waymo. Pan led Tesla’s autonomous factory efforts and later became a chief architect at autonomous driving company Neolix.
The pair came up with the idea for Industrial Next while working together at Tesla. Pankau’s first encounter with Pan was literally tripping over him as Pan was asleep on a factory catwalk after pulling an all-nighter. Although the two didn’t get along at first, they soon realized they shared an obsession with getting things done and had complementary skills.
After years of watching cutting-edge vehicle and self-driving technology get held back by decades-old factory equipment, the founders realized that manufacturing needed to be rebuilt.
“We had all these fancy things that we could do on cars. I could run machine learning algorithms to design a car for me. But I couldn’t figure out how to program a robot, and this was pretty common for engineers at Tesla,” Pankau said. “You had this massive divide, right? You had people who are really good at what they’re doing–designing cars and designing self-driving systems–and then you had them effectively stumped at the factory looking at this equipment from the 1980s. And so we started rethinking what this should look like using the technology that we have today and using everything that we know today.”
The two kept thinking about their frustrations with industrial equipment even after moving on to their next jobs. They stayed in touch, often reminiscing about the machines that never functioned the way they wanted, and eventually decided they could do better.
“I was at Waymo at the time, kind of bored out of my mind because I was missing that pace of Tesla,” Pankau said. Pan, he added, was in a similar position at Momenta, a developer of self-driving systems in China. Pan recalled their conclusion: “We’re like, we’re not getting any younger, and we’re still obviously passionate about it. We still keep complaining about industrial technology. Like, this is three years later, we should start the company.”
Pankau notes that traditional industrial robots are typically programmed to perform highly specific, repeatable tasks. As a result, even a small change in the process or product can cause the robot to fail or trigger costly downtime, which forces manufacturers to simplify their products for repeatability.
Making robots truly flexible presents a different challenge. They need enormous amounts of training data and, unlike AI models trained on the internet, robotics lacks the vast datasets needed to teach machines how to perform complex physical tasks.
“We can make robots do all these cool things like dance around, because there’s data for that, but we can’t make them assemble high-precision things,” Pankau explained. “This is where we’ve made a lot of progress on using simulated environments to do these high-precision and high-dexterity tasks. The secret sauce for the robots that we have is that we have given them an understanding of the process in general, but we build that understanding using an extremely high-fidelity simulation engine that is close to the real dynamics to where we can let the robot do these kinds of high precision tasks almost without seeing the parts at all.”
In other words, the robots practice in a highly detailed virtual world that closely mimics real-world physics. Industrial Next’s robotic stations can be reconfigured, combined, and redeployed across product lines. New tasks are taught through simulation and demonstration, rather than hard-coded scripts.
Pankau explained that some of the startup’s workstations are already used in making one of the world’s most popular smartphones. They handle tasks that manufacturers had tried and failed to automate for years, such as threading a delicate flex cable and snapping a tiny connector cap into place. (He wasn’t at liberty to disclose the customer.) He also described a “film peeling” station, where their AI-powered robots strip protective film off camera modules and buttons at or above human speed with 100% accuracy, even when moved to a new phone model and production line they have never seen.
“We started this company because that is the kind of performance that we wish we had at Tesla, where we were bypassing robot stations because we couldn’t program them effectively enough using traditional technologies,” Pankau said. “Now we want to take this to more complicated tasks than just building a phone. We ultimately want to take this to building a full car end-to-end without any human touching ever.”
To check out more of the Startup Battlefield — along with a slate of established founders and VCs whose takes on the industry you won’t want to miss — join us at Disrupt, happening this week in downtown San Francisco.

articles.title: Exclusivo Prime: Motorola Razr 60 tem 2.º menor preço do ano em até 12x • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Exclusivo Prime: Motorola Razr 60 tem 2.º menor preço do ano em até 12x
Motorola Razr 60 (256 GB) com tela POLED flexível de 120 Hz e 12 GB de RAM sai por menos da metade do preço original, em oferta do Amazon Prime no prazo
O Razr 60 de 256 GB está saindo por R$ 2.699 em até 12x sem juros exclusivo para assinantes Amazon Prime. O celular dobrável da Motorola, com tela POLED flexível de 120 Hz e 12 GB de RAM, atinge o 2.º menor preço de 2026 com desconto de 51% sobre o original de R$ 5.499.
Esta é uma das melhores ofertas recentes para quem busca um dobrável em parcelas que cabem no bolso.
O destaque do Razr 60 é sua tela POLED interna flexível de 6,9″. Com taxa de 120 Hz e brilho de até 3.000 nits, ela reproduz cores realistas com alta fluidez nas transições, além de ter visibilidade garantida em qualquer ambiente. A externa POLED de 3,6″ suporta Always-On e ações rápidas.
Seu chip MediaTek Dimensity 7400X e os 12 GB de RAM oferecem alto desempenho ao rodar apps em multitarefa, games e soluções do Moto AI. Os 256 GB de armazenamento disponibilizam espaço interno razoável para guardar vídeos e fotos localmente.
O kit de câmeras é composto de uma wide de 50 MP com OIS e uma ultrawide de 13 MP, que capturam belas cenas com grandes ângulos, e uma frontal de 32 MP que tira ótimas selfies. Todas filmam em 4K.
O corpo de alumínio com dobradiças de titânio do Razr 60 é reforçado pelo vidro Gorilla Glass Victus sobre a tela externa, resistente a acidentes diversos. Já a certificação IP48 adiciona proteção contra poeira moderada e mergulhos acidentais.
Sua bateria de 4.500 mAh suporta carregamento rápido de 30 W. Segundo a fabricante, o gadget é capaz de receber uma carga para 12 horas de uso em apenas 15 minutos, recurso ideal para usuários com agendas corridas.
O Razr 60 de 256 GB (R$ 2.699 em até 12x sem juros exclusivo Amazon Prime) foi atualizado para o Android 16 e deve receber mais dois updates do sistema operacional. O celular da Motorola traz conectividade 5G, Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 5.4 e NFC.

articles.title: Hackers turn business backup servers into crypto mines after sneaking malware disguised as Microsoft Edge
articles.text:
Hackers turn business backup servers into crypto mines after sneaking malware disguised as Microsoft Edge
Servers used as a failsafe in case of a cyberattack, became targets of cyberattacks themselves
- Attackers exploited critical AhsayCBS backup software flaws to compromise organizations’ backup servers
- Intrusions deployed webshells and disguised XMRig cryptominers for persistence and stealth
- Researchers urge immediate patching, restricted access, and full system reimaging if compromised
In a particularly brazen hack, threat actors were seen targeting the servers that businesses use as backups in case of a cyberattack.
The vulnerabilities used in this attack have since been mitigated, but since the attack is currently ongoing, organizations using this particular backup method are urged to apply the fixes immediately and secure their premises.
AhsayCBS backup utility
At the core of this incident is a backup utility called Ahsay Cloud Backup Suite (or AhsayCBS), a server-based backup management platform developed by a company of the same name, based in Hong Kong.
Businesses, managed service providers (MSP), and IT admins use it to manage backups for their devices and clients across a range of virtual and physical servers, databases, and various software environments, with the tool widely used by IT service providers to manage their clients' data.
Security researchers Huntress noted that on October 4, 2026, two flaws in AhsayCBS were publicly disclosed: CVE-2026-105113, and CVE-2026-105134. The former is a medium-severity vulnerability affecting the checkSysPwd function, and can lead to improper authentication. The latter is a critical-severity flaw affecting the Replication Receiver component, which could lead to unauthenticated remote code execution as NT AUTHORITY/SYSTEM on the host.
“The API contains an authentication bypass that could allow for a random token to substitute valid credentials,” the researchers explained. “After exploitation, a threat actor configured a malicious receiver and dropped a Java Server Page (JSP) webshell into the application directory served by the CBS application.”
Just three days later, threat actors started exploiting these bugs - the first one to bypass authentication, and the second one to gain code execution and deploy webshells on exposed systems. The webshells served primarily as droppers, deploying a range of stage-two executables.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Mining crypto
Huntress also saw threat actors deploy a popular cryptominer called XMRig. This is a legitimate open-source miner that uses the computer’s hardware, electricity, and internet, to mine the Monero currency and deposit it to the attackers’ wallets.
Monero is the go-to currency for unsolicited crypto mining since it is designed as a privacy-first coin that is very difficult to trace across the blockchain.
The attackers went to lengths to hide XMRig on these backup servers. They disguised them as a Microsoft Edge process and installed them as fake Edge update services. They also made sure it hid when someone looked.
A script (apparently written by AI) shuts down the miner whenever Task Manager is opened. The same script would close Task Manager after an hour.
Backups are perceived as one of the strongest protections against ransomware attacks. Virtually all cybersecurity organizations and thought leaders are advising organizations deploy backups and frequently maintain and control them, to make sure they are not outdated or otherwise corrupted. The fact that they can be compromised with relative ease should be cause for alarm. Businesses who were struck could consider themselves lucky to have only gotten an XMRig infection and not a full-blown ransomware encryptor.
That being said, as of October 8, at least five organizations were already targeted, Huntress said. Therefore, it is essential all organizations using AhsayCBS apply the provided patch as soon as possible. All versions of the utility, through 10.3.4 are impacted, it was said.
Besides applying the fix, organizations should also restrict AhsayCBS management interface web access, since the exploit targets the external accessible web app service on the host. “Access should be limited to trusted IP addresses only or require VPN,” Huntress says. “If any of the IoCs listed in this blog have been uncovered, companies should carry out a full host re-image from a trusted backup; as attackers have been able to hide secondary backdoors for extended persistence.”

articles.title: Apple reveals new Apple TV 4K and HomePod Mini with Siri AI
articles.text:
Apple has unveiled several new products, all coming to Canada. These devices include the HomePod Mini 2, the new Apple TV 4K, the new Home Collection with LG and Schneider, and the new HomeView.
The new HomeView is now available for pre-order and will release on November 13. Apple’s cool new device launches in Starlight, Space Grey, Silver, and Rose Pink, and can sit on a tabletop or be wall-mounted.
The HomeView costs $429; learn more here.
New Apple TV 4K
The new Apple TV 4K costs $429. Like most other Apple devices, you can use the new Siri AI and ask the Apple TV 4K, “Show me some documentaries with cute animals,” and the set-top box will show documentaries with cute animals. You can also ask it to “play that show my friend Mark texted me about,” and it’ll start playing that series — in our demo, it was Ted Lasso.
The new Apple TV 4K also has its own far-field microphones, meaning you can speak to Siri directly without pressing the Apple TV remote. The remote finally plays sound, so if you can’t find it, you can ask the Apple TV, “Hey Siri, where’s the remote?” and Siri Remote Find My will play the recognizable “Find My” jingle. It also has Precision Finding now, so you can locate it more easily.
The new Apple TV 4K is available for pre-order today and ships October 30.
HomePod Mini 2
Alongside the new Apple TV 4K and the HomeView, the Cupertino tech giant also unveiled the HomePod Mini 2. The smart speaker comes in green, blue, pink, space grey and silver. It also has Siri AI with access to broad world knowledge and personal context, so you can ask Siri to play a song you were talking to your friend, Danielle, about.
Lights will glow to match album art for some immersion. You can now use AirPlay from your iMac and set the HomePod Mini 2 as the default speaker for better sound. You can also pair them with another for surround sound, which is great if you use your iMac for gaming. You can also set up to four with the new Apple TV 4K for better surround sound, or pair them with two HomePods Gen 2s for even more immersion.
The HomePod Mini 2 costs $199 and is available for pre-order, with release on October 30.
Apple Home Collection
Apple has teamed up with LG for a new lineup of accessories. This includes a new Indoor Camera that can tilt down when you get home for privacy. A new Floodlight with Camera that lights up whenever someone walks by.
There’s also a new video doorbell that chimes through your HomeView or HomePods when someone rings, and it has two cameras. Person-to-package: one camera points directly at incomers, and another points downward so you can see packages.
These three devices launch in November.
LG also has a new Smart Deadbolt Lock that unlocks when your iPhone or Apple Watch approaches the door. The Smart Deadbolt Lock works with up to six devices, but you can tap it to show the PIN code option. And I thought it was cool that you flip up the door lock to reveal a keyhole. Last but not least, the two companies revealed a new thermostat.
These devices launch in December.

articles.title: TCL Showcases 5G AI CPE X5 at Network X 2026
articles.text:
Tuesday, October 13th 2026
TCL Showcases 5G AI CPE X5 at Network X 2026
TCL, a global leader in consumer electronics, showcases its flagship 5G AI CPE X5 at Network X 2026. Positioned as a comprehensive agentic AI 5G CPE, X5 features natural-language interaction, AI network optimization, application-aware QoS, proactive diagnosis and self-recovery, and an extensible AI service platform—making connectivity more reliable and effortless for households while helping reduce operators' O&M workload. 
The X5 is designed for homes and small businesses seeking a premium broadband experience, from remote work and gaming to smart-home connectivity. Recently, it was named a 2026 IFA Innovation Award Honoree.An AI Agent That Turns User Intent into Action
The X5's unified agentic architecture enables its AI agent to interpret user intent and coordinate sensing, decision-making, execution and recovery. Instead of navigating individual settings, users can express a desired outcome. For supported tasks, the agent can coordinate network checks, traffic prioritization, mode switching and compatible-device control. For example, a user could ask the X5 to optimize the network for a gaming session, and the agent can adjust supported settings based on network conditions.
Specialized AI Engines for Adaptive 5G and Wi-Fi Connectivity
The X5 applies specialized AI engines across the connectivity path, from 5G reception to indoor Wi-Fi coverage.
For cellular connectivity, AI analyzes signal quality to help select the antenna configuration for better reception. Its 8Rx architecture combines four directional C-band antennas with up to 13 dBi gain and four omnidirectional C-band antennas, delivering up to 51% higher downlink throughput than a 4Rx design in lab testing. Supporting 3GPP Release 18, X5 offers a theoretical peak downlink rate of 7.01 Gbps.
For indoor Wi-Fi, AI-assisted signal-path selection, together with congestion detection and channel adjustment, helps maintain fast, stable connectivity.
Proactive Network Self-Care, from Diagnosis to Recovery
X5 monitors Wi-Fi, LAN, cellular connectivity and system operation through a closed-loop process: detecting conditions, diagnosing supported issues, performing recovery actions, verifying results and recording outcomes. Supported recovery scenarios include certain congestion conditions, module anomalies, resource overload and parameter drift. 
Network health reports provide visibility for users and support teams. Where integration is enabled, cloud management and operator systems link local diagnostics with further assistance.
Smarter Traffic, Power and Access Management
Local AI QoS recognizes supported gaming, streaming and video-call traffic, prioritizing selected latency-sensitive flows when applications share the connection.
Adaptive power management adjusts power modes based on usage scenarios and application traffic. Device identification helps users spot unfamiliar devices, while AI-assisted traffic analysis can identify certain unusual access patterns. Parental controls and guest-access settings offer additional household management options.
Beyond Connectivity: A New Connected-Living AI Hub
TCL presents a broader vision for the X5 as a connected-living AI hub, bringing together on-device computing, a unified AI OS and a Home Computing Center. The envisioned architecture aims to support local multi-agent scheduling and offline execution of supported tasks, with an emphasis on user control over personal data.
Integrated model and skill stores, alongside a unified runtime, are envisioned to support capability expansion and developer deployment. Operators could explore customized AI agents and service packages, with selected capabilities extending to compatible NAS devices, AI cameras and mesh networking equipment.
Beyond the X5, TCL showcases the prplWare-certified TCL LINKHUB HH516 5G FWA CPE, Wi-Fi 8 CPEs and routers, kids' smartwatches, and TCL Tbot, a smart desktop companion designed to extend the kids' smartwatch experience. Across its connectivity portfolio, TCL is exploring AI, next-generation Wi-Fi, 5G and 5G-A technologies to help operators develop more adaptive and user-friendly connectivity services.

articles.title: Martin Shkreli livestreamed himself violating lifetime pharma ban, FTC says
articles.text:
Martin Shkreli—the ex-pharmaceutical executive infamous for illegally hiking the price of a lifesaving anti-parasitic drug by more than 4,000 percent and getting a seven-year prison sentence for the fraudulent scheme he used to do it—has been under a lifetime ban from the pharmaceutical industry since 2022.
However, according to the Federal Trade Commission and the attorneys general of seven states, Shkreli has “flagrantly and repeatedly” violated that ban nearly the entire time—allegedly by trading stock in dozens of drug companies and discussing the industry during livestreams on social media.
On Tuesday, the FTC and the seven states asked a federal judge to hold Shkreli in contempt for the alleged violations. The states include New York, California, Illinois, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Virginia—the same states that joined the FTC in suing Shkreli in 2020 over the “elaborate anticompetitive scheme” involving the anti-parasitic drug, Daraprim. The scheme raised the price from $17.50 per pill to $750 per pill virtually overnight, while blocking generic competitors from entering the market.
“Egregious” conduct
In 2022, the federal court recognized the “seriousness” of issuing such a lifetime industry ban, but ruled that “Shkreli’s egregious, deliberate, repetitive, long-running, and ultimately dangerous illegal conduct warrants imposition of an injunction of this scope.” The ban, among many things, “explicitly prohibits” Shkreli from owning stock in pharmaceutical companies and making public statements that could influence a pharmaceutical company’s business, according to the FTC and the states.
With the alleged violations, the FTC and the states are now seeking to force Shkreli to divest from all pharmaceutical companies and pay a fine equal to his profits from trading pharmaceutical company stocks. They also want the court to lay out “clear and escalating consequences” if Shkreli violates the ban in the future, including further financial penalties and incarceration.

articles.title: Framework Laptop 12 (Wildcat Lake) review: Growing up amid an unprecedented shortage
articles.text:
Tom's Hardware Verdict
The Framework Laptop 12 is a highly portable and repairable budget laptop, but it’s lacking features compared to the competition and lands at a higher price — unless you’re willing to supply your own RAM and SSD.
Reasons to buy
- + Decent performance for single-channel DDR5
- + Highly repairable and customizable
- + Easy to save money if you already have RAM and SSD
Reasons to avoid
- - Configurations often reach about $1,000
- - Display is middling and locked to 1080p60
- - Webcam quality is poor
Why you can trust Tom's Hardware
Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
When Framework introduced the Laptop 12 early last year, it offered an affordable, repairable, and relatively capable laptop, especially aimed at students. Between a 2-in-1 convertible design, a touchscreen with an optional stylus, the slim frame, and a $699 starting price, it was an attractive option. The updated Framework Laptop 12 targets that same group, though it’s entering a very different market, with some of the biggest brands gunning to become frontrunners for the best college laptops. Framework still makes one of the best laptops on the market with the Laptop 13 Pro, but the entry-level market is a different beast, especially today.
Apple’s MacBook Neo has prompted a wave of more affordable Windows laptops, with Intel’s Wildcat Lake taking center stage in devices like Dell’s refreshed XPS 13. The Framework Laptop 12 provides competitive performance with these devices, though at a higher price point and with less premium amenities.
The 1080p, 60Hz display is a reminder that the otherwise-premium-feeling Laptop 12 is a budget device, and although the Laptop 12 starts at just $549 without memory or storage, it ends up around $200 to $300 more expensive than the competition when fully configured. The laptop begs a question: how much are you willing to pay for repairability?
Design
Like Framework’s previous Laptop 12 with 13th-Gen Intel CPUs, the updated version with Wildcat Lake comes in a variety of colors: Black, Gray, Lavender, Bubblegum, and Sage. Our review unit, as you can see, is the Lavender variation. At the time of writing, you need to purchase the DIY version to choose your color; the prebuilt version is currently only available in Sage.
Unlike Framework’s more expensive Laptop 13 Pro, you don’t have the option to customize the color of the bezels, and only Gray and Lavender keyboard options are available now (though, presumably, Framework will expand these options). USB-A and USB-C modules come in a wide array of colors, as well, though other expansion modules are limited to a standard silver color. Framework also offers an optional $59 stylus, matching the color options available for the Laptop 12.
The Framework Laptop 12 is a highly portable device, though perhaps not as thin and light as you’d expect out of a 12-inch laptop. It's 0.72 inches thick and clocks in at 2.8 pounds, which is thin enough and light enough, though not on the level of its enclosed competitors. The MacBook Neo weighs about the same at 2.7 pounds, but it’s covered in aluminum and it’s 0.5 inches thick. The XPS 13 with Wildcat Lake is much lighter at 2.2 pounds, thinner at 0.5 inches, and also finished with aluminum.
Considering the bulk of modularity, the fact that Framework managed to get the weight and thickness of the Laptop 12 close to closed-door competitors is remarkable. However, the fact remains that you’re often paying a premium with the Framework Laptop 12 compared to the Neo and XPS 13 and, in both cases, getting a laptop that feels less like a premium ultrabook out of the box.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Although the Framework Laptop 12 isn’t finished in aluminum, it still has a metal structure. On top is plastic, which is then coated with thermoplastic polyurethane to absorb impacts. That leads to a plastic feeling externally, though with a smooth, slightly grippy surface that feels good in the hands.
Framework offers an optional backlight on the keyboard (our review unit didn’t have one), as well as four module slots for expansion ports. The back two support Thunderbolt 4 and DisplayPort Alt mode, and all four support USB 3.2 Gen 2 speeds and USB-PD. A 3.5mm headphone jack is standard on the Framework Laptop 12, regardless of the additional modules you choose.
Specifications
| CPU | Intel Core 7 350 | 
| Graphics | Intel Xe3 (2 cores) | 
| Memory | 16GB LP | 
| Storage | 1x 16GB DDR5-5600 SODIMM | 
| Display | 12.2-inch, 1920x1200, touch, 60Hz | 
| Networking | Intel BE213 Wi-Fi 7 / Bluetooth 6.0 | 
| Ports | Up to 4 user-selectable expansion cards | 
| Camera | 2MP sensor, 1080p30, hardware privacy switch | 
| Battery | 50Whr | 
| Power Adapter | 60W USB-C GaN (optional) | 
| Operating System | Fedora 44 | 
| Dimensions (WxDxH) | 11.29 x 8.42 x 0.72 | 
| Weight | 2.8 pounds | 
| Price (as configured) | $1,491 ($1,384 without expansion cards and power adapter) | 
Productivity Performance
This isn’t our first outing with Intel’s Wildcat Lake, so we went into this review with a good idea about what to expect from the Framework Laptop 12’s performance. Our test machine came with the highest-end chip Framework offers in this laptop, which is the Core 7 350. It’s a 6-core / 6-thread CPU with a maximum turbo clock of 4.8 GHz, and it can operate between 15W and 35W.
If you’re unfamiliar, Wildcat Lake is the younger, weaker sibling of Panther Lake. It uses Intel’s cutting-edge 18A node but with several cut corners. For starters, the 350 comes with just two faster P-cores (the remaining four are an LPE cluster). It also comes with just 6MB of last-level cache, half of what you get with Panther Lake.
The cores matter less here than the memory, however. Wildcat Lake exclusively uses single-channel DDR5 or LPDDR5X, regardless of capacity (support goes up to 64GB). In practice, that often means you need to overbudget your capacity, at least compared to something like the MacBook Neo with unified memory. Performance drops at 8GB with Wildcat Lake (see our Dell XPS 13 review).
The Core 7 350 comes in behind in single- and multi-core performance in Geekbench 6 compared to the A18 in the MacBook Neo (though multi-core to a much lesser extent). Compared to the 6-core Core 5 320 in the XPS 13, the Framework Laptop 12 is in lockstep with multi-core speed, and just shy of 5% ahead in single-core speed.
Compared to full-fat Panther Lake in the Framework 13 Pro, Wildcat Lake actually looks better than expected. The 13 Pro here is for context, not as a true comparison point; it costs a few thousand dollars. What’s interesting in Geekbench is how the X7 358H in the Framework 13 Pro scales, relative to the Core 7 350.
The X7 358H is a 16-core chip with a 4.8 GHz boost and access to up to 80W of total power (though much of that is allocated to the 12-Xe3-core GPU). Despite more than doubling total core count, and offering a doubling of P-cores, we’re not seeing twice the performance. And, even with access to less power, the Core 7 350 is within 5% of Panther Lake’s single-core performance.
With Geekbench, Apple silicon tends to perform especially well, particularly in single-core tasks, so keep that in mind.
Even with a bit of extra clock speed, however, the Framework Laptop 12 with the Core 7 350 came in behind the Core 5 320 in the XPS 13 in Handbrake. Here, the Geekbench swing toward Apple levels out; the A18 was 8% ahead in Geekbench 6 multi-core, but it’s less than 3% ahead here in Handbrake.
The Panther Lake-based 13 Pro gives some much-needed context, showing compounding factors between higher core counts, higher power limits, and true dual-channel memory. Again, it’s a far more expensive laptop, and the Framework Laptop 12 performs in line with our expectations for laptops in this class.
Perhaps the biggest takeaway is how similar the Core 5 320 is, at least in this laptop. You get an extra 200 MHz on the CPU and 100 MHz on the GPU with the Core 7 350, which isn’t moving the needle a ton here given how limited Wildcat Lake is as a platform. That’s good news, as the Core 5 320 will save you $220 in the Framework Laptop 12 compared to the Core 7 350.
Unfortunately, many of our gaming tests for laptops won’t run on Linux, and given that devices are often shipped back, we can’t go back and retest a dozen devices. That’s not too important here, though. The Core 7 350 has just two Xe3 cores, as do other Wildcat Lake chips, which doesn’t provide enough horsepower to power most titles.
We were able to achieve 30 FPS in Civilization VI at 1080p, which underscores the limitations of the integrated graphics. Intel’s dual-core Xe3 is plenty capable of running Balatro, Vampire Survivors, or whatever 2D sidescroller is currently popping off on Steam. Otherwise, it’s there to give you a display output.
Display
The display is what separates the Framework Laptop 12 from the various other Wildcat Lake-based devices we’ve seen in the wake of the MacBook Neo, and not for the better. Color performance, especially, is weak in our testing, and although peak brightness is in line with similar laptops, the 60Hz refresh rate is a severe downgrade compared to other devices, as is the 1080p resolution.
For metrics, you can see the display peaked at 451 nits, right in line with the MacBook Neo and Framework 13 (non-Pro). However, gamut coverage is poor, with just 64.9% of the sRGB gamut measured, compared to wide-gamut coverage on the competing machines. This is a “budget” laptop, but it’ll easily run over $1,000 with most configurations, and the display is not worthy of that price.
The XPS 13 provides some important context. It doesn’t get as bright — though, it’s hard to split hairs over 50 nits — but it comes with a 120Hz refresh, a higher 2.5K resolution, and it’s a touchscreen like the Framework Laptop 12. That gap in display performance would be understandable with a big gap in price, but that’s not the case. In fact, the Framework Laptop 12 clocks in at $1,271 with a Core 5 320, 16GB of memory, and 500GB of storage. The XPS 13, meanwhile, is $1,000 for that configuration.
Framework naturally needs to cut corners at this price, and it needs to engineer its devices to be repairable and upgradable. So, it’s hard holding the Framework Laptop 12 to the standard of a device like the XPS 13 that doesn’t come with those serviceability upsides. Still, the display is a consistent reminder that this is a budget laptop, whereas with the XPS 13 and MacBook Neo, it’s easy to forget that when doing day-to-day web and office task, due to the premium screens and build quality.
Keyboard and Touchpad
The Framework Laptop 12 comes with a standard keyboard/touchpad combo unit, which is available in several different layouts. There’s currently just a gray and lavender option for the keyboard unit, though presumably Framework will expand its offerings to cover the other colors available on the Framework Laptop 12 (at least with an American English layout).
I achieve 85 WPM with 99% accuracy in a MonkeyType test, compared to 92 WPM at 97% accuracy on my desktop (using the keyboard I type on every day). The keys have standard 19mm spacing and generous 1.5mm of key travel, which makes it comfortable to type on, even considering the small footprint of the Framework Laptop 12.
The touchpad is naturally small given the size of this device, and it’s mechanical, leading to sharp dips during presses on the bottom corners and no responsiveness near the top. It’s a serviceable touchpad, what you’d expect to see on this class of device. Just don’t go in expecting to be spoiled with a large glass surface or haptics.
Upgradeability
Framework built its brand on upgradability, so it’s no surprise that the Framework Laptop 12 earns near-perfect marks here. Like other devices, you can ship the Framework Laptop 12 pre-assembled, or as a barebones system that can accept your own M.2 2230 SSD, DDR5 SODIMM, and operating system. Even then, you can swap out the keyboard, display, mainboard, and ports if you choose (though only within the Framework Laptop 12 form factor).
However, the Framework Laptop 12 brings up the important distinction between serviceability and upgradability. The Framework Laptop 12 is the gold standard (among all Framework devices) for serviceability.But the Wildcat Lake chip brings up concerns about upgradability with its single-channel memory interface.
You can upgrade the memory up to a 64GB DDR5-6400 SODIMM, but there’s only one physical memory slot on the board. Wildcat Lake exclusively uses single-channel memory; it’s not simply a single-channel configuration for a budget price point. You can upgrade to more capacity down the line, but you can’t simply add in a second SODIMM to double your RAM.
You won’t find a more serviceable laptop on the market (outside of the other options from Framework) than the Framework 12, but you primarily have two narrow upgrade paths: more storage and more memory capacity, but not a true dual-channel configuration. Hopefully Framework will continue this line in the future, allowing you to swap the mainboard.
On the serviceable end, however, Framework makes things simple. You get a matching Torx screwdriver with the laptop that can detach the bottom cover. The cover has eight captive screws, so you don’t need to worry about losing them, and it’s primarily there to keep everything together; you actually service the laptop from the top, under the keyboard.
Considering you’re meant to go inside the laptop, Framework has everything clearly labeled, along with QR codes that link to repair guides for various components. With our barebones kit of modules, the laptop was powered on and assembled within five minutes, and this is my first time ever assembling a Framework device from scratch.
Battery Life
Our typical laptop battery tests are based on Windows, and we can’t replicate the testing process on Linux. Framework assured us that Fedora 44 offers the best experience out of the box, so that is what we tested. Instead of a direct comparison, we designed a basic web browsing test loop to see how long the 50WHr battery would hold up away from a charger.
About 9 hours is the answer, with a 9:16 average across three runs. We ran the laptop through a series of live websites with the screen set to 150 nits, Wi-Fi on, and Bluetooth disabled for the test. Again, we can’t make direct comparisons with Windows laptops, but getting around a full day of work is solid for the small 50Whr battery. And with USB-C charging, you can pretty easily top off with a portable GaN brick.
Audio
The stereo 2W speakers inside the Framework Laptop 12 are surprisingly powerful, considering the size of the machine, though the quality of the speakers and dual internal microphones is a clear cut corner to reach the more affordable price of the device. Thankfully, there’s a 3.5mm headphone jack built in (it doesn’t take a module slot), along with Bluetooth 6.0 support for wireless headphones.
The microphone poses a larger issue than the speakers. It’s heavily compressed, which helps make your voice come through clearly, though at the cost of heavy background noise (including keyboard and trackpad noise). You’ll want to use something like EasyEffects in Linux to clean up the microphone audio.
As for the speakers, they’re not as bad as they could be. As mentioned, they’re loud considering the size of the device, and they didn’t distort at full volume. They’re tuned for this type of device, as well. Rather than overemphasizing the highs or pumping too much low-end and exposing distortion, the speakers in the Framework Laptop 12 have a heavy emphasis on the upper midrange.
This range, somewhere between 500Hz and 4kHz, is typically described as “boxy,” and that emphasis works well for the small drivers in the Framework Laptop 12. It implies a low end that the drivers aren’t actually capable of producing. Further, the higher-end of this range, around 1kHz to 2kHz, is where many human voices fall, with sharp consonants pushing higher-end harmonics that come off as harsh. Again, the emphasis helps, allowing voices to come through clearly, without sounding tinny.
Heat
The Framework Laptop 12 stays fairly cool, even under load. The hottest point we measured on the laptop was the underside, directly in the middle, which peaked at 101 degrees Fahrenheit (about 38 degrees Celsius). Under normal usage in a browser with a handful of tabs open, there’s very little noticeable heat, even at this hottest point.
Up where your hands are, we measured 94 degrees Fahrenheit (about 34 degrees Celsius) between the G and H keys on the keyboard, and 86 degrees Fahrenheit (30 degrees Celsius) on the touchpad. That’s warm for your hands, but again, the heat only crops up during heavy load.
Webcam
It’s unsurprising for a laptop at the price of the Framework Laptop 12, but the webcam quality is poor. The camera oddly uses a 4:3 aspect ratio, and the 2MP sensor creates an image more reminiscent of a watercolor than a sharp, Full-HD picture. It struggles with low-light especially, with even moderate shadows in an otherwise brightly-lit room showing visible noise.
The image above was taken in my office in the middle of the day. A window behind me was fully open, about three and a half feet away, and I have a lamp serving somewhat as a key light about three feet off-screen to my left. I’m on the second floor of a two-story house, on a hill without any trees obstructing sunlight (and it was a sunny day). There was a generous amount of natural light in the room.
Yet, you’d think I was sitting in near darkness from the webcam image. The stark brightness from the window darkens my face, filling it with visible noise, as the camera struggles to handle the dynamic range. Sitting in front of an unobstructed window during the middle of the day is the time and place where you’re likely to have the webcam turned on, and it fails that test.
Software and Warranty
Framework offers a standard one-year limited warranty on the Framework Laptop 12, with an optional three-year warranty available for $89 extra. You can read over Framework’s limited warranty, but the limitations are fairly straightforward. Normal wear and tear, damage due to negligence or misuse, and use of third-party parts (or first-party parts from third-party sources) will void the warranty.
Broad warranty protection isn’t as important here as it is elsewhere, however. If, for example, your USB-C port stops working, you can just buy another one rather than going through the RMA process and potentially paying for a repair on the other side (even if you’re under warranty).
You’re free to bring your own OS, but Framework also offers the Framework Laptop 12 with either Windows 11 or Fedora 44 pre-installed. Framework normally uses Ubuntu; however, Fedora 44 has moved to the newer Linux 7.1 kernel, which has optimizations specifically for Wildcat Lake. Using a slower-moving distro like Ubuntu is fine, though you’ll want to make sure to manually upgrade your kernel (and packages) for the best performance if you’re not already using a distro with kernel 7.1 or newer.
Configurations
Framework offers three mainboard configurations: Core 3 204, Core 5 320, or Core 7 350. As we covered in the performance section, the Core 5 320 in the XPS 13 offered largely similar performance to the Core 7 350 in the Framework Laptop 12, so that seems like the sweet spot here. The Core 3 304 is effectively a single-core CPU, with just one P-core alongside a four-core LPE cluster, and it lacks a fingerprint reader, which is available with both other mainboards.
With the DIY edition, Framework ships the laptop without memory, storage, or expansion cards. There’s a single SODIMM slot for memory and a single M.2 2230 slot for the SSD. Framework offers up to 2TB of PCIe 4.0 storage at checkout, as well as up to 48GB DDR5-5600 (again, via a single SODIMM). Framework has USB-C, USB-A, HDMI, Ethernet, 10G Ethernet, DisplayPort, microSD, and SD card modules available, ranging from $10 to $99.
There aren’t any display options aside from the standard 60 Hz 1080p panel in our unit. For the keyboard and trackpad, Framework offers backlit and non-backlit options in various different native layouts.
Framework offers prebuilt versions of the Framework Laptop 12 at a discounted price. The Core 3 304 comes with 8GB of memory ($699), the Core 5 320 comes with 16GB (1,099), and the Core 7 350 comes with 32GB (1,399), and all three configurations use 512GB of storage. All of the configurations come with Framework’s standard expansion card bundle: two USB-C, a USB-A, and an HDMI module.
Dell starts higher with the XPS 13 at $799, but that’s with the Core 5 320 and 8GB of memory. Jumping up to 16GB, the XPS 13 is $999 with the Core 5 320, $100 less than the preconfigured Framework Laptop 12.
Bottom Line
The Framework Laptop 12 is caught between an unprecedented memory and storage shortage and a wave of budget-oriented Windows laptops that skip the repairability angle in favor of better trimmings out of the box. At the same price, it’d be a solid alternative with understandable downsides. The killer for the Laptop 12 is that you’ll likely spend more on it compared to other Wildcat Lake options.
With the Core 5 320, the Framework Laptop 12 is nearly $300 more expensive than the XPS 13, when both are configured with 8GB of memory and 500GB of storage. The Acer Swift Air 14 is $700, and a similarly configured Framework Laptop 12 is $1,074 before adding on the extra cost of a power adapter and modules. For many Wildcat Lake devices, we see prices top out around $1,000; with the Framework Laptop 12, you’ll often spend at least $1,000, assuming you push beyond the Core 3 304.
Modularity comes at a cost, which is more relevant in the case of the Framework Laptop 12 where $100 or $200 makes all the difference in value (it’s less relevant up at the Framework Pro 13, where you expect premium pricing). That extra cost is especially damaging here, when Framework’s competitors are offering better display performance (and more pixels) and all-aluminum bodies for less money.
There are situations where the Framework Laptop 12 is a great option, even compared to the other Wildcat Lake devices on the market. If you already have a SODIMM module you can harvest from other devices, along with an SSD, this is a cheap way to get some of Intel’s latest silicon. But for everyone else, unless you don’t mind paying significantly more for repairability, there are better options available that typically cost less, look better, and feel more premium.
Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

articles.title: Hostinger cut server response times by 35% – here's how to speed up your website even further
articles.text:
Hostinger cut server response times by 35% – here's how to speed up your website even further
Mario Bañares Colastra, Head of Web Hosting at Hostinger, explains how they've sped up users' websites – and why it won't cost you anything
When Hostinger told me that they had cut server response times by 35%, all without investing in additional hardware or infrastructure, I was both impressed and intrigued.
Typically, hosting providers have to invest a notable sum to improve response times – the cost of which is then handed back to users in the form of subscription increases. 
I wanted to know more. How did they do it? What does better server response times actually mean for users? Will subscription costs increase? 
I caught up with Mario Bañares Colastra, Head of Web Hosting at Hostinger, to get some answers.
Why did Hostinger decide to look at altering code and architecture instead of investing in more hardware or infrastructure?
We had already looked at the hardware route. Putting the CDN on all web hosting plans would have required roughly doubling our server count. Making the CDN itself more efficient was the better option.
That worked. We cut the computing resources needed to run the CDN by 45 to 50%, with no new servers or hardware. The result is faster sites for customers. Even sites that don’t use the CDN got faster because our servers are under less pressure overall.
Can you briefly walk us through the process you followed to audit your setup and identify areas where performance could be improved?
We measured first, then fixed. 
We set up dashboards for each server and monitoring based on real visitors’ experience, so we could see how the CDN performed in practice. Then we looked closely at where the processing power (CPU) was going. Encrypted connections and image processing stood out.
Before changing the certificates, we checked that visitors’ browsers and devices would keep connecting without problems. After the change, we checked the results against real-user data.
Which area turned out to be the biggest bottleneck in your existing infrastructure? How did you overcome it?
The biggest drain on processing power was encrypted connections and image processing.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
For encryption, we moved our SSL certificates from RSA to a more efficient type called ECDSA, which cut the CPU used for SSL operations to about a third. We also adopted kernel TLS and improved session resumption, so returning visitors cost less to serve.
For repeated work, image conversions now happen once and get reused across the network instead of being repeated in several places. Requests also go through the CDN location closest to where the website is hosted, over connections that are already open and ready to use.
A 35% cut in server response times sounds impressive, but what does that actually mean for small businesses using Hostinger?
It means our customers’ websites start responding faster when someone opens them. On average, that’s about a quarter of a second sooner. It sounds small, but it happens on every visit, to every page.
Across our infrastructure, the average wait fell from 965 milliseconds to 714, about 26%. On our older servers, it was 35%, which is where the number comes from. These are still early results.
Speed also depends on things like image sizes and plugins, so results will vary from site to site.
The change also helped our lower-priced plans. Their servers used to be busier than the ones for our higher plans, and now they are less busy, which gives them more room to work.
There’s more to come. Subdomains, such as shop.yoursite.com, weren’t included in the earlier rollouts. We’re enabling the Hostinger CDN on them this quarter too, so the improvement could be even bigger for sites that use subdomains.
As website assets continue to get heavier, what else can small businesses be doing to prepare their websites for the future?
Heavier pages mostly come from images, scripts, and plugins. Start with the basics:
- Images. Use modern formats like WebP or AVIF. Hostinger CDN can also resize and convert images on the fly, so you don’t need to change your site.
- Caching. Turn on browser caching, and for WordPress use a caching plugin.
- Plugins and scripts. Keep analytics, chat widgets, and extra fonts to the ones you really use, since each one adds requests.
- Lazy loading. Load images below the fold only when visitors scroll to them.
- Monitoring. Check resource usage and measure Core Web Vitals. A good goal is a page load in under two seconds.
Ideally, the platform handles as much of this as possible, so business owners don’t have to become performance experts.
Why did you decide to roll this out to all users for free?
Once the CDN became cheaper to run, we decided every customer should get it, not only those on higher plans. We offer it at no additional cost.
Our optimization cut the resources needed to run it drastically, so there was no good reason to keep it for higher-priced plans. It also took pressure off our lower-tier web hosting servers, which helps customers and our infrastructure at the same time. We believe improvements like this should be standard, not something people pay extra for.
Owain has been building websites and online stores for his own and his client's businesses for over 8 years. Having taken on a role at TechRadar Pro in 2023, he now leads on all website builder and CRM content, spending his days researching, testing, and reviewing some of the best website building and CRM platforms on the market. He also has a passion for helping people get a great deal on website builders, delivering the best coupon and promo codes on the market. With an extensive background in business, Owain holds a BA(Hons) in Business and Marketing and has written for several leading publications including MarketingProfs, Website Builder Expert, Digital Doughnut, and NealSchaffer.com.

articles.title: La Ley de Propiedad Horizontal lo aclara y los expertos coinciden: "Puedes aparcar dos vehículos en tu garaje si cumples con las normas"
articles.text:
Si hay algo que une a España es que no hay una comunidad de propietarios donde no haya algún lío. Los hay de todo tipo, capaces de plantar una piscina hinchable en un edificio de los años 60 o de denunciar a un vecino por tener un perro en casa. Pero entre los menos exóticos, hay uno que se repite con cierta asiduidad: ¿puedo meter dos vehículos en mi plaza de garaje?
Dos (o tres o cuatro o cinco) vehículos por el precio de uno. Un garaje comunitario es ese espacio dividido en pequeñas parcelas privadas con entrada, salida y un paso común para el movimiento de los vehículos. Por defecto, podríamos pensar que si el aparcamiento tiene 100 plazas, el número de vehículos que puedan cobijarse bajo techo será otro centenar.
Las dudas surgen cuando un vecino utiliza esa misma plaza para guardar dos vehículos. Un coche y una moto suele ser lo más habitual pero pensemos, por ejemplo, en un coche y una o más bicicletas o, sencillamente, en cuatro o cinco motos. Y ahí empiezan los conflictos.
Lo que dice la Ley de Propiedad Horizontal. Lo más evidente cuando nos preguntamos sobre esto es acudir a la normativa general para los edificios o los garajes comunitarios. La respuesta más repetida en diversos artículos de Internet es que acudamos al artículo 9.1 de esta normativa.
En dicho artículo se mencionan diferentes obligaciones del vecino. Las que encajan con estos casos son las siguientes:
a) Respetar las instalaciones generales de la comunidad y demás elementos comunes, ya sean de uso general o privativo de cualquiera de los propietarios, estén o no incluidos en su piso o local, haciendo un uso adecuado de los mismos y evitando en todo momento que se causen daños o desperfectos.
b) Mantener en buen estado de conservación su propio piso o local e instalaciones privativas, en términos que no perjudiquen a la comunidad o a los otros propietarios, resarciendo los daños que ocasione por su descuido o el de las personas por quienes deba responder.
Sin embargo, como vemos, esta redacción sólo sirve para asentar las bases de una conducta, señalar qué está o no permitido en líneas muy generales. Sencillamente se establecen los criterios básicos para especificar que dentro de tu zona privada puedes hacer el uso que quieras del mismo siempre y cuando no perjudiques al resto de propietarios.
¿Entonces? Por lo tanto, no hay ninguna norma de la Ley de Propiedad Horizontal que especifique cuántos vehículos se pueden estacionar en una plaza de garaje. "Realmente, donde hay que mirar primero es en los estatutos de la comunidad de propietarios", nos explica María del Carmen Martín, administradora de fincas colegiada en Madrid.
"La Ley de Propiedad Horizontal simplemente es una base, un mínimo. Son el andamiaje de la normativa. Realmente, son los estatutos los que pueden o no poner un límite. Hay comunidades de vecinos donde se especifica que sólo puede haber un vehículo por plaza y otros en las que no", especifica la colegiada.
La clave. Si no se ha establecido un número de vehículos por plaza, el meollo del asunto reside en si el propietario ha excedido o no los límites de la misma. Y es que contar con dos o más vehículos en el interior de la plaza no exime de cumplir los límites. Si por tener una moto y un coche aparcados uno de los dos ocupa, aunque sea unos centímetros, la plaza contigua o las zonas comunes el vecino puede ser denunciado.
Esto es importante en plazas especialmente pequeñas. Por ejemplo, si nuestra plaza de garaje mide 4,50 metros y nuestro coche mide 4,85 metros de largo, irremediablemente estaremos ocupando las zonas comunes. En ese caso, si un vecino alega que está sufriendo un perjuicio a la hora de maniobrar, por ejemplo, no podremos estacionar el coche. O, llegado el caso, nos podrían denunciar por esto mismo.
Y ojo con el seguro. Javier Iriarte, también administrador de fincas colegiado en Madrid, nos recuerda que es importante revisar las cláusulas de los seguros. "Algunas pólizas sólo cubren los daños en zonas comunes y otras tienen en cuenta los vehículos que hay dentro", señala Iriarte. Eso sí, no todos los casos son iguales.
"Por ejemplo, hay seguros donde se especifica que se indeminizará por plaza de garaje pero no se detalla número de vehículos. En otros, al contrario, sí se pone límite a estos. En ese caso, si ocurre un accidente y tenemos dos o más vehículos podríamos quedarnos sin el dinero", nos recuerda este administrador de fincas.

articles.title: Mitel WX bets next phase of unified communications will be won on the floor, not in the meeting room - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Mitel WX bets next phase of unified communications will be won on the floor, not in the meeting room
For the better part of my 30-year career as an analyst, unified communications has been designed around the person at a desk, bouncing between meetings, chat and email. That made sense when the pandemic pushed everyone onto video.
It makes far less sense when roughly 80% of the global workforce doesn’t sit at a desk at all. In fact, I’ve argued that front-line, non-deskbound workers have been forgotten by most of the UC industry, which is why so many nurses, warehouse workers and others rely on consumer devices and tools.
That’s the gap Mitel Networks Corp. is targeting with Mitel Workforce Experience, which the company recently launched. Mitel WX brings voice, messaging, meetings, contact center and vertical applications into a single client that adapts to the worker’s role rather than the device. Following a pre-briefing I attended with Eric Hanson, Mitel’s executive vice president and chief marketing officer, and Martin Bitzinger, executive vice president of product management, it’s apparent that “toggle tax” across disjointed applications has plagued users for years, so Mitel’s direction addresses a real problem.
Legacy UC is built for everyone, but optimized for no one
Hanson opened with a line that captures the problem with most UC platforms today.
“Many in the industry have attempted to build something that addresses the needs of everyone, but is optimized for no one,” he said. He’s right. The major platforms were built for knowledge workers and then pushed out to everyone else, which is how a nurse or plant technician ends up with a client designed around calendar invites. Those workers live in Epic or a dispatch console, and when something goes wrong, they pick up the phone.
Hanson also made a point I’ve been making for years: Communications was treated as a mature, almost commoditized part of the stack and “wasn’t really deemed to be strategic until it didn’t work.”
Mitel supported its thesis with a Vanson Bourne study it commissioned, which surveyed about 2,000 workers in Canada, France, Germany and the U.K. The study found that 57% of workers waste time switching among an average of seven tools, 79% reach for voice when rapid action is needed, and frontline workers are twice as likely to use unapproved tools.
It’s vendor-funded, so treat it as directional, but it aligns with what I hear from information technology leaders: When the sanctioned tool doesn’t fit the job, workers default to WhatsApp and IT loses control.
Starting over rather than bolting on
One of the more interesting decisions Mitel made was architectural. Mitel WX isn’t a MiCollab refresh or a rebrand of the clients Mitel inherited from Unify. “We basically started with a blank sheet of paper,” Bitzinger said. Only foundational functions, such as voice, are baked into the core client. Everything else is a plugin that administrators enable by role. While this is a longer path to a commercially available product, it will likely lead to greater success down the road because the code is cleaner and purpose-built.
In the demo, a hospital desk worker who also handles contact center queues sees chat and call queues, along with an electronic health record panel, on a single screen. An environmental services worker in the same hospital sees a streamlined view with work group log-in and task completion. A doctor driving in takes calls on a work number via Apple CarPlay or Android Auto. Calls migrate between mobile and desktop rather than being transferred, a small detail that matters when the caller is a patient.
Bitzinger stressed that IT, not the user, owns role design. “It can’t be left up to the user to do all of those things,” he said. That’s the right call. Frontline workers won’t customize their tools, and configurability without governance creates clutter. Administrators manage templated roles in Mitel Central, including across multiple domains common in health systems built through acquisition.
Control is the real product
For Mitel, WX’s competitive differentiation is deployment flexibility. Though every vendor supports public cloud today, Mitel also lets customers use hybrid, private cloud, on-premises, and edge deployments, with the same client built on a common application programming interface for both its CloudLink cloud back end and on-premises Mitel Central. Asked whether a customer could run Mitel WX fully air-gapped, Bitzinger answered: “They can run it completely air-gapped, completely on-prem in their basement if that’s what they prefer.”
The underrated feature is private push notifications. Most mobile UC apps rely on Apple and Google push services to ring a phone. WX can deliver push notifications over the customer’s own network, so calls and alerts still arrive in a hospital running private 5G or on a site that loses its internet connection. For regulated and mission-critical environments, that’s a meaningful differentiator.
Hanson noted that only about 25% of the industry’s 450 million to 500 million seats have moved to the multitenant public cloud and argued that hybrid is increasingly “a deliberate strategy” rather than a way station. With sovereignty pressure building in Europe and resilience concerns everywhere, I agree.
Mitel has a large European install base, and the deployment flexibility will serve it well in that region, where data sovereignty is a major issue, particularly in regulated verticals. I’ve discussed this with Tom Boyle at the NHS, who told me, “I need to ensure our clinicians can make calls regardless of what macro issues happen around the globe, so we will keep our communications system on-prem for the foreseeable future.”
Where the questions remain
The rollout of Mitel WX is phased. Initial availability begins in November, with full platform availability expected in 2027. MiVoice Business support is prioritized, with OpenScape Business and OpenScape Voice for the largest enterprises to follow in the next couple of quarters. OpenScape customers should receive firm dates before planning migrations.
Mitel will release artificial intelligence capabilities after launch. Mitel’s position on AI is that it makes people more capable rather than unnecessary, countering the view that “agents replace everyone,” particularly in contact centers, although I am seeing that opinion start to change. The Mitel AI Services Framework will include MCP support, and the incremental AI in the Elite tier is still to come.
Bitzinger’s view that “voice is the natural UI” for AI makes sense for front-line workers, and Mitel has decades of voice expertise to support this. Now it needs to ship.
The widget model for WX is only as good as its ecosystem. Mitel will build the core integrations itself and rely on services and technology partners for the rest. Bitzinger was candid about the channel, noting that most partners won’t become vertical workflow integrators: “Not for the overwhelming majority of channel partners. No illusions there.” That honesty is welcome, and integration depth will determine how quickly Mitel WX moves beyond early adopters.
Finally, there’s Microsoft Corp. Teams and Zoom Communications Inc. Mitel frames Mitel WX as complementary to both for knowledge workers. That’s sensible given the share those two vendors hold, but it means WX must win on the frontline against health care specialists and the frontline offerings from the big platforms.
Mitel has a real and growing opportunity. Hanson said two large, longtime customers, one in the U.S. and one in France, are already pushing to start migration plans after seeing MWX at Mitel’s User Group. Though the installed base is the “low-hanging fruit,” both Avaya and NEC have large install bases looking to move off those platforms as quickly as they can due to a lack of innovation. Moving a customer off an incumbent can be challenging, but Mitel can offer a “like-for-like” option for businesses that have stayed with a company such as Avaya because moving to the cloud doesn’t support the business.
Advice for IT leaders
- Map communications by role. Inventory your frontline, contact center, and knowledge worker roles and the tools each role uses. That’s the baseline for judging any role-based client.
- Audit your shadow IT. If frontline staff coordinate via consumer messaging apps, you already have a compliance problem.
- Test resilience, not features. Ask how calls and alerts are delivered when the internet path, a cloud region or a push service goes down.
- Get integration specifics in writing. “Integrates with EHR” can mean a deep workflow or a browser tab. Demand to see the integrations you need running on your systems.
- Use the in-place upgrade. Existing Mitel customers should take advantage of the migration path and the dual-run period to pilot Mitel WX with a single high-friction frontline group first.
Final thoughts
For Mitel, the WX strategy makes sense. Rather than chasing only the knowledge worker, where Microsoft and Zoom are entrenched, it targets the underserved frontline majority with a role-aware client, genuine deployment choice and voice at the center. Execution of the platform roadmap, the integration ecosystem and the AI layer will determine whether Mitel WX becomes Mitel’s growth engine or merely a better client for its installed base. Either way, it’s exciting to see UC come to the factory floor and hallways rather than to yet another meeting.
Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.
