articles.title: Flock faces lawsuit after deputies allegedly used its cameras to retaliate against man who sued sheriff
articles.text:
WTF?! It's not like Flock and its dystopian spying system need any more bad publicity, but here we go: the company and officials from a sheriff's office that uses its cameras are facing a lawsuit from a man who says deputies ran his car through Flock's camera network in retaliation for him suing the sheriff over a previous arrest.
Tyler Murkerson has named Flock, Coweta County, Sheriff Lenn Wood, two sheriff's office employees, and three unidentified operators in his lawsuit. It also seeks class-action status, representing people whose vehicles were searched by Georgia law enforcement without documented investigative justification.
Murkerson previously sued the sheriff and two deputies in Coweta County, alleging that they violated his constitutional rights by forcing him to the ground, using a Taser on him, and arresting him in a gas station parking lot over an alleged seatbelt violation. The suit claims that this happened despite Georgia's seatbelt statute not applying on private property. The criminal charges against him were dismissed in June 2023, and his civil rights lawsuit was resolved in 2026.
While the suit was pending, it's alleged that Coweta County deputies used Flock's ALPR network and associated state and federal law enforcement databases to surveil Murkerson.
It's also claimed that audit records show a surveillance period for Murkerson's 2024 Toyota Camry spanning 197 days, and five searches were attributed to the Coweta County Sheriff's Office, each reaching more than 6,000 agency camera networks nationwide.
Only two of the five searches by Coweta County Sheriff's Office have been disclosed. Their operators are listed as "r.fau" and "w.fau," which the suit says correspond to defendants Randall Faulkner and William Faulkner. The other three operators are sued as John Does.
Murkerson said he only found out about these searches after his cases ended, using HaveIBeenFlocked.com, which we previously covered.
The reasons that were typed into the disclosed searches were "info" and "37." The complaint argues that neither corresponds to any investigation, case, incident, or call for service. It also alleges that William Faulkner used "37" for most searches, providing a case number in just four of his thousands of queries.
Under Georgia law, plate data may only be accessed as part of a law enforcement agency's investigation into an offense or activity. Misusing that data is a crime.
Murkerson also believes he was being followed and watched by the Coweta County Sheriff's Office. He ended a six-year business relationship servicing a neighboring police department's vehicles because he no longer felt safe continuing that work while he was being surveilled, the lawsuit says.
The complaint also accuses Flock of enabling these searches by accepting free-text explanations instead of requiring a verifiable link to an investigation.
Flock has announced mandatory case codes and misuse detection by the end of 2026. Murkerson seeks damages and the deletion of unlawfully obtained records.
Flock is rarely out of the headlines these days. Recent stories include a Florida county's discovery of 14 unauthorized Flock cameras, 11 of which remained unclaimed; a federal judge who ruled a warrantless Flock search unconstitutional and threw out drug evidence; and an engineer who built a Flock-like camera to detect police cars and said officers visited him afterward.
Meanwhile, AOC, Bernie Sanders, and Jeff Merkley have introduced legislation that would largely prohibit federal use of automatic license plate readers and withhold certain federal grants from state and local governments that use them.

articles.title: Backstage 1.55 Adds Scaffolder Task Recovery and Removes Deprecated Catalog APIs
articles.text:
The Backstage project has released version 1.55 of its open-source developer portal framework, adding automatic recovery for Software Template tasks that crash or time out. The release also removes a set of deprecated catalog APIs and moves the search module to Elasticsearch 8, so platform teams have several breaking changes to work through before they upgrade.
Task recovery sits behind a new scaffolder.taskRecovery configuration section. When it is enabled, the scaffolder resumes a task from the last completed step, keeps task secrets until the task reaches a terminal state and persists completed step outputs so later steps can read them. The release notes warn that actions used by recovered tasks should be idempotent or use checkpoints, because a resumed task can run an action a second time. The new section replaces three experimental flags, which still work as fallbacks.
The feature responds to a long-standing request. In April 2025, on a GitHub issue tracking scaffolder task retries, Manoj Azad wrote, "Currently, having to re-run the entire scaffolder process can be not only inconvenient but also problematic from a technical standpoint." The 1.55 feature covers tasks interrupted by a crash or time-out, which addresses part of that request.
Workspace serialisation is optional and needs a separate provider module. The new database provider has a 50 MB limit and is intended for development, and the release notes point production installations to the GCP module or a similar external store.
Most of the upgrade work sits in the breaking changes. The catalog backend drops the catalog.enableRelationsCompatibility option, so entity relations now return only targetRef, and it removes the deprecated CodeOwnersProcessor and AnnotateScmSlugEntityProcessor in favour of community modules. The Elasticsearch module now requires Elasticsearch 8.19 or later, although the AWS and OpenSearch providers are unaffected, and custom code that reads raw client responses needs updating. TechDocs strips MkDocs plugins that are not on a built-in allowlist, and teams that need extra plugins must list them under techdocs.generator.mkdocs.dangerouslyAllowAdditionalPlugins. Further breaking changes affect Backstage UI link components, the GitHub repository creation action, incremental ingestion permissions and the Sentry scaffolder action.
Several changes target governance and speed. The scaffolder.requireScmUserCredentials option, first added in the 1.54.6 patch, requires user-provided credentials for supported GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket and Azure DevOps actions. Permission policies that deny unknown permissions must now explicitly allow scaffolder.template.dry-run to keep template dry runs working. Michael Todorovic, a senior SRE at Veepee, changed the GitLab merge request and push actions to compare files locally. "publish:gitlab:merge-request was taking 5–15 seconds against a self-hosted GitLab," he wrote. "It turned out almost all of that was the action asking GitLab for information it already had." The change cuts API requests for a repository of a few hundred files from roughly 300 to under ten, and a step that took 5 to 15 seconds down to about 3 seconds. Core plugins such as the catalog, search and TechDocs now load their pages only when they render, which reduces the initial app bundle.
Since 15 September, the maintainers have shipped three patch releases. Version 1.55.1 fixed the new backstage-cli pm verify-patches command and TechDocs add-ons on the new frontend system, while 1.55.2 and 1.55.3 fixed how TechDocs handles MkDocs Markdown extension configuration.
The release also lists security fixes in seven packages, including the OIDC and Cloudflare Access auth providers and the proxy backend. The Cloudflare Access provider now requires the application audience in its configuration. The next minor version is already in pre-release, with 1.56.0-next.2 published on 6 October.

articles.title: The Paris Auto Show is full of interesting cars Americans can’t have
articles.text:
Perhaps the days when auto shows debuted new models aren’t entirely over. The big trade shows for cars were a gateway drug for many, expos where you could see the newest models of today and the concepts of tomorrow. But automakers increasingly got tired of sharing the spotlight with each other. New reveals moved offsite to events the night or even the week before the show itself. One by one, brands pulled out of auto show after auto show until there was little left to see. And then the pandemic hit.
But the news out of Paris, where its auto show held media day yesterday, seems like we stepped back into a time when automakers would debut new cars aplenty. That retro vibe extends to the cars themselves, with plenty of familiar nameplates reimagined.
France’s Renault has a long and glorious history of delightful concept cars, and more on what it brought to Paris later. But the star of the show was arguably Stellantis, with strong work from Citroen, Peugeot, and Fiat, to name but three. But this article is meant to irritate you, because I’m pretty sure none of the stuff you’re seeing here will come to the United States. And it’s doubly irritating considering what Stellantis’ brands do offer us over here, doubling down on the same malign trends I saw back in 2020: did you know they’re about to relaunch a V8 Hellcat-powered Charger?
EVs can be small and cheap, apparently
The European concepts show us that, as those Kneecap chaps have it, there’s a better way to live. A sense of utopia was responsible for the original Citroen 2 CV; it had to be cheap enough for a farmer to buy it and rugged enough to get produce to market without breaking it. I’m not sure whether the 2 CV Concept also has to be able to transport eggs across a rutted field without breaking any (although the glove box is a clue), but Citroen says that affordability, lightness, practicality, and versatility were top of mind during the design process. The press release probably didn’t need to also say the company imbued it with distinctive character or charm; that’s quite obvious from the design.

The interior feels particularly refreshing compared to the touchscreen overload we’re usually presented. It might be stripped back, but it still has plenty of whimsy—the display in front of the driver has a bande dessinée theme, and the radio is portable and removable from the car. Technology fans don’t despair, there’s still the 8-inch touchscreen, but this too features more of Belgian comic artist Jean-Luc Delvaux’s work.
I’m even confident some of that whimsy will make it into production, because Citroen is going to build the 2 CV within the next two years, it says, and at a starting price of just 15,000 euros ($16,766). That slots it between low-speed microcars like the Renault Twizy, Citroen Ami, and the Fiat Topolino (which you can buy if you live in Michigan), and superminis like Volkswagen’s Polo.

Audi’s first attempt at a supermini was the esoteric A2, an aluminum and aerodynamic experiment from the wild days of Ferdinand Piëch. Like the original, the Audi A2 e-tron is an efficient little thing—its most efficient car ever it says, with a WLTP rating of 4.9 miles/kWh (100 km/12.8 kWh). As one might expect, I was a big fan of the original A2, which was always a rarer sight on the roads than it deserved to be. I can definitely see that car in the A2 e-tron’s design, and the promised efficiency sounds impressive even if there might not be quite the same excessive and cost-ineffective overengineering under the skin. I can’t see any way that Audi brings this car to America, just like we never saw the first A2, or the A1.

The Peugeot 205 GTi was a Gallic alternative to the late ’80s-era Golf GTIs that Americans will be familiar with, and it’s into this well that Peugeot dipped for Paris. Or rather, the wild 205 T16 Group B rally homologation special that the 205 GTi gave birth to, a car that won the world Rally Championships in 1985–86. Like the Renault 5 Turbo 3e from last year, the E-T16 Concept shows us that hatchbacks needn’t just be humble devices for running errands; they can excite, too. I’m not entirely sure about that multifunction steering wheel, though.
What if I need something bigger?
“But Jonathan, I don’t live a block from a metro station, and I need something a bit bigger to cope with my family,” you say. It is true that cars like the 2 CV or ID. Polo will be too small for some. This is true for Europeans as well, and both Renault and Fiat had something for these segments.

The original Fiat Multipla is another underappreciated car from the late ’90s. The styling was challenging for some, but it was a masterclass in space efficiency, seating six in two rows of three abreast. Rather than simply copying that, but with a slab of batteries under the cabin, the Fiat Multiplay explores the idea of a vehicle that’s adaptable, transforming from a three-row people carrier to a pickup. The front passenger seat can be reconfigured as a lounger, and there’s a “Petsenger” seat—a modular mounting point that allows you to swap in a pet bed, child’s car seat, storage compartment, or small table.

The original Renault Espace was very much loved and created the people-carrier segment out of thin air, at least in Europe. The familiar one-box shape remains for the new E-Space Concept, though with massive 23-inch wheels at the corners, the proportions are a little more Hot Wheels or Matchbox than the 1984 version. (Even in Europe, car designers are drawn to oversized wheels.)
There is a criminal lack of electric minivans on the market today, and the only one available here in the US is the VW ID. Buzz. And that sold so poorly that VW suspended imports for a model year. Which probably tells you how likely a US launch for a production E-Space would be.

That said, I sincerely hope it will go into production.

articles.title: Google lanza Gemini 4 Argon, su IA más potente hasta ahora
articles.text:
Google ha lanzado Gemini 4 Argon, su modelo de frontera más poderoso a la fecha. Tras meses de retrasos y de ceder terreno a Anthropic y OpenAI, el gigante tecnológico contraataca con una nueva IA enfocada en flujos de trabajo completos. Gemini 4 llega con mejoras en razonamiento, programación y tareas de larga duración.
Si bien Google ya había anunciado Gemini 4 Argon a finales de septiembre, el modelo no se encontraba disponible. La tecnológica lo ofreció primero a un grupo de socios especializados en ciberseguridad para evaluarlo. La buena noticia es que el modelo de Google ya se puede usar en la app de Gemini.
De acuerdo con Google, Gemini 4 Argon está diseñado para proyectos de ingeniería de software, conocimiento empresarial en áreas como derecho y finanzas, así como también en defensa en ciberseguridad. La compañía coloca a esta versión como el comienzo de la próxima era de su inteligencia de frontera, un modelo que tendrá lo suficiente para medirse con Claude, ChatGPT y otras IA poderosas.
El cambio más notable con respecto a la versión anterior es que Argon responde de forma más directa y con menos titubeos. Gemino 4 dejará atrás los clichés y las respuestas con muchas repeticiones que no llevan a ningún lado, algo que veíamos en la generación anterior. En tareas de larga duración, la IA informará su progreso con más frecuencia para que sepas en qué punto va sin que tengas que preguntarle.
A diferencia de su predecesor, Argon tiene un límite de generación de 1 millón de tokens, lo que le permite razonamientos y flujos de trabajo más extensos en una sola ejecución.
Gemini 4 Argon es una bestia en programación y ciberseguridad
En las primeras pruebas de rendimiento, Gemini 4 Argon logra un buen puntaje en DeepSWE v1.1, un benchmark que mide el desempeño en tareas de desarrollo de software real. Google afirma que sus ingenieros lo usan a diario, desde tareas de depuración hasta migraciones de bases de código de gran tamaño. Entre los casos de uso destacados se encuentran la optimización de algoritmos para computación cuántica y la reducción del uso de memoria en centros de datos.
Fuera de la programación, Gemini 4 Argon tiene un enfoque marcado en la ciberseguridad defensiva. El nuevo modelo de Google puede encontrar, validar y corregir vulnerabilidades de software. En la prueba de CWE-bench v1, que mide la capacidad de la IA para remediar fallos de seguridad, Argon supera a Claude Opus 5.5 y comparte el primer lugar con GPT-6 Astra y Grok 4.7. La tecnológica menciona que ha trabajado con empresas como Wiz, que ya usa Gemini 4 en sus sistemas de defensa.
Otros hitos del nuevo modelo incluyen el descubrimiento de múltiples vulnerabilidades en bases de código complejas que abarcan 20 lenguajes de programación. Gemini 4 Argon es más eficiente que 3.8 Flash Cyber en descubrir la superficie de ataque, identificar vulnerabilidades y producir pruebas de concepto para validarlas.
Gemini 4 Argon ya está disponible para los suscriptores de Google AI Pro y Ultra a través de la app de Gemini para macOS.

articles.title: Licube wants to be the fuel provider to the fusion power industry — see how at TechCrunch Disrupt | TechCrunch
articles.text:
If fusion power pans out, and there are signs that it will, the world will need a lot more lithium.
That’s the bet behind Licube, a startup that has licensed technology from Hirosaki University in Japan, to purify lithium-6, the form of lithium that fusion plants need to make their own fuel, out of naturally occurring lithium.
The reason comes down to the fuel supply. A lot of things have to go right for fusion power to hit the grid, and one of them is the fuel. Most planned plants would run on a mix of two fuels, deuterium and tritium. Deuterium is easy to come by, but tritium is extremely rare in nature, and it’s an open secret in the fusion world that there isn’t enough of it to power every planned plant.
The proposed workaround is to make tritium on site, inside the power plant itself. A fusion reaction gives off a stream of fast-moving particles called neutrons. Startups plan to surround the reactor with a blanket of lithium, so that when a neutron strikes a lithium atom, the atom splits into helium and tritium. The tritium can then be collected, purified, and fed back into the reactor as fuel.
Not all lithium does this job equally well. It comes in two slightly different forms, lithium-6 and lithium-7, named for their weights. Lithium-6 is far better at capturing neutrons and producing tritium, but it makes up only about 7.5% of natural lithium, and the rest is the heavier lithium-7. Separating the two is difficult, and there is little capacity to do it today, so the world doesn’t have enough lithium-6 either.
Licube sees a big market in solving that problem. “If fusion comes online, it should be a $50 billion market by 2040,” Yohei Kiguchi, co-founder and CEO of Licube, told TechCrunch.
Licube is one of 20 startups that are presenting onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco as part of the Startup Battlefield pitch competition.
While fusion has the potential to capture a significant chunk of the multitrillion-dollar energy market, fusion startups are still years away from building their first power plants.
“Fusion is the biggest market in the future, but we also understand the future might be late by a few years,” Kiguchi said.
Until fusion becomes a major market, Licube plans to use the same technology to purify lithium for use in semiconductor, pharmaceutical, fission reactors, and spacecraft industries.
The core technology is based on the electrolyzer, a device that uses electrical current to drive chemical reactions. In Licube’s case, lithium is dissolved in a liquid on one side of a ceramic membrane. As electrical current flows from one side of the membrane to the other, lithium-6 moves faster. Licube can then draw off that liquid and separate the lithium-6.
The goal is to enrich the lithium to at least 99.995% lithium-6. Fusion companies can feed that highly enriched lithium into their fuel breeding systems.
Kiguchi was inspired to start Licube after visiting ITER, the experimental fusion reactor being built in the south of France. He said he was living a couple of hours’ drive away in Monaco after retiring from his previous company, Enechange, an energy-switching platform network in Japan.
“I found out that I was too young to retire,” he said. “I’m an energy guy. I want to do something bigger.”

articles.title: The Metro 2039 Collector's Edition is available now — here's where to pre-order it and other editions
articles.text:

If you're interested in the other editions only, then the pressure probably isn't so high. Certainly not with the standard edition in terms of stock anyway; you'll be able to find this at launch naturally, but the pre-order bonuses might make it tempting.

articles.title: AI causes uproar in mathematics as experts warn against sharing research with LLMs after OpenAI shares 722 manuscripts and proofs — professor argues that the field must focus on building community over raw solutions
articles.text:
AI causes uproar in mathematics as experts warn against sharing research with LLMs after OpenAI shares 722 manuscripts and proofs — professor argues that the field must focus on building community over raw solutions
Mathematics is a collaborative field, now disrupted by AI
Last week, OpenAI shared over 400 results for longstanding mathematical formulas that have troubled humans for decades; now researchers say it could take years for humans to validate and prove all the AI-driven work. But while analysts try to check the work of the unnamed OpenAI internal frontier model that found these alleged solutions, mathematicians argue this kind of AI-powered research and release threatens the field itself.
There's even the claim that by leaping from a prompt to a solution without a clear working in between, there is little benefit to these solutions in the first place. Mathematicians and the field itself may not be able to build on the results, as they don't know how they were achieved, nor has the development of such solutions produced new fields of mathematical understanding.
To make matters worse, there are suggestions that the growing confluence of mathematical and cybersecurity capabilities of frontier AI could bring into question the sanctity of cryptography itself. Alongside raising serious concerns for national security and modern digital systems, it could also put trillions of dollars worth of cryptocurrency at imminent risk.
Over 722 manuscripts dropped
The official count for OpenAI's maths solution release was 722 manuscripts, but with only 300 of the results formalized — digitizing human-readable formulas so they can be computer-verified — it's very difficult to know what's legitimate research. Some of the researchers The Verge spoke to found nonsense explanations within the reports, formulas that don't make sense, and some research that has already been completed by others.
The burden of proving the veracity of OpenAI and its model's claims is very much on the mathematical community, too. OpenAI didn't release the name of the model it used to generate these results, nor the prompts that generated them — despite those recommendations from the Advisory Group on Mathematicians and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI).
OpenAI has at least published changelogs for its GitHub repository of the results, making it clearer where mistakes were made. But with several retractions and corrections already, it seems clear that it didn't check over the results in any great detail before releasing them.
It's this brashness, the pace of releases, and OpenAI's seeming disinterest in remotely slowing down its progress in the field that have so many mathematicians up in arms.
A looming threat becomes immediate
Mathematics isn't the first field to suffer a major upheaval because of AI. Writers first felt the looming threat with the release of ChatGPT in 2022, and both visual and musical artists faced the same concerns shortly after. Artificial intelligence is impacting almost every industry in some way, but while there are some potential benefits for its use in the field of mathematics, researchers within the field are concerned about the impact this may have on the collaborative nature of the field and how it might discourage future mathematicians from exploring it.
Speaking to Business Insider, mathematics professor at NYU, Tristan Buckmaster, said that OpenAI's release had upended the world of many early-career mathematicians, suggesting it had wiped out their whole research programs. Alongside their own research being invalidated by some of OpenAI's solutions, he suggested that some were now fearful that, by using AI tools, researchers had inadvertently contributed to the results, raising the potential of them not using advanced tools in the future and being less likely to talk about their research publicly.
This could cause huge problems for mathematics as a whole, argued mathematics professor at Northwestern University, Bryna Kra. Highlighting how collaborative maths is, with researchers sharing ideas, research data, and formulas, she is now extremely concerned that OpenAI has made mathematicians more secretive, reducing their ability to work together towards solutions and build on each other's research.
Professor of mathematics at the University of California, Terence Tao said on Mastodon that "many fewer seminars, workshops, collaborations, or other activities are being generated from these results compared to traditional breakthroughs." He argued mathematics may need to pivot to value "progress more holistically," by elevating the role of community building over raw solutions.
Researchers have described an atmosphere of extreme anxiety, that whatever they're working on could be invalidated overnight. That can undermine job applications, grant proposals, and those building the early components of their academic careers. Understanding and developing core mathematical capabilities at a high level can take years. AI dumps eradicating years of effort in such a haphazard fashion risk making it seem a near-pointless endeavour.
With swirling rumors of yet more releases from OpenAI, and potentially companion releases from other AI labs chasing the same headlines, the morale in many mathematical fields is extremely low.
Cryptography
With how much mathematics underpins key components of our digital world, it's no surprise that major changes in the pace of its development could have a domino effect elsewhere. One proposed potential minefield is the fertile ground of cryptography.
Associate professor of computer science at Johns Hopkins Whiting School of Engineering, Matthew Green, said on social media that he believes the congruence of mathematical developments and cybersecurity capabilities could result in AI that can defeat encryption as we know it.
While that raises potential concerns for all manner of fields that rely on encryption to protect the security of sensitive data, it could open up the cryptocurrency industry to wholesale theft, potentially impacting trillions of dollars of digital tokens.
Not everyone agrees with Green that this is an inevitability. British cryptographer — and one of the few people accused of being Bitcoin developer Satoshi Nakamoto — Adam Back, described these claims as nonsense and that there was little suggestion that just because AI can do certain mathematics now, that they'll be able to defeat encryption at some unnamed date in the future.
Ethereum creator Vitalik Buterin urged calm too, stating on Twitter/X that nobody should rush to move their tokens to a new wallet or panic over wallet security. However, he did argue that AI had the potential to one day be a far more dangerous threat to the sanctity of cryptocurrency than quantum computing.
While it doesn't appear that cryptography is a field AI is set to invalidate just yet, it's clear that it poses a potential threat to mathematical researchers and the core underlying 'way of doing things.' Much like it has just about everywhere else.
Researchers are adjusting to it, but the dust isn't likely to settle anytime soon, and in the meantime, OpenAI and its contemporaries may just move on to a new field to focus on as it continues to chase relevance and profitability.
Jon Martindale is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. For the past 20 years, he's been writing about PC components, emerging technologies, and the latest software advances. His deep and broad journalistic experience gives him unique insights into the most exciting technology trends of today and tomorrow.

articles.title: The new Apple TV 4K powered by Siri AI is your smart gateway to entertainment and gaming - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Apple has revealed the next generation of Apple TV 4K, which provides a more immersive home theatre experience and is supported by Siri AI.
With Siri AI and Apple Intelligence on board, users can find their favourite movies and TV shows through a full-screen experience even faster.
There are built-in far-field microphones so Apple TV can hear users talking from across the room.
Apple TV 4K can also be paired with up to four HomePod mini 2 or HomePod second-generation speakers to create a home theatre surround set-up.
Apple TV 4K can also act as a smart home hub monitor and control several products and accessories via the Home app.
Apple TV 4K (4th Generation) will go on sale on November 13 and will be priced at $449.
“The new Apple TV 4K is our most immersive home theatre experience yet,” said Bob Borchers, Apple’s vice president of Worldwide Product Marketing.
“With Siri AI, finding something to watch becomes a full-screen, conversational experience, and with built-in far-field microphones, it’s completely hands-free.
“Pair it with HomePod for the best surround sound setup we’ve ever offered, and it makes managing your Apple Home accessories easier than ever.
“Now, alongside HomeView and HomePod mini 2, it’s part of the most connected Apple Home we’ve ever built.”
Apple TV 4K brings Siri AI into a rich full-screen experience which is more capable and conversational with personal context understanding so it can take even more action as well as making it easier to find the latest entertainment options.
Responses appear in a subtle overlay that doesn’t take over what you’re watching.
With an Apple intelligence-enabled iPhone the Siri AI on Apple TV can also access a user’s personal context to answer requests like “Play the show Jo recommended”.
Apple TV 4K is powered by the A19 chip, which offers 50 per cent faster CPU performance and 2x faster GPU performance than the previous model.
This means it’s more responsive with faster navigation and smoother animations.
Apple TV 4K is also your connection to Apple Fitness+ to turn your home into a workout studio, along with access to Apple Arcade and the App Store library of games.
Apple TV 4K (4th generation) goes on sale on November 13 and will be priced at $449.

articles.title: TFG London cyberattack disrupts systems at Hobbs and Whistles retailers
articles.text:
TFG London detected a cybersecurity incident that impacted IT systems used by the Phase Eight, Hobbs, and Whistles premium fashion brands.
The company disclosed earlier today that several IT systems remain unavailable, although physical stores remain open for customers.
According to the press release, the incident has not affected the group’s other brands, Inside Story and White Stuff, or its operations in Australia and Africa.
TFG London is the UK subsidiary of South Africa’s The Foschini Group, which owns the aforementioned five fashion and homeware brands.
As of mid-2026, the group operated 649 retail locations globally and reported annual sales of £488 million ($646M).
The company said it detected the cyberattack on October 11 and immediately activated its incident response and business continuity plans, bringing in external cybersecurity experts to help contain the threat.
TFG London is investigating whether any customer information has been compromised, and says it will notify affected individuals or organizations if it data has been affected.
BleepingComputer could not find any threat actor publicly claiming the TFG London breach.
The incident at TFG London comes shortly after another UK fashion retailer, ASOS, suffered a data breach after hackers sent push notifications to users of its mobile app.
The company later confirmed that attackers used social engineering to steal an employee’s login credentials and gained unauthorized access to customer data, including names, contact details, and account information.
At this time, TFG London has not confirmed any customer data exposure, but clients of Phase Eight, Hobbs, and Whistles are advised to remain alert for potential phishing and social engineering attacks.
Earlier this week, rumors emerged about an attack at Swedish multinational clothing company H&M, claimed by an attacker saying they were with the ShinyHunters group and threatening to leak stolen data.
Responding to our request for a comment on these allegations, an H&M spokesperson said they were looking into these claims, although current evidence didn't indicate a breach.
“We are aware of information circulating online regarding a potential cyber security incident and are currently investigating the claims,” the H&M spokesperson told BleepingComputer.
“At this time, we have not found any indications that our data environment has been compromised.”

articles.title: 15 startups selected for Google for Startups Accelerator: South Africa programme - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Fifteen startups have been selected for the Google for Startups Accelerator: South Africa, a three-month programme designed to support growth-stage, AI-driven startups with equity-free funding, technical mentorship and access to Google’s advanced AI technologies.
The programme forms part of Google’s plan to support 50 South African startups between 2024 and 2028. Each selected startup receives up to ZAR1 million (US$60,000) in equity-free funding, allowing founders to retain full ownership of their business while using the capital to accelerate growth.
They also gain direct access to Google’s AI tools, cloud infrastructure and models, including hands-on access to Gemini, helping them strengthen their products and enhance their technical capabilities.
Applications for the latest cohort opened in July, and received over 1,000 expressions of interest. From that, 15 South African-led, revenue-generating startups have been selected for the 2026 cohort.
They include Ambani Africa, an African language learning app that helps children connect with their mother tongue; Anvaya Legal AI, an AI legal assistant that speeds up research, drafting and document review; Boleka Africa, a community-based fintech helping underbanked adults access fair credit, savings and payments; Bro, a mobility platform connecting passengers with affordable transport; and Buddy Learning, an AI tutor on WhatsApp that delivers low-data, multilingual tutoring.
Also selected are Daedalis, which builds verified data infrastructure and enterprise AI for supply chains; Dataseka, an AI analytics platform that turns scattered business data into usable insights; Fly n Pay Later, a travel fintech that lets people book flights and pay in manageable installments; Kasicoach, an AI mentorship platform on WhatsApp and Telegram for township and rural youth; and Muna Africa. infrastructure that helps retailers run circular fashion resale programmes.
The cohort is completed by Propela Health, a marketplace connecting African healthcare professionals with global employers; Scale, which lets startups launch and issue card products; Thuto, an ed-tech building AI tools to improve learning outcomes; Tradeflow, an AI platform that automates supplier invoicing and ordering for restaurants; and Zumii, a WhatsApp platform that sources, packs and delivers school stationery to parents.

articles.title: Tech30 2026: Meet the startups building India’s next generation of technology
articles.text:
Tech30 2026: Meet the 30 startups building India’s next generation of technology
From spacetech and defence to clean energy and advanced materials, YourStory's Tech30 spotlights 30 promising startups developing technologies for India and beyond.
India’s startups are no longer just finding new ways to use existing technology. A growing number are building the technology itself, from satellites and autonomous robots to advanced materials, medical diagnostics and cleaner construction methods. Their work is taking them into sectors that demand years of research, specialised expertise, and significant investment, with the potential to change how industries operate.
This shift is at the heart of TechSparks 2026, YourStory's flagship startup-tech summit, themed ‘The New Tech Order’. One of its key highlights is Tech30, YourStory's annual selection of 30 promising startups working on technologies that could shape India’s future.
Sridhar Vembu, Chief Scientist and Co-founder of Zoho Corp, unveiled and presented this year's Tech30 at TechSparks 2026. Speaking on ‘Prosperity cannot be imported: The road to tech independence’, he emphasised the need for India to develop technologies that address its own challenges.
"The new tech order is to learn to solve our own problems — foundational problems from agritech to material science to lasers, and also AI. But AI is not to be the be all and end all of it,” Vembu said.
Yoonmin Cho, APJ Lead, Snowflake for Startups, and Amar Dixit, CEO, WOI India, also joined Vembu in celebrating this year's Tech30 cohort on stage.
Chosen from a pool of applicants, the startups are evaluated by a jury of experienced members of the startup ecosystem, along with YourStory's senior editorial and research teams. The Tech30 report was unveiled at TechSparks 2026, bringing attention to companies working across a range of sectors and technologies.
This year’s selection reflects the growing ambition of Indian startups to develop their own technologies and apply them to practical problems. From improving industrial processes and strengthening critical infrastructure to developing new products and markets, these companies are working on challenges in India and overseas.
Here are the 30 startups selected for Tech30 2026.
Apollyon Dynamics
Apollyon Dynamics develops autonomous drones and counter-unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) systems for defence applications. Its portfolio includes high-speed interceptor drones such as Ahuti Mk II, designed to neutralise hostile drones, and Nightshade ADX-1, an autonomous strike platform.
Arctus Aerospace
Arctus Aerospace is developing high-altitude, long-endurance unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) that operate at around 50,000 feet and can remain airborne for up to 24 hours. Equipped with onboard AI for autonomous navigation, obstacle avoidance, and flight planning, its platforms are designed to provide persistent aerial surveillance and high-resolution imaging for defence, agriculture, infrastructure monitoring, and disaster response.
Attox Research Laboratories
Attox Research Laboratories develops diagnostic technology to accelerate antibiotic sensitivity testing and help address antibiotic resistance. Its flagship device, Bactolizer, analyses electrical signals from patient samples using specialised algorithms to identify effective antibiotics and appropriate dosages in around two hours, compared with the 24–48 hours typically required by conventional methods. The system uses a reusable testing unit and disposable cartridges designed for hospital settings.
Balisto Agritech
Balisto Agritech has developed the Balisto 130 Pro, an electric farm machine that combines multiple agricultural operations, including weeding, sowing, spraying, rotavating, and harvesting, on a single platform. Powered by detachable batteries, the machine can be controlled through an onboard dashboard or remotely, while an internet-connected system enables cloud-based monitoring and remote diagnostics.
CaliperAI
CaliperAI builds AI infrastructure for robots and autonomous machines, using sensor fusion, localisation, and perception to help them navigate the physical world. Its platform captures, analyses, and annotates data from cameras, LiDAR, and navigation sensors, supporting the development of autonomous systems.
CraftifAI
CraftifAI builds AI software that automates development for embedded systems, edge AI, and IoT devices. Its Orbit platform generates, compiles, and validates code directly on target hardware, helping companies develop software for robotics, drones, industrial equipment, and automotive systems.
Curium Life
Curium Life is developing AI models that interpret surgical videos, anatomy, and operating-room workflows to support surgeons during procedures. Its technology aims to provide real-time guidance, identify anatomical structures, and flag potential risks, alongside tools that analyse CT scans to assess preoperative risks and abdominal-wall conditions.
Dognosis
Dognosis is developing BreathEasy, a non-invasive cancer screening test that analyses a person's breath to identify potential cancer risk across multiple cancer types. The system combines trained dogs' ability to detect cancer-related chemical patterns with brain-computer interfaces and machine learning to interpret their responses, flagging higher-risk individuals for confirmatory tests such as imaging and biopsies.
Ecopath
Ecopath turns industrial waste into construction materials, replacing conventional cement with alternatives designed to cut emissions and water use. Its EcoConcrete supports applications ranging from road construction to masonry products, while its soil-stabilisation and waterproofing solutions address other infrastructure needs.
Enerzolve Smart Technologies
From battery storage to grid infrastructure, Enerzolve works on the power electronics and instrumentation needed to manage electricity reliably. Its technology portfolio spans bidirectional power converters, software-driven solid-state transformers, and ultrasonic water, gas, and energy meters, serving utility developers, data centres, and defence organisations.
EON Space Labs
EON Space Labs’ MIRA imaging payload is now in orbit following a launch aboard SpaceX's Falcon 9, marking a milestone for its space-imaging technology. The startup develops electro-optical and infrared systems for space, aerial, and ground surveillance, including imaging payloads, gimbals, and fixed surveillance equipment, with more than 90% of its components built domestically.
Evoxia
Agricultural residues could offer an alternative route to producing polysilicon, a critical material for solar panels and semiconductors. Evoxia is developing a plasma-based process to turn this feedstock into high-purity silicon, reporting 6N purity in laboratory validation and targeting lower energy consumption and emissions than conventional production methods.
Folium Sensing
Folium Sensing turns standard optical fibre cables into sensors that detect vibrations, temperature changes, and mechanical strain over distances exceeding 100 km. Its AI-powered monitoring system helps identify pipeline leaks, railway-track cracks, and security threats across critical infrastructure.
Harvested Robotics
Harvested Robotics' RAKSHAK uses computer vision to identify weeds and high-powered lasers to remove them without damaging crops. Mounted on a tractor, the device can eliminate 80–100 weeds per minute, offering farmers an alternative to chemical herbicides and manual weeding.
Hyperonic Engineering
Hyperonic Engineering develops hydrogen technologies for mobility and industrial applications, including its H35 dispenser for safe, precision-controlled refuelling. It is also developing microgrids that combine electrolysers, hydrogen storage, and fuel cells for decentralised power generation.
Hypersonic Technologies
Hydrogen production need not come with direct CO₂ emissions or a single output. Hypersonic Technologies is developing plasma-based reactors that split methane and other gas feedstocks into hydrogen and solid carbon black, which can be used in tyres, plastics, paints, and coatings.
ImmunitoAI
Designing antibodies from scratch is the focus of immunitoAI, whose AbInitio platform uses AI to create proteins that bind to specific disease-linked targets. Trained on 3D protein structures, the system generates candidate antibodies for laboratory testing, with potential applications in cancer, autoimmune disorders, blood diseases, and neurological conditions.
Integra Robotics
Integra Robotics equips factories and defence teams with modular robots built for hazardous and hard-to-reach environments. The hardware ranges from robotic arms and underwater manipulators to mobile platforms capable of carrying 500 kg, while software uses field-operation data to train and improve machine capabilities.
Kubo Care
Kubo Care uses 60 GHz radar and AI to monitor older adults at home or in care facilities, detecting falls without cameras or wearable devices. Its system also tracks movement patterns, sleep interruptions, and vital signs to flag potential health changes, while alerting caregivers to events such as bed exits and wandering.
Metastable Materials
Discarded lithium-ion batteries contain valuable metals that Metastable Materials recovers for industrial reuse. Its proprietary recycling process separates lithium, nickel, cobalt, and copper without adding chemicals, supplying recovered materials to industries such as glass, ceramics, stainless steel, and automotive manufacturing.
MiCoB
From army bunkers to residential structures, MiCoB uses robotic 3D concrete printing to automate construction. Its integrated technology combines specialised concrete mixes, printers, and digital design software, enabling the company to produce structures with less labour and material waste; it has delivered more than 650 3D-printed structures across 13 states.
MumbaiSemi
MumbaiSemi's DhruvaPro chip enables satellite navigation receivers to work across India's NavIC system and global constellations including GPS, Galileo, and BeiDou. The fabless semiconductor startup is also developing integrated circuits for wireless communications, AI hardware, autonomous vehicles, and low-power IoT devices.
Neo San
Instead of transporting non-recyclable dry waste to disposal sites, Neo San's machines process it where it is generated, using induction heating to reach temperatures of 1,200 degrees Celsius. Its range handles between 25 kg and 500 kg or more of waste daily, serving buildings, hospitals, and industrial facilities, with the resulting ash tested for use in construction.
Pramatra Space
Pramatra Space is working on encryption systems designed to withstand future quantum-computing threats. Its integrated photonics chip generates entangled photons to create secure encryption keys, which the startup aims to distribute through fibre networks and satellites to protect enterprise communications and critical infrastructure.
Red Balloon Aerospace
Red Balloon Aerospace is building platforms to operate in near-space, the region between conventional airspace and outer space. Its portfolio includes high-altitude balloons, tethered aerostats, and autonomous stratospheric airships designed for long-duration communications, remote connectivity, disaster response, and surveillance missions.
Sanyark Space
Sanyark Space is developing low Earth orbit satellites to improve navigation accuracy from metres to centimetres. Its constellation will transmit correction data and stronger signals to support precise positioning, timing, and more resilient communications for defence and infrastructure applications.
Segritech
Segritech uses computer vision and deep learning to grade fruit by size, colour, and surface defects, processing up to two to three tonnes an hour with 95% reported accuracy. Its machines currently sort produce such as pomegranates and apples, while the startup is developing an autonomous robot to harvest fruit directly in the field.
SpaceFields
SpaceFields develops solid-propulsion systems for rockets, unmanned aerial vehicles, and defence applications, with capabilities spanning composite propellants, rocket motors, and energetic materials. Its portfolio also includes an aerospike rocket engine, while its in-house technologies are backed by 32 patent filings, 11 of which have been granted.
TeraLumen Solutions
Terahertz waves are at the core of TeraLumen Solutions’ imaging and testing systems. Its TeraXPLOR platform supports research and spectroscopy, while TeraNIM detects defects and measures coating thickness in industries such as aerospace, automotive, and oil and gas. The company is also developing a system for detecting cancer margins during surgery.
Yaanendriya
Yaanendriya develops motion sensors, navigation systems, and control software for autonomous machines, from drones to surgical robots. Its positioning technology is also being adapted for GPS-denied environments, including underwater and indoor settings.

articles.title: Placer un morceau d'aluminium derrière votre box internet : à quoi cela sert-il et pourquoi le faire aujourd'hui ?
articles.text:
Placer un morceau d'aluminium derrière votre box internet : à quoi cela sert-il et pourquoi le faire aujourd'hui ?
Placer une feuille d'aluminium pliée en arc de cercle derrière votre routeur Wi-Fi peut améliorer le débit de plus de 50 %, selon une étude menée par des chercheurs de Dartmouth College. Le principe repose sur la physique des réflecteurs paraboliques : l'alu concentre les ondes radio vers la pièce visée au lieu de les laisser se disperser dans toutes les directions. Coût de l'opération : zéro euro et trente secondes de pliage.
L'idée paraît tout droit sortie d'un tutoriel douteux sur Facebook. À ne pas confondre avec l'astuce de la pièce de monnaie posée sur la box, qui relève du pur mythe : ici, une équipe de chercheurs du département d'informatique de Dartmouth College a démontré en 2017 que l'aluminium, correctement positionné derrière un routeur, fonctionne comme un réflecteur parabolique capable de rediriger les ondes radio vers une zone ciblée.
	
Avec un investissement d'environ 35 dollars et en définissant les besoins de couverture, on peut fabriquer un réflecteur sur mesure qui surpasse des antennes coûtant plusieurs milliers de dollars.
Le principe est celui d'un phare de voiture : le réflecteur courbé concentre le faisceau dans une direction au lieu de le laisser se disperser à 360 degrés. Les ondes Wi-Fi, émises sur les bandes 2,4 et 5 GHz, rebondissent sur la surface métallique et convergent vers la pièce visée. Les zones mortes reculent, le débit grimpe.
Comment l'aluminium redirige les ondes Wi-Fi
L'équipe de Xia Zhou, aux côtés de chercheurs de l'université de Washington, d'UC Irvine et de Columbia, a développé un logiciel baptisé WiPrint qui modélise la couverture d'une pièce et calcule la forme optimale d'un réflecteur. Les résultats, présentés à la conférence ACM BuildSys 2017 aux Pays-Bas, montrent qu'un simple écran en aluminium surpasse des antennes directionnelles vendues plusieurs centaines d'euros. Un test mené par le site Pocket-lint en août 2025 a mesuré une hausse du débit descendant de 58 % avec une feuille d'alu courbée placée derrière un routeur domestique.
La méthode en pratique (et ses limites)
Découpez une feuille d'aluminium d'environ 30 cm de long, à la hauteur de votre routeur. Pliez-la en forme de C, face brillante vers l'intérieur, et placez-la derrière l'appareil, ouverture orientée vers la pièce à couvrir.
Si votre routeur possède des antennes externes, la feuille doit les dépasser de quelques centimètres. Les gains varient selon l'agencement du logement, l'épaisseur des murs et le modèle de routeur.
Eric Siu, responsable produit senior chez Linksys, rappelait en 2017 dans Popular Science que la FCC encadre la puissance maximale d'émission dans chaque direction. L'astuce reste légale à usage domestique, mais elle concentre le signal : ce que vous gagnez devant, vous le perdez derrière.

articles.title: Meta dégaine Muse Wonder et revient en force dans la course à l'IA
articles.text:
Meta veut jouer dans la cour des grands. Ce lundi 12 octobre, le groupe américain a levé le voile sur Muse Wonder et Muse Wonder Full, ses « modèles les plus performants à ce jour ». Selon Meta, ces nouvelles IA rivalisent avec les meilleurs modèles d’OpenAI et d’Anthropic. Pour Mark Zuckerberg, Muse Wonder est « une catégorie de modèles bien plus grande et plus avancée, qui nous amène à la pointe » de la technologie. Le patron de Meta assure même que ses équipes travaillent « déjà à l’étape suivante »,
 Introducing Muse Wonder, our new family of frontier models with state of the art performance for personal and professional agentic work. https://t.co/NKHrybrGKQ
— Mark Zuckerberg (@finkd) October 12, 2026
Muse Wonder, le fruit de la réorganisation de Meta
De l’aveu du milliardaire, il a fallu « une grande quantité de puissance de calcul et d’investissements, ainsi qu’un travail scientifique très rigoureux », pour mettre au point les modèles Muse. Dans un communiqué de presse, Meta rappelle que sa division IA sort d’une vaste réorganisation interne. Le géant a notamment mis sur pied une équipe chargée de développer des produits d’intelligence artificielle très avancés, le Meta Superintelligence Labs, avant de licencier 600 employés de son ancienne division dédiée à la recherche fondamentale sur l’IA. En parallèle, Meta a embauché une armée de chercheurs spécialisés dans l’IA dans toute la Silicon Valley.
« Il y a quatorze mois, nous avons entamé une refonte de nos efforts en IA, et nous sommes passés de la reconstruction de nos fondations à la conquête de la frontière », résume Meta, soulignant que Muse est le résultat de ces efforts de réorganisation.
À lire aussi : « Pas assez prudents » : un responsable OpenAI claque la porte et descend l’approche des rois de l’IA
Meta à l’assaut d’OpenAI et d’Anthropic
Muse Wonder est taillé pour fonctionner avec des agents, c’est-à-dire des IA capables d’accomplir des tâches à votre place. Deux fonctions sont particulièrement mises en avant par Meta. Baptisée Active Memory, la première fonction permet à l’IA de retenir ce qui compte pour vous d’une conversation à l’autre. La seconde, intitulée Active Focus, permet à l’IA de garder le cap quand une tâche se complique. En cas de difficultés, l’IA change d’approche, corrige ses erreurs et vous demande des précisions si nécessaire. L’objectif de Meta est d’éviter qu’un agent ne se perde en route lors d’une recherche complexe ou d’un projet de grande envergure.
D’après les tests réalisés par Meta, Muse Wonder Full dépasse Claude Fable 5.1 d’Anthropic et se classe juste derrière Claude Opus 5.5 sur l’indice Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, qui résume les capacités d’un modèle d’IA. Il devance aussi GPT-6 Astra d’OpenAI dans certains domaines bien précis, notamment en droit et en développement de logiciels. Par contre, Muse Wonder pèche par un coût d’utilisation bien supérieur à la concurrence, ce qui représente un frein sur un marché de plus en plus axé sur les IA abordables.
À lire aussi : Gemini 4 Argon s’attaque à ChatGPT et Claude : Google dévoile son IA la plus puissante
Meta affirme avoir pris des précautions pour éviter les dérives. L’entreprise de Menlo Park indique avoir entraîné ses modèles à ne pas divulguer d’informations privées sans autorisation, à refuser les demandes nuisibles et à mieux résister aux cyberattaques. Le groupe veut aussi permettre aux développeurs de se servir de Muse Wonder pour débusquer des failles dans leur code. Ces derniers mois, plusieurs incidents impliquant des agents IA ont fait les gros titres. Meta AI a également dérapé en piratant une entreprise en toute autonomie. C’est pourquoi Meta a mis l’accent sur les gardes fous de ses nouveaux modèles.
Le retour en force de Meta
Avec Muse Wonder, Meta signe un retour très attendu sur le devant de la scène de l’IA. Pionnier des modèles ouverts avec Llama, le groupe a par la suite accumulé du retard face à OpenAI, Anthropic et Google. Pour rattraper son retard, le géant des réseaux sociaux a confié les rênes de ses IA à Alexandr Wang, fondateur de Scale AI. L’homme a pris la tête du Superintelligence Labs en décembre dernier, dans le sillage du départ de Yann LeCun. Le pari de Meta est évidemment colossal. Meta prévoit jusqu’à 145 milliards de dollars d’investissements cette année, principalement dans l’IA. Sans surprise, Meta espère que les abonnements à Muse, dont le lancement est une réussite en dépit de plusieurs incidents de sécurité, pourront lui offrir une nouvelle source de revenus et réduire sa dépendance à la publicité en ligne.

articles.title: Apple lance une caméra, un thermostat et une serrure connectée
articles.text:
Avec son écran HomeView (299 $, environ 265 € hors taxes), officialisé ce mardi 13 octobre après plusieurs mois de rumeurs, Apple entend devenir un acteur majeur du marché de la domotique. Il y a néanmoins un frein à son ambition : le catalogue de la multinationale est limité, alors que l’idée est bien de piloter un maximum de choses chez soi. Voilà pourquoi Apple a annoncé ce qu’il appelle l’Apple Home Collection, une gamme de produits conçus par des tiers pour une expérience complète.
Apple n’a pas choisi n’importe qui : LG, qui lui a déjà fourni des écrans pour Mac (les UltraFine 4K et 5K) quand le Studio Display n’existait pas encore, et Schneider Electric (cocorico). La stratégie est simple à comprendre. Quand un client Apple ira chercher son HomeView en Apple Store, il pourra repartir avec des accessoires 100 % compatibles et parfaitement intégrés à l’écosystème Maison. « Il suffit d’un simple toucher avec votre iPhone, et tout est géré depuis l’application Maison d’Apple – aucune application ni aucun compte séparé n’est nécessaire », indique Apple.
LG et Schneider, partenaires domestiques d’Apple
Des sonnettes, caméras ou thermostats compatibles avec l’application Maison existent déjà par milliers chez d’autres marques, grâce aux certifications Works with Apple Home et Matter. Ceux de LG et Schneider Electric gardent la marque de leur fabricant, mais ils ont été conçus avec Apple, et le label Apple Home Collection doit rassurer l’acheteur. Matthew Costello, vice-président de l’ingénierie matérielle d’Apple, promet : « En travaillant en étroite collaboration avec les leaders du secteur LG Electronics et Schneider Electric, nous avons conçu chaque accessoire pour qu’il fonctionne parfaitement avec Apple Home, afin que la gestion de votre domicile soit simple, fiable et confidentielle. »
Dans le détail, LG propose :
- Une sonnette équipée de deux caméras (une orientée vers l’avant pour les visiteurs, l’autre vers le bas pour les colis), avec un son qui peut sortir du HomeView, d’un HomePod ou d’un HomePod mini (250 $) ;
- Une caméra de surveillance avec des projecteurs qui s’allument en cas de mouvement détecté, et une vision nocturne en couleur (400 $, environ 355 € hors taxes) ;
- Une caméra d’extérieur, avec vision nocturne (300 $, environ 270 € hors taxes) ;
- Une caméra d’intérieur, qui bascule automatiquement vers le bas, pour cesser de filmer, dès qu’un membre du foyer rentre. On peut aussi l’orienter depuis l’application Maison (200 $, environ 180 € hors taxes) ;
- Une serrure, qui peut s’ouvrir automatiquement à l’approche d’une personne pourvue d’une clé numérique sur son iPhone ou son Apple Watch. Elle intègre aussi un pavé numérique et une fente cachée pour une clé de secours (350 $, environ 310 € hors taxes) ;
- Un thermostat intelligent, avec un écran de 2,4 pouces (200 $, environ 180 € hors taxes) ;
- Un capteur de température et d’humidité (40 $, environ 36 € hors taxes).
De son côté, Schneider Electric a conçu :
- Un thermostat intelligent (200 $, environ 180 € hors taxes) ;
- Un capteur d’humidité et de température (40 $, environ 36 € hors taxes).
Pas d’abonnement propre aux caméras, mais il faut payer quand même. L’historique des vidéos (dix jours) est stocké dans iCloud+ : le forfait 50 Go couvre une seule caméra, celui de 200 Go jusqu’à cinq, et seule l’offre 2 To permet un nombre illimité. Pour profiter de l’ensemble, il faut aussi un concentrateur (HomeView, HomePod, HomePod mini ou Apple TV 4K) et un iPhone à jour pour l’appairage.
Apple Home Collection arrivera en décembre aux États-Unis et au Canada, ainsi qu’au Royaume-Uni pour la sonnette et les caméras. Certains accessoires ne suivront qu’au début de 2027. Rien n’est annoncé pour la France : Apple ne vend pas HomeView dans l’Union européenne, faute de Siri AI sur iOS dans l’UE, et dit chercher une solution avec Bruxelles.

articles.title: Epic confie tout le code de son jeu pour Disney à l'IA : un virage inédit pour un grand studio
articles.text:
Epic Games reporte la sortie de son jeu Disney, et change de méthode. La société ne veut plus de code écrit à la main : tout sera confié à l’intelligence artificielle (IA). Une décision sans précédent pour un grand studio, qui pourrait marquer un tournant.
En 2024, Disney annonçait un investissement majeur d’1,5 milliard de dollars dans Epic Games. De quoi octroyer au studio un accès aux personnages du géant du divertissement, mais aussi sceller un partenariat majeur portant sur plusieurs jeux, avec l’ambition de bâtir un univers commun. Le premier projet résultant de cette alliance est un jeu de tir mêlant Marvel et Star Wars, initialement prévu pour mars 2027. Une date désormais repoussée.
« Fini le code écrit à la main »
Car d’après des informations recueillies par le très bien renseigné Bloomberg, les équipes d’Epic ont reçu une consigne claire : adopter une production « AI first », c’est-à-dire bâtie d’abord autour de l’intelligence artificielle grâce à des outils comme Claude, spécifiquement cité. « Fini le code écrit à la main », aurait écrit l’un des directeurs du jeu dans un message interne, tandis que tous les visuels seraient « générés par des workflows IA complets ».
Ce changement de cap est justifié, en interne, par le retard pris par le projet, car l’entreprise aurait sous-estimé les effectifs et le temps nécessaires pour le mener à bien. » Chez Epic, nous sommes en pleine phase de réorientation majeure : nous réaffectons les développeurs afin de les préparer à accélérer au maximum le développement de l’IA », écrit Tim Sweeney, le P.-D.G, dans une publication sur X.com.
« L’objectif n’est pas de faire la même chose avec moins de monde, mais de permettre à chacun ici de créer plus et mieux, et de faire profiter toutes les équipes qui utilisent Unreal de ces avancées », promet-il. Concrètement, l’humain supervise l’ensemble, mais c’est bien la technologie qui génère toutes les lignes de code. De quoi laisser les employés pantois.
Un précédent inédit pour l’industrie ?
Ce pivot pourrait avoir d’importantes répercussions dans le monde du jeu vidéo, tant le moteur Unreal Engine est omniprésent. Il s'agit, d'ailleurs, de la première fois qu’un grand studio tente une telle expérience. Mais il n’est pas certain que l’écosystème soit favorable : selon une enquête de la Game Developers Conference, 36 % des professionnels utilisent l’IA générative, mais surtout pour la recherche et le brainstorming, bien plus que pour le code. Et 52 % estiment qu’elle nuit à l’industrie, contre 30 % l’an dernier.
De son côté, le patron d’Epic imagine un secteur dans lequel l’IA est légion, avec de petites équipes capables de créer des mondes immenses. C’est donc sans surprise qu’il juge absurdes les mentions « IA » imposées par Steam. Reste à voir si les joueurs seront convaincus, et rien n’est si sûr.
Pour rappel, Epic Games a supprimé plus de 1 000 postes au mois de mars…

articles.title: Could crypto give startups an edge? (Sponsored) | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Crypto can mean very different things to a startup. For one company, it could make international payments easier. For another, it might become part of a new financial product. And for plenty of businesses, it could simply be something they have no real need for.
Watching the Bitcoin price gives founders a sense of what is happening in the market, but it does not tell them whether crypto belongs in their own business.
Bitcoin crossed €74,222 ($85,000) on September 22 after ETF inflows hit €539.9 million ($617.6 million) in the previous session, according to Reuters reporting published by The Economic Times. That kind of movement is hard to ignore. It is also not necessarily the information a founder needs when deciding whether to adopt digital assets.
The better question is much more practical: where, if anywhere, could crypto make running a startup easier?
Why are startups exploring crypto?
Part of the interest comes down to how blockchain networks operate. They can run continuously, and digital assets can move between countries without following exactly the same route as a conventional bank payment.
For a young company working internationally, that can be interesting. A customer could be based in one country, contractors in another and suppliers somewhere else. Add different currencies and banking systems to the mix, and moving money can become even more complex.
Crypto is also becoming less separate from the financial system around it. Binance Research’s September 2026 Macro and Market Insights report found that equity holders’ share of crypto exposure rose from 64% to 72%. That suggests traditional market participants are playing a larger role in digital assets, too.
Where might it actually help?
There’s no standard crypto package that makes sense for every startup. A fintech business could have a clear use case, while a small software company selling locally might struggle to find one.
International payments are one possibility. A business dealing with customers or suppliers overseas could use digital assets as an additional way to move money. There are other options. A company could accept crypto payments from customers, build a product around tokenised assets or use existing blockchain networks as the infrastructure behind a financial service.
Smart contracts could also automate certain transactions where the conditions are straightforward.
Where does it get complicated?
The obvious concern is volatility. A company holding digital assets has to account for changes in their value. Even when crypto is only being accepted as payment, someone still has to decide how it will be stored, converted and recorded. And then there are the rules.
A startup operating across several countries can’t necessarily assume that the same approach will work everywhere. Digital assets, payments and taxation can all bring different requirements depending on the market.
Security is another practical issue. Blockchain transactions can be hard to undo, so losing control of a wallet or exposing private keys is not something a business can afford to treat casually. But there is an even more basic question worth asking: why use crypto in the first place?
If a startup already has a payment system that works and its customers are happy with it, adding crypto could simply create another thing to manage. There is little point taking on extra cost and complexity for the sake of having a new technology on the website.
Which startups might have a reason to try it?
Fintech startups are the clearest fit. Businesses working with payments, financial products or digital assets can use blockchain infrastructure as part of what they already do.
Other startups have more specific opportunities. An international marketplace could accept crypto payments. A gaming company could use blockchain for digital ownership. A creator platform could build services around digital assets.
Stablecoins are another option for businesses that want to accept crypto payments without holding large amounts of more volatile assets.
The key is having a clear use case. Startups don’t need to adopt crypto across the business. They can test one application and see whether it delivers a practical benefit.
What should a founder work out first?
Before adding a digital-asset feature, it is worth getting back to the basics. Ask what the technology is supposed to improve. Find out whether customers actually want the feature. Check the rules in every market involved. Decide who will handle security and custody.
Think about what happens if an asset’s value moves sharply. And, perhaps most importantly, work out whether the new system can slot into the tools the business already relies on.
Those answers will vary from startup to startup. There is no reason for a company with no obvious crypto use case to force one into its operations.
Crypto does not have to be the whole story
The growing overlap between crypto and traditional finance gives startups more choices, but choice doesn’t mean obligation.
For some founders, digital assets could solve a genuine problem or open up a service that would otherwise be difficult to build. For others, conventional financial infrastructure will remain the simpler route.
That’s probably the healthiest way to look at crypto in the startup world. It is a tool to consider, not a strategy in itself. If it makes something work better, there is a reason to explore it. If it does not, there is no need to force it.

articles.title: Nigeria's data consumption hits 90% of 2025 total in eight months
articles.text:
Nigerians consumed 11.94 million terabytes of internet data in the first eight months of 2026, around 90% of the volume recorded throughout 2025, pointing to growing demand through more intensive use of internet services.
In August alone, consumption reached 1.76 million terabytes, according to the Nigerian Communications Commission’s latest industry statistics.
The surge in internet data consumption intensifies pressure on Nigeria’s telecom operators to expand network capacity as users consume more data through existing and new connections. Operators must therefore accommodate rising traffic while maintaining service quality.
Part of the increase comes from additional internet connections. Osita Odafi, a telecom industry expert, said NCC figures showed approximately 800,000 new internet subscriptions in August alone, expanding the pool of connections generating data traffic.
But new subscriptions are only part of the explanation. Existing users are also using more data-intensive services, he said, particularly video platforms such as YouTube, TikTok, Instagram Reels and Netflix. High-definition streaming and autoplay can further increase consumption.
“The critical question is no longer just how many Nigerians are connecting to the internet, but how intensively they are using it,” Odafi told TechCabal.
He also pointed to online banking, digital payments, cloud services, remote work tools, online education, and AI applications as drivers of demand. His assessment identifies potential drivers rather than a measured breakdown of how much traffic each activity generated.
The growing adoption of 4G and 5G is also supporting more data-intensive activities. 4G’s share of mobile subscriptions rose from 54.31% in July to 54.77% in August, while 5G increased from 4.74% to 4.92%. Together, the technologies accounted for approximately 60% of mobile subscriptions.
Monthly consumption was lowest in February, at 1.26 million terabytes, before rising to 1.4 million in March and crossing 1.5 million in June. By August, it had reached 1.76 million terabytes.
Faster connections can make streaming, cloud applications and other demanding services easier to use. Their rising subscription share does not, however, establish how much of the increase in consumption came from either technology.
Nigeria recorded 197.42 million telecommunications subscriptions in August, an increase of approximately 2.31 million, or 1.18%, from July. Data consumption therefore grew faster than total telecommunications subscriptions over the month.
The two indicators measure different things. Telecommunications subscriptions include connections used for voice and other services, while data consumption measures the volume of internet traffic. Subscription figures also count connections, not unique individuals.
The more relevant comparison is with internet subscriptions, including the approximately 800,000 additional connections in August. Even then, determining consumption per connection would require a consistent comparison of internet subscription totals and traffic over time.
MTN recorded 84.56 million internet subscriptions in August, followed by Airtel with 56.94 million and Globacom with 15.76 million. MTN and Airtel accounted for most subscriptions among the three networks.
For operators, sustained growth in consumption means more traffic to accommodate, whether it comes from additional connections or heavier use of existing ones.
“Continued investment in fibre infrastructure, network capacity and spectrum will be vital to accommodating this growth while maintaining service quality,” Odafi said.
He also identified zero-rated access to educational platforms, an initiative the NCC introduced on October 1, as a potential source of further demand. Under the initiative, eligible users are qualified to receive up to 100 megabytes of free daily data allowance to access designated educational platforms.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. articles.title: Une loi solaire et des canicules : comment l'Allemagne a freiné ses heures de prix négatifs — Frandroid
articles.text:
Cette année, il était presque impossible de passer à côté de l’information : les heures de prix négatifs de l’électricité se sont multipliées presque partout en Europe. Résultant principalement de l’essor du solaire et de l’éolien, le phénomène témoigne des difficultés croissantes à équilibrer la production et la consommation d’électricité.
Lorsque l’offre dépasse largement la demande, les prix peuvent en effet passer sous zéro. Mais alors que de nombreux pays européens enregistrent une hausse de ces épisodes, l’Allemagne, pourtant engagée dans le développement massif des renouvelables, fait figure d’exception. Le nombre d’heures concernées y est en baisse cette année.
Une baisse de 13 % sur l’ensemble de l’année ?
Au 27 septembre, l’Allemagne avait enregistré 463 heures de prix négatifs depuis le début de l’année, contre 511 à la même période en 2025. Pour la première fois en quatre ans, le pays voit diminuer ces épisodes. Selon les estimations du cabinet d’analyse Kpler, citées par Bloomberg le 28 septembre, leur nombre devrait diminuer de 13 % sur l’ensemble de l’année, en glissement annuel.
Sur l’ensemble de 2025, l’Allemagne avait cumulé 576 heures de prix négatifs, d’après le cabinet britannique Ricardo. Avec 463 heures au 27 septembre, le pays se retrouve désormais derrière la France, qui en compte 520 sur la même période.
La réforme solaire allemande, entrée en vigueur le 25 février 2025, semble porter ses fruits cette année. Elle supprime la rémunération garantie des installations solaires de plus de 2 kWc mises en service depuis cette date, dès que les prix de l’électricité deviennent négatifs ; pour celles de 2 à 100 kWc, la règle s’applique une fois le compteur intelligent installé. Cette loi, appelée Solarspitzengesetz, ou « loi sur les pics de production solaire », vise à réduire les coûts du soutien public et à limiter les injections d’électricité lorsque la production est déjà excédentaire.
Avant la réforme, la rémunération n’était suspendue qu’après plusieurs heures consécutives de prix négatifs, si bien que les exploitants pouvaient continuer à injecter leur production en touchant leur tarif garanti pendant la plupart de ces épisodes. Désormais, ils n’ont plus intérêt à injecter pendant ces heures et réduisent ou suspendent leur production. Les heures non rémunérées ne sont pas perdues pour autant : elles donnent droit à une prolongation de la période de soutien de 20 ans.
La loi touche aussi les particuliers équipés de panneaux. Tant qu’elles ne disposent pas d’un compteur intelligent, les nouvelles installations de 2 à 100 kWc ne peuvent injecter que 60 % de leur puissance sur le réseau. Les petites installations de moins de 2 kWc, comme les kits solaires de balcon, ne sont pas concernées par la suppression de la rémunération.
La hausse de la demande électrique durant l’été aura également été bénéfique pour le réseau allemand. Le recours accru à la climatisation pendant les vagues de chaleur a fait progresser la consommation, permettant d’absorber une bonne partie de l’électricité solaire. Selon les données de l’institut Fraunhofer reprises par Bloomberg, la consommation a progressé de 10 % sur un an de mai à juillet, alors que les températures dépassaient parfois les 40 °C. À cela s’ajoute une production éolienne plus faible en mai et en juin, selon Kpler, ce qui a limité les volumes d’électricité disponibles sur le marché.
La France et l’Espagne battent leur record
Pendant ce temps, d’autres pays européens battent leur record d’heures à prix négatifs. C’est notamment le cas de la France, qui en comptabilisait déjà 520 à la fin du mois de septembre. Le chiffre dépasse le total enregistré sur l’ensemble de l’année 2025, qui s’élevait à 513 heures. Si le développement des énergies renouvelables a contribué à cette évolution, RTE pointe aussi le retard pris dans l’électrification des usages, qui empêche la consommation de repartir à la hausse.
L’Espagne enregistre également un niveau historique. À la fin du mois de septembre, le pays avait dépassé les 700 heures de prix négatifs, soit une hausse de 31 % par rapport à l’année précédente. L’abondance de la production solaire et l’insuffisance marquée des capacités de stockage en sont les principales causes. Le pays peine en outre à écouler son excédent d’électricité, faute d’interconnexions suffisantes avec ses voisins.
Pour l’Allemagne, le répit pourrait toutefois être de courte durée. Le pays s’est fixé pour objectif de couvrir 80 % de sa consommation brute d’électricité avec des énergies renouvelables d’ici 2030, contre 60,7 % sur les trois premiers trimestres de 2026. Si le développement du solaire et de l’éolien se poursuit à ce rythme, la question de l’équilibre production/consommation restera centrale. Le stockage, les solutions de flexibilité et l’électrification des usages devront progresser au même rythme pour éviter le retour des heures négatives.
Dans un livre blanc publié en 2025, le cabinet Montel projetait, dans son scénario de base, environ 1 600 heures de prix négatifs par an en Allemagne d’ici 2030. Il estimait toutefois que la règle introduite par la Solarspitzengesetz pouvait en réduire nettement le nombre.
