articles.title: New BCEAO rules double mobile money wallet limits
articles.text:
13 octobre 2026
Hello 👋,
Welcome back to Francophone Weekly by TechCabal, your weekly deep dive into the tech ecosystem across French-speaking Africa. For readers who want to understand Francophone Africa beyond headlines—through markets, startups, and systems. New editions of the newsletter will land directly in your inbox every Tuesday at 12 PM WAT.
By default, this newsletter is in French. If you’re reading this in your email inbox, click the “Read in English” button below to switch to the English version. If you’re reading on our website, you can either click the button below or toggle the language selector at the top right-hand side of the page to view the English edition.
Six jours après avoir rendu gratuits les petits transferts de mobile money, la Banque Centrale des États de l’Afrique de l’Ouest (BCEAO) a de nouveau légiféré. Le 8 octobre 2026, le Gouverneur Jean-Claude Kassi Brou a signé l’Instruction n°020, qui modifie le cadre de 2015 applicable aux établissements de monnaie électronique (EME) dans les huit pays de l’Union Économique et Monétaire Ouest-Africaine (UEMOA). Elle entre en vigueur le 2 novembre 2026, le même jour que la nouvelle tarification de la Plateforme Interopérable de Système de Paiement Instantané (PI-SPI), la plateforme de paiement instantané de la banque centrale.
Le titre est simple : un client peut désormais détenir deux fois plus sur un portefeuille de mobile money. Le détail compte davantage, et une modification a reçu bien moins d’attention que les plafonds.
1. Ce que dit l’instruction
            Source de l’image : Financial Afrik.
       
        
    
L’instruction réécrit deux articles de l’Instruction n°008-05-2015.
L’Article 31 régule les plafonds. Un client identifié peut désormais détenir jusqu’à 4 millions de FCFA (6 850 dollars) auprès d’un même émetteur, tous comptes et instruments confondus. Le plafond précédent était de 2 millions de FCFA (3 425 dollars). Au niveau des rechargements mensuels, le cumul des rechargements d’un même client auprès d’un même émetteur ne peut dépasser 15 millions de FCFA (25 700 dollars) par mois, contre 10 millions (17 100 dollars) auparavant.
Aucun des deux plafonds ne s’applique aux distributeurs ni aux accepteurs — commerçants et agents — agissant dans le cadre de leur activité professionnelle.
La réglementation prévoit également deux dérogations. Un émetteur peut demander à la BCEAO de dépasser l’un ou l’autre plafond. La demande doit préciser les motifs, la durée, le plafond sollicité et les contrôles renforcés mis en place. La BCEAO peut assortir son accord de conditions, en limiter la durée ou le retirer.
L’Article 34 précise où dort l’argent des clients : la contrepartie — c’est-à-dire l’argent réel qui garantit la monnaie électronique en circulation — ne peut être placée qu’en dépôts à vue et à terme auprès de banques ou d’institutions de microfinance (IMF), ou en titres de créance émis ou garantis par les États, les institutions régionales ou les sociétés cotées à la Bourse Régionale des Valeurs Mobilières (BRVM). Les dépôts à vue doivent représenter à tout moment au moins 65 % de l’encours de monnaie électronique, contre 75 % sous les règles de 2015. La BCEAO peut fixer des seuils différents pour chaque émetteur en fonction de son profil de risque.
À qui cela profite vraiment
Pas à l’utilisateur type. Les EME agréés affichaient 1 923,2 milliards de FCFA (3,3 milliards de dollars) en circulation fin 2025 pour 60,6 millions de comptes actifs, selon la Commission Bancaire, le superviseur bancaire régional de l’UEMOA. Soit une moyenne d’environ 32 000 FCFA (55 dollars) par compte actif. Pour l’utilisateur médian, le plafond de 2 millions n’a jamais été contraignant, et celui de 4 millions ne le sera pas davantage.
Le plafond pèse sur un groupe plus restreint : les commerçants qui règlent leurs achats de stock en une fois, les petites entreprises qui gèrent leur trésorerie sur un portefeuille, les ménages liés à la diaspora qui reçoivent des sommes importantes, et tous ceux qui paient frais de scolarité, loyers ou acomptes fonciers. Pour eux, l’ancien plafond obligeait à sortir l’argent du portefeuille vers le cash ou un compte bancaire, ou à le répartir entre plusieurs émetteurs. Le plafond de 2 millions datait de 2015 : le doubler relève autant du rattrapage que de la réforme.
« Ces plafonds avaient été pensés pour une époque où la monnaie électronique servait à de petits transferts. Aujourd’hui, c’est le compte de dépenses de millions de personnes dans la région. La BCEAO aligne les règles sur la réalité, et c’est une bonne nouvelle pour tous ceux qui devaient fractionner leur argent ou revenir au cash, » dit Regis Bamba, cofondateur de Djamo, la fintech ivoirienne qui propose des comptes numériques, des paiements, de l’épargne et des services d’investissement en Afrique de l’Ouest francophone.
« Pour nos clients, entrepreneurs, freelances, familles, c’est la fin d’une contrainte qui ne correspondait plus à leur quotidien, » dit Bamba.
Ce qui change pour les fintechs
Pour les émetteurs de monnaie électronique, les gains sont doubles : des soldes plus élevés et plus de rendement sur la contrepartie.
Un portefeuille qui peut contenir 4 millions de FCFA et recevoir 15 millions par mois peut servir de compte d’exploitation à une petite entreprise. Associé aux transferts interopérables gratuits à partir du 2 novembre, il devient un substitut crédible au compte courant de base.
Abaisser le seuil des dépôts à vue de 75 % à 65 % permet aux émetteurs de placer jusqu’à 35 % de leur contrepartie en dépôts à terme et en titres, contre 25 % auparavant. Ce revenu compte plus que jamais depuis que la PI-SPI a supprimé les frais sur les petits transferts. Les EME ont déclaré un bénéfice net cumulé de seulement 16,9 milliards de FCFA (29 millions de dollars) en 2025. Dix points supplémentaires d’une contrepartie en croissance, placés à terme, constituent une compensation réelle.
Le coût, c’est la conformité. La BCEAO a annoncé qu’elle serait particulièrement vigilante sur le suivi des transactions et la maîtrise des risques. Les émetteurs dont les outils de lutte contre le blanchiment des capitaux et le financement du terrorisme (LBC/FT) étaient dimensionnés pour de petits soldes devront les mettre à niveau avant le 2 novembre.
Ce qui change pour les institutions de microfinance
Les IMF se trouvent des deux côtés de cette instruction. En tant que lieux de placement, elles peuvent recevoir des dépôts à vue et à terme des émetteurs. Un seuil de dépôts à vue plus bas favorise les placements à terme, et les IMF rémunèrent généralement mieux les ressources à terme que les banques. Certaines IMF pourraient y trouver une nouvelle source de financement significative, auprès d’émetteurs en quête de rendement.
En tant que concurrentes pour l’épargne, elles perdent du terrain. Beaucoup de clients d’IMF y gardent de petits soldes parce que l’institution est proche et inspire confiance. Un portefeuille qui peut contenir jusqu’à 4 millions de FCFA, envoyer gratuitement et payer les commerçants instantanément dispute directement ces soldes. Les IMF ont par ailleurs jusqu’au 30 juin 2027 pour se connecter à la PI-SPI. D’ici là, leurs clients ne peuvent pas déplacer leur argent aussi facilement que les utilisateurs de portefeuilles.
Ce qui change pour les banques
Les banques subissent une version plus discrète de la même pression. Les comptes courants de petites entreprises et les comptes salaires d’entrée de gamme sont les plus exposés, car le portefeuille couvre désormais l’essentiel de ce que ces clients attendent d’une banque, hormis le crédit.
Deux facteurs atténuent le choc. D’abord, l’essentiel de la contrepartie finit toujours dans les banques : au moins 65 % doivent rester en dépôts à vue, et une grande partie du reste ira probablement en dépôts à terme bancaires. Les banques gardent l’argent, mais perdent la relation client. Ensuite, les banques peuvent elles-mêmes émettre de la monnaie électronique et participent déjà à la PI-SPI. Celles qui construisent un portefeuille compétitif gardent les deux.
L’effet plus subtil : dix points de contrepartie qui passent du dépôt à vue au dépôt à terme donnent aux banques des ressources plus stables, mais plus chères.
La newsletter continue après cette publicité.
Fondateurs. Investisseurs. Décideurs politiques. Leaders d’entreprise. Moonshot 2026 rassemble les personnes qui façonnent l’écosystème technologique africain en matière d’IA, de commerce, de climat, d’entreprise et de culture. Mettez votre marque en avant dès aujourd’hui.
2. Comment la concurrence évolue
            Des marques de paiement mobile font la promotion de leurs services à Deux Plateaux, à Abidjan, le 20 janvier 2023. © Issouf SANOGO/AFP
       
        
    
Les deux mesures d’octobre vont dans le même sens. La PI-SPI rend gratuit le déplacement de l’argent entre institutions. L’Instruction n°020 permet de garder davantage d’argent dans un portefeuille. Ensemble, elles réduisent les raisons qu’a un client de quitter son portefeuille pour une banque.
Les plus grands émetteurs en profitent le plus. Wave, Orange Money et MTN MoMo ont la base d’utilisateurs pour transformer des plafonds plus élevés en contrepartie plus importante, et les équipes de trésorerie pour bien la placer. Les petits émetteurs obtiennent les mêmes droits, mais moins de contrepartie à faire fructifier. Les fintechs qui opèrent sous la licence d’un partenaire n’en profitent qu’indirectement.
Les zones grises
- « Par émetteur » veut dire multiplication. Le plafond s’applique par client et par émetteur. Un client détenant des portefeuilles chez trois émetteurs peut conserver 12 millions de FCFA (20 550 dollars), contre 6 millions auparavant. L’instruction ne traite pas de l’agrégation entre émetteurs, que seule la BCEAO peut observer.
- Clients entreprises. Distributeurs et accepteurs sont exemptés. Les entreprises qui utilisent des portefeuilles pour la paie ou les paiements fournisseurs ne sont ni l’un ni l’autre : elles restent soumises au plafond de 4 millions, sauf dérogation obtenue par leur émetteur. L’instruction ne crée pas de catégorie « client entreprise ».
- Clients non identifiés. L’article 31 de 2015 permettait aux émetteurs de mettre à disposition des porteurs non identifiés jusqu’à 200 000 FCFA (340 dollars) par mois. Les comptes rendus publiés du nouveau texte ne portent que sur les clients identifiés. On ne sait pas encore si cette franchise est maintenue, modifiée ou supprimée.
- Pouvoir discrétionnaire de la réglementation. La procédure de dérogation précise ce qu’un émetteur doit fournir pour dépasser les plafonds, mais ni le délai de réponse de la BCEAO ni ses critères. Un pouvoir discrétionnaire sans délai favorise les émetteurs qui entretiennent les relations les plus étroites avec le régulateur.
- Seuils fondés sur le risque. La BCEAO peut fixer des règles de placement différentes par émetteur. C’est une bonne pratique de supervision, mais des concurrents peuvent ainsi opérer sous des règles de liquidité différentes sans que le marché le sache.
Le bon et le moins bon
Le bon est réel. Les plafonds étaient dépassés, et les relever fait entrer davantage de valeur dans un système supervisé plutôt que de la renvoyer vers le cash. Commerçants, petites et moyennes entreprises (PME) et ménages aux paiements irréguliers gagnent un outil utilisable. Les émetteurs obtiennent une source de revenus qui compense en partie la gratuité des transferts.
Le moins bon est circonscrit, mais mérite d’être nommé. Abaisser le seuil de liquidité de 75 % à 65 % au moment même où les soldes peuvent doubler demande à l’argent des clients de travailler davantage, alors même qu’il y en a plus. En cas de retraits massifs chez un émetteur, une part plus faible de la contrepartie serait immédiatement disponible. Les règles de cantonnement de 2015 — comptes dédiés, rapprochements quotidiens — s’appliquent toujours et restent la principale protection. Des soldes plus élevés augmentent aussi l’enjeu de la fraude et du piratage de comptes pour chaque client touché.
Rien de tout cela ne plaide contre la réforme. Cela plaide pour suivre deux choses après le 2 novembre : la rapidité et la transparence avec lesquelles la BCEAO statue sur les dérogations et les seuils propres à chaque émetteur, et la capacité des émetteurs à adapter leurs dispositifs LBC/FT aux montants qu’ils sont désormais autorisés à détenir.
La newsletter se termine ici.

articles.title: Un important séisme oblige un avion d’Air France à faire demi-tour en plein vol
articles.text:
Un vol d’Air France à destination du Panama a dû faire demi-tour alors qu’il survolait l’océan Atlantique. La raison n’est pas un téléphone chargé à l’aide d’une batterie externe ou un bracelet connecté portant un étrange nom Bluetooth, mais une catastrophe naturelle survenue à proximité du lieu de destination. Le vol d’Air France est ainsi parti de l’aéroport Paris-Charles-de-Gaulle pour y revenir quelques heures plus tard. L’aéroport qui dessert la ville de Panama City a depuis repris ses activités et un nouveau vol a pu être programmé.
Un avion d’Air France obligé de faire demi-tour alors qu’il se situait au-dessus de l’Atlantique
Ce vendredi 9 octobre, à 16 h 45 (heure française), le vol AF490 d’Air France, assuré par un Airbus A350-900, a décollé de l’aéroport Paris-Charles-de-Gaulle avec comme destination l’aéroport international de Tocumen, qui dessert Panama City, la capitale du Panama. Un vol somme toute assez commun, mais les passagers ont entendu à bord une annonce à laquelle ils ne devaient pas s’attendre : l’avion allait faire demi-tour alors qu’il volait déjà depuis plusieurs heures et qu’il se trouvait au-dessus de l’Atlantique. Retour au point de départ donc, c’est-à-dire l’aéroport de Paris-Charles-de-Gaulle.
Autant dire qu’Air France n’a pas eu d’autre choix. À 19 h 56 (heure française), un important séisme de magnitude 7,7 et d’une profondeur de 12,6 kilomètres a frappé le Panama. L’épicentre a été localisé à environ 12 kilomètres à l’ouest-sud-ouest de Pitaloza Arriba, à quelque 200 kilomètres de Panama City et de son aéroport international de Tocumen.
 🔴 Séisme à Panama : le vol Air France AF490 qui devait relier Paris CDG à Panama City fait demi-tour au dessus de l’Atlantique et rentre en France. https://t.co/asgLaxo3Sl pic.twitter.com/VHXE9pPsF8
— air plus news (@airplusnews) October 9, 2026
L’aéroport international de Tocumen a donc pris la décision de suspendre ses activités jusqu’à nouvel ordre, obligeant le vol AF490 à faire demi-tour. Ce demi-tour s’est par ailleurs effectué dans le calme, contrairement à celui du Boeing 777-200ER de British Airways qui a récemment rencontré un problème technique en survolant l’Irlande.
Un nouveau vol a pu être programmé
En réalité, l’aéroport international de Tocumen a suspendu ses activités seulement quelques heures, le séisme n’ayant pas impacté cette région. L’aéroport a indiqué dans un communiqué partagé sur X : Avant la reprise, les pistes, les voies de circulation, les installations aéroportuaires et la tour de contrôle ont été inspectées. Aucun dommage empêchant la reprise des opérations n’a été signalé. Air France a donc pu programmer un nouveau vol et les passagers ont cette fois-ci bien pu atteindre leur destination. Notons tout de même que si ce séisme survenu au Panama a causé des blessés et des dégâts matériels, aucun décès n’a été recensé à l’heure où nous écrivons ces lignes.

articles.title: Jonathan es una tortuga, tiene 194 años y acabamos de descubrir por qué su ADN envejece tan lentamente
articles.text:
El secreto de la longevidad extrema siempre ha sido un tema que ha fascinado a la ciencia, pero para saber cómo se puede vivir más de 200 años, a veces no hay que mirar a los humanos, sino a un apacible reptil que lleva caminando por este planeta desde antes que se inventara la bombilla, como es Jonathan. Esta es una tortuga gigante que, a sus 194 años, ostenta el récord de ser el animal terrestre más longevo del mundo.
Su razón. Aguantar durante todos los años hace que la gente busque el porqué. Y aquí la ciencia ha decidido asomarse al interior de sus células gracias a un equipo internacional que ha secuenciado su genoma y su metiloma para entender la razón por la que Jonathan no envejece como el resto de animales.
Un simple frotis. Para entender un poco mejor a Jonathan, no hizo falta someterle a dolorosas pruebas, sino que solo bastó con raspar la mucosa bucal del animal. A partir de esta muestra, un equipo internacional comparó su ADN con el de otras tortugas gigantes de Aldabra mucho más jóvenes.
El resultado. Lo que encontraron en el código genético fue un arsenal biológico muy importante, puesto que se pudieron identificar hasta 287 genes con variantes exclusivas de Jonathan. Pero lo interesante es que muchas de estas variantes están íntimamente ligadas a la supresión de tumores y a la reparación del ADN.
Aunque no se queda aquí, ya que Jonathan posee copias extra de un gen encargado de codificar una proteína que "limpia" el organismo eliminando las células senescentes, que son las famosas "células zombi" que causan el envejecimiento y algunos cánceres.
No hay envejecimiento. Sin embargo, tener buenos genes no es toda la historia, puesto que la clave también está en cómo se expresan en el organismo. Aquí el metiloma nos da muchos datos, puesto que nos indica cómo están activados o desactivados estos genes, y los investigadores vieron que, en general, su epigenoma mostraba signos de desgaste coherentes con un anciano de 200 años.
Pero había una excepción que nos ha dado una clave dentro del envejecimiento, y es que los interruptores genéticos asociados a sus mitocondrias se conservaban intactos, como los de una tortuga joven.
Las mitocondrias son las fábricas de energía de las células y el estudio revela que las regiones de baja entropía en el ADN de Jonathan están fuertemente enriquecidas en promotores de genes vinculados a la cadena de transporte de electrones mitocondrial y al metabolismo del ARN. A partir de esto, los autores proponen que la extrema longevidad de Jonathan podría sustentarse en una eficiencia mitocondrial inusual, puesto que si su motor celular "no pierde fuelle", entonces las funciones vitales están casi intactas.
No es caso aislado. Aunque todo esto parece impactante, la realidad es que hay precedentes en la historia, como en España. En nuestro entorno, en 2019, un equipo de la Universidad de Oviedo secuenció el genoma de otra tortuga llamada Solitario George. Aquí ya se encontraron variantes en genes de reparación del ADN y la inflamación, que Jonathan viene a confirmar.
Hay relación entre las tortugas y los humanos, y un ejemplo puede ser el de Maria Branyas, que falleció a los 117 años y cuyo genoma fue analizado por el Instituto Josep Carreras. Y aquí se vio algo similar, puesto que se encontró un epigenoma más joven de lo normal, baja inflamación y un microbioma envidiable, haciendo que tengamos ahora mismo encima de la mesa un puzle del envejecimiento.

articles.title: IA tem menos regras que uma caixa de leite, diz Microsoft • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
IA tem menos regras que uma caixa de leite, diz Microsoft
Presidente Brad Smith compara IAs a produtos cotidianos, enquanto CEO Satya Nadella defende um “freio de emergência” para interromper modelos.
As inteligências artificiais estão sujeitas a menos exigências de segurança do que produtos cotidianos, como máquinas de lavar e caixas de leite. É o que afirma o presidente da Microsoft, Brad Smith, que defendeu regras mais rígidas e a criação de normas de monitoramento e responsabilização das empresas por acidentes.
Em entrevista à BBC, Smith disse que “toda caixa de leite que você vê na mercearia passa por regras de segurança e inspeção” e que, por isso, “sabemos que ele é seguro”. Para ele, é esse tipo de confiança que a indústria precisa gerar para a IA.
Entre as medidas que possibilitariam isso estão notificações de pessoas afetadas por incidentes e avaliações independentes de sistemas avançados antes da liberação pública. A defesa de regras mais rígidas também se soma à posição do CEO da Microsoft, Satya Nadella, favorável à criação de mecanismos para pausar ou desligar modelos de IA que apresentem comportamentos inesperados.
Em uma publicação no X, Nadella afirmou que as empresas precisam considerar a possibilidade de seus sistemas serem comprometidos e garantir que pessoas autorizadas possam interromper suas operações. “Devemos presumir que um modelo está comprometido e contê-lo desde o início”, escreveu o CEO.
“Pense nisso como um freio de emergência. Qualquer pessoa autorizada deve ser sempre capaz de pausar ou desligar um modelo no meio de uma tarefa. Modelos mais avançados exigirão tecnologias de contenção mais avançadas que precisamos padronizar.”
– Satya Nadella, CEO da Microsoft
O mecanismo, conhecido como kill switch, permitiria interromper uma tarefa caso o sistema representasse algum risco. Nadella também defende separar o modelo de IA dos mecanismos responsáveis por coordenar e executar suas ações, além de padronizar tecnologias de contenção.
A cobrança contrasta com a preferência do governo de Donald Trump por uma abordagem mais favorável à autorregulação do setor. O presidente dos Estados Unidos reuniu no fim de setembro representantes de gigantes da tecnologia, incluindo OpenAI, Anthropic, Google e Meta, para a assinatura de um compromisso de segurança que prevê colaboração com mecanismos de supervisão e auditorias.
Smith elogiou a iniciativa, mas afirmou que compromissos voluntários não são suficientes para garantir que todas as empresas adotem práticas responsáveis.
“É um bom passo, é um passo necessário… Mas não acho que seja suficiente por mais tempo […] as empresas boas farão o que você pede. São as companhias que não são responsáveis que devem nos preocupar.”
– Brad Smith, presidente da Microsoft
OpenAI, Anthropic e Meta estiveram entre as desenvolvedoras de IAs que afirmaram ter tido problemas com modelos em treinamento “fugindo” de ambientes de testes, acessando a internet e inclusive hackeando sistemas de terceiros, como no caso do repositório Hugging Face.
As revelações acabaram promovendo, ainda que indiretamente, as capacidades agênticas de alguns modelos e deram mais força aos críticos das práticas de segurança das empresas.

articles.title: Undecimal Bio lands €16 million to develop targeted RNA medicines beyond the liver | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Cambridge-based Undecimal Bio, a spin-out from Eleven Therapeutics advancing targeted delivery of siRNA therapeutics, today announced a €16 million ($18 million) Seed financing round to expand DELiveri, its proprietary AI-enabled platform for identifying conjugates that can direct RNA medicines to defined cell types.
The round was co-led by 4BIO Capital and IQ Capital, with participation from Verve Ventures, Harel Tech, Entree Capital, Kerna Ventures and Saras Capital. The funding will also be used to progress Undecimal’s renovascular programmes and enable expansion of the team at their laboratories based at the Cancer Research UK Cambridge Institute.
“The hard problem in RNAi was never the silencing, it was getting the molecule to the right cell,” says Dr. Yaniv Erlich, CEO and co-founder of Undecimal Bio. “Our in-vivo validated DELiveri platform can screen large chemical spaces at an unprecedented pace, generating massive data for our legions of AI agents to decipher the structure-activity relationship and score the best candidates. We are excited to bring these advances to develop the next generation of siRNA therapeutics for the benefit of patients.”
Undecimal Bio’s Seed financing comes amid a series of European investments in RNA-based therapeutics, targeted drug delivery and AI-enabled biotechnology platforms in 2026.
Related announcements include Dublin-based Aerska‘s €32 million Series A to advance RNA interference medicines targeting neurological diseases, Paris-based WhiteLab Genomics‘ €23.2 million Series B for AI-driven genomic medicine design and delivery, and Cambridge-based STORM Therapeutics‘ €47.5 million Series C to progress RNA-modifying cancer treatments.
In the UK, Thalia Therapeutics also secured €3.1 million to develop its RNA therapeutics portfolio, while London-based Helical raised €8.4 million for its AI-powered pharmaceutical R&D platform.
Alongside additional investments in Spain’s Gate2Brain, Belgium’s Sightera Biosciences and the UK’s Houdini Bio, these announcements represent approximately €125.9 million in 2026 funding, rising to €141.9 million including Undecimal’s round.
Founded in 2026, Undecimal pairs massive scale combinatorial chemistry with transformer-based AI to guide siRNA therapeutics into the tissues that need them.
According to the company, RNA interference has transformed the treatment of liver-expressed diseases, but reaching tissues beyond the liver remains a key obstacle limiting the broader potential of the modality. DELiveri addresses this challenge as a technology that screens massive-scale combinatorial libraries of candidate ligands, converting cells to act as molecular radars that detect productive delivery at single molecule resolution.
This high throughput data is analysed by agentic AI to decode the resulting structure-activity data and identify conjugates capable of carrying siRNA into target cells.
Undecimal is initially applying the DELiveri platform in renovascular diseases, which pose significant unmet clinical need. Existing treatments of these indications largely address symptoms rather than the underlying etiological factors.
Th company believes that targeted siRNA delivery holds the potential to bring the digital-like precision of genetic medicines, enabling durable, target-specific silencing of the disease-driving pathways.
The Board of Directors comprises representatives of 4BIO Capital, IQ Capital and Harel Technologies, together with co-founders Dr. Yaniv Erlich and Shaul Ilan. Alongside the financing, Verve Ventures joins the Board as an observer.

articles.title: Apple launches next generation HomePod mini with better audio quality, Siri AI and new colours - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Apple has launched the latest generation of the HomePod mini speaker which has support for Siri AI and is available in a range of impressive new colours.
The HomePod mini 2 has enhanced audio with Siri AI coming in a future software update to enable the new and more conversational personal assistant.
It can understand your personal context, has a solid broad world knowledge and works across more apps to bring even more capability to the HomePod mini 2.
HomePod mini 2 will be priced at $229 and will be available in stores on October 30.
It will be available in pink, green, blue, white, and midnight.
“HomePod mini 2 brings together Siri AI, gorgeous new colours, and incredible audio,” said Kaiann Drance, Apple’s vice president of Worldwide Home Product Marketing.
“With Siri AI, it understands you better than ever, drawing on personal context and broad world knowledge to make music discovery even richer.
“It fills a room with sound on its own, which gets even bigger in a stereo pair or with multiroom audio, and when paired with the new Apple TV 4K, it delivers our most immersive home theatre setup yet.
“And with just your voice, HomePod mini makes it easy to securely control your accessories and run automations across the connected home.”
The HomePod mini 2 provides room-filling audio through a single speaker and can be linked with another HomePod mini to create a stereo pair.
And when paired with the new Apple TV 4K, users can connect up to four HomePod mini 2 speakers to create a surround sound system.
When paired with an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPhone or iPad, the HomePod mini 2 can answer all your questions and tap into your personal context to find out what you need.
It can connect to other apps like Messages and Timers while playing your favourite music.
On the audio side, HomePod mini 2 offers 360-degree sound from its small footprint whether it’s used as a single speaker, in a stereo pair or as a multi-room audio setup.
The new HomePod mini can also be used as a speaker for Mac and expand the sound for your movies and gaming, along with FaceTime and video calls.
One new feature is Sound Glow, which transforms the top of the speaker into a visual canvas that glows and pulses in time with the music.
The song’s album artwork from Now Playing can also create a colour-matched light experience, which means it’s unique to every song.
HomePod mini 2 can control your smart home products including locking and unlocking doors, lowering blinds, and turning off the lights at bedtime.
The HomePod mini 2 is available to pre-order now and will go on sale on October 30 with a price of $229.
Siri AI will not be available for HomePod mini 2 at the time of launch – it will be installed in a future software update.

articles.title: Gemini 4 Argon begins rolling out in Gemini app and Antigravity, but only if you pay
articles.text:
Google revealed Gemini 4 Argon a few weeks ago, saying that it needed to move cautiously toward a full release because of the potential for nefarious use. Google seems to have worked all that out pretty quickly, though. Argon is beginning its wide rollout today, but it’s only coming to paying users at this time, and even those on lower-tier plans won’t have full access.
Nothing about Gemini 4 Argon’s capabilities has changed. Google still points to the benchmarks it published late last month as evidence of the model’s advanced reasoning and agentic coding capabilities. The model is supposedly trained to refuse malicious instructions, and an automated misalignment monitor can stop processing if it detects an unintended workflow. Google claims Argon needs that because it’s so capable.
The company has a few new examples of how Argon has helped inside Google, where it has been used by thousands of Googlers. Argon has reportedly been instrumental in making YouTube’s comment system more efficient. Argon identified redundant emoji rendering that, when eliminated, dropped server load by 45 percent. Engineers also turned Gemini 4 loose on the proprietary drone physics simulator used in Project Wing, and the AI found critical bugs that had been in the codebase since 2018. Google also notes that Argon has advanced its robotics program, showing a measurable step increase in embodied reasoning.

articles.title: Exclusive: Rivian's startup Mind Robotics hires former Ford EV chief Doug Field | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Doug Field has worked on EVs at Ford and Tesla, the not-so-secret car project at Apple, and was employee No. 1 at Segway. Now the executive is turning his attention to Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe’s latest project: Mind Robotics.
Field has been hired as president of Mind Robotics, an industrial AI and robotics venture Rivian created last year. The news, shared onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 (taking place October 13-15 in San Francisco), is another sign that Mind Robotics is getting ready to scale up its early operations just one year after its founding.
Scaringe will still be involved with Mind Robotics, but the day-to-day aspects of the business, including product, engineering, and operations, will be handled by Field.
Mind Robotics, which has already amassed more than $1 billion in backing from Accel, Andreessen Horowitz, Eclipse, Kleiner Perkins, and the venture arms of Volkswagen and Salesforce, is building a full stack for industrial manufacturing. The purpose-built robots will run on foundation models with a goal of automating industrial and manufacturing tasks at scale.
Unlike the humanoid robots being developed by Tesla and others, Scaringe says Mind Robotics won’t attempt to mimic all the biomechanics of a human. The startup is also using Rivian as “a live, high-volume manufacturing environment for model training and deployment,” with Rivian being Mind Robotics’ first customer.
Scaringe said on the Disrupt Stage Tuesday that he wanted someone like Field to help run Mind Robotics, and so he called him up to ask for a recommendation.
“Him and I then really began digging into how important it is that we really think deeply and very intentionally about how we develop robotics and deploy robotics into our society, into our economy, and we found such alignment in how we thought about this from the overall mission of the business, but even more important, we found really deep alignment just in how we both work and how we build teams,” he said.
Field left Ford in April after five years shaping the automaker’s electric vehicle and technology strategies. His departure was part of a wider reorganization of the automaker’s leadership. Prior to Ford, Field led Apple’s Project Titan, the electric, autonomous car project that was canceled in 2024. He also served as senior vice president of engineering at Tesla, where he oversaw development of the Model 3 and got the sedan through “production hell.”
“Integrating AI and robotics is one of the most important — and difficult — engineering challenges of our time,” Field said in a statement. “Mind has assembled an exceptional team and has a unique advantage: the ability to deploy and learn inside a real, high-volume factory from day one. I’m thrilled to join RJ in building a team, culture, and technology that will redefine what we can make in America.”
Mind Robotics is the second company that Scaringe created outside of Rivian, following Also, a micromobility play that’s starting with high-end e-bikes. Like with Field and Mind Robotics, Scaringe is involved as chairman at Also but has tapped someone to run the day-to-day: Chris Yu, the former chief product officer of Specialized.
Mind Robotics and Also operate as stand-alone companies, but Rivian has minority stakes in both. The company reported owning about a third of each startup as of June 30, 2026.

articles.title: Mira el impactante tráiler de 'Narnia: El sobrino del mago', lo nuevo de Greta Gerwig
articles.text:
Greta Gerwig, la directora que logró aclamación mundial por Barbie, está de regreso con Narnia: El sobrino del mago. La nueva película de la saga Las crónicas de Narnia acaba de lanzar su esperado tráiler, revelando los primeros detalles de lo que veremos una vez que llegue a los cines (y luego a Netflix).
El primer tráiler de Narnia: El sobrino del mago nos permite conocer un poco más sobre la tónica que le imprimirá la cineasta a esta adaptación de la obra literaria de C. S. Lewis. Si bien ya habíamos visto algunas primeras imágenes de la producción a través de la revista Empire, faltaba ver realmente cómo se plasmaría la visión de Gerwig en el plano audiovisual.
La realidad es que Narnia: El sobrino del mago promete generar reacciones de lo más divisivas. Ya sucedió en el último tiempo cuando Greta Gerwig reveló que su idea para esta adaptación era la de crear una ópera rock con guiños a artistas icónicos como The Who y David Bowie. Lo mismo, cuando se anunció que la voz del león Aslan está a cargo de Meryl Streep. El primer tráiler llega con Stairway to Heaven de Led Zeppelin para generar gran impacto.
Si bien Narnia: El sobrino del mago será la cuarta película basada en los trabajos de Lewis, servirá como reinicio de la franquicia. Tengamos en cuenta que el libro El sobrino del mago es el primero de la saga en orden cronológico, aunque fue el sexto (y penúltimo) en publicarse en la década de 1950. A continuación puedes ver el tráiler de la adaptación cinematográfica.
Narnia: El sobrino del mago se estrenará en cines, y luego en Netflix
Si bien Netflix se encuentra detrás del desarrollo de Narnia: El sobrino del mago, la película llegará a los cines antes que a la plataforma de streaming. Esto se debe a un acuerdo de distribución que la empresa ha firmado con Columbia Pictures y Sony Pictures International.
Según la sinopsis oficial de Narnia: El sobrino del mago, al tocar un anillo mágico dos niños son transportados al antiguo mundo de Charn. Allí, por error despiertan a una poderosa y malvada hechicera de su sueño eterno. Sedienta de poder, ella no dudará en destruirlo todo y a todos a su paso. Pero el gran león Aslan hará despertar con su canción una nueva esperanza, un nuevo mundo: Narnia. Un lugar donde todo es posible.
El elenco de Narnia: El sobrino del mago incluye a David McKenna (Digory Kirke), Beatrice Campbell (Polly Plummer), Emma Mackey (Jadis), Meryl Streep (Aslan), Carey Mulligan (Flora Kirke) y Daniel Craig (Andrew Ketterley), por citar solo a algunos.
Narnia: El sobrino del mago se estrenará en cines el 12 de febrero de 2027, mientras que el 2 de abril se añadirá al catálogo de Netflix.

articles.title: 9 things we learned from the big Apple 'Welcome Home' event — including a new HomeView smart display and fresh Apple TV 4K
articles.text:
Apple 'Welcome Home' event — 9 things we learned and all the launches, from the Apple HomeView to a new Apple TV 4K
A host of new products
After treating us to the grand unveiling of the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo handsets in September, Apple returned in October to launch some notable device upgrades in the smart home and streaming categories.
There are refreshed versions of the Apple TV 4K and the HomePod mini, plus an Echo Show-style smart display called the HomeView. The HomeView is evidence of a renewed focus on the smart home from Apple, as are the devices being made by LG Electronics and Schneider Electric that the HomeView can connect to.
We've also got Siri AI rolling out across the board, which in theory should mean more intelligent and more useful AI conversations. Here's our full recap of what was announced, with links to specific articles if you want to read more.
1. The HomeView is Apple's first smart display — and it comes in two versions
Apple just jumped into smart displays: the HomeView is a competitor to the Amazon Echo Show and the Google Nest Hub, giving you a 7-inch screen that lets you control smart home devices, chat to Siri AI, play music, and much more. You can choose between a HomeView on its own rotating stand, or a HomeView designed to be wall-mounted.
A curated list of Apple apps can run on the HomeView, including Calendar, Safari, FaceTime, Weather, and Apple TV. If you like what you see, the HomeView costs $299 / £299 / AU$449 in Silver, Starlight, Rose Pink, or Space Gray. Preorders are open today, with sales and shipping starting on Friday, November 13.
- Read the full story: I've seen Apple's HomeView smart display in action — it looks like the Apple Watch and classic G4 iMac had a baby, and it could make the Echo Show irrelevant
2. You need an iPhone or iPad to use the HomeView
Before you put your cash down for Apple's new smart display, read the small print. You need to have an iPhone or an iPad handy to set it up, and these connected mobile devices also provide a lot of the HomeView's personalized context — your messages, appointments, reminders, podcasts, and playlists for example.
3. The Apple TV 4K has finally been refreshed (with a big price hike)
We're pleased to see the launch of a brand new Apple TV 4K, but less enthused about the increased price: the new model will set you back $299 / £299 / AU$449, up from $199 / £199 / AU$299 (Wi-Fi) and $249 / £249 / AU$399 (Wi-Fi and Ethernet) for the old models, which are no longer going to be on sale from Apple.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
You do get more for your money though. The upgrades here include a new Siri Remote that can make a sound when you're trying to find it, Siri AI on board, a faster processor, and three far-field mics for more "hey Siri" voice control options. Preorders are opening today, with a shipping and on-sale date of Friday, November 13.
- Read the full story: New Apple TV 4K finally brings HomePod Dolby Atmos surround sound and a Siri Remote you can’t lose — but its price has been hiked to $299
4. The new Siri Remote works with older Apple TVs
The fourth-generation Siri Remote that comes with the 2026 Apple TV 4K — the one that can make a sound when you're trying to find it, and can be tracked down using Precision Finding on the latest iPhones — is compatible with older Apple TV models too.
That means it'll work with the Apple TV HD and previous Apple TV 4K models. It'll be available to buy separately, but we're still waiting on pricing details.
5. You can pair the new Apple TV 4K with four HomePod speakers
One of our favorite new features on the Apple TV 4K is the ability to pair it with up to four HomePods as its audio system.
That could be four 2nd-gen HomePods, four HomePod mini 2s, or two of each, it's up to you. Naturally, that could be a pretty pricy combo if you're starting from scratch though — an Apple TV 4K and four HomePod mini 2 units would cost $895 / £895 / AU$1,365, for example.
Still, you're still able to use a single HomePod or a stereo pair with the new Apple TV 4K as well, just like before.
6. The HomePod mini 2 is here, but it doesn’t have Siri AI (yet)
Considering the first HomePod mini launched in November 2020, an updated version was well overdue, and it's now arrived. It comes with a speedier chipset, and a modest price bump to $149 / £149 / AU$229. Preorders are open now if you want to put your money down, with the speaker shipping and going on sale on Friday, October 30.
You've also got new colors to pick from — Green and Pink models are available, alongside the previous White, Midnight, and Blue (Yellow and Orange get dropped) — and the LEDs on top of the speaker can change color to match the artwork of whatever you're listening to. Siri AI is supported as well, but it's coming in a future software update (there's no confirmed date yet).
- Read the full story: The HomePod mini 2 is here, but while the upgrades are subtle, the price hike isn’t — and you'll have to wait for Siri AI
7. There’s no Siri AI update for the second-gen HomePod
While the HomePod mini 2 will get the all-singing, all-dancing Siri AI update eventually (Apple hasn't set a specific date), the 2nd-gen HomePod launched in 2023 won't be getting the smarter AI.
Apple hasn't yet said why, but presumably the on-board processor just isn't fast enough for the extra demands of the AI.
8. Apple has co-designed new smart home gadgets with LG and Schneider Electric...
It's fair to say Apple's smart home ambitions have been limited somewhat by a lack of compatible gear — there's just not the range of products you get that work with Google Home or Amazon Alexa for example — but improvements are coming. A new doorbell and smart lock, plus cameras, sensors, and thermostats, are on the way.
These new gadgets are appearing under the label of the Apple Home Collection, though these are actually joint efforts between Apple and both LG and Schneider Electric. It means if you do buy a new HomeView smart display, you're going to have a wider choice of smart home devices to connect it to, and more hardware is likely to be in the pipeline.
- Read the full story: Apple Home is getting a new doorbell, cameras, and smart lock — but Apple isn’t making them
9. ...but you won’t be able to buy them everywhere
When it comes to the availability of the Apple Home Collection, these devices might not be sold as widely as we might like.
Shipping is scheduled for December across the board, but it looks like the LG Door Lock will only be available in the US and Canada, while the doorbell and cameras are limited to the US and the UK — at least for now.

articles.title: OpenAI employee arrested for allegedly planting a bug in a conference room
articles.text:
An OpenAI engineer was arrested after the company said it discovered a “sophisticated recording device” hidden in one of its offices. The employee was identified as Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national. Alfozan is charged with using or endeavoring to use a device to intercept oral communications, according to a press release from the Department of Justice.
OpenAI employee arrested for allegedly planting a bug in a conference room
The recording device was apparently discovered plugged into a TV’s USB port in an executive meeting room.
OpenAI’s post about the incident says it used its AI models to “understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier.”
As noted by the DOJ, OpenAI found the device plugged into a TV’s USB port in an executive conference room, where discussions about “highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information” often take place.
Alfozan didn’t have access to this room, but CCTV footage allegedly showed him “near the executive conference room on multiple dates prior to the device’s discovery,” according to the DOJ. Footage also captured Alfozan appearing to look behind the TV where the device was installed, federal prosecutors claim.
The device was covered in toilet paper and installed on or around September 28th. Its contents were encrypted. Additionally, the DOJ claims OpenAI security discovered a bag Alfozan left in another room inside the company’s office, where they found his wallet, ID, and another recording device.
OpenAI says it fired the employee and referred the incident to the FBI. Alfozan was arrested Friday and has remained in custody since, appearing in federal court for the first time on Tuesday.
We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices. We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work.
At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated.
We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance. Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states, and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats.
Update, October 13th: Added information from the DOJ.

articles.title: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
articles.text:
Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
Why the open-closed AI debate is more complicated than it seems
MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here.
Late last month, Anthropic released a report arguing that the model GLM-5.3 poses a major cyberattack risk. The report’s core concern is that the powerful new model, released in August by the Chinese company Z.ai, is freely available for anyone to download and modify. Anthropic’s assertion is only the latest move in a long-running debate about whether frontier AI models should be made open, like GLM-5.3, or should stay locked behind the doors of the frontier labs.
These days, much of the debate about how to handle open models is playing out in public—and there’s a lot of money resting on its outcome. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has a lot to gain if people continue buying their own hardware to run open models, advocates enthusiastically for the United States to develop more of them, whereas Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, who runs a company that could be undermined by cheap, powerful models, advocates for a more cautious approach. But beneath all these commercial incentives, there is real substance to disagreements about open models.
“I think a lot of the way you come down on the openness debate is influenced by how you come down on the AI debate,” says David Gray Widder, an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Information. Those who are concerned about AI safety warn that open models can easily be misused by bad actors, whereas those who focus more on AI’s practical potential urge that this power should not sit behind the closed doors of just a few big companies, and that open models could help spread it more widely.
There are a range of ways to handle open models between banning them entirely and releasing them willy-nilly. But any approach that a government or a society might take still involves trade-offs between safety and democratization. Deciding whether to support or limit the production of open models requires understanding those risks and benefits in depth.
What are the benefits of open models?
Let’s start with the basics. A closed model, like the models that power ChatGPT and Claude, can only be accessed through a website, app, or API. An open model, on the other hand, can be directly downloaded: The details about its internal structure, encoded in a long series of numbers known as the model weights, are publicly available. Such models are sometimes called “open-weight models,” to distinguish them from models for which even more information, such as details about the training procedure, is available.
Right now, closed models are more capable than open models—as of publication, the top eight models on the Artificial Analysis LLM leaderboard are all closed, though open models are only a handful of months behind in development. But there are several reasons why someone might opt to use an open model rather than a closed one. Because open models are downloadable, people can run them on their own computers or hard drives. They can even retrain them to behave differently, if they have the expertise and resources to do so.
If you’re an academic researcher working to understand and improve AI systems, you almost certainly need to work with open models in your research. When working with closed models, researchers can’t do much more than send prompts and observe the responses. But researchers can observe the inner workings of open models, as well as the “chain of thought” that the models use to think through a problem before answering. They can also combine multiple open models to build new systems, compress them to make them more efficient, and fine-tune them for new applications.
Businesses, too, have reasons to prefer open models. Even if you depend on an external provider to run them for you, open models still typically cost less than closed models, according to a recent report from Mozilla. And if businesses want to use AI to process sensitive data or proprietary information, running a local model on their own hardware may be the best way to keep their operations secure.
But perhaps the most important quality of open models is that they challenge the tight control the frontier labs have over how most of us use AI. “The clearest, biggest argument [for open models] is around preventing mass concentration of power—it is about making sure that this foundational technology is a public good,” says Elizabeth Seger, senior policy advisor at the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change. “I think we’re at this juncture where the question of who controls the infrastructure that allows AI to operate is as big of a question as who gets to control information on the internet.”
Seger sees the future of AI playing out in different ways, depending on the role that open models have. In one possible future, frontier AI systems are controlled entirely by select people, companies, or governments, and as those systems grow more powerful, those groups have increasing control over what our world looks like. The world’s most sophisticated hacking models, for example, are currently all made in the United States, so it’s entirely up to US companies and the US government whether other countries can use them to shore up their own cyber defenses. If those companies remain in the lead, we could in principle wind up in a world in which the United States is capable of hacking any other country, but no one is capable of hacking it.
Frontier open models could change that balance. “If every individual had a loyal-to-them AI system that was safe [and secure], I think that would be a much less concerning world than one in which they have to just rely on a government that says, ‘Yeah, we’ve got a super intelligent AI system, it’s got this plan, it’s inscrutable to all of you, just trust us,’” says Hamish Hobbs, director of AI policy at the Centre for Long-Term Resilience.
But open models are not a geopolitical panacea. Paul Azunre, who cofounded Ghana NLP, an organization that builds open-source AI tools for low-resource Ghanaian languages, notes that open models can also function as a way for companies to benefit from the labor and expertise of less-privileged nations and consolidate more power in their own hands. He identifies a pattern in which AI companies release models openly, observe how the community uses and modifies them, and then integrate those same improvements into their own products—without any credit or compensation for the people who originated those innovations. Mark Zuckerberg himself has said that the ability to integrate community improvements into Meta’s stack is a key benefit of releasing open models.
“I think the ideal of open source is a very noble one, and there’s a lot of value that it brings,” Azunre says. “But the way it’s actually implemented in practice, it tends to be a very extractive approach.”
Are open models riskier than closed ones?
The past few months have made it clear that safety remains a gnarly problem for closed models. There’s the autonomous hack that OpenAI agents executed against Hugging Face in July, but human misuse is a real threat too: According to a recent risk report from Anthropic, several extensive hacking operations have been undertaken with the assistance of Claude.
So closed models are risky enough—and open models would likely be much easier to exploit. Before Anthropic passes a user’s query to one of its closed models, it uses automated systems to detect whether that query relates to hacking, biological weapons, or other risks. When it detects that users have outsmarted those filters, it can shut down their accounts. But when someone downloads a model and runs it on their own hardware, there’s no filter checking whether their prompts are safe, and there’s no way to revoke their access to the model.
There are other important lines of defense. AI companies train their models to refuse harmful requests—so even if a bad prompt gets through Claude’s filters, there’s a good chance that the model will still say no. In principle, this same defense could work for open models, because it’s intrinsic to the model itself. Unfortunately, researchers have shown that it’s surprisingly easy to retrain a “safe” open model to agree to engage in the behaviors it was previously trained to avoid.
Because of these facts, some people have argued that open models are simply too dangerous to release. An open model capable enough to walk someone through synthesizing a virulent new pathogen, for example, could prove catastrophic in the wrong hands.
But it would be a vast oversimplification to deem open models dangerous and closed models safe. The defenses that AI companies build around their closed models are far from perfect, and people misuse those models all the time, as the Anthropic risk report makes clear. Even though open models have even fewer defenses against misuse, bad actors might still opt to use closed models because they are more accessible than open models with similar capabilities, which require lots of expensive computer chips to run locally (and even more chips if you want to retrain them).
In fact, some experts who spoke with MIT Technology Review argued, by analogy to open-source software, that open models have safety advantages over closed models. Open-source tools, such as the Linux operating system, are often seen as safer than their closed-source counterparts because their vulnerabilities have been probed and patched by a vast community of online contributors. Similarly, communities of researchers can more easily test open models for security flaws, though fixing those flaws is trickier than rewriting a line of code.
Open models can also be deployed more broadly than closed models for cyber defense. Any tool that can be used for hacking can also be used to prevent it: Defenders hack their own software to uncover flaws in need of patching. Anthropic has shown how this can work for closed models with its Project Glasswing initiative, which enables some trusted companies to use its most capable models for cyber defense. But plenty of other companies were left to fend for themselves.
Open models, however, can be used much more widely. After it was hacked by OpenAI agents, Hugging Face emphasized the fact that it had to depend on an open model to analyze the hack, because questions about it triggered the closed models’ security filters.
Nevertheless, many experts still perceive open models as riskier than closed models. The time-tested open-source security logic doesn’t necessarily hold up when dealing with tools as powerful as today’s—and tomorrow’s—models. “Where it gets complicated is when you start taking seriously the one-off instances of particularly catastrophic incidents that might be lower probability, but if they happen would be disastrous,” says Seger. If a wildly powerful open hacking model were dropped into the world today, for example, a bad actor could devastate our technological infrastructure before anyone had a chance to shore up their defenses. An event like that could be impossible to recover from.
The risks can look even more dramatic when you consider what models might do of their own accord. The OpenAI Hugging Face hack only occurred because the company’s models were being tested with many of their cybersecurity guardrails removed, and open models have very few guardrails in the first place. If open models did decide to misbehave, it might be difficult to detect what was happening because they are so decentralized. For this reason, people who take seriously the purported catastrophic risks posed by rogue agents, such as Dario Amodei, tend to be more skeptical of open models.
Can we make open models safer—and more open?
A few years ago, the debate about open models had an all-or-nothing framing: Either you supported open models because of their potential to fight concentration of power, or you rejected them because of the safety risks. These days, however, people are expending a lot of effort to find some middle ground. One way they are doing that is by devising techniques to mitigate the safety risks of open models.
Most of the safety tools used for closed models, such as filters and monitoring, aren’t applicable to open models, but there are other possibilities. Some researchers are interested in trying to train models that are never exposed to training data that teaches them about bad or otherwise undesirable behavior—an open model that never learns about hacking, for example. But purging training datasets of all references to misbehavior without harming model performance remains a challenge.
Other researchers are working to build models that are resistant to retraining, so that an open model’s safety training can’t be so easily removed. The theory behind these “tamper-resistant” models makes a lot of sense: If you repeatedly try to retrain a model to be unsafe and reinforce any resistance that the model shows to that retraining, eventually you’ll get a model that’s fortified against future retraining attempts. In practice, however, no current approaches to making models tamper-resistant hold up against all tampering attacks, according to a recent preprint.
But Saad Hossain, an engineer at the AI medical imaging company Deep Breathe and the paper’s lead author, hopes that future techniques will prove more effective. “My reason for optimism is that it’s a very active area of research, and a lot of people are trying to come up with new and better methods,” he says.
If the risks of open models are less black-and-white than they might at first seem, so are the benefits. Publishing the internal structures, or weights, of models might not be enough to disrupt AI-mediated concentration of power. “I think there are very genuine benefits to open source in terms of deconcentrating power, but they’re not sufficient in themselves,” Hobbs says. Open weights are a bare minimum standard for open models: Researchers can learn much more about how models work if they have access to details about their training, including the data on which they were trained, but AI companies are typically reluctant to divulge this information.
Accessibility matters for open models too. Without computer chips that can run sophisticated models, you can’t actually use the model weights, even if you have them. Those chips have become prohibitively expensive as AI companies snap up more and more of them. “Openness is a floor, not a ceiling, for what we need to do to ensure that our technological futures benefit everyone,” Widder says.
Real openness—not only open weights, but also open training data and accessible hardware—could also bring more risks, of course. If everyone has access to advanced AI hardware and advanced models to run on it, then anyone could potentially be a hacker. But there are strategies for mitigating these risks. Many experts advocate for some version of staged release, in which models start their life closed and gradually become more and more freely accessible as their safety is assured.
Figuring out exactly how to implement such strategies will require striking a careful balance between the risks and benefits of open models. But if open models are a necessary element of a positive AI future, as some experts believe, that effort will be well worth it.

articles.title: Agentic AI Automates RTL Waveform Analysis And Debugging (Columbia, Google)
articles.text:
Researchers at Columbia University, Google DeepMind, and Google published a technical paper titled “Back to the Future: Rethinking EDA Infrastructure for Agentic Systems in Chip Design Verification.”
Abstract
“The unprecedented computational scale of modern artificial intelligence depends on complex, multi-billion-transistor Systems-on-Chip, yet the workflows that verify these chips remain stubbornly manual. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have made rapid inroads into Electronic Design Automation (EDA), approximately 74.6% of existing studies target static Register-Transfer Level (RTL) code generation, leaving post-simulation verification and interactive waveform debugging largely untouched. We introduce Back-to-the-Future (BTTF), an end-to-end agentic framework that closes this infrastructural gap. BTTF distills massive, unstructured simulation dumps into a normalized relational SQLite database and couples it with a collaborative multi-agent orchestration engine that translates natural-language verification queries into schema-aware SQL while correlating signal anomalies with versioned RTL repositories. Across a 150-query benchmark, BTTF attains 95.33% execution accuracy, charting a practical path toward autonomous EDA verification.”
Find the technical paper here. October 2026.
Yang, Je, Ivan Lobov, and Thomas Karpati. “Back to the Future: Rethinking EDA Infrastructure for Agentic Systems in Chip Design Verification.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2610.06790 (2026).

articles.title: Turning the connectivity gap into a blockchain opportunity - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
African technologists and entrepreneurs are applying blockchain in innovative ways, creating a new financial infrastructure for the continent with wide-ranging benefits, including for the humanitarian sector.
Through its Blockchain Ventures investment programme – supported by Ethereum Foundation and GSR Foundation – UNICEF Office of Innovation provides funding and technical assistance to emerging market startups building innovative blockchain-based solutions.
Unreliable and expensive internet access locks millions out of the digital economy, but as XMesh founder Benjamin Yan explains, blockchain could help equip ordinary people to act as a hyper-local connectivity provider and earn an income from their unused bandwidth.
What problem were you trying to solve when you came up with XOneFi?
I love adventure travelling and I use Starlink in remote areas. I was paying a fair amount of money for that service and I’d find that people around me also wanted to get online, but there was no way to share the connection and there was no way to charge people who want to use my internet, so that’s when I began thinking about a usage-based solution for sharing the internet.
How does XOneFi work?
Anyone with an internet connection can become a provider. They purchase their upstream connection, and then install an XOneFi-enabled router, set their rate and they are good to go.
Nearby customers can use their phones or computers to discover the network, purchase internet access by time or data usage, and the XOneFi firmware meters the session and automatically sends the payment from the customer to the provider.
Where does blockchain come in, and why is it essential?
The blockchain is valuable because we are facing an open network with many independent providers and customers who don’t know the infrastructure owners.
Blockchain is fully transparent, offers tamper-resistant usage accounting – so that providers and customers cannot cheat– and automated micro payments. If a customer is paying $4 a month, maybe every hour you are only paying several cents, which is a very small amount of money, and without blockchain we really cannot transact that.
How are prices set so they work for providers and customers?
We provide a default rate, but providers can adjust it based on their own payment for the internet. When the customer connects they see how much they need to pay and, if they agree, they click, and the transaction starts.
How does the connectivity gap you are bridging affect children and schools?
School administrators tell us connectivity issues are really a big problem: their internet is not reliable, the data rate is very low. Sometimes they cannot sustain a Zoom call or YouTube video, and you can’t even talk about coding or using AI. It is really a missed opportunity for the kids to get a better education, to get the opportunities that they want.
Why did you choose Nigeria to test XOneFi?
Nigeria is a growing economy with big cities and a large population of young people looking for opportunities. They want to utilise the digital economy to improve their living standards.
What is happening on the ground now?
We are running a pilot project at two Nigerian schools and planning to expand to community centres and business centres. Our chief financial officer and our director – both are women – are really moving things forward and identifying and solving challenges on the ground.
Looking ahead, what is your vision for connectivity and local digital economies?
The ultimate vision is that a child or any other user does not need to know where the connection comes from – whether it’s fibre, cellular, satellite or any other technology – but will be able to find an affordable network that they can use. For providers, they can operate their own access points, earn income and reinvest in the hardware to get a better connection. So, everyone has the opportunity to become a mini, hyper-local provider of connectivity, and everyone can get affordable and reliable internet.

articles.title: Ivanti warns of Connect Secure zero-day exploited in attacks
articles.text:
Ivanti urged customers on Tuesday to immediately patch an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability in the Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) remote access gateway.
Formerly known as Pulse Connect Secure and originally Juniper Pulse, the enterprise-grade ICS SSL VPN provides remote employees, contractors, and hybrid workforces with secure access to corporate and cloud resources.
Tracked as CVE-2026-104935, this high-severity authentication bypass zero-day affects ICS versions 22.8R2.4 and earlier, 25.1.2.2 and earlier, and 25.1.1.1 and earlier.
Remote threat actors without privileges can exploit CVE-2026-104935 in low-complexity attacks that don't require user interaction to execute arbitrary commands on targeted ICS appliances.
"At the time of disclosure, Ivanti is aware of limited exploitation in the wild. We are working directly with those organizations while making information, updates and remediation available to the broader customer community. If you are running one of the impacted versions, Ivanti recommends you act immediately," Ivanti said.
"Customers should review the security advisory, upgrade to the fixed version as soon as possible, and run the Integrity Checker Tool regularly."
Internet threat watchdog Shadowserver now tracks over 5,500 ICS instances exposed online, but there is no information on how many are honeypots or have already been secured against ongoing attacks.
Exploited since at least October 3
Cybersecurity firm Volexity, which found and reported the flaw, revealed earlier today that a previously unknown threat actor it tracks as UTA0576 has chained the CVE-2026-104935 vulnerability since at least October 3 with two other flaws to achieve unauthenticated root-level code execution on fully patched devices.
"Notably, UTA0576 deployed no malware or web shell. Instead, the threat actor re-exploited the device for every command it ran and tampered with logs to cover its tracks, evading Ivanti’s Integrity Checker Tool," Volexity said.
While Ivanti has patched two flaws, it is still working to address a privilege escalation vulnerability that UTA0576 exploited as part of the same chain.
Threat intelligence company Defused also confirmed Volexity's report, saying that it caught the first signs of CVE-2026-104935 exploitation in the wild starting October 1.
Hackers have frequently exploited Ivanti vulnerabilities, often as zero-days, because they provide a quick way to breach enterprise networks and steal sensitive customer and corporate data.
Ivanti has also patched several other Connect Secure zero-days exploited in the wild over the past several years, some of them chained in widespread attacks to deploy malware.
It addressed an authentication bypass (CVE-2023-46805) and a command injection (CVE-2024-21887) in early January 2024, and a server-side request forgery (CVE-2024-21893) two weeks later.
More recently, it fixed a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability tracked as CVE-2025-0282 in January 2025 and a second RCE flaw (CVE-2025-22457) that China-linked cyber spies have exploited since at least mid-March 2025.
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged 36 vulnerabilities across various Ivanti products as actively exploited in the wild since November 2021, 12 of which ransomware gangs have also abused.
Ivanti has over 3,000 employees, a network of over 7,000 partners, and more than 40,000 customers worldwide using its IT asset management solutions.

articles.title: Sridhar Vembu says India must prioritise tech sovereignty over spending billions on GPUs
articles.text:
Sridhar Vembu says India must prioritise tech sovereignty over spending billions on GPUs
Zoho co-founder Sridhar Vembu says India should prioritise infrastructure and foundational technologies over heavy GPU spending to build lasting prosperity and reduce dependence on foreign countries.
Zoho Chief Scientist and co-founder Sridhar Vembu believes investments should be directed towards building infrastructure in India rather than purchasing graphics processing units (GPUs), amid the current euphoria around artificial intelligence (AI).
“If I earn $10 billion right now, as a government, I will spend the money on Bangalore infrastructure, Chennai infrastructure, all that. There's no point spending $10 billion on GPUs right now,” Vembu said in the inaugural keynote address at the 17th edition of TechSparks 2026, YourStory’s flagship event.
Vembu made the argument against the backdrop of growing excitement and anxiety around AI advancements, particularly concerns about job losses among technology professionals.
“Our world is all revolving around software tech. Approximately 97% of the population doesn't care, and they are only on the consuming side of it,” he said.
According to Vembu, technology investments should extend beyond software to other sectors, including agriculture and manufacturing.
He cited China, South Korea, and Taiwan as examples of countries that have leveraged technology to boost food production and drive economic prosperity.
“We need a lot more know-how to inject into agriculture to grow more food,” Vembu said, and added, “Israel is able to grow food in the desert.”
To achieve this, Vembu called for India to build sovereignty in foundational technologies and reduce its dependence on foreign countries. He warned that the current geopolitical tensions could leave the country vulnerable to disruptions in access to critical technologies.
“The priorities should go towards foundational and upwards. Then only can we build durable prosperity. Prosperity that stays with us.”

articles.title: CMF de Nothing dévoile deux nouvelles enceintes portables à moins de 100 euros
articles.text:
La marque CMF appartenant au constructeur britannique Nothing vient de dévoiler sa première gamme d’enceintes portables baptisée CMF Speaker Series. Nous retrouvons pour l’instant deux modèles : la CMF Speaker S et la CMF Speaker M. Si ces deux enceintes se veulent abordables et facilement transportables, elles présentent une différence au niveau de leur taille et de leurs performances sonores. Spécificités, prix, date de lancement : voici tout ce qu’il faut savoir.
La CMF Speaker S
Cette enceinte audio se veut facilement transportable, notamment grâce à son format compact et son point d’attache intégré qui permet de fixer un mousqueton. L’enceinte peut ainsi être accrochée à un sac et transportée en extérieur. Au passage, précisons qu’elle est certifiée IP68, c’est-à-dire résistante à la poussière et à l’eau.
Côté audio, la CMF Speaker S dispose d’un haut-parleur large bande de 45 mm et de deux radiateurs passifs. Elle affiche une puissance de 10 W RMS et couvre une plage de fréquences allant de 70 Hz à 20 kHz.
La CMF Speaker S est disponible dès maintenant au prix de 59 euros sur le site de Nothing et chez certains partenaires à partir de novembre.
La CMF Speaker M
Avec sa plus grande taille, l’enceinte Speaker M promet un son plus ample et plus puissant que la Speaker S, tout en étant également facilement transportable grâce à sa poignée intégrée. Il est toutefois ici davantage question d’une enceinte à placer au sein d’une pièce ou à amener lors d’un rassemblement avec d’autres personnes. Cette enceinte est par ailleurs également certifiée IP68 (résistante à la poussière et à l’eau).
Côté audio, la CMF Speaker M est équipée d’une architecture à caisson fermé à double haut-parleur, composée d’un woofer dédié de 25 W associé à un tweeter de 10 W, pour une puissance de sortie RMS de 35 W sur une plage de 60 Hz à 20 kHz.
La CMF Speaker M est disponible dès maintenant au prix de 99 euros sur le site de Nothing et chez certains partenaires à partir de novembre.
Les points communs de ces deux enceintes audio
Notons quelques points que les deux modèles ont en commun : des boutons de commande physiques intégrés aux enceintes, un algorithme qui ajuste automatiquement le son en temps réel, la fonction Ultra Bass (qui ajoute de la profondeur contrôlée dans les graves) et quatre préréglages d’égalisation personnalisables depuis l’application Nothing (« Balanced », « More Bass », « More Treble » et « Voice »).
Notons également qu’il est possible de connecter deux enceintes S ou deux enceintes M pour restituer un son stéréo, tandis que le mode « Party », basé sur Auracast, synchronise la lecture sur deux enceintes compatibles ou plus, y compris des modèles pris en charge par d’autres marques. Nothing annonce jusqu’à 18 heures d’autonomie à 50 % du volume avec la fonction Ultra Bass activée. Une charge de 10 minutes permettrait par ailleurs de bénéficier d’une heure d’écoute.
Les deux modèles sont disponibles en blanc, gris foncé, orange et turquoise. Certaines façades et certains boutons sont par ailleurs interchangeables. Il reste maintenant à voir ce qu’il en est dans les faits.

articles.title: Écran AMOLED 120 Hz et stockage de 512 Go : le POCO M8 5G est à 229 €
articles.text:
Le smartphone POCO M8 5G 8/512 Go est à 229 €
Le POCO M8 5G associe un écran AMOLED de 6,77 pouces à 120 Hz, un processeur Snapdragon 6 Gen 3 et une batterie de 5 520 mAh compatible avec la charge 45 W.
Amazon propose le POCO M8 5G 8/512 Go noir à 229 €, contre un prix conseillé de 303 €. L’écart atteint 74 €, soit environ 24 %. Cette offre concerne un appareil neuf, vendu et expédié par Amazon. Attention à bien sélectionner le modèle M8 et la configuration avec 512 Go de stockage.
Un écran AMOLED 120 Hz et 512 Go de stockage
Le POCO M8 5G possède un écran AMOLED de 6,77 pouces, affichant 2 392 × 1 080 pixels. Son taux de rafraîchissement monte à 120 Hz dans les applications compatibles pour rendre les défilements et les animations plus fluides. Le téléphone dispose également de deux haut-parleurs compatibles Dolby Atmos pour les contenus multimédias.
Cette version associe le Snapdragon 6 Gen 3 à 8 Go de mémoire vive et 512 Go de stockage. Cette capacité laisse de la place pour les applications, les photos et les vidéos téléchargées, même si une partie est occupée par le système. Un emplacement hybride permet d’ajouter une carte microSD à la place d’une seconde carte SIM. La connectivité comprend la 5G et le NFC.
Une batterie de 5 520 mAh dans un boîtier de 7,35 mm
Le smartphone intègre une batterie de 5 520 mAh compatible avec la charge rapide 45 W, dans un boîtier annoncé à 7,35 mm d’épaisseur pour 178 g. Le chargeur secteur n’est pas inclus : il faut donc prévoir un adaptateur compatible pour profiter de la charge rapide. La durée d’utilisation dépend des applications, de la luminosité et des conditions de réseau.
Pour la photo, le M8 combine un capteur principal de 50 Mpx, un capteur de profondeur de 2 Mpx et une caméra avant de 20 Mpx. Il peut filmer en 4K à 30 images par seconde avec la caméra arrière. Un lecteur d’empreintes intégré à l’écran complète l’équipement.
