articles.title: Workday is using TypeSafe's Jev to build user interfaces on the fly
articles.text:
Workday is using TypeSafe’s Jev to build user interfaces on the fly
Workday on Tuesday made Sana, its AI assistant, the new home screen for its HR, finance, and IT software. If you’re not an HR pro, that may not be all that exciting for you, but the way the team built this is maybe one of the most interesting use cases of Jev, TypeSafe’s decision model. Workday is building the user interface on the fly — and all of that is managed by Jev.
In a demo during a press briefing ahead of the announcement, a question about a paycheck brought up a card with the amount hidden behind a click, for example, while a request for time off produced a date picker, with Sana filling in the rest of the form.
Sana, which Workday bought for $1.1 billion last year, is available now, and admins can roll it out to their users without making it the default.
Picking components instead of writing them
Joel Hellermark, Workday’s chief AI officer and Sana’s founder, said in a press briefing that the usual approach to generative UI, in which a model generates the full interface, is “quite slow.”
“If you use a classification model instead and you just give it all of the design components to pick from, you can literally do it instantly,” he said.
Workday gave Jev every atomic component in its design system and hard-coded none of the selection logic, Hellermark said, though the team also had to get data preloading right. In the demo, the paycheck card appeared before he finished typing, for example.
TypeSafe claims Jev answers in 70 to 500 milliseconds, which makes it ideal for this kind of real-time use case.
In many cases, Hellermark said, AI that works through real interface elements does significantly better than pure back-and-forth chat.
A model built to choose
According to TypeSafe, developers send Jev application data and a set of typed questions, and it returns a pick from a list of up to 255 options, a score, or a yes-or-no answer, each with a probability attached. It doesn’t generate text.
TypeSafe launched Jev on Sept. 15 with a $40 million seed round led by DCVC. On Friday, it said it raised an $870 million Series A, led by Andreessen Horowitz, at a $7.5 billion valuation. TypeSafe says a third of the Fortune 500 already use Jev but hasn’t named them. Andreessen Horowitz’s own announcement puts the figure at 25 percent, and TypeSafe’s only published case study features Jack & Jill, an AI recruiting marketplace.
There is no dearth of competition in this field, of course. OpenAI, Amazon, Cloudflare, and Perplexity have already shipped their decision models too, with Microsoft following on last week.
A pattern developers are already testing
Using Jev and similar models for building user interfaces isn’t completely new, though. CopilotKit, an open source framework for adding AI copilots to apps, published a recipe in which Jev picks which prebuilt panel to show, with an OpenAI model as the fallback.
Vercel Labs is testing a Jev mode in json-render, its framework for rendering AI-generated UIs from developer-defined components.
Andrew King, who leads solutions architecture at app developer Very Good Ventures, wrote last month that handing every closed question (one with a fixed set of answers) to Jev cut his generative dashboard’s median render time to 3.8 seconds, from 29 seconds with a frontier model composing it. His tests ran on synthetic data.
“A shape nobody anticipated cannot appear on screen,” King writes. Anything Jev answers with less than 50 percent confidence goes to a language model instead, a setup he calls “a cage with a door.”
In a test on OpenRouter’s blog using the Banking77 intent-classification set, Jev answered in a median 175 milliseconds and scored 81 percent accuracy. Claude Opus 5 scored 84.4 percent but took 2.3 seconds and cost about 22 times as much.
TypeSafe’s own documentation says Jev struggles with counting, arithmetic, and dates, leans toward whichever option is listed first, and doesn’t treat injected content as hostile by default.
Workday hasn’t said how large its design system is or what Sana does when no combination of components fits. King wrote in September that he was keeping client data off Jev because the vendor was “weeks old with no published security certification yet.” TypeSafe now offers a SOC 2 Type II report on request.
What leaves Workday
Workday recently added TypeSafe to its list of subprocessors, the outside companies that can process customer data (the ones you only think about when a SaaS service you subscribe to emails you about a change of subprocessors that you promptly forget). This entry, it’s worth noting, covers all of Workday’s product lines, not just Sana, for natural language processing, intent classification, and confidence scoring.
According to TypeSafe, Jev runs only on its hosted API and processes data in the U.S., and the company offers zero data retention to enterprise customers.
Staying inside Workday
Hellermark also showed Sana working inside Anthropic’s Claude. That’s an AI-to-AI integration, Gerrit Kazmaier, Workday’s president of product and technology, said in the briefing, and users lose the Jev-driven interface and some context along the way.
Workday’s May partnership with Google Cloud already covers A2UI, Google’s spec for agents to describe interfaces that host apps then render. MCP Apps, a Model Context Protocol extension, brings interactive UI into Claude and ChatGPT. Neither shows up in Workday’s announcements this week, so for now, it seems, employees who reach Sana through Claude get the conversation without the date picker.

articles.title: Le créateur de Linux a utilisé Claude Code pour modifier son propre noyau… et c'est une petite révolution
articles.text:
Linus Torvalds a publié dans son propre dépôt une série de huit patchs pour le noyau Linux, conçue avec Claude Code.
Le créateur de Linux a baptisé sa branche noref-filemap-read-with-llm, et le suffixe dit tout : le code, les programmes de test, la revue des problèmes ouverts et le premier jet de la lettre d'accompagnement viennent de l'assistant d'Anthropic. Les benchmarks, eux, ont tourné sur sa machine. C'est la première fois qu'il crédite un agent pour une série touchant à la gestion mémoire du noyau dans son propre arbre, un cran au-dessus de ses usages précédents, limités au débogage.
Un compteur disputé par tous les cœurs du processeur
Le chantier vise le cache de pages, la zone de mémoire vive où le noyau garde les fichiers récemment lus. Quand plusieurs threads lisent de petits morceaux du même fichier, chaque lecture prend puis relâche une référence sur la page concernée, deux écritures atomiques sur la même ligne de cache. Les cœurs se la disputent.
Les tentatives précédentes copiaient les données dans un tampon sans référence, puis validaient après coup, mais butaient sur des courses que cette validation ne détecte pas, comme une page libérée puis réinsérée au même index. Torvalds supprime plutôt la cause : une page sortie du cache ne retourne à l'allocateur qu'après une période de grâce, ce qui permet à un lecteur de copier directement vers le tampon utilisateur, sans référence ni limite de taille de lecture.
Selon Hwbusters, avec huit threads sur un fichier, le coût noyau par lecture tombe d'environ 2 950 à 725 cycles, et le débit passe d'environ 10 millions à 30-33 millions de lectures par seconde. Avec un seul thread, le gain est de l'ordre de 10 %.
Une branche pas encore fusionnée dans le noyau
La branche repose sur Linux 7.3-rc6 et pour le moment rien n'est fusionné : les utilisateurs d'Ubuntu ou d'une autre distribution ne verront donc aucun changement. Torvalds espère de plus gros gains sur des machines plus grandes ou multi-sockets, sans avoir rien testé de tel.
Le contraste avec son discours d'il y a deux ans est net : en octobre 2024, il résumait l'industrie de l'IA à « 90 % de marketing et 10 % de réalité ». Il refuse toujours que l'IA signe le code à la place du développeur, et le sujet continue de diviser l'écosystème : un développeur a démissionné avec fracas quand Debian a autorisé le code produit par IA. Reste à savoir comment les mainteneurs de la gestion mémoire accueilleront la série.
Pour le noyau, vous êtes plutôt du camp qui accepte du code assisté par IA tant qu'un humain signe, ou de celui qui préfère l'écarter ?

articles.title: Whiterock deploys €82 million to support SME growth across Northern Ireland | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Belfast-based fund manager Whiterock has announced their investment of €82 million (£70 million) in Northern Ireland SMEs across their two funds – both backed by the British Business Bank.
The two funds are the Growth Capital Fund and the Investment Fund for Northern Ireland.
Paul Millar, Chief Executive of Whiterock, says: “Whiterock has been supporting local SMEs’ growth for over 14 years, and our strong, dedicated team has spotted investment opportunities across multiple sectors from advanced manufacturing to tech to consumer products.
“We are an NI based funder with local knowledge, and we find that local businesses really value the insights and partnership that we bring to the table. We are proud of the resounding success of our equity and debt funds since they launched in early 2024 and we hope to continue working as the go-to strategic partner for local companies to achieve their growth ambitions.”
Whiterock’s investment milestone comes amid wider British Business Bank activity aimed at increasing access to finance for UK businesses in 2026.
EU-Startups has reported comparable commitments of €58 million to London-based Soho Square Capital, €46 million to FPE Capital, up to €11.5 million to Ascension Ventures, €11 million each to SFC Capital and Fuel Ventures, and up to €53.6 million to Zinc Capital Management.
Together, these commitments represent approximately €191 million in financing for investment managers supporting businesses at different stages of growth. Including Whiterock’s €82 million already deployed across Northern Ireland, the announcements account for approximately €273 million in reported financing activity.
EU-Startups previously covered Whiterock’s €7.7 million investment in Belfast-based Drinksology Kirker Greer and its €1.8 million funding package for Solarfix in 2024.
Sue Barnard, Senior Investment Manager at the British Business Bank, adds: “Reaching £70 million of investment in Northern Ireland businesses is an important milestone and demonstrates the impact that public and private finance can have in supporting ambitious smaller businesses to grow.
“Through the British Business Bank’s programmes, we are proud to work with fund managers such as Whiterock to increase access to finance for businesses that can drive jobs, innovation, and economic growth across the region. The breadth of businesses supported through these funds highlights the importance of a diverse funding landscape, and we look forward to seeing the continued impact of this investment across Northern Ireland.”
Founded in 2012, Whiterock manages over €420 million (£255 million) across five funds. Its Growth Capital Fund provides minority investments in scaling Northern Ireland companies, with capacity for further follow on funding as required.
Since 2024, Whiterock has invested €47 million (£40 million) into 15 companies across Northern Ireland, including Drinksology, MANTIS and Around Noon, through its €88 million (£75 million) equity fund and a further €35 million (£30 million) invested into 60 companies through its €71 million (£60 million) IFNI debt fund, supporting NI SMEs such as Neighbourhood Café, Nomadic Watches, Axial 3D and BLK BOX.
To date, the company has deployed in excess of €224 million (£190 million), which has leveraged over €177 million (£150 million) of further funding from other funders, and supporting the creation of over 3000 jobs.
A prime example of its investment thesis is Neighbourhood Café, which since opening its new site in February 2025 with loan support has delivered strong growth and is reportedly on track to more than double its revenue in FY26, its first full year of trading from the expanded premises. The business now serves an average of 11,000 guests per month across its café operations.
Building on this performance, management is focused on growing its events offering as a key driver of future revenue diversification and revenue growth.

articles.title: Biotecnología: este es el plan para para filtrar la sangre de bebés con sepsis en Europa
articles.text:
La empresa austríaca Efferon recibió el 22 de abril de 2026 la primera certificación europea para un dispositivo que filtra la sangre de bebés y chicos con sepsis. Es el primero de su tipo aprobado en la Unión Europea para uso pediátrico.
El dispositivo, llamado Efferon NEO, obtuvo la marca CE MDR, el equivalente europeo a la aprobación de la FDA (la agencia que autoriza medicamentos y dispositivos médicos en Estados Unidos), otorgada por el organismo certificador 3EC International.
La sepsis es una de las principales causas de muerte infantil en el mundo: provoca más de tres millones de muertes de chicos por año y representa la mitad de todos los casos de sepsis a nivel global, según datos de la compañía. Entre los pacientes más vulnerables, la mortalidad llega al 50%.
Los números del estudio clínico
La aprobación se apoyó en el estudio multicéntrico LASSO NEO, que incluyó a 78 chicos de entre un mes y 14 años tratados en ocho centros médicos. De ellos, 32 recibieron el dispositivo y 46 integraron el grupo de control con el tratamiento habitual.
La mortalidad a 28 días fue del 9% en el grupo tratado con Efferon NEO, frente al 35% en el grupo de control, una diferencia estadísticamente significativa. Los chicos tratados también dejaron de necesitar respirador y medicación para sostener la presión arterial antes que el resto.
El puntaje pSOFA, que mide la gravedad de la falla multiorgánica en pediatría, bajó a 4,9 puntos al séptimo día entre los chicos tratados, frente a 7,8 puntos en el grupo de control. La mitad de los pacientes tratados dejó de necesitar respirador artificial hacia el sexto día, contra el día 37 en el grupo de control.
El jefe de terapia intensiva del Centro Médico Multidisciplinario Infantil de Tecnologías Médicas Avanzadas de San Petersburgo, Mikhail Rusak, participó del estudio y calificó el resultado de inesperado. “Hasta ahora, ningún estudio de gran escala había mostrado un efecto de la adsorción de endotoxinas sobre la reducción de la mortalidad”, señaló.
Cómo funciona el filtro de sangre
El dispositivo extrae la sangre del paciente, la hace pasar por un cartucho con un material polimérico y se la devuelve filtrada. Ese proceso elimina al mismo tiempo las endotoxinas, sustancias tóxicas que liberan las bacterias, y las citoquinas, las moléculas que disparan la inflamación descontrolada que caracteriza a la sepsis.
“Desde que se demostró la eficacia de Efferon LPS en pacientes adultos con sepsis, quedó claro que negarles a los chicos el acceso a esa terapia que puede salvarles la vida sería simplemente poco ético”, dijo el cofundador y director de tecnología de la empresa, Ivan Bessonov.
Según explicó el propio Bessonov, el dispositivo ataca al mismo tiempo dos frentes del problema: el origen bacteriano de la infección y la respuesta inflamatoria descontrolada que el cuerpo desencadena para combatirla.
La versión pediátrica se diseñó para adaptarse al menor volumen de sangre que circula en el cuerpo de un bebé o un niño, a diferencia de un cartucho pensado para adultos. Puede usarse en pacientes de hasta 18 años.
El cofundador y director ejecutivo de Efferon, Dima Romashin, describió la certificación como “un hito central, no solo para la empresa, sino para la medicina crítica en general” y dijo que la compañía entra así “en un mercado de 40.000 millones de dólares que las soluciones existentes dejaron desatendido durante mucho tiempo”.
Expansión y próximos pasos
La tecnología de Efferon, que incluye tanto la versión para adultos como la pediátrica, ya se usó en más de 25.000 tratamientos en más de 40 países, entre ellos Australia, el Reino Unido, Alemania y Arabia Saudita.
La versión específica para chicos, Efferon NEO, ya se utiliza en unidades de terapia intensiva de unos 30 países, entre ellos hospitales europeos, Arabia Saudita y Tailandia, según datos de la empresa citados por TechCrunch.
Romashin, un emprendedor serial que asumió como director ejecutivo de Efferon a principios de este año para comercializar la tecnología, suele señalar que la sepsis en general mata a más de 11 millones de personas por año en el mundo, entre chicos y adultos, muy por encima de la inversión y la atención médica que recibe la enfermedad.
Efferon fue seleccionada este año entre las 200 startups de la competencia Startup Battlefield de TechCrunch Disrupt 2026. La compañía nació en 2016 a partir de tecnología desarrollada por investigadores de la Universidad Estatal de Moscú y hoy tiene su sede central en Villach, Austria.
Esa tecnología generó hasta ahora más de un millón de euros en ingresos acumulados, de acuerdo con cifras publicadas por la empresa.
La empresa espera cerrar este año con 2 millones de dólares en ingresos anualizados y ya prepara la presentación de su pedido de aprobación ante la agencia de medicamentos de Estados Unidos, a través de una vía regulatoria pensada para dispositivos que atienden a poblaciones de pacientes reducidas.

articles.title: Microsoft is shutting its Nairobi engineering centre
articles.text:
Microsoft is winding down its Africa Development Centre (ADC) in Nairobi, putting nearly 400 jobs at risk and reversing a seven-year effort to make Kenya a hub for building technology for global markets.
Two employees, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, told TechCabal that staff at the centre, housed in Dunhill Towers in Nairobi’s Westlands district, were called to a meeting on Monday morning and asked to meet with their managers by Friday, October 16, to discuss exit options, including severance terms.
The closure comes seven years after the company pledged more than $100 million to develop African tech talent, to make Nairobi one of its engineering hubs outside the US. It would unwind a project built on the promise that African engineers could build products for global markets without leaving the continent, raising questions about Microsoft’s long-term plans for engineering in Africa.
“We are communicating directly with employees in Kenya about proposed changes to our engineering operations,” a Microsoft spokesperson told TechCabal on Monday. “We recognise the uncertainty this brings and are keeping those discussions private. Microsoft remains committed to Kenya and will continue to have employees in the country while supporting the country’s ongoing digital transformation and innovation ambitions.”
The statement did not confirm the centre’s closure or specify how many employees would remain or when the changes would take effect.
Two other employees, who asked not to be named as they aren’t authorised to discuss the matter, told TechCabal they expect their meetings with supervisors to focus on severance terms rather than on whether they will stay.
“Our case is sealed; we just didn’t know when,” one employee said.
Another person familiar with the matter said fewer than 10 employees are expected to remain, including staff in sales and recruiting, two in Microsoft Customer and Partner Solutions (MCAPS), which manages customer and partner relationships, and employees working on AI for Good, Microsoft’s initiative to apply AI to social and environmental challenges.
Microsoft’s seven-year bet on African engineering
When Microsoft launched the Africa Development Centre (ADC) in 2019, Michael Fortin, then a corporate vice president, said it would allow engineers to do “meaningful work from their home countries” while working within a global engineering organisation. Microsoft planned to hire 100 engineers by the end of 2019 and grow the workforce across Nairobi and Lagos to 500 by 2023.
By December 2022, Microsoft President Brad Smith said the Nairobi centre employed more than 450 engineers. The centre had met its original hiring ambition, making it harder to explain the closure as a failure to deliver on its initial promise.
The Nairobi closure follows Microsoft’s May 2024 decision to shut its sister centre in Lagos, a move the company said at the time would not affect its operations in Kenya. The Lagos closure caught staff by surprise, while Nairobi employees say they had seen signs of trouble for some time.
On Monday, Kenya’s ICT Minister William Kabogo said he met a Microsoft delegation led by Jeff Bullwinkel, the company’s vice president and deputy general counsel for Europe, the Middle East and Africa, with its East Africa team headed by Angela Ng’ang’a.
Microsoft briefed him on “its evolving operations in Kenya in the context of its global restructuring,” Kabogo said, while he pressed the company on “protecting jobs at Microsoft’s Nairobi engineering centre.”
The company reaffirmed its long-term commitment to Kenya, he said, and both sides agreed to draft a joint action plan. Neither has disclosed what the plan will contain or whether it could change a decision employees describe as final.
Microsoft has yet to disclose why it is closing the Nairobi centre, and people familiar with the matter point to several possible factors. The decision comes amid a wider round of cuts at the company, which announced about 4,800 job cuts in July 2026, or roughly 2.1% of its workforce, following about 15,000 cuts in 2025.
The reductions come as Microsoft pours record sums into AI infrastructure, raising questions about which parts of its business will continue to receive funding. A remote engineering centre could come under pressure, though no public evidence links the Nairobi closure directly to the global cuts.
Kenya has also struggled to advance another major Microsoft initiative. The $1 billion data centre that Microsoft planned with Abu Dhabi-based G42 in Olkaria has stalled amid concerns about electricity capacity and disagreements over the Kenyan government’s ability to guarantee payments for the facility’s capacity. President William Ruto has cited the country’s limited power supply as a problem. However, government officials have said the project has not been abandoned.
A third possible factor is the cost of maintaining a large local workforce, particularly its tax bill. One employee told TechCabal that Microsoft’s Kenyan employees generate at least KES 1.5 billion ($11.6 million) in annual Pay As You Earn (PAYE) taxes for the Kenya Revenue Authority. TechCabal could not independently verify the figures.
The closure would return hundreds of engineers to a job market Microsoft helped reshape when it opened the centre in 2019. The company recruited talent from Kenyan banks, telcos and technology firms to build its local engineering team.
Seven years later, those employers and other technology companies will be among the places its departing engineers may look to next, raising questions about where the specialised talent built at the centre will go and whether Kenya can retain the skills and experience it took Microsoft years to assemble.

articles.title: Production Patterns for Agents, Evals, and LLM Costs: QCon AI New York 2026
articles.text:
Once AI is in production, code arrives faster than it can be reviewed, token costs rise, evals have to be good enough to act on, and agents need permissions and guardrails. QCon AI New York 2026 has confirmed sessions from senior engineers who have worked through these problems in systems they run. The conference takes place December 15-16 at The Westin Jersey City Newport, about five minutes by PATH train from the World Trade Center. It is for senior engineers and technical leaders making decisions on production AI.
What the sessions offer is hindsight. The senior engineers presenting have already made these decisions and run the results in production. They describe the system and the numbers behind it, letting another team compare an approach against its own constraints before committing.
Identity and authorization for agents in production
The QCon AI opening keynote describes two bad options for giving an agent production access. Teams hand it a long-lived service account and hope, or scope access too narrowly until it cannot finish its task. Nancy Wang, who founded and scaled AWS Data Protection, provides alternative solutions in When Software Becomes a User: Identity and Authorization for Agents in Production.
See what those controls look like on a live platform. Implement guardrails that sit on the server, including rate limits and peer approval for production changes, from Ronak Nathani, who led the move to Kubernetes at LinkedIn. He presents Inside LinkedIn's Kubernetes Ops Agent: Skills, Tools, and Guardrails, detailing an operations agent working across 500,000+ nodes and 5M+ pods. Together, the two talks give a team an authorization model and a working set of guardrails to compare with its own.
Whether a change is safe to ship, and what it costs to run
An eval is useful when engineers trust the score enough to ship or hold on it. Fabio Flores, who leads foundation development for Agentic Ordering at DoorDash, will argue that engineers should apply one judge to both simulated and production sessions so improvements measured before launch carry into production. He presents From Signal To Impact: The Eval Loop Behind DoorDash's Agentic Ordering System.
Agent workloads that worked as prototypes can become too expensive in production as context grows. Tejas Chopra, who previously worked on distributed caching infrastructure at Netflix, will explore how to implement prompt compression and ordering that increases provider cache hits. In Make Each Token Count: Compression, Caching, and Retrieval for Production LLM Context, he covers tiered storage for conversation history and the failure modes his team hit.
When AI writes code faster than teams can review it
Human review becomes the bottleneck as AI tools generate more code. Min Chen, who leads the move to AI-native software engineering at LinkedIn, suggests engineers should filter low-confidence findings before developers see them. She presents High-Signal AI Code Review That Adapts to Your Codebase at Scale. The system reviews tens of thousands of pull requests a week across roughly 10,000 repositories, and she explains how the team measures whether suggestions make it into merged code.
Faster output does not help every organization equally. Nathen Harvey, who leads DORA at Google Cloud, will explore how to assess AI maturity beyond adoption metrics and identify which existing problems AI is likely to make worse. He argues in Building in the AI-First World: Scale Brilliance, Not Bottlenecks that AI amplifies what an organization already does well and what it does badly.
What teams take back
The QCon AI Program Committee invites senior practitioners who are doing something other teams can learn from. The talks are vendor-neutral with no hidden product pitches, so each one is an account of what a team built and why. With one speaker for every eleven attendees, there is also time for a follow-up question for the person who built the system. The aim is for teams to return with patterns ready to adopt and costly mistakes they can avoid.
All confirmed talks are on the QCon AI New York 2026 sessions page.

articles.title: Meta Says Hackers Took Code, Personal Data of 1,500 in GitHub Breach
articles.text:
Meta is notifying roughly 1,500 people, most of them employees in the US, that their personal information was impacted after hackers got into some of the company’s GitHub repositories.
The intrusion was detected a few weeks ago. According to the tech giant, an outside group gained access to the repositories using an employee’s stolen credentials.
Meta’s security team shut down the attackers’ access and brought in GitHub and law enforcement. Notifications to the impacted individuals started going out on Tuesday.
Meta told SecurityWeek that 99% of the data the hackers took was business data, in the form of software code related to some of its products. The remaining 1% was personal data.
That personal data had been added to the repositories by mistake and should not have been there, as storing it on GitHub went against company policy. Meta has not said what types of personal information were involved.
The company also noted that a significant portion of what looked like personal data was actually synthetic or anonymized test data. As a result, the attackers may not readily be able to tell genuine records apart from test data.
Based on its investigation with GitHub so far, Meta does not believe the hackers were specifically after its data.
Meta is also notifying regulators, and the people whose information was involved are being offered credit and dark web monitoring services.
“This was not a vulnerability in any Meta product, and Meta’s internal systems were not breached. Meta business data held in a GitHub repository was improperly accessed using an employee’s stolen credentials – this included a small amount of personal data for a limited number of people, most of whom were Meta employees,” a Meta spokesperson told SecurityWeek.
In response to the incident, Meta rotated secrets it found in the affected repositories. It also hardened its product security to address risks stemming from access to its business data.
The company is working with its teams that use GitHub to keep user data off the platform. As a second line of defense, it is adding controls for proactive scanning to detect any user data uploaded by mistake.
“We’ve since rotated secrets found in the repositories, implemented new controls to prevent user data from being stored in GitHub, and worked with GitHub on additional measures to protect our repositories,” the spokesperson said.

articles.title: CXMT president says company’s first 4F² DRAM will be a server DDR5 RDIMM due by year-end — vertical transistors cut each memory cell’s footprint by a third on paper, but no speeds or capacities yet
articles.text:
CXMT president says company’s first 4F² DRAM will be a server DDR5 RDIMM due by year-end — vertical transistors cut each memory cell’s footprint by a third on paper, but no speeds or capacities yet
CXMT expects to sell a memory cell that Samsung and SK hynix have only shown in research papers so far.
CXMT expects to launch its first 4F² product, a server DDR5 RDIMM, by the end of the year, company president Cao Kanyu said in remarks reported by Yicai. The memory will be built on a denser cell layout, not yet commercialized, using vertical transistors to reduce the cell’s footprint by about one-third on paper. No speeds or capacities have been announced yet for the new product.
Cao spoke about the new RDIMM at the Integrated Chips and Chiplets Conference on Saturday. A 4F² cell is 2F by 2F at about two-thirds the area of current 6F² cells at the same feature size, and designs so far all stand the transistor up. The company has produced research and patent filings on the technology with papers in 2021, 2023, and 2025, and an 8Gb full-array research example was demonstrated at IEDM 2023.
Cao said CXMT’s version, the Vertical Surrounded Gate (VSG) transistor, has a channel that stands vertically with the gate wrapped around it, allowing stronger gate control with less leakage. Most importantly, standing the transistor up shrinks the cell. CXMT now has more than 300 published patent families tied to 4F², he added. The report says the industry as a whole is moving toward 4F² with 3D solutions that decouple DRAM and CMOS processes, combining them with wafer-level hybrid bonding, which allows logic and cell density to be optimized independently. Cao also covered CXMT’s own hybrid-bonding work, which began in 2019, with published patents.
Aside from this announcement, China’s primary DRAM maker has been in the news lately for its manufacturing and market-share gains. Its fifth-generation G5 DRAM technology platform, announced Sept. 20, is in mass production. TrendForce puts CXMT’s share of global DRAM revenue at 9.5% in the second quarter, up from 7.6% in the first, good for fourth place. Last November, CXMT showed off DDR5-8000 and LPDDR5X-10667. It has revealed itself as a manufacturer to be taken seriously by the biggest existing players.
Samsung showed off a 16Gb, 10nm-class 4F² DRAM design in its ISSCC 2026 paper in February. That one also used vertical-channel transistors (VCT), with the array bonded on top of the periphery using wafer-to-wafer hybrid copper bonding. The company claims the bonding raises dies per wafer by more than 20% with the same design rules. In April, The Elec reported that Samsung had a working 4F² VCT die on its sub-10nm “10a” process, with mass production targeted for 2028. Later South Korean reports clouded that date: the VCT version has since been split off as “D0a-V” with no timeline, and there is no firm timeline for adopting 4F².
SK hynix laid out plans at VLSI 2025 for a 4F² vertical-gate platform and 3D DRAM at nodes of 10nm and below, with circuitry bonded under the cell array. The April report also puts SK hynix’s 4F² debut at the 10b node, one step after Samsung’s 10a. Micron’s plans remain less clear, with no widely reported 2026 statement.
The announcement is perhaps more interesting for what wasn’t mentioned: capacity, speed, die density, process node, named customers, or intended volume. All we have is a date and a purported cell design, admittedly well-supported by the literature, but no product that has been tested by anyone outside of CXMT. Beyond Cao’s talk, CXMT hasn’t posted a release about the product in its Chinese or English newsrooms.

South Korean reports have said that CXMT’s initial products may only partly use 4F² and that producing stable units at volume is a separate challenge. With about 11 weeks left in the year, it will be interesting to see what CXMT actually delivers.

articles.title: Apple’s first smart display is the 7-inch HomeView for $299
articles.text:
Apple opened preorders for the HomeView smart home hub today.
The HomeView is a 7-inch smart display and speaker that aims to be a central access point for up to six members of a family to access and control Apple’s ecosystem of devices, apps, and the Siri generative AI chatbot that’s currently in beta.
Users can speak to HomeView to control smart home devices, such as, for example, telling Siri to close the smart blinds or activate smart locks. HomeView can also show a livestream for up to nine video feeds simultaneously.
“With a supported iCloud+ subscription, HomeView works with compatible cameras to deliver intelligent, end-to-end encrypted recognition of people, familiar faces, pets, packages, and vehicles, notifying the household the moment someone arrives at the front door. With video descriptions for HomeKit Secure Video footage, HomeView helps users quickly understand what happened in a video clip without even watching it,” Apple’s announcement said.
Competing with devices like the Amazon Echo Show, HomeView uses its integrated camera to identify who’s using it and show them their profile, which users can personalize with their preferred apps and widgets. Users can connect their HomeView profile to their Apple Intelligence-supporting iPhone or iPad and use the hub to access their Messages, Calendar, Reminders, and FaceTime.
“With an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad, Siri AI does more for each person—taking action across apps and surfacing relevant information from Messages and Calendar, playlists on Apple Music, and more by drawing on their personal context,” Apple’s announcement says.

articles.title: ChatGPT's answers could soon contain invisible watermarks — here's why OpenAI wants to change the way AI text works
articles.text:
ChatGPT will soon start secretly watermarking its answers — here's what that means for the text you copy and share
OpenAI is complying with the EU AI Act by inserting a watermark into generated text
I wrote earlier this year about Claude’s decision to comply with the EU AI Act, which requires all AI-generated text to be identifiable as AI, and start to insert a watermark into its text. Rather than limit this to EU customers, however, Anthropic decided to roll the feature out globally, which seemed a bit of an overreaction at the time.
OpenAI has now announced that it is following suit, but limiting the geographical areas of impact to the EU only. It is going to start inserting watermarks into generated text, but only for ChatGPT customers who live in the EU. That means that US and UK users won’t be affected at all.
OpenAI announced the change on October 5 saying: “Over the coming weeks, we will add an invisible watermark to eligible ChatGPT and Codex text output in the European Union.”
Inserting the watermark
To insert the watermark, which involves subtly changing the word choice for generated text, OpenAI is using a system of its own called textGrain. A note on the OpenAI website says: “Our text watermarking technology, textGrain, adds an invisible statistical signal to the model’s word choices. Our detector looks for that signal to assess whether a passage contains an OpenAI watermark. More details about how textGrain works can be found in our technical report, which will be updated with additional details in the coming weeks.”
Like many people, I find that idea that the word choice of the AI that I’m paying to use is now being influenced by a watermarking algorithm, not by what’s optimal for me the customer, to be deplorable. I’m not saying that the resulting text will automatically be worse because of the watermark, but it certainly won’t be optimal.
It also sounds like it’s an easily broken solution that is full of holes. To detect AI text that’s produced using textGrain's watermarking a special AI detection tool needs to be used, which it’s currently unavailable to the public. OpenAI says it is providing detector access to researchers and expert organizations and that approved researchers and expert organizations can apply starting today.
“The tool will report whether it detects an OpenAI watermark”, continues the OpenAI article “without identifying the user or revealing their prompts or conversations. Given the risk of missed watermarks and false positives, we are not making it publicly available at launch.”
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
So if the detector tool isn’t being made public it begs the question, what is this supposed to accomplish?
A box-ticking act?
The OpenAI article specifically says that detectors are prone to errors. That “shorter or more constrained text is harder to detect”, and that “editing can weaken the watermark”. It already sounds flawed, but what happens if you try and circumvent it completely by asking ChatGPT not to write in a way that can be detected, or to not use textGrain. Will it do it?
All of which leads me to conclude that the move by OpenAI looks a lot like a box ticking exercise to comply with the EU AI Act, which it is forced to do, since it requires generative AI providers to make generated text identifiable in a “machine-readable way”
It’s reassuring to hear that the changes are only going to be implemented inside the EU and that the text will remain private when the detector is used, but I suspect most ChatGPT users would rather OpenAI concentrated on producing the best possible answers rather than making those answers easily identify as AI-generated.
There’s also something fundamentally strange about a system that deliberately changes the words an AI chooses, without telling you which ones, to insert a watermark that can potentially be removed simply by editing the text. If the goal is to make AI-generated content more transparent, then surely the answer should be something that actually works, rather than an invisible signal that nobody outside a select group can even check for themselves.

articles.title: Flox Intelligence is building AI to keep wildlife away from trains, airports, and roads | TechCrunch
articles.text:
When I was eight, I remember our train to Mumbai ground to a halt with a great noise. When we started moving again, a good eight hours later, someone pointed out a mangled tail, of all things, hanging from a branch close to the tracks.
The train, you see, had apparently hit a wild bison at full speed, and the impact damaged the engine so badly that it had to be towed away for repairs. For a long time, I thought such things only happened in places like rural India, but I learned a few years ago that wildlife and infrastructure do not mix anywhere on the planet.
The FAA estimates that wildlife strikes have cost U.S. civil aviation about $272 million a year on average between 1990 and 2025. In France, the rail operator SNCF says wandering animals affect more than 8,000 trains across the country each year and are among its five leading causes of delays. In Brittany, 120 trains hit animals in 2023 alone, disrupting 660 services and causing more than 15,000 minutes of delays.
Reading about all that damage, to both infrastructure and animals, inspired Sara Nozkova (pictured above on the left) to develop a wildlife-deterrent system that works differently from the sirens, lights, fences, falcons, and culling traditionally used to keep animals away from roads, train tracks, airports, and other infrastructure.
“I was convinced the answer was not a louder deterrent,” she told TechCrunch.
After spending 13 years working in transportation and autonomous vehicles, Nozkova had learned how quickly the systems we build to navigate roads and other controlled environments fail once nature enters the equation.
“We have taught machines to be brilliant, but only inside the environments we engineered for them,” she said. “Cities, factory lines, warehouses. Fixed geometry, known objects. Stepping outside into nature, I saw firsthand how the same machines quickly go blind. Because nature is complex and always alive.”
So instead she joined the AI lab at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm and started working on a system that could change its deterrent responses based on what an animal nearby is doing, and even what kind of animal it is.
That work turned into Flox Intelligence, which spun out of KTH in 2020 and is one of the finalists at this year’s Startup Battlefield 200 pitch competition at TechCrunch Disrupt, taking place this year at Moscone West in San Francisco October 13-15.
Flox makes edge devices that process data on-site rather than in the cloud. Like autonomous vehicles, they use perception systems to sense their surroundings, but theirs are trained on wildlife behavior. A motion sensor wakes the device when it detects movement, triggering a camera that uses on-device models to identify nearby animals. The device then emits a species-appropriate sound to scare them away.
Nozkova says the system learns from experience, too, and varies its responses so animals don’t get habituated to repeated signals.
The company currently sells battery-operated devices that can be mounted on poles, trees, and other structures. It also offers a software platform that shows clients where the devices are deployed and what’s happening on the ground. The platform can also generate reports for regulatory compliance and for uses like biodiversity monitoring. The longer-term goal is to make the software portable enough to run on machines that work outside, including trains, cars, and drones.
Nozkova says about 150 Flox devices are live in North America, Europe, and Australia at airfields and airport perimeters, road and rail corridors (especially fence ends and crossings along wildlife corridors), national parks, agricultural land, urban areas, mining sites, and critical infrastructure such as electrical substations.
The company sells edge units up front, then charges an annual software and AI subscription after the first year. Flox also has OEM partnerships with companies that pay an annual fee to deploy its software on vehicles, like trains. Train manufacturer Alstom is one such partner.
The company expects to end 2026 with revenue of about $1.5 million, Nozkova said.
As unique as Flox’s product and approach are, the startup is not without competition. Robin Radar’s Scarecrow also uses species-specific distress calls to disperse birds and it records the activity, while iCHASE sells a system that detects birds with computer vision and targets them with a moving laser, adjusting its response as needed.
Nozkova says her moat is the breadth of the system and the data Flox has collected in the field, which she calls “ground truth on what actually makes a moose or a grizzly bear move safely.”
“Physical AI is walking out of the factory and into the messy, alive outdoors,” Nozkova says. “Every machine that operates outside — trains, trucks, drones, tractors, robots — will need to understand nature, and nature intelligence is the next layer of the perception stack. Almost nobody is building it.”
The company has raised about $5 million across pre-seed and seed rounds so far, with the seed round led by Unconventional Ventures and Tilia Impact Ventures. Co-investors across the rounds include GENIUS NY, Norrsken, Satgana, and angel investors, Nozkova said.
The company is now opening a $10 million Series A, which would mostly go toward growing from about 150 devices to several thousand deployed units and extending the underlying system beyond its current wildlife use cases.

articles.title: Las nuevas aspiradoras de Roborock llegan con más potencia y menos mantenimiento
articles.text:
Las aspiradoras de fregado se han convertido en uno de los electrodomésticos más importantes del hogar. Si bien los robots aspiradores han tomado la delantera, muchos prefieren el control manual para decidir las zonas en las que se enfocará más. Para estos últimos, Roborock ha lanzado dos aspiradoras con buena succión y funciones para acabar con todo tipo de suciedad.
La primera de ellas es la Roborock F25 BX Gen 2, una aspiradora que ofrece una potencia de succión de 20.000 Pa con una presión constante de 20 N sobre el suelo y un rodillo que gira a 450 rpm. La marca afirma que su nuevo modelo puede eliminar el 99,99% de las bacterias en superficies y cuenta con certificación TÜV SÜD para demostrarlo.
En términos de diseño, la Roborock F25 BX Gen 2 cuenta con tecnología FlatReach 2.0 que le permite reclinarse hasta 180°. El cuerpo cuenta con un centro de gravedad bajo y giro de hasta 70º para maniobrar alrededor de los muebles, mientras que la altura de 12 cm te permitirá meterla bajo la cama o el sofá sin perder la potencia de succión. También se incluyen ruedas optimizadas para facilitar el desplazamiento y superar umbrales o juntas del suelo.
Pasando a la limpieza, la F25 BX Gen incorpora un sistema JawScrapers que combina rascadores de presión constante con cuchillas en forma de diente de tiburón. El sistema antienredos está diseñado para atrapar cabellos y evitar bloqueos. También se incluye tecnología DirTect, que monitoriza la suciedad en tiempo real y ajusta la succión y el caudal de agua, mientras que la base lava el rodillo con agua y aire caliente a 90 ºC, dejándolo completamente seco.
Roborock F25 LT Gen 2
El segundo dispositivo que presentó Roborock es una aspiradora que debuta con muchas de las funciones de su hermano mayor. La F25 LT Gen 2 comparte la succión de 20.000 Pa, el rodillo de 450 rpm y el diseño reclinable FlatReach 2.0, que le permite llegar a 180° para limpiar bajo muebles con altura de hasta 13 cm.
Su sistema JawScrapers monta un peine de 141 dientes de 3 mm, inclinados a 30°, junto a un rascador recto flotante que presiona el rodillo de forma constante. Al igual que vemos en la F25 BX Gen 2, este modelo cuenta con certificación de SGS, que le atribuye una tasa de enredos del 0% y una eliminación del pelo del 100%. El depósito de agua limpia se encuentra en la parte inferior, lo que baja el centro de gravedad, aligera el manejo y genera hasta 20 N de presión descendente.
Otras novedades incluyen tecnología Full-Link, que extiende el secado al conducto de aire para reducir la humedad y el riesgo de que se forme moho. También se integra un sistema EasyClean, el cual separa residuos sólidos y líquidos, facilitando el mantenimiento.
Ambos modelos montan una batería de 4.000 mAh que permite limpiar hasta 480 m² con una sola carga y pesan 8,2 kg.
Precio y disponibilidad de las nuevas aspiradoras de Roborock
- La Roborock F25 BX Gen 2 ya está disponible en España con un precio de venta recomendado de 399 euros. Si la compras antes del 1 de noviembre, puedes obtener una oferta y pagar solo 249 euros a través de la web de Roborock y Amazon.
- La Roborock F25 LT Gen 2 también está disponible en España y es ligeramente más barata. El precio sugerido es de 349 euros, pero existe una promoción de lanzamiento y solo tendrás que pagar 219 euros si la consigues en la web de Roborock y Amazon.

articles.title: AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models
articles.text:
AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models
Most startups fail. A new industry is giving their data an afterlife in AI.
When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup this year, he didn’t think its data was worth much: the users were anonymous, the company just a few years old. But he’s since turned the firm’s digital archives into real money. He’s netted roughly $25,000 for his code base and a still-pending amount (likely around $15,000) for the workspace data in Google, Notion, Figma, and Slack. “At least all that stuff we were doing for two and a half years is worth something to someone somewhere,” he says.
The sale was brokered by a company called SimpleClosure, part of a new growth sector in tech: businesses catering to dying startups. Estimates from Carta and AngelList show shutdowns rising between 26% and 56% annually in recent years, and an end-of-life ecosystem—including coaches, “death doulas,” and firms that help handle the legal, tax, and operational headaches of going belly-up—has emerged. Now tech undertakers are selling the data remains to AI labs.
SimpleClosure added data sales to its services in April. Its Asset Hub platform helps founders sell their code and workspace data—emails, chats, documents. Buyers include foundation AI labs, vendors that construct simulated workspaces for AI training, and mature tech companies building their own models. Asset Hub has handled over 150 deals and expects to return over $10 million to startups by the end of 2026. CEO Dori Yona has seen these transactions, once rare and “somewhat taboo,” become increasingly routine, with 47% of SimpleClosure deals now including code or data sales.
And it’s got company. Industry rival Sunset also has a rapidly growing data resale business. Founder and CEO Brendan Mahony says Sunset values a dying client’s assets by head count, years in operation, volume of data, and how the team used its tools. Particle board, he says, is a good analogy: “This operational exhaust data is like the wood shavings that everyone thought had no value, but it actually has a ton.”
Demand for defunct companies’ data emerged suddenly last year, as AI training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets. Surge AI, for example, buys data to build “reinforcement-learning gyms” where clients’ AI agents practice tasks—think debugging a complex IT architecture or drafting appellate briefs. Nick Heiner, who leads the company’s work on these environments, says he seeks data archives reflecting a range of situations, from disagreements to tricky judgment calls. Heiner explains that one company’s Slack history, if it captures conversations with variety and depth, can be worth more than another’s Slack, email, and calendars combined.
Real archives avoid common errors in synthetic worlds, such as references to dates that don’t exist, but the extent of performance gains remains unclear. No company has yet released tests comparing results of real-world data training with the alternatives. Pricing reflects this uncertainty: Buyers quote wildly different numbers, Heiner says, because valuations are based on “research theses” estimating how many useful tasks come from, say, 100,000 lines of code.
That hasn’t stopped bigger deals from happening. This past August, as part of Spirit Airlines’ bankruptcy, Google outbid the AI data company Mercor to buy the carrier’s decades of data, including 100 million emails, 500 million Teams messages, and 176,000 employee records. The price tag: $10 million. And Bloomberg reported in September that SpaceX’s AI unit is weighing buying data from struggling startups.
Legally, this all could get iffy. Spirit’s flight attendants’ union objected to the sale on privacy grounds, and Greg Ewing, an attorney who advises AI startups, has called such data “legally radioactive.” Suppliers employ data scientists to scrub personally identifiable information and exclude HR records, and buyers say they scrub too. But Ewing points out some of the private details that lurk in emails and calendars: doctor appointments, school pickup arrangements, date-night plans. He describes a “Wild West of AI training” that is only starting to give way to proper licensing agreements and vetted use.
There’s also the question of who profits from these windfalls. The proceeds typically flow to senior creditors and investors—not employees. To Ifeoma Ajunwa, a law professor at Emory University and author of The Quantified Worker, this represents a form of “captured capital.” Legal precedent allows for monitoring to help workers do their jobs, but once a firm is out of business, that justification vanishes. “Employers should have express consent before selling workers’ data,” says Ajunwa, but she adds that there’s no federal law banning such sales.
While many see this new market as a chance for failing businesses to recover some value, these wind-down sales also have limitations. Founders have little to no visibility into who is buying the data and what they plan to do with it. Plus, there’s little assurance they’re getting a fair offer. Data prices will likely stabilize in the coming year, though, unless an AI bubble pops first. Either way, tech’s new undertakers will be there to appraise what’s left.
Matthew King is a technology and environmental journalist based in Baltimore.

articles.title: It looks like Apple Music is getting a new icon
articles.text:
Apple Music’s iconic red app icon has reportedly been replaced with a black-and-white version in the latest iOS 27.2 beta, 9to5Mac reports. The eighth note on the icon also appears to have a slightly sharper angle than the original. A new Apple Music logo was also spotted last month on the Apple Music Hall website, so the company could be refreshing its app icon to match.
It looks like Apple Music is getting a new icon
Apple Music might be going monochrome.
Apple Music might be going monochrome.
According to 9to5Mac, the new icon is a black music note on a white background in light mode, or the opposite in dark mode. The icon’s not the only thing that’s been drained of color, either — 9to5Mac also says Apple Music widgets now have black backgrounds and the app now uses a splash of blue in the tab bar to show the active tab.

articles.title: Apple unveils HomeView - a new smart hub powered by Siri AI and Apple Intelligence - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Apple has unveiled a brand-new product – HomeView – a smart speaker with a 7-inch Liquid Retina display that can meet all your entertainment, connection and smart home needs in one place.
HomeView can do everything from controlling devices and monitoring your home to playing music and making FaceTime calls.
There are two versions of HomeView – one which can be placed on a tabletop and the other that can be wall mounted to fit in any space.
It will be priced at $449 and will go on sale on November 13.
HomeView comes in four colours- silver, starlight, rose pink, and space grey – and includes a matching cable.
The wall-mounted HomeView is available in space grey and silver and has the same 7-inch Liquid Retina display and features, along with rich audio. It can be fixed to a wall using three purpose-built mounts.
HomeView uses the same Face ID security as the iPhone and can recognise up to six different users and is able to access their personal content in Messages, FaceTime, Calendar, Reminders and Find My.
Each person recognised has a personalised home screen with apps and widgets and their content is kept private from others.
And when paired with an Apple Intelligence compatible device, HomeView can also access a user’s personal context, including their calendar, messages, and other relevant information across apps, to provide more personalised and helpful responses.
HomeView allows users to have a conversation with Siri AI and continue that conversation, if necessary, through a private iCloud sync across a user’s other devices, like iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, or Apple Vision Pro.
“Apple HomeView is designed to be shared by everyone in the home yet feel completely personal to each user,” said Greg Joswiak, Apple’s senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing.
“It recognises your face to shift from a household screen to your own experience, fills the room with incredible sound, keeps you connected to the people who matter most with FaceTime, and makes it easy to control your smart home.
“And it’s powered by Apple Intelligence with Siri AI at its core, drawing on personal context from your iPhone to help you find what you need and get more done, all while keeping everyone’s information private and secure.”
HomeView has an aluminium design with a 7-inch Liquid Retina display connected to a domed speaker base with a stainless steel hinge.
This offers a smooth tilt to view comfortably on tabletops of any height like kitchen counters, desks, nightstands and side tables.
The onboard display is adaptive with True Tone able to adjust brightness automatically depending on the light conditions.
Automatic brightness can adjust from 500 nits, which is bright enough to read in a sunlit room, all the way down to 0.3 nits so it’s ideal for a bedside table.
At the heart of HomeView is Siri AI, powered by Apple Intelligence and advanced Apple silicon.
Siri AI is more powerful and conversational, with personal context understanding and on-screen awareness.
Users can personalise HomeView to display information convenient to them.
The HomeView syncs with an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad so it can take action across apps and provide relevant information from messages and calendars.
The Photos face can also bring memories to life with portrait-style depth effects to create a blurred background while keeping the subject sharp.
Users can select a shared album and turn HomeView into a stunning photo frame.
The Flow face can respond to your physical presence and movement and turn the screen into a piece of interactive art and other animations that reflect the time of day, the weather, and the latest sporting events.
On the audio side there are two custom full-range drivers in the display for crisp clean sound, including room-filling spatial audio.
A separate down-firing woofer and two noise-cancelling passive radiators are also built into the base.
The unit is powered by Apple silicon and real-time sensors and offers advanced computational audio to optimise loudness and bass response.
The wall-mounted version also delivers rich sound with two custom drivers and computational audio tuned for on-wall placement.
HomeView allows users to enjoy Apple Music, along with animated art and lyrics on the screen, along with Apple Podcasts, Apple News, Apple TV, and other compatible third-party audio and video apps.
Handoff allows users to continue listening to a song or a podcast they were playing in the car or on a walk by placing their iPhone in front of the HomeView display.
HomeView also makes it easy to connect through FaceTime with CenterStage keeping everyone framed perfectly and centred even if they move around the room.
The intercom feature lets users send a message to a single room or to the whole house via other HomeView and HomePod speakers, along with other personal devices like iPhone, iPad, or Apple Watch.
HomeView is particularly handy in the kitchen and can be your sous chef to convert recipes found on the internet into step-by-step instructions, as well as providing hands-free timer control and help with ingredient tracking.
The new HomeView can also act as a smart home dashboard and view camera feeds, adjust lights, lock doors, and close blinds.
The Home Modular Face provides access to favourite accessories while the Home Camera Face can stream up to nine video feeds at once to keep an eye on the doorstep when you’re waiting for an important delivery or check on your pets in the backyard.
With a supported iCloud Plus subscription HomeView we’ll work with compatible cameras to provide other features like end-to-end encrypted recognition of people, pets, packages, and vehicles.
HomeKit Secure also provides AI descriptions of what happened in a video clip so you don’t even need to watch it.
HomeView will also work with Apple’s Home Collection, which is a new range of smart home cameras, thermostats, and locks designed in partnership with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric.
Apple’s HomeView is available to pre-order now with a price of $449 for the desktop and wall-mounted version. It will go on sale on November 13.

articles.title: Avec ses 7 places et une recharge en 9 minutes, ce SUV chinois bouscule les constructeurs européens
articles.text:
BYD s’attaque aux grands SUV électriques avec un Atto 8 capable d’accueillir sept personnes et de tenir jusqu’à 653 km sans passer à la station. Sa recharge ultrarapide pourrait surtout faire la différence sur les longs trajets, à condition de disposer des bornes capables d’en profiter.
Le Peugeot E-5008 tient un nouveau concurrent sérieux. Dévoilé ce 12 octobre au Mondial de l’Auto de Paris, le BYD Atto 8 est un SUV électrique à sept places qui promet jusqu’à 653 km d’autonomie WLTP. Ce nouveau modèle haut de gamme entend répondre à une préoccupation concrète des familles qui passent à l’électrique, celle de partir chargées sans transformer chaque départ en vacances en expédition.
Une recharge express, à condition de trouver la bonne borne
Les 653 km annoncés concernent la version à propulsion. La déclinaison à transmission intégrale, forte de 775 chevaux, affiche pour sa part 602 km, avec la même batterie de 115 kWh. Ces chiffres restent évidemment ceux du cycle WLTP. Sur autoroute, avec sept personnes à bord, leurs bagages et le chauffage ou la climatisation, l’autonomie réelle sera sensiblement inférieure.
La nouveauté la plus intéressante se joue à la borne. Grâce à sa batterie Blade de deuxième génération et à la technologie Flash Charging, l’Atto 8 pourrait en effet passer de 10 à 70% de niveau de charge en cinq minutes seulement, puis atteindre 97% après neuf minutes de charge totale. De quoi réduire sensiblement l’attente dans les stations-service pendant les grands déplacements.
Sur le papier, l’attente commence à se rapprocher d’une pause classique sur une aire d’autoroute. Encore faut-il trouver une borne capable de délivrer une telle puissance. Le constructeur prévoit d’installer 3 000 bornes Flash Charging en Europe d’ici à la fin 2027, et leur déploiement sera déterminant pour transformer cette promesse en avantage réel.
Sept passagers, mais des bagages à répartir
Avec 5,04 mètres de long, l’Atto 8 joue clairement dans la catégorie des grands SUV. Les sept occupants disposent de trois rangées de sièges, mais il faudra composer avec seulement 270 litres de coffre lorsqu’elles sont toutes utilisées.
Un compartiment de 136 litres sous le capot apporte un peu d’air, tandis que le volume grimpe jusqu’à 1 960 litres une fois les deux rangées arrière rabattues.
BYD soigne également le confort. Les sièges avant et les places extérieures du deuxième rang disposent de fonctions de chauffage, de ventilation et de massage. L’écran central de 15,6 pouces (39,6 cm de diagonale) intègre notamment Google Maps et le Play Store.
Peugeot et les Européens ont encore des arguments
En France, le Peugeot E-5008 Grande Autonomie, assemblé dans l’Hexagone, propose déjà une autonomie voisine de 670 km WLTP. Le nouveau venu ne prend donc pas une avance décisive sur ce terrain. L’écart entre les promesses de recharge est beaucoup plus marqué, puisque Peugeot annonce 27 minutes pour passer de 20 à 80% sur sa version de 97 kWh.
Le marché européen commence par ailleurs à se peupler de grands modèles familiaux électriques. Le Škoda Peaq revendique lui aussi sept places et plus de 640 km d’autonomie, tandis que Renault continue de répondre à cette clientèle avec un Espace hybride.
L’Atto 8 doit arriver au premier trimestre 2027, mais son tarif français reste inconnu. C’est probablement lui qui décidera si BYD tient un nouveau poids lourd du marché ou une impressionnante vitrine technologique. Si sa recharge tient ses promesses, les passagers pourraient en tout cas finir par réclamer une pause bien avant que la voiture doive recharger.

articles.title: Docker Hub flaw let attackers impersonate users, tamper with images
articles.text:
Docker has disclosed a critical vulnerability (CVE-2026-105445) in Docker Hub that let attackers access another user’s container repositories using a personal access token (PAT).
Docker Hub is an online registry for storing, sharing, and downloading container images - templates that package everything needed for an application to run in an isolated environment.
In Docker Hub, a PAT serves as a secret used to authenticate tools and workflows. It allows you to pull, push, or delete container images.
According to a security bulletin from the Docker team, an attacker could create an account and PAT, then convert the account into an organization and name a target user as its owner.
The CVE-2026-105445 flaw stems from Docker Hub reassigning a personal access token (PAT) to a designated organization owner without changing its secret or obtaining the target's consent. This allowed the attacker to use the token to authenticate as the target.
Depending on the token’s scope and the target’s permissions, attackers could pull, push, or delete images in the target’s repositories and accessible organizations.
“Within the scope of the token, a re-assigned PAT acted as the target user at the registry level, meaning an attacker could potentially pull, push, and/or delete images in the target’s repositories and in organizations where the target had access,” Docker explained.
“Because that includes publishing images under a legitimate name, we treated this as a software supply chain risk and rated it critical.”
Although the flaw is critical, Docker noted that it did not provide Docker Hub web access or allow attackers to change passwords, email addresses, or two-factor settings, potentially locking legitimate account holders out.
The vulnerability was introduced on August 26, 2024, when the conversion started reassigning the personal account PAT to the new owner. This occurred without revoking or rotating the secret, and without asking the named owner to confirm the change.
On September 30, 2026, Docker received a vulnerability report describing the issue, confirmed it, and deployed a fix to production less than four hours later.
Docker says it found no evidence of exploitation after examining 304,000 pushes made with transferred tokens and analyzing high-risk public images.
Affected users and organization owners were notified on October 2, and transferred PATs were deactivated on October 8, except for those whose owners explicitly requested to retain them.
Docker says users who didn’t receive a notification should assume they were not impacted and did not need to take any action.
The platform no longer transfers PATs during conversion and requests user consent before naming them an organization owner.
Build your security blueprint for AI-powered attacks
Join Mikko Hyppönen and security leaders from the NFL, CHANEL, and Atlassian for a two-hour digital summit on what AI-speed attacks change, what defenders should stop doing, and how to validate, decide, fix, and re-validate at machine speed.

articles.title: Gemini 4 Argon passe un cap : déploiement mondial et bonne surprise pour les abonnés Pro — Frandroid
articles.text:
Le 30 septembre, Google présentait Gemini 4 Argon, son nouveau modèle d’IA haut de gamme. Par contre, il ne disait pas quand on pourrait s’en servir. Seules des équipes de cybersécurité triées sur le volet (membres du Fairwind Program) y avaient accès.
Ce mardi 13 octobre, Google déploie Argon à l’échelle mondiale pour les développeurs, les entreprises et les abonnés payants de Google AI. Pour nous, utilisateurs, le modèle arrive dans l’application Gemini et dans le Mode IA du moteur de recherche Google.
    À lire aussi : 
Gemini : notre guide pour tout comprendre l’IA de Google
Qui peut utiliser Argon, et à quel prix ?
Côté particuliers, Argon est réservé aux abonnés Google AI Pro et Ultra. La version gratuite de Gemini et l’offre AI Plus, à 4,99 euros par mois, n’y ont pas accès. En France, Google facture AI Pro 21,99 euros par mois et AI Ultra à partir de 99,99 euros. Fin septembre, Google ne citait que les abonnés Ultra parmi les premiers servis. C’est donc une bonne surprise pour les abonnés Pro.
Pour coder avec Antigravity, en revanche, il faut passer à l’abonnement Ultra. Google Antigravity est la plateforme de développement de Google où des agents IA écrivent et testent le code. Elle ne propose Argon qu’aux abonnés Ultra. Les développeurs Android peuvent aussi utiliser le modèle dans Android Studio, soit via Antigravity dans la version de test Canary, soit via l’offre payante de l’API Gemini.
Jusqu’à 330€ d’avantages avec nos offres Hello Prime ou Hello Prime Duo, dont 80€ cash à l’ouverture de compte !
Les développeurs qui passent par l’API paient en fonction de leur consommation, comptée en jetons. Un jeton (token) correspond à un morceau de mot. Jusqu’au 30 novembre 2026, Google fait un prix de lancement : 2 dollars par million de jetons envoyés au modèle (environ 1,80 euro HT) et 10 dollars par million de jetons générés (environ 8,90 euros HT). Ensuite, le prix double, à 4 et 20 dollars (environ 3,60 et 17,90 euros HT). Les jetons déjà envoyés et gardés en cache coûtent 95 % moins cher.
Au tarif normal, Argon coûtera autant que Claude Opus 5.5, le modèle haut de gamme d’Anthropic. Il restera moins cher que GPT-6 Astra d’OpenAI, facturé 10 et 50 dollars.
Google ouvre aussi le Fairwind Program à des centaines de nouveaux partenaires. Ils reçoivent une version d’Argon sans les garde-fous qui limitent ses capacités en cybersécurité. Côté recherche, 10 000 scientifiques pourront aussi utiliser gratuitement le niveau d’usage le plus élevé d’Antigravity pendant six mois, sur candidature.
Ce que Google promet avec Argon
Google présente Argon comme un modèle pensé pour les tâches longues et complexes, dans le code, la finance, le droit, la cybersécurité ou la recherche scientifique. Via l’API, il peut générer jusqu’à 1 million de jetons en une seule réponse,. Il peut donc travailler sur de gros projets sans s’interrompre.
Dans l’application Gemini, Google promet des réponses plus directes et avec moins de répétitions. Un bouton permet aussi de passer de la discussion aux tâches, que Gemini peut accomplir même quand on n’est pas devant son ordinateur. L’assistant se connecte désormais à plus de 40 applications, dont Instacart, OpenTable, Adobe et Shopify. Sur Mac, l’application Gemini intègre en plus l’interface de code d’Antigravity.
Pour appuyer ces promesses, Google cite surtout l’usage qu’en font ses propres équipes. Selon l’entreprise, Argon leur a permis de soumettre plus de 35 % de code supplémentaire écrit par des agents IA. Les retours en arrière, c’est-à-dire les modifications qu’il faut annuler parce qu’elles cassent quelque chose, ont baissé de près d’un tiers. L’équipe de Chrome s’en est aussi servie pour réorganiser un dossier d’environ 6 millions de lignes de code, sur les 40 millions que compte Chromium, la base de code de Chrome. Le travail a pris quelques semaines au lieu de plusieurs mois.
Google met aussi en avant la robotique dans un billet destiné aux développeurs. Argon y obtient 87 % à ERQA, un test qui mesure la capacité d’un modèle à résoudre des problèmes physiques dans un environnement en 3D. Lors d’un essai interne, Argon a regardé la vidéo d’une personne qui jouait au cornhole (un jeu où l’on lance des sacs sur une planche percée). Il a ensuite écrit le code de simulation qui a permis à Apollo, le robot humanoïde d’Apptronik, de réussir sept lancers d’affilée.
Sur les benchmarks, Google met en avant la première place d’Argon au Vals Index. Ce classement de la société Vals AI évalue les modèles sur des tâches de finance, de code, de droit et de fiscalité. Argon y obtient bien 68,9 %, contre 67 % pour Claude Opus 5.5. Restons prudents sur ce point, car le cabinet indépendant Artificial Analysis le classait huitième au général début octobre, cinq points derrière Claude Opus 5.5.
Les abonnés Pro et Ultra peuvent choisir Argon dans l’application Gemini à partir de ce mardi. Les développeurs, eux, ont jusqu’au 30 novembre pour profiter du prix de lancement de l’API.

articles.title: Filtration en sept étapes et rayon d’action de 12 m : l’Electrolux Pure C9 est à 184,99 €
articles.text:
L’aspirateur sans sac Electrolux Pure C9 PC91-4MG est à 184,99 €
L’Electrolux Pure C9 PC91-4MG associe une filtration en sept étapes, un bac sans sac et un rayon d’action de 12 m pour nettoyer les différentes pièces de la maison.
Amazon propose l’Electrolux Pure C9 PC91-4MG gris à 184,99 €, contre un prix conseillé de 249,99 €. L’écart atteint 65 €, soit 26 %. Par rapport au prix le plus bas des 30 derniers jours de 232,71 €, la baisse représente 47,72 €, soit environ 21 %. L’aspirateur est vendu et expédié par Amazon.
Un aspirateur sans sac avec une filtration en sept étapes
Le Pure C9 utilise une technologie cyclonique pour séparer la poussière de l’air aspiré. Son système PureFlow repose sur un circuit étanche, associé à une brosse PowerFlow destinée aux différents types de sols. La poussière est recueillie dans un bac à vider, ce qui évite l’achat régulier de sacs.
La filtration comprend sept étapes, dont un filtre multicouche 3D lavable. Electrolux prévoit un point d’accès commun aux filtres pour faciliter leur entretien. Ce fonctionnement demande néanmoins de vider le bac et de nettoyer les éléments lavables conformément à la notice pour conserver de bonnes conditions d’aspiration.
Un rayon d’action de 12 m et de grandes roues
Cet aspirateur traîneau filaire offre un rayon d’action de 12 m, une caractéristique utile pour couvrir une pièce ou un couloir sans changer trop souvent de prise. Ses grandes roues souples accompagnent les déplacements, tandis que le tube télescopique permet d’adapter la longueur à la position de nettoyage.
La poignée du flexible possède un variateur de flux d’air. L’appareil dispose également d’un enrouleur automatique du câble et de positions de rangement horizontale et verticale. Electrolux annonce un niveau sonore de 72 dB. Le Pure C9 convient ainsi aux utilisateurs qui recherchent un traîneau sans sac pour des séances de nettoyage prolongées, avec une alimentation sur secteur qui dispense de gérer la recharge d’une batterie.

articles.title: Recharge en 5 minutes et 653 km d’autonomie : le BYD Atto 8 arrive officiellement en France
articles.text:
La recharge en 5 minutes devient réalité en France avec BYD qui commercialise chez nous son premier modèle équipé de la technologie Flash Charging. Remplaçant pressenti du vieillissant Tang, l’Atto 8 est encore plus imposant en pointant à 5,04 mètres de long. Il devient ainsi le nouveau porte-drapeau de la marque en Europe. En plus d’être ultra rapide à recharger, le chinois propose dans son portefeuille des technologies de premier plan.
En version de base Design propulsion avec 462 ch et 365 Nm de couple, sa grande batterie de 115 kWh lui permet ainsi de proposer une autonomie de 653 km sur le cycle WLTP. Même si cela ne constitue aucun record, c’est de bon goût pour tenir correctement la distance. Pour faire fondre le chrono, on se rabattra plutôt sur la version Excellence intégrale avec deux électromoteurs produisant en cumulé 775 ch et 775 Nm de couple.
1 500 kW de puissance : la recharge la plus rapide chez BYD arrive en France
Suffisant pour effacer le 0 à 100 km/h en 4,6 secondes. L’autonomie est quant à elle réduite à 602 km, rançon d’un appétit supérieur. Dans les deux cas, le Flash Charging casse la barque avec une puissance de recharge pouvant atteindre les 1 500 kW en courant continu DC. De quoi passer de 10 à 70 % de batterie en 5 minutes et de 10 à 97 % en seulement 9 minutes. Et pour information, 12 minutes seront nécessaires pour faire le 20 à 97 % par -30°C.
Impressionnant, car en France, cette technologie était jusqu’alors réservée à l’exclusive Denza Z9GT. Le seul hic est de trouver une borne compatible : BYD prévoit l’installation de 3 000 points de charge en Europe d’ici fin 2027. Patience car il n’y en a encore aucun en France. Il faudra donc se rabattre en attendant sur des bornes 600 kW qui suffiront déjà à écourter l’attente par rapport aux rivaux.
Un habitacle 7 places digne d’un salon avec réfrigérateur intégré
À bord, c’est l’espace qui prime pour les 7 passagers. Et la qualité, aussi : la marque évoque « des matériaux doux au toucher, notamment du cuir suédé, sur les principales surfaces ». Côté numérique, c’est plutôt classique avec une instrumentation de 10,25 pouces secondée par un affichage tête haute de 26 pouces. Un écran central de 15,6 pouces intégrant les services Google est aussi de la partie.
Les sièges avant et latéraux du second rang sont chauffants, massants et ventilés. La climatisation trizone arrive en série sur toutes les versions. Ajoutons que sur les modèles Design RWD et Excellence AWD se drapent de cuir véritable. L’engin inclut aussi une sonorisation à 21 haut-parleurs et un réfrigérateur avant. Les prix du BYD Atto 8 n’ont pas encore été communiqués.
