articles.title: Digitaler Ausweis auf dem Smartphone: Was Banken an d-you kritisieren
articles.text:
Digitaler Ausweis auf dem Smartphone: Was Banken an der d-you-Wallet kritisieren
Die staatliche Wallet „d-you“ soll im Januar 2027 starten. Nutzer können sich damit per Smartphone ausweisen, amtliche Dokumente speichern und elektronisch unterschreiben.
Grundlage dafür ist die EU-Verordnung eIDAS 2.0, die jeden Mitgliedstaat verpflichtet, seinen Bürgern eine solche Wallet anzubieten. Die Bundesregierung plant dazu entsprechende Regeln im Digitale Identitätengesetz (DIdG), über den Gesetzentwurf stimmt der Bundestag voraussichtlich am Donnerstag ab.
Die Deutsche Kreditwirtschaft (DK), als Interessenvertretung der Banken und Sparkassen, fordert nun Nachschärfungen im Gesetz. Zwar begrüßen die Banken, dass Kunden sich künftig per Wallet geldwäscherechtlich identifizieren können, wenn sie ein Konto eröffnen. Die Institute fordern jedoch, klar festzulegen, dass es ausreicht, die vom Wallet–Verfahren bereitgestellten Daten zu speichern, also dass eine Ausweiskopie weder erforderlich noch technisch umsetzbar ist. Ohne diese Präzisierung könnten Banken sonst vorsichtshalber zusätzliche Nachweise verlangen, wodurch der Vorteil einer schnellen, papierlosen Kontoeröffnung verloren gehen könnte.
Außerdem müsse das Gesetz klarer regeln, wann Banken eine fremde Wallet akzeptieren müssen, wer bei technischen Fehlern haftet und welche Daten ihnen zur Betrugsabwehr zur Verfügung stehen.
Authentifizierung und Autorisierung
Den Banken geht es dabei unter anderem um die Trennung von Authentifizierung (als Sicherheitsabfrage) und Autorisierung, also die Freigabe von Zahlungen.
Grundsätzlich sind sie offen dafür, die Wallet beim Onlinebanking und beim Bezahlen als Sicherheitsabfrage zu akzeptieren, ähnlich wie heute eine TAN-App, allerdings nur dort, wo eine solche Prüfung ohnehin vorgeschrieben ist. Die Banken befürchten, das Gesetz könne sie zur Akzeptanz verpflichten, ohne dass sie die nötigen technischen Nachweise und eine eindeutige Haftungsregelung bekommen. Die DK fordert deshalb eine Klarstellung im Gesetz.
Keine Annahmepflicht
Grundsätzlich unterstützt die Bank die Idee, die Wallet auch für Zahlungen nutzbar zu machen. Eine Verpflichtung der Banken, Zahlungen direkt über die Wallet anzubieten, lehnen sie aber ab.
Jedes Institut soll selbst entscheiden dürfen, mit welchem Verfahren Kunden ihre Zahlungen freigeben. Auch eine pauschale Annahmepflicht im stationären Zahlungsverkehr sehen die Banken kritisch. Kartenzahlungen, Girocard und Bargeldabhebungen dürften nicht durch die Hintertür an die Wallet gekoppelt werden. Bestehende Systeme umzubauen, wäre aus Sicht der Banken technisch, rechtlich und wirtschaftlich sehr aufwendig.
Kunden sollen ihre Bankkarte künftig in die Wallet laden können, ähnlich wie heute bei Apple Pay oder Google Pay. Ob eine Bank das anbietet, soll aber ebenfalls ihre freie Entscheidung bleiben. Die DK wünscht sich auch hier eine eindeutige Formulierung im Gesetz. Außerdem soll eine Einbindung nur mit einem Vertrag zwischen Wallet-Anbieter und Bank zulässig sein.
Neben der staatlichen Wallet können auch Unternehmen künftig eigene Wallets anbieten. Laut Entwurf entscheidet darüber aber das Digitalministerium, und zwar mit der Möglichkeit, seine Entscheidung später zu ändern. Für Investoren ergebe sich daraus Planungs- und Investitionsrisiken, warnen die Banken. Sie fordern daher, private Wallets direkt im Gesetz zu erlauben, bestehende Angebote zu schützen und einen klaren Zeitplan festzulegen.
Streitpunkt Haftung
Eine weitere offene Frage berührt die Haftung in Betrugsfällen oder bei technischen Pannen. Zahlungsdienstleister wollen nicht für Fehler einer Wallet haften, die sie nicht selbst bereitgestellt haben oder kontrollieren können.
Die Banken fordern deshalb: Wird eine Wallet zur starken Kundenauthentifizierung genutzt, soll der Wallet-Anbieter nachweisen müssen, dass die Authentifizierung ordnungsgemäß lief, korrekt protokolliert wurde und nicht durch einen Fehler der Wallet beeinträchtigt war.
Außerdem wollen die Banken ein gesetzliches Recht auf die Informationen, die sie zur Prüfung von Erstattungs-, Haftungs- und Betrugsfällen benötigen. Dazu zählen standardisierte Protokolle, Transaktionsdaten, Angaben zum Wallet-Anbieter und Risikosignale. Bei bekannten Sicherheitslücken oder Zertifizierungsproblemen wollen sie außerdem das Recht haben, eine Wallet abzulehnen oder vorübergehend sperren zu dürfen.
Bedenken zur EUID-Wallet hatten zuletzt auch Sachverständige in einer Anhörung des Digitalausschuss angemeldet. Anfang Oktober bemängelten Daten- und Verbraucherschützer etwa, dass sich die Wallet zum Start nicht pseudonym nutzen lässt. Anbieter könnten mehr Daten abfragen als nötig und aus den Daten Profile bilden.
Die IT-Sicherheitsforscherin Jiska Classen von der Universität Potsdam kritisierte, große Teile der Sicherheitsarchitektur seien noch nicht öffentlich und nicht bewertet. Smartphones blieben ein hohes Risiko, weil viele Geräte keine Sicherheitsupdates mehr erhielten. Über ein kompromittiertes Handy könnten sich unbefugte Nutzer im Namen eines anderen ausweisen, Hotels buchen oder Kredite aufnehmen. Auch sie forderte daher eine eindeutige Haftungsregelung im Gesetz.

articles.title: Votre téléviseur pourrait bientôt héberger une IA malveillante, et ce n'est pas de la science-fiction
articles.text:
Et si votre téléviseur ou votre aspirateur robot hébergeait demain une intelligence artificielle malveillante, à votre insu ? Des chercheurs d’Anthropic viennent de démontrer que ce scénario, encore largement théorique, pourrait devenir réalité plus rapidement que prévu.
On savait déjà que les objets connectés pouvaient être piratés et transformés en relais pour des cyberattaques. Mais avec les progrès de l’intelligence artificielle, une nouvelle menace commence à prendre forme : des logiciels malveillants capables de réfléchir, de s’adapter et surtout de se reproduire sans intervention humaine. Dans une étude publiée le 12 octobre, Anthropic s’est intéressé à ces nouveaux vers informatiques, avec quelques résultats pour le moins inquiétants. Et pour mener leurs expériences, les chercheurs n’ont pas eu besoin de serveurs surpuissants. De simples boîtiers Android TV à quelques dizaines de dollars ont suffi.
Quinze boîtiers Android TV pour faire tourner une intelligence artificielle
Les chercheurs d’Anthropic ont réussi à exécuter Gemma4-26B-A4B, un modèle d’intelligence artificielle de 26 milliards de paramètres, sur quinze boîtiers Android TV vendus environ 55 dollars pièce.
Pour y parvenir, ils ont réparti les calculs entre les différents appareils, chacun exécutant une petite partie du modèle. Le résultat n’a rien de spectaculaire en matière de performances, avec seulement 0,39 token généré par seconde. Mais l’essentiel est ailleurs : une IA relativement complexe peut fonctionner sur un ensemble d’équipements grand public, sans dépendre d’un centre de données.
Les équipes de recherche ont ensuite évalué la capacité de plusieurs modèles à installer leur propre environnement d’exécution sur des machines inconnues. Un modèle de neuf milliards de paramètres y est parvenu sur huit des neuf catégories de matériel testées.
Plus inquiétant encore : des modèles plus puissants ont réussi à enchaîner les différentes étapes d’une propagation autonome, depuis la recherche d'une nouvelle machine jusqu’à l’installation d'une copie. Ces expériences ont toutefois été réalisées dans des environnements simplifiés, notamment avec des accès volontairement peu sécurisés. Anthropic n'a donc pas créé un ver capable d’infecter spontanément des appareils domestiques.
Des boîtiers TV aux autres objets connectés, une menace encore théorique
Le scénario n’est pourtant pas totalement fantaisiste. Les chercheurs évoquent notamment les réfrigérateurs, les fours connectés et les aspirateurs robots, dont certains disposent désormais de processeurs suffisamment puissants pour contribuer à l’exécution d’une IA.
Attention cependant à ne pas confondre puissance de calcul et vulnérabilité. Un appareil équipé d'une puce dédiée à l’intelligence artificielle n'est pas automatiquement capable d’héberger un modèle de langage, encore moins de se laisser infecter.
Les objets connectés constituent néanmoins des cibles intéressantes pour les pirates. Le botnet Kimwolf a déjà compromis près de deux millions d’appareils, principalement des boîtiers Android TV, pour mener des cyberattaques. La menace existe donc, même sans intelligence artificielle.
Anthropic estime que de petits modèles pourraient acquérir les capacités nécessaires à leur propre réplication d’ici la fin de l’année 2026. C’est une projection, pas une certitude. Les chercheurs reconnaissent d’ailleurs que ces vers pourraient mettre plusieurs jours à se reproduire, ce qui laisserait du temps aux systèmes de sécurité pour les détecter.
Il y a un autre risque, plus sournois. Contrairement aux malwares traditionnels, ces IA pourraient apprendre à s’adapter à de nouveaux appareils et poursuivre leur propagation sans serveur central à neutraliser. De quoi compliquer sérieusement la tâche des spécialistes en cybersécurité. Pour l’instant, nos aspirateurs robots se contentent encore de traquer les miettes sous le canapé. Espérons qu’ils ne se mettront pas demain à chercher de nouvelles machines à infecter.

articles.title: Webs que se caen y bots desactivados: la consecuencia inesperada de bombardear centros de datos
articles.text:
Webs que se caen y bots desactivados: la consecuencia inesperada de bombardear centros de datos
Los ejércitos de Ucrania, Rusia e Irán han lanzado varias oleadas de ataques contra estas infraestructuras, provocando pérdidas milmillonarias y, en algunos casos, la eliminación definitiva de datos
Ucrania ha asestado un importante golpe a la infraestructura digital rusa. Los drones ucranios han lanzado desde el pasado jueves una serie de ataques que han destrozado tres grandes centros de datos de Yandex, conocido como “el Google del Kremlin”, a las afueras de Moscú. La aplicación de transporte de viajeros Yandex Taxi y el servicio de pagos del grupo, Yandex Pay, han dejado de funcionar temporalmente. El presidente ucranio, Volodímir Zelenski, incluso aseguró que los bombardeos desactivaron bots rusos.
No es la primera vez que un ejército regular ataca centros de datos. Moscú lleva haciéndolo desde marzo, según ha denunciado Kiev en varias ocasiones. Y, antes que Rusia, lo ha hecho Irán. El pasado 28 de febrero, tras ser blanco de los bombardeos de EE UU e Israel que iniciaron la guerra, Teherán destruyó con drones tres centros de datos comerciales de Amazon Web Services (AWS) en Emiratos Árabes Unidos y Bahréin, lo que causó problemas en el funcionamiento de los servicios en la nube de la región y afectó a los sistemas de pago en el Golfo Pérsico. El ataque tuvo un efecto cascada que se dejó notar en varias zonas de disponibilidad de AWS, incluyendo distintos países de América y la costa este de EE UU.
El hecho de que Rusia y Ucrania estén destruyéndose mutuamente estas infraestructuras, y de que Irán decidiera atacar esas instalaciones nada más arrancar el conflicto bélico (se habla también de bombardeos en Emiratos Árabes Unidos y Arabia Saudí), muestra que los centros de datos están en la mirilla.
“Los centros de datos son objetivos secundarios, justo después de los sitios militares evidentes”, dijo a Forbes Matt McCrann, antiguo ejecutivo de la empresa de defensa contra drones DroneShield, con experiencia en Estados Unidos y Oriente Medio. También ilustra otra cuestión, en el caso de Irán: en la era moderna, ni siquiera una distancia de 11.000 kilómetros es garantía de impunidad. “Los ataques demostraron que la distancia física de un escenario de conflicto ya no es garantía de no recibir los impactos de la guerra”, asegura Tomáš Foltýn, analista de ESET.
El bombardeo iraní de los tres centros de datos de AWS no solo provocó interrupciones de servicios en Oriente Medio y otras partes del mundo, como EE UU, donde servicios como Snowflake, Claude (de Anthropic) o algunas aplicaciones financieras funcionaron con dificultad. Los drones también destruyeron para siempre parte de los datos que se almacenaban en esas instalaciones, algo que no está claro que haya sucedido en el caso de los centros de datos rusos. El ataque sirvió de recordatorio de que la llamada computación en la nube es solo una metáfora: lejos de ser etérea, consta de infraestructuras físicas. Si estas fallan, se puede perder todo.
Un nuevo objetivo militar
Los centros de datos son las tripas de la nube: instalaciones parecidas a naves industriales de última generación repletas de racks de servidores (una especie de ordenadores altos como armarios). En esos procesadores se ejecutan programas en remoto, como los servicios de streaming, y se almacenan datos, como los archivos que se guardan online. Eso es fundamental para el funcionamiento de los servicios online, desde el correo electrónico hasta un editor de textos o una aplicación de banca: si los centros de datos no guardaran archivos y ejecutaran programas en remoto, estos deberían alojarse físicamente en los dispositivos. Sería imposible que los móviles hicieran tantas cosas; deberíamos llevar encima discos duros portátiles.
Además de ejecutar programas y alojar datos, los centros de datos han sumado en los últimos tiempos una tercera función: entrenar y ejecutar modelos de inteligencia artificial (IA), lo que requiere equipar el centro de datos con microprocesadores mucho más potentes (y que consumen más energía). De ahí que el académico Eliezer Yudkowsky, preocupado por que los sistemas de IA puedan rebelarse contra la humanidad, haya sugerido la opción “destruir con un ataque aéreo los centros de datos” de los países que no limiten la potencia de cálculo de estos programas.
Al ser instalaciones intensivas en alta tecnología, que además necesitan un suministro ininterrumpido de energía, los centros de datos son de las infraestructuras más caras que hay. Y eso los convierte en un objetivo atractivo. “Atacarlos tiene mucho sentido desde el punto de vista militar iraní. Son inversiones milmillonarias que surgen de la visita de Trump al principio de su mandato y que van asociadas a otros negocios personales de Trump y su familia en la región”, señala el coronel Ángel Gómez de Ágreda, autor de Un mundo falaz. El nuevo orden global en la era de los algoritmos y la manipulación (Planeta).
Gómez de Ágreda coincide en que los centros de datos están ya entre los objetivos militares. “Se puede argumentar, además, que los centros de datos son objetivos legítimos (no civiles), ya que proporcionan apoyo a operaciones militares”, añade.
Eliminación definitiva de datos
Cualquier empresa puede contratar con alguna operadora de servicios en la nube espacio en sus servidores para guardar datos. AWS es el líder del mercado mundial, con una cuota del 28%, seguido de Azure, de Microsoft (21%), y de Google Cloud (14%), según datos de Synergy Research Group. Normalmente, las compañías optan por centros de datos lo más cercanos posible al mercado en el que operan para reducir la latencia (el tiempo que tarda un conjunto de datos en ir y volver desde un dispositivo hasta un servidor). Una de las claves del éxito de la expansión de Netflix, por ejemplo, fue establecer acuerdos de larga duración con la propia AWS, lo que le permitió servirse de su infraestructura mundial, de modo que el streaming funcionaba razonablemente bien en prácticamente cualquier país.
Tanto AWS como sus competidores suelen construir los centros de datos de tres en tres, en lo que llaman zona de disponibilidad: tres instalaciones prácticamente iguales a pocos kilómetros, de manera que si alguno de ellos falla, la actividad siga gracias a los otros dos. Los datos también se replican en esos conjuntos de centros de datos por si pasa algo.
Pero una cosa es que falle el suministro energético o se interrumpa el funcionamiento de una instalación por avería, y otra muy distinta es que se destruyan los tres a la vez con misiles. Eso es lo que ha hecho Irán en los últimos seis meses con varias oleadas de ataques, y lo que acaba de hacer ahora Ucrania en Rusia.
¿Hay forma de blindarse contra la posible pérdida de datos? Fuentes de AWS aseguran que su recomendación es que las cargas críticas de datos (las que podrían interrumpir la operativa de la empresa, como aerolíneas o banca) sean siempre replicadas. Se puede hacer en otros centros de datos dentro del mismo país o en otros países. Por supuesto, el coste de hacerlo es superior a no tener copias. “La decisión última es del cliente”, dicen esas fuentes.
Desde que empezaron los bombardeos de Irán, AWS conminó a sus clientes a migrar sus datos a otras regiones. La mayoría lo ha hecho, dicen desde la compañía, y han podido restablecer sus operaciones en otras regiones a partir de copias de seguridad. Pero quienes tenían sus datos allí de forma exclusiva los han perdido. Tras trabajar todo el verano en ello, la tecnológica informó el pasado 15 de septiembre de que era imposible recuperar parte de los datos.
No ha trascendido qué empresas se encuentran entre las damnificadas. Sí se sabe que las que han perdido datos son empresas de Oriente Medio. Y, como los pagos se interrumpieron, se cree que los afectados son bancos y entidades de medios de pago. Irán dijo haber impactado también a empresas israelíes, aunque eso no se confirmó. AWS ha mantenido en secreto el nombre de los clientes afectados.

articles.title: Aunque lo niegue en público, Estados Unidos tiene un problema con su dependencia de China para fabricar chips
articles.text:
La industria de los semiconductores de EEUU no es independiente. Actualmente no lo es la de ningún país. Las empresas estadounidenses que se dedican a la fabricación de circuitos integrados, como Intel, GlobalFoundries o Texas Instruments, entre otras, se gastan unos 27.000 millones de dólares al año en equipos de fotolitografía, máquinas de procesamiento de obleas y materiales avanzados.
Los productos de la empresa neerlandesa ASML y las japonesas Tokyo Electron o JSR Corporation son algunos de los más demandados por los fabricantes de chips de todo el planeta. También por los de EEUU. De hecho, el 95% del dinero que las compañías estadounidenses dedican a la compra de los productos y las materias primas que necesitan va a parar a Europa, Japón, y también a sus propios proveedores en EEUU, como Applied Materials, Lam Research o KLA Corporation.
No obstante, hay un matiz que merece la pena que no pasemos por alto: el 95% del que acabamos de hablar se reduce al 68% si nos ceñimos a la procedencia real de esos productos o materias primas, y no a la nacionalidad de la empresa que los produce. Como hemos visto, ASML es de Países Bajos, pero también produce algunas de sus máquinas en Alemania, EEUU y Taiwán. Applied Materials es de EEUU, pero también fabrica en Singapur y Taiwán. Y KLA Corporation produce, además de en su país de origen, en Singapur y China.
UN VISTAZO A...
La presencia de China aumenta si rastreamos los equipos de una forma minuciosa
Si solo contemplamos la sede de los proveedores de equipos para fabricar semiconductores, China únicamente representa alrededor del 1% del suministro directo de máquinas y materiales avanzados para la industria estadounidense. Sin embargo, si en vez de mirar solo hacia la sede rastreamos el lugar de fabricación de esos productos, la participación del país liderado por Xi Jinping se incrementa hasta el 5%. Y si ampliamos el espectro a todo el sudeste asiático esa cifra se incrementa hasta el 10%.
Si nos ceñimos a las máquinas involucradas en la producción de circuitos integrados, EEUU apenas depende de China. Depende, sobre todo, de Países Bajos, Alemania, Japón y Taiwán, así como de sus propios proveedores nacionales. Sin embargo, para fabricar chips no hacen falta solo máquinas; también son necesarias materias primas. Algunas de ellas son escasas, y con frecuencia su mayor productor es China. Este es el auténtico punto débil de la industria de los semiconductores estadounidense.
En 2025 China produjo alrededor de 270.000 toneladas de tierras raras frente a unas 390.000 toneladas extraídas a escala mundial
En 2025 China produjo alrededor de 270.000 toneladas de tierras raras frente a unas 390.000 toneladas extraídas a escala mundial. Estas cifras las ha recabado el Servicio Geológico de EEUU, por lo que presumiblemente son fiables, y ponen encima de la mesa una realidad inapelable: actualmente el país liderado por Xi Jinping produce alrededor del 69% de las tierras raras extraídas en todo el mundo.
Esta cifra intimida, no cabe duda, pero hay otra todavía más impactante: China también domina la industria del procesado al que es necesario someter las tierras raras para que puedan ser utilizadas. Tanto es así que su cuota, si nos ceñimos a la industria global de procesado, asciende al 90%. Con una producción de aproximadamente el 70% del mercado global y un control del 90% de la industria de procesado de las tierras raras, este país asiático tiene la sartén bien agarrada por el mango. Por mucho que lo lamenten EEUU y sus aliados.
De hecho, durante los últimos tres años China ha utilizado su dominio sobre las tierras raras como una herramienta de presión sobre sus rivales. La industria de los semiconductores no solo de EEUU, sino también de Taiwán, Corea del Sur y Japón es vulnerable. Y reducir su dependencia de China exige mucho más que trasladar algunas fábricas. EEUU en particular se enfrenta a un problema estructural que le obliga a reconstruir casi por completo su cadena de suministro, especialmente la de las tierras raras y otros minerales estratégicos sin los que su industria de los chips difícilmente podría sostenerse.

articles.title: Circle Gas has $67 million in carbon credits awaiting delivery
articles.text:
Circle Gas, the UK parent of Kenyan pay-as-you-cook liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) supplier M-Gas, reported $67 million in contracted carbon credits awaiting delivery and $57 million in cash prepayments in 2025, according to its financial statements.
The company’s dependence on carbon-credit revenue exposes the financial risks facing Kenya’s clean-cooking businesses, where government authorisation can determine whether contracted credits deliver their expected value.
The company’s accounts, filed in September, show the financial stakes. Circle Gas lost $39.3 million in 2025, held $1.1 million in cash at year-end and reported net liabilities of $156.7 million. It needs about $28 million in new funding to finance its growth plans.
Carbon credits are central to the economics of clean cooking businesses such as M-Gas. The company supplies LPG in small, affordable amounts with smart meters so households can pay as they cook. Revenue from the resulting emissions reductions can help support that model. Koko Networks, another Kenyan clean-cooking company, entered administration after the government declined to authorise the carbon-credit sales on which its business depended.
Circle Gas’s annual report says it received a “Letter of Acceptance” confirming that its carbon-credit projects met eligibility criteria and could proceed to apply for a “Letter of Authorisation.”
M-Gas announced in January 2026 that its clean-cooking carbon project had received a Letter of Approval. The report does not clarify whether this is the same document it calls a Letter of Acceptance.
Kenya’s carbon-market rules distinguish project approval from authorisation to transfer credits internationally. Under the relevant framework, the final authorisation requires government approval and determines whether specified emissions reductions can be transferred abroad.
Circle Gas did not respond to a request for comment.
The value of carbon credits
Circle Gas reported $67 million in contracted carbon credits yet to be delivered as of the end of 2025, and $57 million in cash already received as prepayments against carbon-credit contracts. The first figure represents credits awaiting delivery, while the second is money buyers have already paid.
The accounts do not disclose how much of the contracted portfolio depends on the outstanding authorisation or how much of the prepayments remains available.
Circle Gas says authorised credits can command significantly higher prices than credits sold in advance. It has not disclosed the expected premium. The company also excludes the higher value from its financial projections, leaving the potential upside outside its current funding assumptions.
Circle Gas grew revenue to $40.8 million in 2025 from $36.1 million, but remained loss-making, with a $39.3 million loss after tax. Its cash reserves fell to $1.1 million, while net liabilities climbed to $156.7 million from $116.5 million.
The company says it needs about $28 million to fund its 2026 growth plans. Without additional funding, it expects to limit investment and remain stagnant.
“At the date of approval of these financial statements, the additional third-party funding of approximately US$28.0m necessary to finance continued growth funding for the base case in 2026 is yet to be fully secured, and there is no certainty that funding will be available to the Group (Circle Gas),” the statement said.
The losses and funding needs cannot be attributed solely to the outstanding authorisation. But the delay leaves a potentially more lucrative source of carbon revenue uncertain as Circle Gas seeks new capital.
Koko’s carbon debt
Koko Networks built a business selling subsidised bioethanol stoves and fuel to low-income households, relying on carbon-credit sales to cover part of its operating costs. When the Kenyan government declined to authorise those sales, the company lost access to a revenue stream it needed to sustain the business.
Koko shut down in January 2026, laying off more than 700 employees. Its Kenyan and UK entities entered administration in February. The administrators now face the task of recovering money owed to creditors, with the carbon credits held by its UK arm a central asset. Without a sale, FirstRand Bank is owed $60 million, while other unsecured creditors are owed about $171 million.
Koko’s collapse shows how a clean-cooking business can accumulate substantial debts when it cannot sell the carbon credits expected to fund its operations.
The government rejected Koko’s application in early February 2026, with Trade Cabinet Secretary Lee Kinyanjui saying the volume of credits sought could have exhausted Kenya’s allocation for international transfers, leaving other projects in agriculture and manufacturing with little room to sell their credits abroad.
Unlike Koko Networks, Circle Gas has not had its authorisation request rejected. M-Gas announced that its project had received a Letter of Approval. However, Circle Gas’s accounts indicate it is still seeking a Letter of Authorisation and do not disclose how much of its contracted carbon credits depends on it.
Koko is the clearest warning of what is at stake: carbon credits may be recorded as assets, contracted to buyers and used to secure financing, but they cannot generate the expected cash if the company cannot sell them.
Kenya’s carbon-credit rules give the government control over which emissions reductions can be sold abroad, leaving companies exposed to decisions that can affect their revenues and debts.
Circle Gas secured earlier approval for its project but is still seeking authorisation, leaving the value and delivery of some contracted credits uncertain.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. articles.title: Mercado de criptomonedas: cuál es el valor de ethereum
articles.text:
Ether, comúnmente llamada como ethereum, es la moneda digital #2 en cuanto a términos de capitalización de mercado, por lo que se trata de una de las divisas digitales que más despierta el interés entre los mineros (creadores de las criptodivisas).
Ethereum es una plataforma de blockchain de código abierto que se ejecuta con el uso de su moneda nativa, llamada ether o ETH, por lo que a pesar de que la gente usa estos nombres como sinónimos son cosas distintas.
Ether es un token que se utiliza específicamente en la blockchain ethereum para pagar transacciones. Este token es responsable de impulsar casi todo lo que ocurre en la red, misma que puede ser usada por cualquier persona para crear y ejecutar contratos inteligentes, que son programas de software que se ejecutan de manera autónoma y sin la intervención del usuario.
De acuerdo con el portal de Binance, la moneda digital solana actualmente cuenta con 122.1M de unidades creadas.
La cotización de ethereum para este día a las 14:05 horas (UTC) es de 2505.76 dólares, es decir, que la criptomoneda tuvo un cambio de -0.95 % en el último día.
Por otro lado, registró un cambio de 0.0 % con respecto a su valor hace una hora. En cuanto a su popularidad, se ubica en la posición #2.
Valor de la criptomoneda Ethereum
Ethereum 2.0: las claves
Tras varios meses de retraso y con el temor de que ya nunca pasaría, finalmente el 15 de septiembre de 2022 Ethereum llevó a cabo su tan ansiada fusión o actualización al nuevo nivel 2.0 con la promesa de mejorar la experiencia de los usuarios de esta criptomoneda.
“The Merge”, inglés para “La Fusión”, es una transformación en la forma en que Ethereum procesa las transacciones y en cómo se crean nuevos tokens de Ether.
Esta fusión se trata de la combinación de la cadena de bloques de Ethereum con una nueva cadena de bloques separada conocido como proof-of-stake, el cual reduce el consumo de energía de la cadena de bloques de Ethereum en un 99,9 %, según sus propios desarrolladores, lo que la vuelve más “amigable” con el ambiente al tiempo que las transacciones serían más baratas.
Sus defensores creen que la fusión hará que Ethereum resulte favorecido con respecto al máximo rival, Bitcoin, pues podría aumentar su uso.
En el proceso Proof Stake los propietarios de Ether bloquearán cantidades establecidas de sus criptomonedas para verificar nuevos registros en la cadena de bloques, ganando nuevas monedas además de su criptografía “participada”.

articles.title: Building agents that transact with Anchor Browser and AgentCore payments | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Building agents that transact with Anchor Browser and AgentCore payments
AI agents increasingly need to access web resources that are priced per request. For example, premium datasets charge by the query, research APIs meter by the call, and paywalled publishers gate content behind payment. When an AI agent encounters one of these resources, the server returns HTTP 402 Payment Required. The agent has no built-in payment mechanism, no budget attached to the session, and no programmatic way to satisfy the request. The task stalls and requires manual intervention.
Anchor Browser with Agentic Payments handles machine-to-machine payment workflows on behalf of the agent. Developed in collaboration with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center Partner Agent Factory, it’s now available on AWS Marketplace. This post covers how Anchor Browser integrates with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments so that AI agents can pay for x402-protected pages and APIs autonomously. The x402 protocol is an open standard for HTTP-based machine-to-machine payments. A server responds with 402 Payment Required along with the amount, accepted payment methods, and payment address that the agent uses to complete the transaction.
Anchor Browser is a cloud-based browser automation solution purpose-built for AI agents. Each agent session runs inside a managed browser environment that maintains authentication state, handles navigation, captures network requests, and provides a live view of page interactions.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides capabilities to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments is a fully managed capability within AgentCore that AI agents can use to discover, access, and pay for APIs, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and web content autonomously. AgentCore payments manages wallet connectivity, enforces configurable spending limits at the infrastructure layer, and processes payments through the x402 protocol. It also provides observability into payment attempts, approvals, denials, and settlements through Amazon CloudWatch.
When an agent running in Anchor Browser encounters a 402 response, AgentCore payments authorizes and completes the transaction within the configured budget. The workflow continues without interruption.
Challenges
When an autonomous agent encounters an x402-protected resource, the workflow stalls. The agent makes a request, such as fetching a premium research report or calling a paid data enrichment API, and the server responds with HTTP 402 Payment Required. Without a mechanism to pay, the task that was supposed to run autonomously now requires human intervention.
Today, developers must build the entire payment stack. This effort spans four categories of complexity:
Payment protocol handling
- Detecting and parsing the 402 challenge from the HTTP response, and distinguishing payment-required responses from other 4xx errors.
- Constructing the correct payment header with the cryptographic proof in the exact format the merchant expects.
- Supporting multiple payment schemes (exact, upto, and protocol variants) without hardcoding vendor-specific logic into the agent.
- Maintaining compatibility across x402 merchant implementations that might vary in challenge format, supported stablecoins, or settlement timing.
Security and key management
- Storing a private key to sign payments, requiring secure key storage within an environment exposed to untrusted inputs.
- Managing wallet lifecycle operations, including key rotation, credential refresh, and provider failover.
Operational resilience
- Resubmitting the original request with the payment header while preserving session state, cookies, and request context.
- Providing idempotency, which is essential for wallet operations.
- Enforcing per-session and per-transaction spend limits with real-time budget tracking across concurrent agent executions.
Observability and compliance
- Capturing every payment attempt, approval, denial, and settlement in audit logs for compliance and reconciliation.
Without a managed payment service, the agent must internalize the entire payment stack. On every x402-protected call that returns a 402 response, the agent must orchestrate the full payment flow internally, including:
- Signing the proof.
- Attaching the correct header.
- Retrying the request.
- Settling the transaction.
- Logging the result.
Each of these steps requires custom code that developers must build, secure, and maintain. Figure 1 illustrates this architecture. The agent contains eight tightly coupled components (Wallet, Private Keys, Budget Controls, Sign Proof, Attach Header, Retry Logic, Settle Payment, and Logging). The agent connects to an x402 API with a 402 challenge flowing back and a retry flowing forward.
The security considerations extend beyond the engineering effort.
Uncontrolled spending. Without hard spending limits enforced at the infrastructure level, a bug, retry loop, prompt injection, or inadvertent access can trigger unintended payments. An agent retrying a paid endpoint in a loop continues to authorize payments until manual intervention occurs.
Key exposure. When private keys reside inside the agent runtime, they share an execution environment with untrusted web pages, third-party tools, and external dependencies. These vectors might inadvertently disclose the credentials that control real funds.
Signing flow exposure. If the signing infrastructure is accessible from the runtime, a threat actor can attempt to access the key or redirect payments to an address under unauthorized control. Effective mitigation requires that the key doesn’t enter the runtime in the first place.
Browser-based agents introduce an additional constraint: the payment must occur within the same browser session. Otherwise, session recordings and live view no longer match what actually executed.
Solution
Anchor Browser and AgentCore payments address this complexity by moving the entire payment stack into managed infrastructure.
Unlike a stateless tool call, Anchor Browser provides a real cloud browser with persistent identity, repeatable and deterministic workflows, and the session context needed to log in, navigate, and finish tasks reliably. Authentication, navigation, network requests, recordings, and live view happen inside the same browser session. When a payment is required, the transaction happens within that session. The recording captures the full sequence from request to 402 to payment to content delivery. Anchor agents include a built-in x402 tool that handles paid API calls natively within the browser context. The built-in tool requires no changes to existing Playwright, Puppeteer, or Chrome DevTools Protocol-based workflows.
AgentCore payments serves as the payment layer. At the center of the service is the Payment Manager, the top-level resource that coordinates payment operations for the AWS account. Creating a Payment Manager requires specifying an authorizer type and an IAM role. AgentCore then provisions a corresponding workload identity in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity.
The remaining components connect the Payment Manager to external wallet infrastructure:
- A PaymentConnector integrates the Payment Manager with an external wallet provider, either Coinbase Developer Platform (Coinbase CDP) or Stripe Privy.
- A PaymentCredentialProvider stores wallet provider credentials securely in AgentCore Identity.
- A PaymentInstrument identifies the specific wallet address from which funds are drawn.
Anchor Browser sets up wallets through AgentCore payments using a supported wallet provider, without placing wallet secrets or private keys inside the agent runtime. AgentCore payments handles wallet operations through the configured provider. For endpoint discovery, AgentCore provides a curated Coinbase x402 Bazaar MCP server through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, so agents can discover available pay-per-use x402 endpoints programmatically.
AgentCore payments restructures the payment architecture. Sensitive operations move out of the agent runtime and into a managed service layer. The Anchor Agent holds only two payment-related components: a budget session and the x402 tool. The infrastructure, including authentication, wallet secrets, payment limits, observability, and payment proof signing, resides in the AgentCore payments layer. Figure 2 shows the Anchor Agent connecting to the AgentCore payments managed layer, which handles wallet provider integration with Coinbase CDP or Stripe Privy.
How the payment flow works
The following steps describe what happens end to end, from the moment a browser session encounters an x402-protected resource to the moment the agent receives the response and continues the task.
- Anchor Browser creates a dedicated AgentCore PaymentSession for the browser session. When the session starts with x402 turned on, Anchor Browser provisions a PaymentSession through AgentCore payments, linking the browser session to a configured payment instrument and budget.
- The browser receives an HTTP 402 Payment Required response. The agent navigates to a URL or makes a fetch or XMLHttpRequest (XHR) request. The merchant responds with a 402 challenge specifying the amount, accepted payment methods, and payment address.
- The browser selects a compatible payment method. Anchor Browser reads the 402 challenge payload and matches the requested payment method against the instrument linked to the PaymentSession.
- AgentCore verifies the session budget and generates the cryptographic payment proof. AgentCore payments validates that the payment amount falls within the session spending limit. The service then signs the transaction using the configured wallet provider (Coinbase CDP or Stripe Privy) and returns the cryptographic proof. No key material enters the browser or agent runtime.
- The browser retries the original request with the payment header. The browser attaches the signed proof as PAYMENT-SIGNATURE for x402 v2 or X-PAYMENT for x402 v1, then retries the original request exactly once.
- The merchant verifies and settles the payment, then returns the protected resource. The merchant validates the cryptographic proof, settles the transaction on-chain, and serves the content. The agent continues the task.
Wallet credentials remain with AgentCore and the configured wallet provider throughout this flow.
Prerequisites
Before you begin, make sure that you have a valid Anchor Browser API key (ANCHOR_API_KEY). To create one, see the Anchor Browser Quick Start guide.
Setting up automatic x402 payments
Setting up agentic payments for Anchor Browser requires one session property. Set session.x402 to true. The property defaults to false. When enabled, the browser session can automatically access x402-protected websites with payments signed by AgentCore payments and retried inside the same browser session. Enabling session.x402 authorizes the browser to make real payments from the configured payment instrument.
The following examples show how to create a payment-enabled session for Anchor Browser using cURL and JavaScript:
cURL
JavaScript
After connected through Chrome DevTools Protocol, the agent navigates normally. You don’t need to include a wallet key or payment header in your automation code. The browser handles 402 challenges, payment signing, and retries transparently for document navigation, fetch, and XHR requests.
Payment session limits and behavior
Anchor Browser enforces the following guardrails at the session level through AgentCore payments integration. Each payment-ready browser session operates within configured spending and time constraints. For specific limits, refer to the Anchor Browser technical documentation.
If the merchant response is malformed, no compatible network is offered, the budget is exhausted, or AgentCore payments rejects the payment, the browser returns the original 402 response to the page unchanged. Your automation code can then handle the 402 as a standard HTTP error.
The x402 session property controls payments to third-party resources only. The property doesn’t replace Anchor credits and doesn’t pay for the browser session.
Automation code for Anchor Browser
Your automation code for Anchor Browser remains unchanged. The following example demonstrates that no payment-specific code is required:
No wallet logic, no payment header construction, and no retry code. The agent navigates to the URL. If the server returns 402, Anchor Browser coordinates with AgentCore payments to sign the payment proof, retries the request with the appropriate payment header, and delivers the content to the page. Your automation code receives the final rendered page with no indication that a payment occurred.
This pattern applies uniformly to paywalled journalism, licensed financial data, gated API documentation, metered research databases, and other resources that gate content behind a 402 challenge.
Using the built-in x402 tool for API calls
Paid resources aren’t limited to web pages. Many are APIs that expect POST, PUT, or other HTTP methods. Common examples include data enrichment services, premium inference endpoints, and licensed content APIs. For these use cases, Anchor Browser agents include a built-in x402 tool that you call like a standard HTTPS API within the browser context.
Your agent makes the API call through fetch or XHR. If the server returns a 402 challenge, the browser coordinates payment signing through AgentCore payments and retries the request with the signed payment header. Your code receives the response as though the endpoint were free. The tool isn’t tied to a specific vendor, model, or framework. Payment operates as a session-level capability beneath your existing tooling, and no changes to agent code are required.
Your automation code doesn’t receive wallet credentials. Automatic payments are available only when session.x402 is set to true and remain subject to the spending and expiration limits described in the previous section.
Key benefits
This integration moves payment from application code to the infrastructure layer:
No payment infrastructure to build. No wallet SDK to integrate, no 402 response parser to write, no retry loop to implement, no header construction logic to maintain, and no custom audit logging to build. AgentCore payments manages the entire payment stack.
No changes to existing tooling. Playwright scripts, Puppeteer automations, Chrome DevTools Protocol commands, and agent flows in Anchor Browser continue to function exactly as before. Payment is a session capability attached to the browser, not a modification to agent logic, prompts, or tool definitions.
Private keys don’t enter the runtime. Signing and settlement happen inside AgentCore payments. The service communicates with Coinbase CDP or Stripe Privy through secure credential storage in AgentCore Identity. The agent runtime doesn’t have access to key material that can move funds.
Budgets are enforced at the infrastructure level. Every session operates within defined spend limits that AgentCore enforces before authorizing a payment. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability provides full payment audit trails through Amazon CloudWatch. When a session reaches the spending limit, AgentCore payments denies the payment.
Paid tasks complete successfully. Paid GET pages load. Paid API calls return responses. The agent completes the workflow rather than stopping at a 402 response and requiring manual intervention.
Billing is consolidated. Anchor Browser settles third-party x402 charges in credits on the same invoice as browser session time. There’s no separate crypto custody to manage, no USDC balance to monitor, and no on-chain settlement for the finance team to reconcile.
Conclusion
Anchor Browser, integrated with AgentCore payments, equips AI agents to handle x402 payment challenges autonomously for paywalled web pages and paid API endpoints. Wallet credentials stay out of agent code, and no custom payment infrastructure is required.
As more of the web moves to per-request pricing, agents that lack a payment mechanism can’t complete tasks involving paid resources. This integration addresses that gap: agents complete paid workflows end to end, operating within defined budgets, with full observability through AgentCore Observability, and without cryptographic key material in the runtime.
To get started, explore the following resources:
- Automatic x402 payments in Anchor Browser
- AgentCore payments developer guide
- AgentCore payments with browser integration
- Anchor Browser on AWS Marketplace

articles.title: AWS Reworks EventBridge Custom Buses for Enterprise-Scale Event-Driven Architectures
articles.text:
AWS has introduced an enhanced Custom Event Bus for Amazon EventBridge, targeting a problem that often emerges when event-driven architectures move beyond a single team or AWS account: the event infrastructure itself becomes fragmented. The new model allows organisations to create a single event bus shared across multiple AWS accounts, while adding native event ordering, retention and replay, content-based deduplication, simplified subscriptions and a new pricing model.
The change addresses an architectural tension in enterprise AWS environments. Organisations commonly use multiple accounts to provide isolation between teams and applications, but this can lead to EventBridge buses being connected through cross-account rules and forwarding configurations. As the number of consumers grows, the resulting topology becomes harder to govern and understand, while forwarding the same event through multiple buses can introduce additional processing and routing costs. AWS's new model instead positions a central bus as an organisational event backbone, with individual teams managing their own subscriptions.
The enhanced Custom Event Bus can be shared across AWS accounts using AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM). A platform team can therefore establish a central event bus while allowing application teams to publish and subscribe from their own accounts. AWS says the new bus supports up to 10,000 subscribers by default, with the option to request a higher quota.
This changes the governance model as much as the technical one. Rather than a platform team configuring every cross-account connection, it can establish the boundaries around the central bus while individual application teams manage their own subscriptions, filtering, targets, retries, and failure destinations. That creates a separation between platform-level governance and application-level event consumption, potentially reducing the amount of infrastructure work required to onboard another consumer.
AWS also introduces synchronous invocation for targets such as AWS Lambda. This can remove a pattern where teams place Amazon SQS between EventBridge and Lambda primarily to provide stronger processing acknowledgement. The result is a bus that can support both conventional asynchronous event consumption and workloads where ordering and processing confirmation are important.
The new Subscriber resource is another important change to the EventBridge model. Previously, consumers were typically represented through combinations of rules, targets, and retry configurations. The Subscriber resource brings filtering, target configuration, retries, and dead-letter destinations together into a single consumer definition. It also supports variable start times, which can be used when onboarding a new consumer or replaying historical events.
The bus itself also becomes more useful as a durable event backbone. Events can be retained for a configurable period of between one and 365 days, allowing consumers to start from an earlier point in the event history or recover after application failures. AWS also supports JSONata transformations and can deserialize Avro and Protocol Buffers payloads into JSON for filtering and routing.
The enhanced bus adds content-based deduplication, allowing EventBridge to identify retries of the same event based on its payload. AWS says matching events received within a five-minute window can be collapsed, providing exactly-once semantics for that specific deduplication scenario. This does not remove the need for application-level idempotency, particularly where events are replayed or processed across regions.
AWS has also changed the pricing model. Rather than allowing costs to compound with every cross-account and bus-to-bus forwarding hop, the enhanced bus uses an ingress and egress throughput model, with publishers paying for events ingested and subscribers paying for events delivered. This more closely aligns cost with the amount of event data entering and being consumed from the central bus rather than the number of intermediate routing steps in the architecture.
The enhanced EventBridge model moves into territory traditionally associated with enterprise event brokers and streaming platforms such as Apache Kafka, but the two technologies still address somewhat different architectural needs. Kafka is fundamentally a distributed event-streaming platform built around durable logs, partitions, and consumer groups, giving engineering teams extensive control over high-throughput streaming workloads and consumption semantics. EventBridge remains a managed, serverless event-routing service, with AWS handling the underlying infrastructure while providing filtering, routing, retention, transformations, and integration with AWS targets. The new capabilities therefore make EventBridge more capable as an enterprise event backbone, but they do not turn it into a direct replacement for Kafka in every streaming architecture.
Importantly, AWS is not replacing the existing EventBridge model immediately. Existing custom buses continue operating unchanged and are now labelled Custom event bus-classic, while the enhanced bus is introduced as a separate resource. Organisations can therefore adopt the new architecture incrementally rather than having to redesign existing event-driven applications as part of the launch.
The enhanced Custom Event Bus is initially available across selected AWS Regions in North America, Europe and Asia Pacific, and can be created through the AWS Management Console, CLI or EventBridge APIs.

articles.title: XWorm RAT Evolves Into Surveillance Platform
articles.text:
The XWorm RAT developers have expanded the malware’s capabilities with fresh plugins that turn it into a surveillance platform, cybersecurity firm Netskope reports.
A sophisticated, multi-functional Windows RAT first observed in 2022, XWorm provides attackers with full control over the infected systems, offering keylogging, screenshot capture, webcam access, and payload execution capabilities.
The malware’s developers have been constantly updating its codebase and adding new functionality, and the threat has remained highly active, with Netskope observing over 1,200 incidents across 100 organizations during the third quarter of the year.
Alongside new variants, the developers have also increased the number of plugins XWorm supports, from 35 in July 2025 to 46 in October 2026.
Some of these have been clearly designed for surveillance: enabling location tracking, live audio streaming, webcam capture, and interactive control over authenticated browser sessions.
“The Maps plugin provides victims’ GPS location without a user prompt. The Microphone plugin streams live audio from the victim’s device. HBrowser hijacks authenticated browser sessions without touching credentials, bypassing MFA entirely. Webcam capture is also available on demand,” Netskope says.
According to the cybersecurity company, the activity surrounding XWorm has increased since a cracked version of its builder was released publicly in June 2025, and the source code for RAT’s 6.4 version was leaked in August 2025.
With the addition of the HBrowser plugin, the RAT moves beyond harvesting credentials and user data from browsers: it provides the operator with a real-time view of the browser and can relay attacker inputs to the browser.
Operator’s interactions are encoded as command-and-control (C&C) commands, transmitted over the standard XWorm AES-encrypted communication channel, and executed on the victim’s system.
“The victim machine receives them and executes the corresponding input on the active browser window. The operator receives a continuous stream of screenshots. From the operator’s perspective, it is a full remote browser session. Every authenticated tab is accessible, bypassing the need for logging in and dealing with MFA,” the company explains.
The Maps and Microphone plugins allow operators to monitor the victim’s location and to capture audio without privilege escalation and without a user warning.
“XWorm continues to evolve and has now added surveillance capabilities. Since its builder and source code were leaked, we expect continued upgrades and use of this toolkit,” Netskope notes.

articles.title: Some AI researchers are taking up smoking because they believe artificial intelligence will cure cancer
articles.text:
WTF?! The promise that AI is going to cure cancer has failed to materialize, but some AI researchers are so sure it'll happen one day that they've taken up smoking. That's according to Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar, who says this comically bad idea is a sort of flex to show others how much faith they have in the technology.
Sankar made his claim during an interview on CBS's Face the Nation on Sunday. The exec talked about Pascal's quote of how there is a God-shaped vacuum, or hole, in the heart of every person, and how many AI workers in Silicon Valley had filled that hole with the machine god that is AI (or AGI, as he calls it).
As an example of this unwavering faith in their Warhammer 40,000-like machine god, Sankar claims that many AI researchers have started smoking as a way of signaling to other researchers how much they believe in AI.
"'I believe so much in AI that it's going to cure cancer. So I will – I'm showing you my chips are all in.' So there is kind of this mass psychosis social delusion around it," the Palantir executive said.
Assuming this is true, and it very well may be, given some people's fetishism of AI, it's very stupid and a bit sad. Even if AI did help scientists develop effective treatments for some cancers, smoking can cause several different types of the disease.
Moreover, there's the time it takes to test these treatments in clinical trials, and let's not forget the numerous other non-cancerous but still potentially fatal conditions smoking can cause. So maybe think twice before deeply inhaling those tar-filled toxins into your spongy lungs.
Despite being filled with health-obsessed types like Bryan Johnson, there have been several recent articles about how smoking is making a comeback in certain tech circles, so maybe some of what Sankar says is true. Or perhaps in these uncertain times we live in, the smokers think there might not be a future to worry about – ironically, a big part of that is driven by the threat from rogue AI.
While not on the level of curing cancer, an AI-generated drug was reported last month to have shown signs of a different breakthrough: slowing the aging process. There were some caveats, of course, the big one being that changes in aging markers don't prove we'll soon be living to 150 or older.

articles.title: One of Spain’s largest recent FinTech deals sees ID Finance secure €545 million to scale Plazo | EU-Startups
articles.text:
ID Finance, a Barcelona-based FinTech group, has announced €545 million of debt and equity funding to support further growth for their flagship consumer finance app; Plazo.
This funding saw participation from Spice Expeditions, WashU, Kingsway Capital and global investment firm i80 Group, who provided asset-based financing. EU-Startups previously covered ID Finance in October 2019, when the Barcelona-based group secured over €1.7 million through crowdfunding.
Alexander Dunaev, co-founder of ID Finance says: “This investment is a strong vote of confidence in Plazo and in the model we’ve built to modernise consumer credit in Spain. Plazo tripled its portfolio in 2025 and reached profitability, proving that responsible, AI-driven underwriting and a genuinely better product experience can scale together.
“This new capital from some of the most reputable global investors in FinTech lets us build on that foundation, expand Plazo’s product suite and keep pushing on innovation, including through Turrón“.
ID Finance’s debt and equity financing comes amid wider investment activity in European consumer credit, flexible payments and specialist lending during 2026.
According to EU-Startups’ coverage, London-based Plend secured a credit facility of up to €58.3 million, fellow UK FinTech Vuelo raised €64 million for its travel financing platform, and Manchester-based Firenze secured €6.8 million for investment-backed lending.
In Spain, Madrid-based BCAS raised €30 million in debt financing to expand its flexible education payment solutions. Meanwhile, Paris-based Aria announced €247 million in equity and debt financing capacity for its embedded B2B finance platform.
Together, these five announcements represent approximately €406 million, rising to around €951 million when including ID Finance’s latest transaction.
Tamir Saeed, Managing Partner at Kingsway Capital, adds: “It has been a pleasure to partner with ID Finance over the last few years, supporting their mission to provide access to financial services to all consumers in Spain and Mexico. We are pleased to continue investing in this exciting next phase of ID Finance’s journey, exemplified by the high growth and disruptive potential of new products like Plazo and Turron.”
Founded in 2015, ID Finance provides alternative lending in both Spain and Mexico, specialising in providing innovative financial solutions. Plazo plays a key role in this strategy. Launched in 2021, the app brings together debit and credit solutions on a single platform.
As part of its continued expansion, ID Finance recently launched Turrón by Plazo, a flexible payment solution that enables customers to make online and in-store purchases. Turrón combines an e-money account, debit card and Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL) solution.
The addition of BNPL services marks another step towards in creating Spain’s “go-to” consumer credit platform.
Peter Frank, Managing Director at i80, says: “ID Finance has done a tremendous job of managing risk while growing the portfolio. We’re delighted to deepen our relationship and increase the scale of the asset-based financing that will support Plazo’s next phase of growth as it continues to modernise consumer credit in Europe.”
Today’s transaction is reportedly one of the largest closed by a Spanish FinTech in recent years and comes two years after the €134 million ($150 million) debt financing round provided by i80 Group in early 2024, that was utilised to grow Plazo’s credit portfolio.
In 2025, the Group reported €243 million in revenue, while profit nearly doubled in the same period. Plazo achieved bottom line profitability in 2025 as its revenue grew 300% YoY, growing client base to over 400,000 users.
Together with additional financing, Plazo is expected to grow another 300% in 2026, supported by AI-powered technology infrastructure.

articles.title: They war-gamed dimming the Sun. It went even worse than you think.
articles.text:
When it comes to deciding the fate of the planet, Colleen Golja always thought science and reason would have a seat at the table. That was until one morning last September in London, when the climate researcher took part in the first in a series of war games. The goal: to prevent an uncontrolled global race to develop a technology aimed at cooling the planet but that comes with vast, unknown risks that could reshape life on Earth.
“I thought that would be such an easy thing. Like, we can all agree to do ethical research and make sure it’s for the better of all humans,” she told WIRED. “And boy, was I wrong.”
The simulation, titled Exploring Geopolitical Tipping Points and Climate Cooling Strategies, saw a couple dozen foreign-relations experts, scientists, military personnel, and former government officials from across the world convene in a meeting room at Queen Mary University of London. After making introductions over coffee and little yogurts, they sat at tables arranged in a square with the name of the country or organization each person was playing: national governments, climate NGOs and nonprofits, indigenous groups, and tech companies. Golja was assigned to provide technical advice to help participants make scientifically literate decisions.
The point of the game was to stress-test the world’s response to a group of prospective technologies known collectively as solar radiation modification. These technologies promise to reverse global warming by reflecting away a portion of the sunlight reaching Earth, for example by spraying particles of sulphur dioxide or some other manufactured substance into the atmosphere. The cooling effect of this kind of solar geoengineering is widely accepted. It would mimic the well-known impacts of large volcanic eruptions, which temporarily cool the planet by half a degree or more. But the fallout is less certain—and less equal. Some regions will suffer: Models predict drying in sub-Saharan Africa and more intense tropical storms in the Atlantic. The cooling effect would also last only as long as the geoengineering continued; after that the global temperature could shoot back up with wild and hard-to-predict effects.
Until recently, the idea of solar radiation modification was a speculative niche of climate science. That has changed fast. Private firms are exploring solar geoengineering as a commercial opportunity: Last year, a US-Israeli startup called Stardust Solutions raised $60 million, and in May it released details of a suite of new inventions it claims would give humans the ability to dial down the global temperature as desired. In August, Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX might be a candidate for delivering geoengineering interventions, threw his voice behind solar geoengineering, writing on X: “Space satellites to control temperature and massive geo-engineering will be needed or it will be game over.”
The world is going to have to make decisions about how to govern this technology much sooner than most policymakers imagine, Cynthia Scharf, a former UN advisor, told WIRED. “It’s not 15 years from now; it’s in the next decade, easily.”
It was against this backdrop that Danielle Young, an assistant professor in international relations at Leeds University, arranged the war game. Its setting was a hastily convened UN committee charged with coordinating the international response to developments in solar geoengineering. The game unfolded over simulated meetings set at three points in time: the present, September 2027, and September 2028. Each step ratcheted up the stakes, with the game creators introducing new advances in sunlight-reflecting technology. As in real life, no one knew all the facts, and players had to respond to events that were bringing the world closer to a full-scale attempt at deploying solar geoengineering tech, even when they may not have a full picture of what had truly occurred—or what any of the others were up to.
The first session set the tone. Distrust and disinformation dominated. As participants discussed rules governing outdoor experiments in an attempt to agree an international deal, players representing both the US and China told the group they could not sign a deal that constrained their pursuit of research considered to be in their “national interest.” Nor could they accept a deal that would see their superpower rival taking the lead technologically. Speaking to WIRED, Jeffrey Nielsen, a major in the US Army who played the role of a US national security attaché, summarized the position as “worse than no deal at all is any deal that favors China.”
Tensions escalated when the team running the simulation handed the Russian delegates an “intelligence report” indicating they had found a plane near the Bering Strait believed to be involved in a US geoengineering research program. The US team—which was indeed flying research missions—accused Russia of disinformation.
Meanwhile, the US became convinced China was also conducting research and developing its own program. Beijing’s representatives had tried to insert language into a mooted deal that would ensure no retroactive punishment for past experiments. Then, China approached a player representing SpaceX to float the idea of a technology-sharing program. In a private discussion away from the group, the SpaceX player immediately reported the Chinese approach to the US team. The US demanded an international investigation. The finger-pointing continued, and countries abandoned the talks. The Canadian representative called it a “humiliating defeat.”
At the end of the session, Nielsen was pumped. He’d busted China and derailed any prospect of a global deal. In the context of the game, he told WIRED, it was a “humungous victory” for the Americans. But Young, the researcher who designed the scenario, said the Chinese were not, in fact, conducting experiments in the game. Mutual suspicion meant all parties left the room believing the others were moving as quickly as possible to build their own geoengineering capability.
What played out in the first session reflected “the likelihood, in my opinion, of the geoengineering arms race,” says Nielsen, who clarified he was speaking to WIRED in a private capacity and not representing the views of the actual US government. Most experts agree it would take a superpower’s reach to ensure the safe passage of planes needed to deliver payloads of dust to the stratosphere in a geoengineering exercise. But neither the US nor China would lightly cede control over the global thermostat, says Nielsen, and distrust and poor communication are a significant risk: “Any action related to the issue by one actor can be perceived as malintent by the other.”
The threat of falling behind a rival is “a very strong driver of research and development of capability,” a former British diplomat with a background in national security told WIRED. “But that’s not at all the same thing as deployment.” There are similarities with nuclear arms dynamics—though solar radiation management, unlike nukes, has more obvious benefits as well as downsides, many of which are poorly understood. “There is an interdependence here,” says the former diplomat, who was not involved in the game and spoke on condition of anonymity to preserve relationships. “It’s not an inherently zero-sum game.”
Scharf, who represented the US government alongside Nielsen in the game, told WIRED a “scientifically transparent international collaboration” between China and the US “might be the best we can do in terms of fending off a very dangerous competition between the two. But I certainly cannot imagine that happening under the Trump administration.”
Compounding the problem is a lack of information. Geoengineering has historically been viewed with suspicion and often ignored by the scientific mainstream. One researcher told WIRED he’d experienced ostracization and barriers to academic progression owing to his interest in the technology; he no longer works in the field.
This lack of scientific interest greatly frustrated Golja, who spent much of the game watching as a bystander while political posturing dominated. Given the low level of knowledge around solar radiation modification and its side effects, she was one of very few experts who could help the participants understand the climate impacts of what they were discussing—yet she was largely ignored.“I was just so surprised about how little anyone actually cared about the science,” she says.
In the next sessions, the organizers tried in vain to nudge the talks back toward the realities of climate change. The participants received frequent notifications of climate disasters. These barely registered. Golja had prepared an “emulator,” a real-world demonstration of the best available science on how solar radiation management might affect weather patterns in different regions. It was ignored. If country representatives asked her anything, it was usually a leading question looking for data that would serve their ends or frame a rival’s proposal as reckless.
Then, during the last day, players were trying to find a way to respond to reports that a major plume of aerosols had been detected. In the game, this had been caused by a joint US-Saudi test of Stardust’s technology, though not everyone knew this. Finally, scientific advice was at a premium. Countries needed to know how to establish a monitoring network of satellites and other observational tools in order to prevent tests like this from happening in secret. A player representing an NGO called the Climate Futures Cooperative approached Golja, offering her money to fund such a scheme.
“Great. Fabulous. Why wouldn’t I do that?” she recalls thinking.
But it soon came out that the Climate Futures Cooperative was actually backed by the fossil fuel industry. The organizers had recognized that fossil fuel companies and major producing countries like the US and Saudi Arabia would have a clear interest in removing barriers from the development of a technology that could combat climate change without having to immediately stop burning coal, oil, and gas. The shadowy NGO spent the game subtly wrecking the vibe and carping about process—though mostly they just sat back and let it burn. Some players—Russia, the US, SpaceX and Stardust—figured out the CFC was not what it seemed, says Young. “But they assessed it was to their benefit and didn’t draw attention to it.” Then the CFC chose its moment to offer money to Golja, only to crater her credibility, isolating and fragmenting the voice of science in the room.
“It was a whole mess,” says Golja.
That final lesson in fossil fuel realpolitik was about all Golja could endure. By the end of the last day, she was in tears.
At no point did the countries in the game agree to a deal, despite multiple proposals being put forward. European countries and Canada tried to build support for safeguards and open scientific research, but the talks constantly got bogged down by delay tactics and veered into tense showdowns over duelling strategic interests. In their final report, the researchers running the simulation—whose work was sponsored by the UK government-funded Advanced Research and Invention Agency—concluded that “strategic competition and state sovereignty drove the simulations, not climate concerns.”
Simulations like this one are not supposed to predict the future. The outcomes depend on the design of the game and the relative personalities and experience of the players. Many of those in the room lacked first-hand diplomatic and national security experience. The UN forum, which organizers selected as the game’s setting, may also not be as effective as talks between smaller groups of major countries. But the experiment in London echoed and refracted through the real world, during and after the months it was running.
In March, two papers from conservative US think tanks urged the Trump administration to take the lead on solar radiation modification and counter China’s threat. One memorably invoked a new, MAGA-coded term: “Weather sovereignty.” This month, the Observer newspaper in London revealed that the UK Ministry of Defense had paid a deep tech security consultancy to conduct research into sunlight reflection. Then, last week, the British government released its first official policy paper on the field, backing further research but stating firmly that it did not support deployment and “does not plan to do so.” Stardust has continued its lobbying of the US and governments around the world; CEO Yanai Yedvab told WIRED its job was getting easier as, unlike before, “the majority of policymakers … are already aware of this technology.”
Stardust has always maintained that it will not conduct large-scale outdoor experiments, let alone full deployment, before global governance is in place. “We are developing a very powerful tool,” Yedvab says. “When you develop this kind of powerful technology—and you have many precedents—national interests will play out. We’re not naive about it.”
Meanwhile, drivers of the climate crisis are intensifying. During the time span of the game, efforts to curtail the use of fossil fuels were being undermined by rising energy costs and political hostility. Week after week, an incredible summer of drought and heat pounded Europe. In the final week of August, the collapse of a glacier on the Tibet-Nepal border fulfilled the prophecies of decades of climate scientists, killing more than 1,450 people.
In the months since the simulation ended, Golja has reevaluated many things. On a corkboard behind her desk, she has pinned up a note to herself, laying out a vision for life in a world ruled by narrow geopolitical self-interest rather than science, evidence, and reason. Her answer: She plans to return to the small coastal town where she grew up in Connecticut and use her expertise to help local climate groups build the seawalls and coastal erosion buffers they will need to cope with the inevitable. “To try and make a difference where it feels like I actually have traction,” she says. After what she saw, pursuing science in the hope of informing global decisions no longer held as much appeal. “Now it feels a little bit more personal.”
Wired.com is your essential daily guide to what's next, delivering the most original and complete take you'll find anywhere on innovation's impact on technology, science, business and culture.

articles.title: Get an RTX 5070 Ti gaming laptop for just $1,449 — Walmart has slashed $700 off this Gigabyte A16 Pro
articles.text:
Get an RTX 5070 Ti gaming laptop for just $1,449 — Walmart has slashed $700 off this Gigabyte A16 Pro
A really great price.
A pre-built desktop or gaming laptop is one of the best ways to sidestep some of the worst pain of AI-driven price increases when it comes to PC gaming. If you're on the hunt for a powerful gaming laptop, this Gigabyte Gaming A16 Pro is now just $1,449 at Walmart.
● Check out this deal at Walmart
This laptop comes with a 16-inch IPS display clocking in at 2560 x 1600. It's powered by Intel's Core 7 240H, a Raptor Lake-H refresh CPU with 10 total cores. However, the star of the show is undoubtedly the mobile RTX 5070 Ti GPU, which will excel at gaming on the go.
AI development has seen the price of individual PC parts skyrocket in recent months. 32GB of DDR5 6000 RAM now costs $450, with storage and graphics cards also enduring significant price hikes. One of the best ways to dodge these hikes is to buy a laptop, where increases are trickling down more slowly.
Get an RTX 5070 Ti gaming laptop with Intel Core 7 240H 10-core CPU, 32GB of RAM, 1TB SSD, and 165Hz IPS display.
With 10 cores (six performance and four efficient cores), the CPU in this rig is ideal for both gaming and productivity on the go. Paired with the RTX 5070 Ti gaming GPU, it will have no trouble running most games at the 2560 x 1600 resolution. The RTX 5070 Ti has 12GB of VRAM and 5,888 CUDA cores, making it ideal for this resolution.
For the price, this laptop also has a generous supporting cast, notably 32GB of DDR5 RAM (a rarity in cheap gaming laptops these days), and a 1 TB SSD for storing your games.
Otherwise, you get HDMI 2.1 connectivity, USB 3.2, USB-C with DisplayPort, 3.5mm audio connectivity, and Wi-Fi 6E, as well as Bluetooth v5.2.
This would be an ideal laptop for someone looking to do some gaming on the go while also supporting productivity workloads, possibly a college student. It would also make a great upgrade for anyone currently using an older-generation laptop.
