articles.title: 'VisionQuest' (★★★½☆), el remake de 'Inside Out' de Marvel es una gran heredera de 'WandaVision'
articles.text:
Llega por fin al Universo Cinematográfico de Marvel la serie de VisionQuest, su nuevo proyecto para Disney+. El título tendrá una vez más como protagonista al superhéroe de Paul Bettany. Solo que esta vez no es la misma versión que conocemos, sino su reinicio, la Visión Blanca. El proyecto, además, traerá varios regresos muy esperados como el de Ultrón y el de Tommy Maximoff. Y, sobre todo, servirá para cerrar la Trilogía de Wanda, siguiendo la estela de las series Bruja Escarlata y Visión (2021) y Agatha All Along (2024).
En VisionQuest, Visión, reiniciado y tras escapar de quienes pretendían convertirlo en arma, ha permanecido oculto. En busca de un nuevo propósito, consulta a las distintas IA integradas en su programación, incluidas F.R.I.D.A.Y., E.D.I.T.H., J.A.R.V.I.S. y el infame Ultrón.
Su discreta existencia llega a su fin cuando una recompensa por su captura lo obliga a huir junto a Thomas Shepherd, un misterioso joven que podría ser su hijo reencarnado. Mientras evita ser capturado, Visión deberá enfrentarse a su propia naturaleza, resistir la influencia de Ultrón y desentrañar el enigma de su joven acompañante si quiere sobrevivir.
El remake de Inside Out
Hay algo genial en la propia concepción de VisionQuest. Y es que la serie establece todo un mundo digital en el que Visión puede relacionarse con el resto de IAs. Todas ellas con forma humana y con su propia personalidad muy marcada, se convierten en los improbables huéspedes de una alocada casa. Las dinámicas entre ellas son el gran punto fuerte del proyecto, aunque no siempre se explota del todo ese potencial.
En cualquier caso, este universo digital no deja de estar dentro de la cabeza de Visión. Por tanto, el paralelismo que se traza con Inside Out, la aclamada película de Pixar, es irremediablemente evidente. Cada IA acaba representando, de alguna manera, uno de los aspectos de la personalidad de Visión. Su responsabilidad, su atrevimiento, sus dudas... Y es la relación de todas ellas juntas lo que le completa.
Es también una serie muy abiertamente heredera de Bruja Escarlata y Visión. Porque en aquella también se creó todo un mundo en el que Wanda pudo tener la vida que quería, más o menos. A nivel temático, las reminiscencias son claras. Otra vez se trata el dolor y la pérdida, aunque en esta ocasión desde un prisma diferente. Porque VisionQuest nos habla del trauma y de la identidad. De quien lo ha perdido todo, pero sobre todo de quien se ha perdido a sí mismo y no sabe reencontrarse.
Esos aspectos de salud mental nos recuerdan a WandaVision para cerrar perfectamente la Trilogía de Wanda. Además, a nivel narrativo y si bien es cierto que Agatha All Along sorteó en buena medida los acontecimientos de WestView, aquí los fans pueden esperar todo lo contrario. Los comentarios y referencias a aquella primera serie de Marvel para Disney+ son constantes. Sobre todo en la trama de Tommy, que va creciendo con el paso de los episodios.
El regreso de Ultrón
Como decimos, las dinámicas entre las IAs de VisionQuest son de largo el mejor punto de la serie. Pero si hay una que se lleva la palma es, no cabe la menor duda, Ultrón. El actor James Spader regresa a Marvel para encarnar de nuevo al villano, esta vez no solo como su voz sino también como su cuerpo humano. Y con un papel bastante protagónico, se roba por completo la serie.
Su visión maquiavélica del mundo, su evolución y su clara manipulación ¿emocional? hacia el héroe hacen de él, otra vez, un villano que se siente rico, inteligente, complejo, lleno de capas. Marvel lo tenía muy desaprovechado al haberse deshecho de él en una sola película, pero por fin le recuperan y le dejan brillar un poco más. Spader está impresionante en el papel, que le encaja como anillo al dedo.
Baches y acelerones
A nivel puramente forma, VisionQuest también va a satisfacer a los fans porque consigue generar un cierto comentario sobre la IA bastante interesante. El mundo digital de la mente de Visión es bonito, elegante. Pero a la vez también tiene un cierto componente inquietante. Hay pequeños detalles muy sutiles y repartidos que hacen que todo se sienta como si, efectivamente, lo hubiera generado una Inteligencia Artificial.
El creador, Terry Matalas, ha dejado claro que para la producción de VisionQuest no se ha empleado ningún tipo de IA. Sin embargo sí se quería reflexionar, o al menos explorar, acerca de los recursos y limitaciones de esta nueva tecnología que actualmente mantiene en vilo al mundo real. Es una inteligencia que, en el fondo, solo replica lo humano, lo que ya existe. No es capaz de crear. Y, como en el caso de Ultrón, alberga peligros reales.
Por desgracia, en VisionQuest no todo son alegrías. Por momentos a nivel emocional la serie se siente un poco distante. Al haber sido siempre un personaje bastante esquivo dentro del UCM, solo los más apegados a la familia Maximoff se sentirán completamente apelados. Y no ayuda ni mucho menos que a toda la historia de la búsqueda de identidad de Visión (y de Tommy), con Ultrón de por medio, se añadan tantas tramas y subtramas.
Al final el conjunto resulta recargadísimo y enrevesado. Hay que descubrir quién es Tommy, si Visión podrá ser "más humano" como su versión anterior, los planes ocultos de Ultrón, enfrentarse a diferentes villanos, desentrañar el misterio de una identidad oculta... Son tantas cosas a las que hacer frente que, al final, VisionQuest acaba un poco perdida en sí misma. Sobre todo en los episodios centrales, su ritmo se atasca y va a trompicones, a veces muy acelerada y en otras ocasiones excesivamente lenta y repetitiva. Por fortuna, el final es épico, solvente, siguiendo con acierto la fórmula típica de Marvel.
Date de alta en Disney+ ahora y ahorra gracias a la suscripción anual, con la que podrás disfrutar de todo su catálogo de series y películas. Acceso a los últimos estrenos, al catálogo de Star y ESPN* y a los mejores documentales de National Geographic.
*ESPN solo está disponible en Latinoamérica. Ahorro respecto a 12 meses de suscripción mensual.
En resumen, VisionQuest es una serie muy entretenida y que sirve como genial desenlace para la Trilogía de Wanda. Tiene problemas con su ritmo y con la cantidad de elementos que incluye, presentando muchas subtramas innecesarias y que quedan exploradas de manera superficial y caótica. Pero en líneas generales gustará, sobre todo a los fans de los Maximoff y de esos fans que buscan en Marvel reflexiones más profundas sobre salud mental, identidad y trauma.

articles.title: Cloudflare’s OHTTP Gateway Refuses to Decrypt Requests That Arrive through Cloudflare
articles.text:
Cloudflare has opened a closed beta of the Cloudflare OHTTP Gateway, a managed endpoint that decrypts Oblivious HTTP requests on an origin’s behalf. The design decision that drew most of the attention is a refusal rather than a feature: the Gateway will not decrypt requests that reach it from Cloudflare Workers or from hosts proxied through Cloudflare.
Oblivious HTTP, standardized as RFC 9458, splits a request across two parties. The client encrypts the inner HTTP request to the gateway’s public key using HPKE and sends the sealed payload to a relay. The relay sees the client’s IP address but cannot read the request. The gateway decrypts it and forwards plain HTTP to the application, so it sees the contents but only ever sees the relay’s address.
That only works if different operators run the two hops. Putting a Worker in front of the Gateway, or proxying the relay through Cloudflare, would route the client-identifying hop and the decryption hop through the same company, so Cloudflare built a product that declines to run in that configuration. Authors Lara Schull and Akshat Mahajan write that the model "requires that the relay and app server be operated by separate, non-colluding parties."
For a team evaluating this, the practical cost is the relay. Cloudflare does not supply one for the Gateway, and says the component is not the hard part, since relays "can run on any infrastructure provider, and they’re simple." The hard part is being in a position to "verifiably promise to your users that you won’t inspect logs with client identifiers." Cloudflare is also renaming its existing Privacy Gateway to Cloudflare OHTTP Relay to separate the two sides.
The Gateway itself binds to a zone and listens at a fixed path, https://your-zone.com/.well-known/ohttp-gateway, which stops a customer from pointing their gateway at another domain. Cloudflare manages the HPKE keys and serves the public keys from that same path in response to a GET, and clients can fetch keys over a different IP address than the one they use for requests. Standard and chunked OHTTP both work, with chunked recommended for performance. Cloudflare Access runs before decryption, so the relay itself can be authenticated with mutual TLS, static service credentials, or custom external logic.
Protection stops at the network layer, and Cloudflare says so. OHTTP "provides privacy at the network level, and doesn’t touch the inner request body," the post notes, adding that "it’s up to you not to send identifying information (e.g. a user’s email address or username) in the request body." Put a session token or an email address inside the sealed request and the gateway operator has the identity the protocol was meant to withhold.
Discussion on Hacker News divided between readers working out where the protocol fits and readers naming what it costs. Commenter johnhess set out the fit:
This separates who sees what. Cloudflare (or any OHTTP gateway) sees who talks to who, but can’t see the content. The service sees the content but not who you are/your IP. You can imagine a lot of threat models where who you talk to isn’t sensitive, nor is "someone talked to them about X" but knowing both facts is a risk.
Commenter gsnedders gave the most detailed comparison, measuring OHTTP against the obvious do-it-yourself alternative of a SOCKS5 proxy:
OHTTP is designed for a relatively narrow use case: stateless requests where you don’t want the gateway to be able to correlate multiple requests from the same client (i.e., it’s not just about hiding the IP address).
Matching that with SOCKS5, he wrote, means a new TCP connection for every request, no TLS session resumption or 0-RTT, and a deliberately conservative ClientHello, because SOCKS5 is unencrypted and carries the destination in the clear. OHTTP keeps the TLS fingerprinting surface away from the gateway and allows long-lived connections from client to relay and relay to gateway, which he called a significant latency win for workloads like DNS over HTTPS. He also named what the design gives up:
With OHTTP, disclosure of the gateway key essentially means the relay can decrypt recorded traffic that used that key (as there is no forward secrecy), whereas disclosure of the client <-> relay and relay <-> gateway keys matters a lot less.
The pointed questions were operational. Commenter arshxyz asked about a product interaction the announcement does not address:
Does Cloudflare’s WAF (which relies on TLS Fingerprinting) stop working if OHTTP is enabled? If not, does this imply the client metadata is read and processed by Cloudflare but not passed on to the application server?
Commenter Joker_vD asked how IP-based banning survives, and commenter blantonl described the position an operator ends up in: "I respect customer privacy. But I also need to know who is abusing my platforms as well." Commenter thayne raised the aggregation point, noting that when one entity serves a large share of the internet it ends up holding a record of which sites a given IP visited and which IPs visited a given customer, while conceding "that is still better than them having the source ip and the content."
If these reactions are representative, the cryptography is not what teams will argue about. Nobody in the thread disputed that the split works as described. The questions were whether a client exists that speaks the protocol, what a self-hosted relay is worth, and what breaks on the Cloudflare side once the client metadata is gone. Commenter ranger_danger asked whether any current proxy, tunnel, or VPN software supports OHTTP as a transport, which is the adoption question for anyone not shipping their own app. On self-hosting, commenter palata pointed out that a relay run for a handful of people defeats its own purpose, because the service then knows any request through it came from that small group. Commenter scosman described the demand side from experience, saying he had wanted this for update checks in otherwise offline transcription software and ended up calling GitHub releases directly. Commenter freedomben questioned charging for it at all, calling a paid privacy add-on "a poor incentive if the goal is to improve privacy generally."
The closest comparison in the thread was Tor, which commenter maayank reduced to "OHTTP is like a two-hop Tor circuit with a predetermined gateway." The difference is scope. OHTTP needs a client that deliberately speaks the protocol to a known gateway, so it is not general browsing privacy. It fits an app vendor that wants telemetry, inference, or a lookup feature without being able to tie each request to a user. Cloudflare cites Flo Health’s Anonymous Mode and Apple’s Private Cloud Compute as production deployments, with Apple’s LiveCallerID as the case where a service accepts OHTTP from a third party. Cloudflare’s Reference Image work with Apple, which InfoQ covered earlier this year, uses the same transport to request timestamps without revealing who asked.
Cloudflare says the Gateway launches this fall, with a closed beta of the self-serve version starting now. It will be sold as a paid add-on to a customer’s zone, and the announcement does not publish a price. Interested teams can register through a waitlist form.

articles.title: High-speed video reveals how honey bee stingers pump venom
articles.text:
Honey bees are known to leave their stingers embedded in tender flesh once they sting you and fly away. Scientists have now determined that the stinger is able to continue pumping venom into its unfortunate victim even after the bee flies away, thanks to a unique double-piston pump-like mechanism, according to a new paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
Different species have evolved different mechanisms for delivering venom, which involves piercing the skin and then pumping venom from a gland or reservoir. Spiders, for instance, have muscles surrounding their venom glands, which contract and eject venom through hollow fangs. Bees, wasps, and ants deliver venom via their stingers, either by contracting muscles around the venom reservoir or through stiff elements called lancets working together to pump venom.
Honey bees (Apis mellifera) add a unique feature: Worker bees fly away after inserting their stingers in the target, leaving the stinger behind. The stinger continues to penetrate the tissue and pump venom on its own, a rare phenomenon known as autotomy. A honey bee’s stinger has three main interlocking elements that form the venom canal: a stylet that widens to form the main pumping chamber and two sharp-tipped lancets that slide back and forth, piercing the tissue and pumping venom into the target. But the precise mechanism by which the pumping action is achieved has never been directly observed.
The authors of this latest paper sought to capture the venom-pumping kinematics of honey bee stingers in order to identify the underlying biomechanics. They collected live worker bees and removed the stingers with forceps just prior to filming. Then they partially inserted those stingers into blocks of artificial gel and captured the pumping action using stereomicroscopy and high-speed color videography. This was followed by a frame-by-frame analysis to better track the movement, which is visible because the structures are semi-translucent.

articles.title: Manage private pricing offers for Amazon Bedrock with managed entitlements | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Manage private pricing offers for Amazon Bedrock with managed entitlements
Managing AI model access across dozens or hundreds of AWS accounts creates operational friction when each workload account must subscribe and accept AWS Marketplace Private Pricing Offers (MPPOs) individually. Amazon Bedrock with managed entitlements simplifies multi-account access to third-party AI models so you can subscribe once from a central account and distribute access across your organization.
In this post, we show you two ways to activate AWS Marketplace Private Pricing Offer (MPPO) entitlements in AWS License Manager. Use the lightweight script when you want a one-time, no-infrastructure fix for received licenses you already trust. Use the CDK automation when you want ongoing event-driven processing that verifies sellers, creates and activates distributed grants.
Why automate grant activation
With AWS Marketplace Private Pricing Offers, you can negotiate custom rates for third-party models on Amazon Bedrock. After an eligible private offer is accepted, AWS Marketplace creates a license in AWS License Manager. In AWS Organizations with all features enabled, organization-level grants are auto-accepted but remain Disabled until you activate them.
Teams often manage this by checking the AWS License Manager console and activating grants manually. Manual checks work, but they add effort and are easy to miss. Until someone activates the grant, negotiated pricing does not apply. The same effort appears as teams adopt new models or renew terms.
Solution overview
The sample repository provides two paths:
- Path 1 – The lightweight path is a standalone script that lists received licenses and prints a dry-run plan. It only creates and activates organization-wide grants when you re-run it with --apply --confirm-account-id. It has no seller allow-list, so use it only when you trust every received license in the management account.
- Path 2 – The event-driven path uses AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) to deploy ongoing automation in your AWS management account.
Choose one of the following implementation paths. Use Path 1 for one-time activation without CDK. Use Path 2 for ongoing event-driven automation.
Path 1: Lightweight script (one-time activation)
Use this path when you need one-time activation without deploying CDK. The script lists every received license in the management account, so use the dry run as your review gate before applying changes.
- Clone the sample repository locally and move into the project directory.
- Run the lightweight script in dry-run mode.
- Review every listed license and confirm that the ISV Partner issuer and account scope match the private offer you expect.
- Apply the reviewed plan from the same AWS Organizations management account.
- After the grant is active, validate the billing path before you rely on the private offer in production. Billing data in AWS Cost Explorer can lag, so use it to compare the effective charge for covered Amazon Bedrock usage after charges appear. For a repeatable check, adapt the sample scripts/bedrock_discount_check.py utility to match your ISV Partner issuer and confirm the expected discount path.
Path 2: CDK automation (ongoing activation)
Use this path when you want new private pricing agreements handled automatically. The CDK stack listens for eligible AWS Marketplace agreement events, checks your seller allowlist, creates distributed grants, and retries activation when License Manager needs more time. The solution contains three components:
- Amazon EventBridge rule: The stack listens for AWS Marketplace agreement events on the default event bus in us-east-1. The rule matches source aws.agreement-marketplace and detail type Purchase Agreement Created - Acceptor, then invokes the AWS Lambda function.
- AWS Lambda function: The function receives the AWS Marketplace agreement event, verifies the seller allow-list, discovers the license, creates the distributed grant, and requests activation with CreateGrantVersion(Status=ACTIVE). The function logs the outcome to Amazon CloudWatch Logs for auditability.
- AWS License Manager entitlements: The grant targets your organization, selected organizational units (OUs), or specific accounts. Negotiated pricing applies only after the grant is activated and reaches ACTIVE or WORKFLOW_COMPLETED.
The following diagram shows the event-driven flow.
Key benefits of this approach:
- Faster time to negotiated pricing. The negotiated rate applies after the distributed grant reaches ACTIVE or WORKFLOW_COMPLETED, without waiting for a manual console check.
- Consistent handling across accounts. The same AWS Lambda function and Amazon EventBridge rule pattern can be deployed for each organization that receives third-party model grants, so activation logic doesn’t vary by operator.
- Built-in audit trail. Every activation attempt or skip decision is logged to CloudWatch Logs, giving you a record of when each grant was activated, deferred, or ignored.
Prerequisites
Before you deploy this path, confirm these prerequisites:
- Use the AWS Organizations management account in us-east-1 with Python 3.12+, AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), and AWS CDK v2 configured.
- Confirm that AWS Organizations uses all features and that the private offer is for a License Manager-backed Bedrock model. Software as a service (SaaS) products are out of scope for this automation.
Implementation steps
- Clone the sample repository locally and move into the project directory.
- Verify or enable organization prerequisites. 
         
         Review any APPLY or MANUAL items before making changes. The bootstrap script can enable License Manager organization integration, License Manager trusted access, AWS Marketplace license-management trusted access, and required service-linked roles.
- Configure deployment inputs. 
         
         Review config/sellers.json. Configure your Organization ID, seller allow-list, notifications, and optional grant targets. By default, grants target the full organization. Use grantTargets to scope grants to selected OUs or AWS accounts.
- Deploy the CDK stack.
- Seed the Amazon DynamoDB seller allow-list from config/sellers.json. Treat the seller allow-list as a security boundary. Verify each seller account ID against your accepted AWS Marketplace private offer or received License Manager license before seeding the table. Don’t add broad or unverified seller entries, because matching sellers can trigger grant creation and activation across your configured grant targets. After deployment and seller seeding, the stack is ready to process eligible AWS Marketplace agreement events. Grant creation and activation happen only for verified sellers in the allowlist, and activation may be deferred until License Manager finishes processing the grant workflow.
- Validate the deployed automation.
- Verify grant activation after an eligible AWS Marketplace agreement event. 
         
         Activation and billing visibility can take hours or days. After the event-driven workflow accepts and activates the grants, confirm the grant state in AWS License Manager, then validate covered Amazon Bedrock usage in AWS Cost Explorer after billing data appears. For a repeatable check, adapt the sample scripts/bedrock_discount_check.py utility to match your ISV Partner issuer and target linked account.
Clean up
If you deployed this stack for testing, remove it to avoid the small ongoing Lambda and Amazon EventBridge charges:
Voice of customer
        “As an AI Care Partner supporting millions of clinician consults every week, Heidi Health relies on third-party foundation models at real scale. Private pricing on AWS Marketplace gives us a cost-effective and efficient way to manage that growth: we can granularly attribute usage and pricing across AWS accounts and organizational units, and automate grant management as we adopt new models. That lets our platform team scale cost governance without scaling manual work.”
— Marcus Lau, Head of Platform Engineering, Heidi Health
Conclusion
This post showed two ways to activate managed entitlements for Amazon Bedrock private pricing offers. Use the lightweight script for one-time activation of trusted received licenses, or deploy the CDK automation when you need ongoing event-driven processing for new AWS Marketplace agreements. Both approaches reduce manual effort and help negotiated pricing apply after distributed grants are activated.
To get started, try the code sample in your AWS management account to automate model subscriptions.

articles.title: Kubo Care uses radar technology to keep senior citizens safe at home
articles.text:
Kubo Care uses radar technology to keep elders safe at home
Bengaluru-based startup Kubo Care uses millimetre-wave radar devices to monitor seniors and detect falls without intrusive cameras or wearables.
As families increasingly live in different cities and countries, keeping ageing parents safe at home can be a challenge. Full-time attendants require trust and may not always be reliable, while video cameras can feel intrusive, particularly in bathrooms, where more than half of serious falls occur. Wearable devices such as smartwatches and panic pendants offer another option, but seniors may forget to wear or charge them.
Bengaluru-based Kubo Care is addressing this problem with a system that monitors movement continuously without recording video or audio, while keeping families informed.
The healthtech startup was founded in 2024 by CEO Ayush Agrawal and COO Anurag Ram Chandran. Agrawal, who previously co-founded senior care ecommerce platform Seniority and worked as an AVP at CARS24, experienced the problem firsthand when his father suffered a stroke and fell while alone at home. He remained undiscovered for hours.
Chandran, a Schwarzman Scholar who previously ran an Indian NGO, became the primary caregiver for his grandmother after she was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease. His experience exposed him to gaps in elderly care.
The two met in early 2024 at Antler’s Bengaluru residency and combined their experience in age-tech to develop a system for monitoring seniors at home.
Monitoring movement through radio waves
Kubo Care’s main device is mounted on a wall or ceiling and uses 60 GHz millimetre-wave (mmWave) radar technology. Similar to how bats use echolocation, the sensor transmits radio signals to map a room in three dimensions, tracking human presence and movement without capturing video or audio.
The system uses proprietary AI to analyse this spatial data and identify patterns of movement. It can detect sudden falls in less than a second while distinguishing them from deliberate movements, such as someone slowly lowering themselves onto the floor.
Beyond emergencies, the software establishes a baseline of daily habits, tracking sleep restlessness, night-time awakenings, and washroom visits. Changes in these routines can help care teams identify possible health issues, including urinary tract infections or gradual vision decline.
Kubo Care holds patents in India and the US for software that converts raw point-cloud data into real-time skeletal models to assess posture and gait. It also has a patented method that reduces false alarms by more than 99%.
The startup develops its technology in-house, including hardware, custom firmware, cloud applications and AI analytics. In larger spaces, its software transfers tracking data between multiple wall-mounted devices, allowing continuous monitoring as a resident moves between rooms, including areas with blind spots.
For institutional operators, the system provides customisable alerts for bed exits, prolonged washroom stays, and wandering. The hardware can also be connected to ambient sensors that measure room temperature, humidity, lighting and air quality.
The information is available through an enterprise management portal for care facility staff and a mobile application for family members.
Global B2B plans
Kubo Care operates on a Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) model and plans to charge senior care operators between $50 and $70 per device per month.
The startup is currently pre-revenue and conducting pilots in India, Japan, and the US. In India, retirement community developers are integrating its hardware into model homes as part of the standard infrastructure.
Over the next year, Kubo Care plans to expand its B2B presence in senior care facilities across Japan, the US and India, while preparing for a broader direct-to-consumer launch.
“We are able to reduce false alerts by over 99% through our patented method,” Agrawal says. “The roadmap over the course of the next year is to establish ourselves in B2B, especially in the US and Japan, the two largest senior living markets in the world, while preparing for a direct-to-consumer launch by late next year.”
Kubo Care is part of YourStory's Tech30 cohort—a showcase of India's most promising startups of 2026, unveiled at TechSparks Bengaluru.
Edited by Teja Lele

articles.title: Installer Windows 11 26H2 sur un PC non compatible devient un jeu d’enfant avec Tiny11
articles.text:
Installer Windows 11 26H2 sur un PC non compatible devient un jeu d’enfant avec Tiny11
L’utilitaire Tiny11 fait peau neuve pour s’attaquer à Windows 11 26H2. Son créateur promet une installation débarrassée des applications superflues et bien moins gourmande en ressources, même sur les PC déclarés obsolètes par Microsoft.
Depuis son lancement, Windows 11 impose des prérequis matériels stricts, laissant de nombreux ordinateurs sur le banc de touche. Microsoft continue d’ailleurs de bloquer les anciennes astuces de contournement, mais le développeur NTDEV ne s’avoue pas vaincu. En déployant une refonte complète de son célèbre utilitaire Tiny11, il est maintenant possible de créer de petits fichiers d’installation, prêts à être placés sur une clé USB pour déployer le système d’exploitation. L’objectif reste clair, à savoir redonner vie aux machines jugées obsolètes, avec cette fois-ci la dernière version en date : Windows 11 26H2.
Une refonte totale de Tiny 11 pour contourner les ultimes blocages de Microsoft sur Windows 11
Le projet Tiny11 n’est pas nouveau, mais il vient de franchir une étape décisive. Après une longue période sans mise à jour majeure, son créateur NTDEV a dévoilé une toute nouvelle architecture pour son outil de création d’images ISO, le format de fichier indispensable pour installer manuellement Windows 11. En plus d’abandonner son ancien design au profit de l’interface WinUI 3, bien plus moderne, elle ajoute une compatibilité avec la récente mise à jour 26H2, tout en offrant de nouveaux outils puissants pour “nettoyer” le système d’exploitation avant même de l’installer.
Concrètement, l’application automatise la suppression des éléments superflus intégrés par défaut dans l’OS. Vous obtenez ainsi une version allégée qui consomme nettement moins de mémoire vive. Cette optimisation s’avère redoutable pour les configurations modestes ou vieillissantes, cœur de cible de Tiny11. L’outil neutralise d’ailleurs les vérifications de compatibilité matérielle lors de l’installation, permettant ainsi à la quasi-totalité des ordinateurs de profiter de cette mise à jour.
La seule véritable limite matérielle concerne l’absence de certaines instructions processeur spécifiques pour faire fonctionner les dernières versions du système d’exploitation. Toutefois, la communauté a déjà trouvé une parade : une fois l’image ISO créée avec Tiny11, il suffit de l’associer à un autre utilitaire nommé POP4.2, pour débloquer les dernières restrictions imposées par Microsoft.
Les autres nouveautés ajoutées à l’utilitaire
Tiny11 offre au passage une interface proposant deux approches distinctes pour créer son fichier d’installation. On a tout d’abord le mode classique, qui se charge de purger automatiquement les applications promotionnelles et les fonctionnalités superflues, tout en préservant des éléments vitaux comme Windows Update ou Microsoft Defender. Et ensuite, pour les utilisateurs les plus exigeants, le mode personnalisé laissant le choix de cocher individuellement les services, applications et composants à conserver ou à supprimer. Vous obtenez ainsi un contrôle absolu sur ce qui tournera réellement sur votre PC.
NTDEV a ensuite introduit une fonction Turbo, conçue pour accélérer drastiquement le processus de création de l’image ISO de Windows 11 en optimisant les ressources de votre ordinateur. Autre ajout pratique, l’application est désormais capable de sauvegarder votre progression. Si la compilation est interrompue, vous pourrez la reprendre sans avoir à tout recommencer depuis le début.
Cette version remaniée est d’ores et déjà disponible en téléchargement sur GitHub.

articles.title: Europe’s Advanced Packaging Gap: Fraunhofer, Swissbit Target the Missing Middle - EE Times
articles.text:
Europe has no shortage of semiconductor research. The harder problem often begins after the prototype works.
A company may need an advanced packaging process for a specialized product, but only at volumes of tens, hundreds, or thousands of units. That can be too much for a research organization to support indefinitely and far too little to interest a conventional high-volume outsourced semiconductor assembly and test provider.
Rolf Aschenbrenner, deputy director of the Fraunhofer Institute for Reliability and Microintegration (IZM), sees that gap regularly. “Companies come to us because their volume is too low to get access to advanced packaging,” he told EE Times. “We can help with prototypes, and in some cases we can also do small-volume manufacturing.”
That doesn’t mean Fraunhofer wants to become an outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) provider. Its role, according to Aschenbrenner, is to adapt packaging processes to customer requirements, demonstrate their viability, and ultimately hand them off to industry. “The goal is that we also transfer our processes,” he said.
The problem is what happens when no industrial manufacturer is ready to take them.
Too small for the OSATs
Aschenbrenner cited fan-out wafer-level packaging as an example. A company developing RF products might require only around 100 wafers per year. For a large packaging provider, that volume barely registers.
“If you go to a large OSAT and ask for 100 wafers per year, that’s nothing for them,” he said. “They won’t do it.”
Fraunhofer has encountered even smaller production runs. Aschenbrenner described one customer making miniature cameras for medical applications that requires only about 20 wafers annually. A single wafer can contain tens of thousands of cameras, making that small wafer count sufficient for the customer’s entire market.
“Twenty wafers per year is the full volume,” he said. “They don’t need more. But nobody else can do those 20 wafers.”
He also pointed to work for a medical technology company on detector arrays for a novel CT scanner. The application requires sensors to be placed very close together; conventional wire bonding creates gaps that can affect imaging performance, so the design uses through-silicon vias to route connections to the backside.
The customer wanted that work performed in Europe, Aschenbrenner said. But again, the volume was too low to attract a conventional packaging house. “There was no company in Europe with the technology available at that volume,” he said. “So we do it.”
For Europe, that problem is especially relevant because many of its industrial strengths lie in specialized markets rather than mass consumer electronics. “We have many small and medium-sized companies that are champions in very narrow areas,” Aschenbrenner said. “They also need access to advanced packaging, and often no one is there to help them.”
The capital requirements make it harder for those companies to solve the problem themselves. Advanced packaging is no longer a matter of buying a few relatively inexpensive wire bonders. Wafer-level packaging lines require substantial investment.
That leaves a missing industrial layer between pilot production and mass manufacturing.
The industrial answer
Swissbit provides one example of how that middle ground might work. The company develops memory and security products in Europe and increasingly uses advanced packaging to move toward system-level products combining memory, controllers, security functions, compute, and potentially AI.
According to Lars Lust, executive director of Swissbit Germany, the company’s core competency is not semiconductor manufacturing. “We integrate semiconductors,” he told EE Times. “Advanced packaging is a must-have for our products.”
Lust argued that low-volume manufacturing doesn’t necessarily have to be uneconomic. The key is to avoid building a unique process flow for every product. “If you have a standard tool chain and a common platform, you can produce low volume in the same way as higher volume,” he said. “You don’t need a new setup every time.”
Swissbit’s own production illustrates the model. The company has roughly 3,500 products in its catalog and around 150 active products moving through production in a typical month. Some products may run in quantities of only hundreds, while others reach thousands or tens of thousands, but they can share equipment, process steps, and tooling.
“We scale over the platform,” Lust said. “If you have a good platform for low-volume products, you can produce them on the same line as volume products.” That changes the economics of the “missing middle.” The challenge is not necessarily low volume itself, but low volume combined with a bespoke process that cannot be reused.
For Europe, that could be important. Rather than trying to replicate the enormous Asian packaging ecosystem built around highly standardized, high-volume products, European manufacturers could aggregate many specialized products onto common advanced packaging platforms.
The handoff cannot come at the end
Lust also sees room for improvement in the way Europe transfers technology from research institutes to manufacturers. He argued that industry should become involved around technology-readiness levels five or six, once early demonstrators have shown that a process works, rather than waiting until researchers have pushed the technology close to production.
“The RTO should not develop everything to TRL seven or eight and then hand it over,” he said. “Industry needs to come in earlier, when the first demonstrators are there, to define applications, requirements, and scalability.” That makes the transition less like a relay race and more like an overlap between research and manufacturing.
Aschenbrenner described Fraunhofer’s current role in similar terms. Its packaging equipment is deliberately close to what’s used in industry, making it easier either to transfer processes or to manufacture initial volumes while an industrial route is established.
But he was clear that Fraunhofer should not remain the manufacturer indefinitely. “We can fill a gap,” he said. “But manufacturing should be industrialized. We are very interested in transferring our knowledge and processes so industry can do it.”
Build around Europe’s actual strengths
Both Aschenbrenner and Lust argued that Europe should be selective about what kind of packaging capacity it tries to build.
Aschenbrenner pointed to automotive and industrial markets, where Europe already has strong customers and specialized requirements. “We have to look at the real applications in Europe,” he said. “Do we really need to copy what is being done for extreme high-performance computing? I don’t think so. We should focus on the needs we actually have here.”
Lust made a similar argument. “Me-too is not the right approach,” he said. “Traditional packaging is already established elsewhere. Europe should strengthen the things it is already good at and scale those strengths into advanced packaging.”
That means complex integration, specialized industrial products, flexible manufacturing, and packaging platforms able to support many different applications rather than one enormous product family.
For Lust, Europe already has evidence that such a model can work. “In the industrial market, Europe is very strong,” he said. “We can handle complexity and variation. The key is to have your own platforms, your own ecosystem, and scale them across different applications.”
The missing piece is turning that capability into sustainable industrial infrastructure.
Fraunhofer can keep technologies alive through the dangerous interval between prototype and volume production. But if Europe wants a resilient advanced packaging supply chain, the final destination cannot be the pilot line.
It has to be industry.

articles.title: OPPO's Find X10 Series will offer a new standard of photo and video quality on a smartphone - Tech Guide
articles.text:
OPPO will launch its new flagship Find X10 smartphone series which includes a Hasselblad True-to-Life Camera and a next-generation LUMO True Image Engine to take your photography to a new level.
The Find X series continues the minimalist design language and uses premium materials and crafted detail that’s all brought together in a new borderless design which includes one piece of sculpted glass that seamlessly flows from the screen to the camera module.
The OPPO Find X10 Pro Max in Luna White has a LUMO camera island in a matte silver metallic finish that houses the True-Colour Cameras and dual flash system.
It’s also complemented by Hasselblad’s signature matte orange accent ring to create a distinctive two-tone finish.
“Find X Series reflects our relentless pursuit of exceptional mobile imaging,” said Pete Lau, SVP and Chief Product Officer at OPPO.
“Together with Hasselblad, we are taking another significant step forward with Find X10 Series, bringing true-to-life detail, colour and tone to everyday photography.
“Simply open the camera and capture the moment as you see it, with no extra settings required.”
The Find X10 camera includes a dual 200MP camera system co-developed with Hasselblad.
The Find X10 Pro Max has the industry’s first triple 200MP camera system, bringing 200MP sensors to the ultra-wide, main, and telephoto cameras for the first time on a smartphone.
Now it’s one thing to have great cameras but the OPPO Find X10 also has next-generation computational photography – the LUMO True Image Engine.
It works with OPPO’s image expertise deliver precise colour and quality.
On the video side the Find X10 Pro Max supports 4K 120fps and 8K 30fps through all three rear cameras, while the Find X10 has the same capabilities on its two 200MP cameras.
The Find X10 is powered by the MediaTek Dimensity 9600M chip while the Find X10 Pro Max is among the first smartphones to include the 2nm MediaTek Dimensity 9000 Pro which offers a major boost to performance and power efficiency.
Both Find X10 models feature a massive 7,150 mAh OPPO silicon carbon battery to 2 days of use on a single charge.
The battery is also engineered to retain more than 80 per cent of its original capacity even after five years of typical use.
The OPPO Find X10 will be available in Glacier Blue, Glow Coral, and Mist Grey while the OPPO Find X10 Pro Max will come in Titanium Grey and Luna White.
Pricing and availability will be announced at the global launch event on October 21.

articles.title: How to Rewrite Apache Spark UDFs for GPU Acceleration with AI Agents | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Enterprise applications have become increasingly demanding. Agentic AI has compounded the need for vast amounts of enterprise data with frequent, complex queries across increasingly large datasets.
Meeting that demand requires greater data throughput without a proportional increase in cost. NVIDIA cuDF addresses this challenge by leveraging the massive parallelism and high-bandwidth memory of GPUs for data analytics. Particularly, the NVIDIA cuDF plugin for Apache Spark brings this acceleration to Apache Spark, the industry-leading platform for big data processing and analytics, to achieve better TCO performance in major workloads.
User-defined functions (UDFs) have long been problematic for accelerated query engines, introducing runtime overheads due to their opaque nature. While UDFs can often be replaced with more performant code, rewriting UDFs has long been a laborious process requiring careful validation.
This post describes how to use agents to rewrite UDFs into GPU-accelerated equivalents within minutes, achieving 22x+ speedups in Apache Spark jobs. We’ll introduce the cuDF skills for Apache Spark, a set of skills to quickly break through the UDF bottleneck for end-to-end development, from testing, to benchmarking, through integration.
The UDF challenge
cuDF achieves seamless GPU acceleration in part due to Apache Spark’s declarative programming interface. The SQL / Dataframe abstractions are powerful because they separate what a query should produce from how the system should execute it. This enables the cuDF plugin to transparently parallelize row-wise operations using the massive SIMD capabilities of GPUs, without any change in user code.
Apache Spark, however, also supports UDFs: custom routines to extend built-in functionality. While useful for implementing bespoke business logic, UDFs break the declarative abstraction—they contain arbitrary user code which the system cannot reason about or parallelize in any general sense. During execution, the GPU accelerator must convert the data from a columnar to row-wise format, and fall back to the CPU to execute the UDF row-by-row:
Thus in an otherwise accelerated query, UDFs have the following drawbacks:
- The UDF incurs a round-trip data transfer overhead due to fallback.
- The UDF forgoes potential compute speedup, had it been written using GPU-accelerated primitives.
Accelerating UDFs
With a small, targeted code change, many UDFs can be rewritten into a GPU-accelerable form by using the right primitives. Rewriting UDFs eliminates the overhead associated with accelerator fallback, and can yield speedups of over 20x.
We outline three approaches to rewrite UDFs:
| Approach | Complexity | Best For | 
|---|---|---|
| SQL | Low, highest level of abstraction | Simple relational logic, e.g. small or inlined functions | 
| cuDF | Medium, more flexibility and control over execution | Most cases, e.g. moderately complex logic like string parsing, nested types | 
| CUDA | High, maximum flexibility and kernel-level control | Most complex or performance critical logic | 
To make these approaches concrete, consider a simple Scala UDF that converts temperature from Celsius to Fahrenheit:
final class ToFahrenheit
    extends Function1[java.lang.Double, java.lang.Double]
    with Serializable {
  override def apply(celsius: java.lang.Double): java.lang.Double = {
    if (celsius == null) null
    else celsius * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0
  }
}
spark.udf.register("to_fahrenheit", new ToFahrenheit)
spark.sql("""
  SELECT
    *,
    to_fahrenheit(celsius) AS fahrenheit
  FROM temperatures
""")
Rewriting the UDF with SQL
The most direct solution for simple UDFs is to replace the UDF with an equivalent Spark SQL expression:
spark.sql("""
  SELECT
    *,
    celsius * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0 AS fahrenheit
  FROM temperatures
""")
This makes the function visible in Spark’s expression tree. During query planning, the cuDF plugin will replace these expressions with their corresponding GPU implementations, keeping the data and execution fully on the GPU.
Rewriting the UDF with cuDF
When SQL primitives are insufficient or undesirable, the UDF can instead operate directly on GPU columns using the RapidsUDF interface, a contract provided by the cuDF plugin. The contract requires a single method, evaluateColumnar:
import ai.rapids.cudf.{ColumnVector, Scalar}
import com.nvidia.spark.RapidsUDF
import scala.util.Using
final class ToFahrenheit
    extends Function1[java.lang.Double, java.lang.Double]
    with Serializable
    with RapidsUDF {
  override def apply(celsius: java.lang.Double): java.lang.Double = {
    if (celsius == null) null
    else celsius * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0
  }
  override def evaluateColumnar(
      numRows: Int,
      args: ColumnVector*): ColumnVector = {
    Using.Manager { use =>
      val scale = use(Scalar.fromDouble(9.0 / 5.0))
      val offset = use(Scalar.fromDouble(32.0))
      val scaled = use(args.head.mul(scale))
      scaled.add(offset)
    }.get
  }
}
The cuDF plugin recognizes instances of the RapidsUDF interface and passes a GPU-resident ColumnVector to the evaluateColumnar function. The function then composes operations from the Java API for cuDF operations to process the column in parallel. This approach provides a richer API for more complex processing.
Rewriting the UDF with CUDA
For highly complex logic that cannot be efficiently composed from existing cuDF operations, a RapidsUDF can invoke a custom CUDA kernel through the Java Native Interface (JNI). We’ve elided the code for brevity, but examples of CUDA conversions can be found in the cuDF examples for Spark UDFs.
Efficient rewrites with AI agents
Despite the performance benefits, UDF rewrites can require significant engineering effort. They demand careful API selection, semantic validation, and performance measurement, while columnar APIs can be unfamiliar to practitioners with less experience in vectorized programming.
Fortunately, much of this work is well suited to coding agents. With proper guardrails, an agent can search unfamiliar APIs, implement candidate rewrites, and iterate quickly while executable tests and performance measurements determine whether each change is acceptable.
Available skills
The cuDF skills for Apache Spark decompose the rewrite into four focused feedback loops. Each skill defines both the work to perform and the evidence required before proceeding to the next stage:
Figure 2. Four skills guide agents through testing, conversion, benchmarking, and optimization, with verification-driven feedback loops at each stage
Scaffolding and design
Reliable agent execution begins with a reliable development environment. The skills provide a complete project template containing the cuDF- and Spark-specific scaffolding required for end-to-end development. This includes test and benchmark harnesses, encoded routines for output verification, and build configuration. By encoding this knowledge into code, the agent can focus on the UDF rather than repeatedly reconstructing specialized infrastructure.
The skills also provide best practices for GPU programming with cuDF, including memory management and configuration. This serves as an advisory tips and tricks reference. To best leverage the power of frontier models, the agent remains free to explore different implementations based on surrounding context and select an approach based on measured correctness and performance.
Performance results
A major consumer technology company used this workflow to convert 30+ UDFs used in production data pipelines into GPU-accelerated implementations. The rewrites preserved the behavior of the original CPU UDFs while removing costly fallbacks from otherwise GPU-accelerated workloads. As an example, the following benchmark shows the resulting before-and-after performance for a UDF in one such workload:
This particular UDF was affecting more than 3,000+ jobs, and in this job, saw a 22x speedup when implemented as a cuDF-enabled RapidsUDF. With the help of agents, these performance gains are much more attainable, enabling practitioners to iterate on rewrites on the order of hours rather than days or weeks, without compromising correctness.
Get started
Converting UDFs to GPU implementations can unlock major speedups and contribute to overall cost savings in GPU-accelerated pipelines. With agent skills, the rewrite process can be made both easy and reliable.
To get started, install the cuDF skills for Apache Spark on GitHub, either directly or using the npx skill installer:
npx skills add NVIDIA/cudf-spark --skill ‘*’
For a deeper walkthrough of the workflow and practical lessons from building it, see the Data + AI Summit session, Coding with AI Agents to Supercharge Your Spark UDFs with GPU Acceleration.
To learn more about GPU acceleration for Apache Spark, follow the cuDF plugin for Apache Spark getting-started guide to unlock better performance and TCO across your Spark pipelines. Visit our webpage to learn more about NVIDIA cuDF: GPU-Accelerated Structured Data Processing, or you can read the docs for more information on NVIDIA cuDF plugin for Apache Spark.

articles.title: Apple lance de nouveaux Apple TV et HomePod mini : voici les nouveautés
articles.text:
L’Apple TV n’avait pas évolué depuis 2022, le HomePod mini depuis 2020. La bonne nouvelle est que l’attente est enfin terminée pour les fans de ces produits : Apple a dévoilé le 13 octobre de nouvelles versions de son boîtier télé et de son enceinte connectée (mais oublie toujours le grand HomePod). La marque a profité de sa conférence « Welcome Home » dédiée à la maison connectée pour dévoiler les nouvelles versions de ces produits avec plusieurs nouveautés. La star du jour est évidemment l’écran HomeView, mais on peut imaginer que les Apple TV et HomePod mini sauront vite trouver leurs publics.
Apple met ENFIN à jour son Apple TV
« Enfin » n’est pas un euphémisme : la dernière Apple TV 4K date d’octobre 2022 et les fans du produit attendent avec impatience une nouvelle génération. Nous recevons souvent des messages de nos lecteurs sur Numerama et une part conséquente d’entre eux concerne des renseignements sur la future Apple TV. Le dilemme est souvent le même : les gens ont des téléviseurs à équiper mais ne veulent pas acheter un vieux modèle alors que les rumeurs annoncent une nouvelle génération depuis deux ans. Et comme le marché des box télé est relativement faible (le Nvidia Shield TV date de 2019 et le Google TV Streamer n’est pas un foudre de guerre), alors l’Apple TV est considérée par beaucoup comme le seul produit du marché.
Le 13 octobre 2026 est le jour de la libération : Apple annonce qu’une nouvelle Apple TV sera disponible le 13 novembre 2026, au prix de 349 € (modèle unique). L’Apple TV passe à la puce A19, celle de l’iPhone 17, ce qui la rend sur le papier plus puissante qu’un MacBook Neo (l’ancien modèle avait l’A15). Apple promet un processeur jusqu’à 50 % plus rapide et des performances graphiques jusqu’à deux fois supérieures, ainsi qu’un décodeur AV1 dédié pour un streaming de meilleure qualité avec moins de bande passante. Cette montée en puissance devrait améliorer la réactivité du boîtier, les graphismes des jeux et permettre de traiter une partie des requêtes Siri directement sur l’appareil.
Aux États-Unis, au Royaume-Uni ou au Canada, l’Apple TV offre des fonctionnalités Siri AI (en anglais et en version bêta), mais pas en France, alors que le produit n’est pas régulé par le DMA européen. La raison : Siri AI exige que le propriétaire du domicile dans l’application Maison ait un iPhone avec Siri AI, ce qui est impossible en Europe. On pourra quand même demander un programme qui pourrait nous plaire, comme c’est déjà le cas aujourd’hui.
L’Apple TV est aussi accompagnée d’une nouvelle télécommande sans grand chamboulement esthétique, mais enfin compatible avec Localiser : on pourra la faire sonner pour la retrouver entre deux coussins. Elle ne sera plus obligatoire pour le pilotage à la voix, l’Apple TV étant équipée de trois microphones à longue portée. Notons enfin qu’on pourra coupler l’Apple TV à quatre HomePod mini 2 ou HomePod de deuxième génération (par paires identiques à l’avant et à l’arrière) pour une vraie expérience sonore digne d’un home cinéma.
Le HomePod mini 2 adopte une puce plus puissante
L’autre nouveauté est encore plus discrète : six ans après le premier modèle, le HomePod mini a enfin un successeur. Il s’appelle le HomePod mini 2 et, à l’instar de l’Apple TV, sera privé de Siri AI en France (aux États-Unis, l’assistant n’arrivera que dans une future mise à jour). Siri sera toujours là pour quelques commandes vocales (exemple : lancer un minuteur) ou gérer sa domotique. Le HomePod mini adopte la puce S10 de l’Apple Watch Series 10, ce qui est une évolution notable depuis la puce S5 de la première génération. Pour l’écoute musicale, elle analyse les morceaux en temps réel pour optimiser la dynamique et le volume.
Apple mise sur de nouveaux coloris pour séduire : blanc, rose, bleu, vert et minuit.
Le HomePod mini 2 sera disponible le 30 octobre, au prix de 169 €.

articles.title: Fitbit : Google met fin au sursis des anciennes versions de l’appli
articles.text:
Vous faites partie des irréductibles qui refusaient de dire adieu à l’application Fitbit ? Vous allez devoir vous faire une raison : une mise à jour renvoie désormais vers Google Health.
En avril dernier, nous vous annoncions la disparition programmée de l’appli Fitbit, remplacée par Google Health. Le nouvel outil, qui intègre notamment un coach IA piloté par Gemini, est loin d’avoir convaincu tout le monde. Certains utilisateurs se sont plaints de dysfonctionnements dus aux hallucinations de la technologie. D’autres ont tout simplement choisi de conserver une ancienne version de l’app Fitbit. Mais Google ne l’entend pas de cette oreille… Explications.
Le sursis pour l’application Fitbit, c’est terminé
Google a beau disposer de moyens conséquents, maintenir deux applications n’est pas raisonnable. Le géant de la Tech avait, en juin dernier, averti que les versions de Fitbit antérieures à la 5.0 perdraient leur support dès le 15 juillet. Mais certains utilisateurs se sont tout de même accrochés à leurs précieuses applications.
Google a donc dû employer la manière forte. Depuis cette semaine, un nouvel écran a fait son apparition sur Fitbit : ce dernier « recommande » de mettre à jour le service, ce qui revient à passer à Google Health. Le problème ? Dans la majorité des cas, il est impossible de passer outre et d’utiliser l’ancienne appli.
Les réactions sont, on s’en doute, plutôt mitigées : « Je suis tombé à genoux ce matin. Je ne peux pas sortir de là. On est obligé de mettre à jour. Je ne me sens pas bien et je suis triste », peut-on notamment lire sur Reddit. Nos confrères de TechRadar ont également recueilli d’autres réactions, tout aussi négatives : « L’appli Google Health est vraiment nulle. Je veux aussi retrouver mon appli Fitbit », « Il ne reste plus aucune des fonctionnalités que j’appréciais dans l’application Fitbit » ou encore « J’ai bien peur de ne plus jamais retrouver ce genre de suivi ».
Pourquoi les utilisateurs ont-ils autant de mal à passer à Google Health ?
Google Health est, pour le moment, loin d’être à la hauteur des exigences des habitués de Fitbit : les badges, profils de sommeil et autres fonctions sociales ont changé, quand ils n’ont pas tout simplement disparu. Un sondage mené par Android Authority a notamment montré que la moitié des répondants n’aimaient pas la nouvelle application. Google a donc beaucoup de pain sur la planche pour séduire les récalcitrants.
En attendant, les notes de mises à jour de Fitbit indiquent désormais qu’ « un compte Google est désormais nécessaire pour utiliser l’application Google Health, la période de migration des comptes Fitbit étant désormais terminée. » Le support de MyFitnessPal explique, quant à lui, que l’API Fitbit s’éteindra fin octobre.
L’heure des adieux a donc sonné : il faudra passer à Google Health, en espérant que l’outil comble vite ses lacunes… Ou aller voir ailleurs.

articles.title: SAP warns of maximum severity OAuth2 SSRF security flaw
articles.text:
SAP has addressed 20 security flaws across multiple products in its October 2026 security updates, including a maximum-severity vulnerability in the Cloud SDK for Python.
The SAP Python SDK is the official programmatic toolkit for developing AI agents and Python applications on the company's SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP) services.
Tracked as CVE-2026-89111, the maximum-severity vulnerability patched this month can be exploited by remote attackers without privileges to steal credentials.
Customers who can't immediately deploy the October 2026 SAP patches can temporarily mitigate the issue by using an allowlist to validate tenant_subdomain values.
"The SAP Cloud SDK for Python contains an OAuth2 SSRF vulnerability affecting multi-tenant BTP applications. An attacker who controls the tenant_subdomain parameter can redirect OAuth2 token requests to an attacker-controlled server, causing client credentials to be exfiltrated," according to a Tuesday advisory.
"Consumer applications can mitigate the vulnerability by validating tenant_subdomain against a known allowlist of registered tenant subdomains before passing it to any SDK call."
Today, SAP also addressed CVE-2026-89110, a critical broken access control vulnerability in the SAP NetWeaver Visual Composer that could let remote attackers with limited privileges fully compromise vulnerable systems.
Another critical flaw patched today in SAP Manufacturing Integration and Intelligence (tracked as CVE-2026-89108) lets threat actors with administrator privileges gain admin control over the underlying system by provisioning an elevated-privilege account on the underlying Java app.
In recent months, SAP has fixed several other maximum-severity flaws in multiple components. For instance, it patched CVE-2026-58231 in the Commerce Cloud cloud-based e-commerce platform in August, which threat intelligence firm Defused flagged as actively exploited in attacks days after it was addressed.
More recently, in September, it also fixed the CVE-2026-44756 memory corruption flaw in the SAP Kernel code, dubbed OVERPASS by Onapsis security researchers who reported it. According to Onapsis estimates at the time, over 10,000 Internet-facing SAP systems use the vulnerable component and may be exposed to attacks that exploit CVE-2026-44756.
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added 14 SAP security flaws to its catalog of actively exploited vulnerabilities since November 2021, three of which were abused in ransomware attacks.
SAP is a German multinational software company that serves 99 of the 100 largest companies worldwide and reported revenues exceeding €36 billion in fiscal year 2025.

articles.title: Hypersonic Technologies is turning methane into hydrogen and carbon black
articles.text:
Hypersonic Technologies is turning methane into hydrogen and carbon black
Chennai-based deeptech startup Hypersonic Technologies is betting on two revenue streams to help industrial customers offset production costs while reducing emissions.
Hydrogen is expected to play a larger role in helping industries cut emissions, but conventional production methods can leave a significant carbon footprint. Chennai-based Hypersonic Technologies is working on an alternative that produces hydrogen alongside carbon black, a commercially useful material used in tyres, rubber and pigments.
Founded in 2023 by Jayaraman Kandasamy and Jayakumar Venkatesan, the climate-tech startup uses staged-plasma pyrolysis to convert methane and biomethane into hydrogen and solid carbon. By producing two materials through one process, it aims to help industrial customers offset production costs while reducing emissions.
Kandasamy has more than a decade of experience in Europe, where he worked on plasma technology for aerospace propulsion and explored converting biomass into fuel and hydrogen-rich gases. After returning to India, he founded Hypersonic Technologies to apply this experience to industrial decarbonisation.
“Our main mission is converting methane and biomethane into hydrogen and carbon black using staged-plasma pyrolysis technology,” he says. “The aim is to decarbonise industries, particularly oil refineries, steel, cement, and fertiliser, while also producing carbon black through the same process.”
One process, two outputs
Plasma pyrolysis uses high temperatures to break down hydrocarbons into hydrogen and solid carbon. Hypersonic Technologies combines dielectric plasma with microwave plasma in two stages, which Kandasamy says can improve efficiency and make the process more stable than a single-stage system.
The technology aims to address emissions associated with conventional hydrogen production. Kandasamy says steam methane reforming, a widely used method, can emit around 10 kg of carbon dioxide for every kilogram of hydrogen produced. Carbon black production also generates emissions.
“Both methods have to move towards cleaner, climate-oriented options. That is why this technology is important,” he says. “Methane is available in several places, where it may simply be flared. Instead, we can use it as feedstock to produce hydrogen and solid carbon.”
The company's prototype is at Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 5, meaning it has been validated in a relevant environment. Its lab-scale system at IIT Madras produces around 500 grams of hydrogen per hour, according to Kandasamy. The technology has received a patent grant, and the startup says it has also been validated through the government-backed NRDC-NETRA programme.
The carbon black produced is intended for industrial applications, including pigments, and the company is exploring higher-value grades. Kandasamy says Hypersonic has held discussions with established carbon black manufacturers about possible collaborations, although the technology is still at an early stage.
“We are looking at producing carbon black that can be used for pigments and other applications,” he says. “The advantage is that hydrogen and carbon black can both be monetised, rather than relying on hydrogen revenue alone.”
Moving from the lab to industry
Hypersonic Technologies is targeting refineries, steelmakers, cement companies, and fertiliser manufacturers. It is also exploring commercial models that could include equipment sales, operating partnerships, and payments linked to output.
Its immediate challenge is scaling the prototype. Kandasamy says the company needs around Rs 5 crore to advance from TRL 5 to TRL 7, with plans for a larger pilot plant once funding is secured. The startup is also seeking government support and has received a Carbon Zero Challenge grant.
“We are a deeptech hardware startup, so we need funding to take the technology to the next level,” he says. “Once we establish a plant producing five kilograms of hydrogen per hour and reach the required validation stage, we can pursue orders from refineries and steel companies.”
Kandasamy says industrial adoption will depend largely on cost, particularly because major manufacturers cannot easily replace existing infrastructure. He sees new facilities as a more immediate opportunity than retrofitting existing plants.
“Industries are very sensitive to cost. They cannot replace existing technology overnight because they have already invested in it,” he says. “But when they set up new facilities, they can evaluate alternatives such as plasma pyrolysis.”
For Hypersonic Technologies, the next step is to demonstrate that its process can produce hydrogen and carbon black reliably and economically at a larger scale.
Hypersonic Technologies is part of YourStory's Tech30 cohort—a showcase of India's most promising startups of 2026, unveiled at TechSparks Bengaluru.
Edited by Teja Lele

Cet airfryer présente le meilleur rapport qualité / prix de notre comparatif
L'airfryer Moulinex Easy Fry Smart & Silence s'affiche aujourd'hui à 84,99 € chez Amazon. C'est actuellement le meilleur rapport qualité / prix de notre comparatif, selon les 41 modèles testés dans notre laboratoire.
Avec l'Easy Fry Smart & Silence, Moulinex promet un airfryer à la fois plus discret et plus simple à nettoyer. Doté d'une interface guidée et de plusieurs programmes automatiques, ce modèle de 5 l vise une cuisson rapide et accessible au quotidien.

Points faibles
- Long à monter en température au centre.

Les performances de cuisson sont globalement convaincantes, même si la montée en température au centre demande un peu plus de patience. Attention toutefois aux temps de cuisson proposés par l'assistant, parfois trop optimistes, et à l'absence de fenêtre de contrôle, qui oblige à ouvrir régulièrement le tiroir pour surveiller les aliments. Au final, l'Easy Fry Smart & Silence réussit son pari principal : être un airfryer efficace et surtout très silencieux, avec quelques côtés pratiques bienvenus.

articles.title: Cyberattaque « opportuniste » contre les supermarchés français : des chercheurs évoquent « une réalité largement sous-estimée »
articles.text:
Des équipements industriels connectés, comme des frigos, peuvent être pris pour cible « avec une facilité déconcertante ». Synacktiv, une entreprise française spécialisée dans la cybersécurité offensive, réagit aux cyberattaques qui ont déréglé les frigos de centaines de supermarchés. Pour Synacktiv, la vague de cyberattaques met en lumière « une réalité largement sous-estimée ».
Des failles connues dans les systèmes de Danfoss
Dans une réaction adressée à 01net, l’entreprise assure que ses chercheurs « connaissent particulièrement bien ces systèmes ». Par le passé, les chercheurs de Synacktiv ont déjà identifié plusieurs vulnérabilités dans des équipements signés Danfoss, le fabricant danois au cœur de la cyberattaque contre les supermarchés. L’entreprise originaire du Danemark a en effet conçu les systèmes de régulation frigorifique qui ont été piratés dans la nuit du 11 au 12 octobre 2026, et qui ont été déréglés à distance par des cybercriminels.
Parmi les vulnérabilités épinglées par Synacktiv, on trouve une faille permettant de contourner l’authentification. Autrement dit, des pirates pouvaient se connecter à des systèmes sans avoir besoin du moindre identifiant. L’alerte est loin d’être récente. Trois ans avant la cyberattaque, Synacktiv a déjà découvert des vulnérabilités sur d’anciens systèmes de régulation Danfoss, les SM800 et SC255/SC355. « Le problème est loin d’être théorique », insiste Synacktiv.
Le CERT-FR, le centre gouvernemental de veille et de réponse aux attaques informatiques rattaché à l’Anssi, confirme d’ailleurs le problème. Dans une alerte publiée ce 12 octobre, il dit avoir connaissance de « nombreuses compromissions » des équipements Danfoss des séries AK-SM et AK-SC. En cause : des interfaces de gestion exposées sur Internet, ce qui est « contraire aux bonnes pratiques », rappelle l’organisme. Il recommande de déconnecter ces équipements d’Internet ou d’en filtrer strictement l’accès. En cas de piratage, les exploitants doivent réinitialiser les boîtiers, appliquer tous les correctifs disponibles et changer leurs mots de passe.
 ⚠️ CERT-FR Alert ⚠️
The CERT-FR is aware of numerous compromises of Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC series.
— CERT-FR (@CERT_FR) October 12, 2026
À lire aussi : 200 000 appareils piratés : ce botnet utilise la blockchain pour brouiller les pistes
Des frigos connectés sans mot de passe
Lors d’un audit réalisé récemment, les experts ont cette fois découvert des systèmes de réfrigération accessibles « directement depuis Internet, sans aucun mot de passe ». Pour mener une cyberattaque, il suffit donc théoriquement de trouver l’appareil en parcourant le réseau. Une fois à l’intérieur, un attaquant peut « arrêter les équipements ou modifier à distance les températures de conservation », ce qui peut avoir des impacts « potentiellement importants sur les marchandises et l’activité des magasins », prévient l’entreprise. C’est peut-être ce qu’il s’est passé lors de l’opération qui vient de semer la pagaille dans des centaines de magasins français.
Le chercheur en cybersécurité français Baptiste Robert affirme d’ailleurs avoir recensé 2 752 « systèmes » Danfoss accessibles en ligne. Plus de la moitié d’entre eux, soit 1 590, se trouvent en France.
 We count 2752 Danfoss “systems” online.
We’re gonna do a quick and dirty thread the old-school way.
First observation: 1590 “systems” out of 2752 are in France
— Baptiste Robert (@fs0c131y) October 12, 2026
D’après les recherches de Synacktiv, les équipements vulnérables sont aussi « parfois accessibles depuis les réseaux internes des magasins ». La société affirme avoir pu prouver ses dires lors de plusieurs tests réalisés dans différentes enseignes. Lors des expérimentations, un chercheur s’est s’introduit dans un lieu pour vérifier que les mesures de sécurité étaient à la hauteur.
« Cet incident n’a rien de surprenant. Un réfrigérateur de supermarché n’est plus un simple appareil électrique ; c’est un système informatisé connecté à un réseau, permettant une surveillance et un contrôle à distance. Si cette connectivité permet une gestion efficace des systèmes de réfrigération, elle les expose également à des risques de cybersécurité, en particulier lorsque les équipements opérationnels fonctionnent pendant des années avec des logiciels obsolètes, sans mises à jour de sécurité régulières et avec des interfaces de gestion accessibles depuis Internet », nous explique Oded Vanunu, responsable de la recherche sur les vulnérabilités chez Check Point Software Technologies, soulignant que « les équipements opérationnels sont souvent conçus pour rester en service pendant 15 ans ou plus, alors que les cybermenaces et les technologies évoluent à un rythme bien plus soutenu ».
L’experte recommande d’abord « d’identifier les contrôleurs et les interfaces de gestion directement exposés à Internet et d’éliminer toute exposition inutile ». De son côté, Benoît Grunemwald, expert cybersécurité chez ESET, estime que c’est « un bon rappel que la cybersécurité ne relève plus seulement des équipes informatiques ». Les « systèmes de froid, de chauffage, de production ou de supervision sont devenus des systèmes numériques à part entière », ajoute l’expert.
À lire aussi : Cyberattaque chez E.Leclerc : une fuite a exposé les données des clients
Une attaque « opportuniste »
À ce stade, les chercheurs de Synacktiv privilégient l’hypothèse d’une « attaque opportuniste », menée en deux temps. Les cybercriminels auraient d’abord repéré les frigos de Danfoss grâce à des moteurs de recherche spécialisés, tel que Shodan. Ce type de moteur permet de retrouver des appareils connectés à Internet, comme des caméras, serveurs, ou des systèmes industriels. Ensuite, les attaquants auraient exploité des failles connues de Danfoss ou des identifiants faciles à deviner pour prendre le contrôle sur les interfaces de gestion. In fine, ils pouvaient envoyer les commandes qu’ils souhaitaient aux frigos de centaines de supermarchés. Les pirates ont alors activé à distance le mode de dégivrage, qui fait grimper la température au-delà des 50 degrés.
« La dispersion géographique des attaques semble conforter cette hypothèse », estime Synacktiv, qui reconnaît toutefois ne pas pouvoir confirmer le mode opératoire exact « à ce stade ».
Pour l’heure, la faille exploitée le 12 octobre n’a pas encore été identifiée. L’attaque n’a pas non plus été revendiquée. Danfoss s’est contenté d’indiquer que « la majorité des logiciels touchés sont obsolètes, et ne reçoivent plus de mises à jour de sécurité ». Quoi qu’il en soit, la cyberattaque risque de laisser des traces. Interrogé par 01net, le Groupement Mousquetaires, à l’origine d’Intermarché et de Netto, estime qu’il y a environ 180 magasins concernés par cette cyberattaque, et que le « retour à la normale » sera progressif.
