articles.title: Juan Luis Arsuaga, antropólogo, sobre la IA: “Ojalá esta vez no ocurra, pero no hay precedentes de un cambio de modelo económico que no produzca conflictos”
articles.text:
Juan Luis Arsuaga, especialista en evolución humana, no es economista, y cuando le preguntan por la inteligencia artificial, contesta con lo que sabe: la historia. “Ojalá esta vez no ocurra, pero no hay precedentes de un cambio de modelo económico que no produzca conflictos”, ha dicho en una entrevista.
Para Arsuaga, el problema empieza cuando cambia la estructura económica y parte del trabajo humano deja de hacer falta, más que cuando una máquina aprende a hacer una tarea. Queda por saber qué pasa con quien deja de ser necesario y quién gana con ello.
Un 46 % más de producción, un 12 % más de salario: la última vez que cambió el modelo
Entre 1780 y 1840, la producción por trabajador en Gran Bretaña creció un 46 % (estimación de Nicholas Crafts y Knick Harley) y el salario real un 12 % (la de Charles Feinstein).
El historiador económico Robert Allen bautizó ese periodo como la "pausa de Engels", por Friedrich Engels, que describió la situación de la clase obrera inglesa en 1845. Según su estudio de 2009, la tasa de beneficio de los empresarios se duplicó mientras los sueldos casi no se movían, y solo hacia mediados del siglo XIX los salarios alcanzaron a la productividad: entre 1840 y 1900, la producción por trabajador aumentó un 90 % y el salario real un 123 %. Allen lo atribuye a la acumulación de capital, que tardó en ponerse a la altura del progreso técnico.
No todos los economistas aceptan que existiera esa pausa. Crafts sostiene que la participación del trabajo en la renta nacional pasó del 57,1 % en 1790 al 59,2 % en 1840, es decir, subió ligeramente, mientras que la serie de Allen la baja del 56,2 % al 49,0 %, y dice que esta choca con todas las demás estimaciones. Se discute con datos de hace dos siglos.
Del conflicto sí hay registro. En 1811, los tejedores de medias de Nottinghamshire intentaron negociar salarios más altos y que los fabricantes dejaran de producir los llamados cut-ups, prendas más baratas que exigían menos destreza y pagaban menos.
Al fracasar la negociación, rompieron 63 bastidores en Arnold y unos 200 más en el condado en tres semanas. Según Kevin Binfield, que ha estudiado el movimiento, los luditas no se oponían a la tecnología en sí, sino al uso de máquinas existentes de maneras que recortaban salarios y producían ropa de mala calidad. El Parlamento convirtió romper bastidores en delito capital, el Gobierno envió a unos 14.000 soldados al centro de Inglaterra y unas dos docenas de luditas acabaron en la horca.
¿Cuántos empleos están en juego? Depende de quién haga la cuenta
La Organización Internacional del Trabajo y el instituto polaco NASK calcularon en 2025 que uno de cada cuatro empleos del mundo (el 24 %) está en ocupaciones expuestas a la IA generativa, una cifra que sube al 34 % en los países de renta alta. Los más expuestos son los puestos administrativos, y lo más probable, dicen, es la transformación de los empleos, no su sustitución.
El FMI había medido en enero de 2024 casi el 40 % del empleo mundial y en torno al 60 % en las economías avanzadas. En estas últimas, según el análisis de su directora gerente, más o menos la mitad de los empleos expuestos podría salir ganando con la IA y la otra mitad sufrir menos demanda, salarios más bajos o menos contratación. Añadía que, en la mayoría de los escenarios, la IA probablemente agravará la desigualdad general.
Exposición no equivale a pérdida de puestos. Funcas estimó en 2026 que la IA podría destruir entre 1,7 y 2,3 millones de empleos en España entre 2025 y 2035, con un abanico de 700.000 en el escenario más optimista a más de 3,5 millones en el más pesimista. Suma además unos 1,61 millones de empleos nuevos ligados a la IA (cifra de otros estudios, con un horizonte algo distinto, 2023-2033), de modo que en el escenario central quedaría una pérdida neta de unos 400.000.
Por ahora, los datos de empleo no detectan destrucción
Eso son proyecciones; lo ocurrido lo recoge el Observatorio Trimestral del Mercado de Trabajo que elaboran Fedea y BBVA Research, publicado en septiembre: algo más del 30 % del empleo en España está en ocupaciones muy o bastante expuestas a la IA generativa, y desde 2022 el empleo ha crecido más en ellas que la media. Florentino Felgueroso, de Fedea, dice que no observan desplazamiento de empleo por la IA.
Los autores de BBVA Research, Rafael Doménech y Juan Ramón García, piden no sacar todavía conclusiones causales: los efectos, advierten, no son automáticos ni homogéneos. Los más expuestos son los trabajadores de 25 a 34 años y los titulados (más del 40 % de quienes tienen estudios superiores, frente al 15 % de quienes tienen la ESO, Educación Secundaria Obligatoria, o menos).
El análisis añade que el PIB por ocupado apenas ha variado desde finales de 2019 y que la productividad por hora ha subido un 2,4 %. La nota no ofrece cifras de salarios.
Más miedo donde hay menos formación
En mayo, el análisis de la Dirección General de Economía y Finanzas de la Comisión Europea partió de una encuesta a 21.207 personas de 18 Estados miembros y cuatro países candidatos, hecha en febrero y marzo.
Alrededor del 54 % usa herramientas de IA y algo menos de la mitad de ellas lo hace en el trabajo; el uso es mayor entre directivos y profesionales. Entre los ocupados que la usan en su empleo, el 41 % teme ser desplazado (un 14 % mucho y un 27 % algo), y ese temor es mayor entre operarios, personas de menos renta y menos formación, y jóvenes. Según el texto, la adopción desigual corre el riesgo de ampliar las disparidades económicas dentro de los mercados laborales y entre regiones. No estima el efecto neto sobre el empleo.
En España, según ADP Research (39.000 trabajadores de 36 países), el 15 % usa IA a diario y el 11 % cree que acabará sustituyéndolo.
Bruselas anunció el 22 de julio un grupo de expertos de alto nivel para estudiar cómo transforma la IA el empleo. Entre las tres prioridades de su estrategia social figuran gestionar esos efectos y reducir las desigualdades. La información publicada no dice cuándo empezará a trabajar.

articles.title: AMD's RDNA 5 graphics cards tipped to arrive in late 2027
articles.text:
Rumor mill: Given the state of the graphics card market, it feels like we'll be waiting forever to see next-generation GPUs. But according to a popular leaker, AMD will launch its RDNA 5 lineup in the second half of 2027 – so the first cards could be here in less than 12 months.
The information comes from Kepler_L2, who has a long history of correctly predicting graphics card releases. The leaker previously said RDNA 5 would land in 2027. Now, the timeframe has been narrowed to the second half of the year.
Writing on the AnandTech forums, Kepler_L2 said Team Red's next-generation cards could be unveiled at Computex 2027 at the earliest, though they're more likely to be announced later that year.
Computex 2027 starts on June 1. That'll be 2 years and 3 months since the RDNA 4-based Radeon 9000 series launched in March 2025. The gap between the Radeon RX 7000 series and RX 9000 cards was 2 years and 2 months, and it was 2 years and 25 days between the Radeon RX 6000 cards and RX 7000. So, the timing fits.
AMD might also depart from its usual habit of launching the higher-end cards first. Previous reports point to the mid-range AT2 GPU arriving in 2027, with the rest of the RDNA 5 family – including the rumored flagship AT0 and lower-end AT3 and AT4 chips – following in 2028.
Kepler_L2 also responded to a question about RDNA 5's potential use of the rumored 4GB GDDR7 memory chips, which are expected to be mass produced in the next two years along with 6GB GDDR7 chips. The leaker believes that 4 GB GDDR7 won't be used for next-generation consumer parts, suggesting they'll be reserved for AI-focused and other enterprise products.
Another unanswered question is the all-important price of the cards. Thanks to the memory crisis, most mid-range GPUs no longer carry mid-range prices, while flagships have reached second-hand car levels. There are opposing opinions about whether things will get better or worse over the next few years, but it's hard to be optimistic.
As for when Nvidia will launch what is presumed to be the RTX 6000 series, another leaker, Kopite7kimi, says it won't be here until 2028. And don't expect to ever see any RTX 5000 Super cards.

articles.title: Un motor de búsqueda alemán ha rechazado a Mistral apostando por modelos IA chinos open-source en su lugar
articles.text:
Cuando se creó Mistral, el objetivo era tener una alternativa europea a los gigantes estadounidenses y chinos de la IA. En este tiempo, ha ido levantando miles de millones de euros en diferentes rondas de financiación y están peleando para poder conseguir potencia de cálculo que los haga competir en las grandes ligas. Su CEO aprovechó la controversia política contra Estados Unidos para afirmar que Europa debía dejar de ser un vasallo tecnológico del país americano, y una de las armas para cuajar son los navegadores.
Meter la IA en el navegador es algo que están haciendo prácticamente todos, ya que es una forma de licenciar tecnología y conseguir usuarios más allá de las grandes empresas que pagan por usar la IA. De hecho, la conjunción entre navegadores europeos y Mistral parecía una buena forma de combatir a las propuestas estadounidenses, y precisamente por eso el encontronazo entre Ecosia y la empresa de IA francesa es tan sonado. Porque no es que ahora el navegador alemán vaya a volver a ChatGPT, sino que se va a ir a modelos chinos.
¿Motivos? Mejor calidad, según la entrevista al fundador de Ecosia publicada por Politico, pero de fondo también están asuntos políticos, energéticos y una contradicción que puede levantar más de una ceja.
Ecosia ataca a Mistral con todo
Hace unos días, el medio Politico publicó una entrevista a Christian Kroll, fundador y CEO de Ecosia, en la que anunció que el buscador con sede en Berlín dejará de usar Mistral como proveedor de IA. La empresa ya 'pasó' de ChatGPT a mediados de año para apostar por Mistral y, ahora, dejará el modelo francés en la cuneta.
Eso no implica que Ecosia deje de usar IA en el navegador, ya que Kroll apunta que irán en busca de modelos abiertos, citando Qwen, GLM y Kimi que "cuestan la mitad y nos dan más rendimiento" Lo que tienen en común es que son chinos, y es una decisión que llama la atención cuando uno de los pilares sobre los que se levantó Ecosia fue la independencia de tecnológicas no europeas.
Kroll da varios motivos por los que se ha tomado esta decisión que impactará en un navegador que está presente en instituciones públicas alemanas y británicas, por ejemplo. Son los siguientes:
- La calidad de Mistral es insuficiente, argumentando que sus modelos "van un año por detrás de la competencia".
- Mistral no es lo suficientemente potente, comentando que han tenido varios problemas técnicos como servidores saturados, achacándolo a que "Ecosia es un cliente demasiado grande para Mistral".
- Mistral no encaja con sus objetivos climáticos por el gran peso de la energía nuclear en el mix eléctrico francés.
- Mistral no es soberano debido a que depende de enormes inversores internacionales (Nvidia, por ejemplo, entre otros).
Son un montón de melones abiertos y desde Mistral no han respondido a Politico, pero el científico jefe de la empresa comentó en una rueda de prensa que animaba a Ecosia a probar su nuevo modelo, incluso con acceso anticipado para que puedan ver si la calidad ahora les satisface. De hecho, el mismo día de la entrevista, Mistral lanzó Large 4, un modelo que algunos analistas han posicionado como unos seis meses por detrás de los de frontera.
En una entrevista posterior en EU-Startups, Kroll intentó ser algo más comedido, argumentando que no se trata tanto de que los modelos chinos sean mejor que Mistral, sino de un cambio de foco a modelos abiertos. Es decir, no es una cuestión que tenga que ver con el país de origen, sino con la propia tecnología.
Apuntaba que quizá usarían Melious, una empresa alemana que ofrece acceso a más de 60 modelos abiertos a través de su API, que reparte consultas entre proveedores europeos y que está centrada en ofrecer el servicio apoyado por energía verde (algo que casa más con los compromisos ambientales de la propia Ecosia).
Pero usen lo que usen, la idea es apostar por esos modelos abiertos. En el caso de Ecosia, la jugada sería usar modelos desarrollados fuera, pero servidos desde infraestructura europea. Ahí es donde entra la mencionada Melious.
La contradicción china
Pero claro, si bien la calidad e infraestructura de Mistral es algo que sólo Ecosia sabe si le ha ido bien o mal, el tema energético y medioambiental es lo que puede hacer que levantemos una ceja en caso de que la compañía empiece a apostar por modelos chinos si no quieren apoyar un modelo francés que puede alimentarse de energía nuclear.
Según RTE, que es el gestor de la red eléctrica francesa, la nuclear aportó el 68,1% de la electricidad francesa en 2025 con una producción baja en carbono que alcanzó el 95,2%. Según las estimaciones, la electricidad francesa emite menos de 20 gramos de CO2 por kWh. Alemania, posicionada en contra de las nucleares y lastrada por el carbón, se sitúa en el rango de los 300 gramos de CO2 por kWh.
En la entrevista, Kroll alude a la nuclear como uno de los motivos para dejar de usar Mistral, pero sin especificar si es por seguridad de la planta, por gestión de residuos o por las emisiones directas.
Si nos vamos a China, aunque es cierto que el gigante asiático es una potencia verde, según la IAE, el 70% de la electricidad que alimentó sus centros de datos en 2025 venía del carbón. La idea es que las renovables cubran el 80% del consumo de esos centros de datos para 2030, pero la incómoda realidad actual es que, en todo el mundo, los picos de demanda de la inteligencia artificial están llevando al traste los compromisos climáticos de los países, volviendo a ese carbón o al gas.
Y luego está la contradicción por la calidad debido a la censura de los medios chinos. Si has jugueteado con alguno, sabrás que hay preguntas como qué ocurre en Taiwán o qué pasó en la plaza de Tiananmén a las que no te va a responder. Puedes dar rodeos, pero tardarás en dar con la respuesta (si es que lo consigues).
Es por ello que hay organizaciones occidentales que dudan de la calidad de los modelos chinos en algo como un buscador debido a esa censura, aunque hay algunos más optimistas como la de Rasmus Rothe, director de la Asociación Alemana de IA, que comentó a Politico que la censura puede eliminarse en gran parte reentrenando el modelo.
El problema es el sesgo de los datos de entrenamiento, algo mucho más difícil de corregir.

Half of yesterday’s TC Daily edition was about IPOs: Airtel Money and OPay. But apparently, we missed an important one: Banque du Caire, Egypt’s sixth-largest commercial bank by assets. Fintech
Pepkor’s $1.3 billion fintech deal draws shareholder pushback
When Pepkor, the South African retailer behind PEP and Ackermans, announced its Flash-Shop2Shop merger in July, the pitch was growth: combine two large merchant networks, build a bigger fintech business, then list it separately. Three months later, the deal is attracting attention for a different reason.
What happened? Some Pepkor directors and investors believe shareholders should have been allowed to vote on the R21.3 billion ($1.3 billion) transaction. Pepkor will own 57.1% of the combined entity, FintechCo. Pieter Erasmus, Pepkor’s chief executive officer (CEO), will indirectly own 13.2%, worth roughly R2.8 billion ($170 million) at the deal valuation, according to the company’s filing.
Erasmus recused himself from discussions and decisions. Pepkor also obtained independent valuations and a voluntary fair opinion. JSE rules did not require a shareholder vote because the deal is classified as a Category 2 transaction—which must be publicly disclosed but does not require shareholder approval—while Erasmus’s interest falls below the threshold that would make it a related-party transaction.
Explain like I’m new here: Erasmus’s link to Shop2Shop is not new. An associated company owned 31.2% of Shop2Shop before the merger, and Flash and Shop2Shop had already been doing business together since 2020. Pepkor disclosed those relationships in previous financial statements.
Between the lines: Pepkor did not need shareholder approval under JSE rules. But some investors still think a deal this important—especially one in which the CEO has a financial interest—should have gone before shareholders. FintechCo is central to Pepkor’s next phase, and its CEO stands to own a valuable stake in the private company being brought into the group. A shareholder vote, even a non-binding one, would have given investors a direct say on that conflict.
Zoom out: Pepkor is moving quickly beyond retail. Financial-services revenue jumped 41.6% in the first half of 2026, and the group plans to launch a bank in April 2027. As more of Pepkor’s growth comes from finance and payments—as it eyes banking—as well as other private deals, investors will care just as much about how those businesses are put together and how fast they grow.
Happy customer service week.
Your success and ours are the same story. Happy Customer Service Week. This year’s theme is The Extra Mile, and it’s the only way we know how to do this. Visit: fincra.com.
Ecommerce
Quickmart cuts founder-linked contracts before IPO
Quickmart’s owners are selling half the supermarket chain to the public. But before those new shareholders come on board, the retailer has been cleaning up some old arrangements with the people who built and owned the business.
What happened? Quickmart terminated several consultancy and management contracts with founder- and director-linked businesses in July, months before its initial public offering (IPO). In 2025 alone, Quickmart paid KES 208.4 million ($1.6 million) in management fees to its parent companies, KES 268.7 million ($2.1 million) to Basic Land Investment, and KES 161 million ($1.2 million) to Resource Business Investments.
Those three payments alone came to about KES 638 million ($4.9 million), roughly 43% of Quickmart’s KES 1.5 billion ($11.6 million) net profit that year.
Explain like I’m new here: Founder-linked transactions are not automatically a problem. Private companies often lean on their owners for property, advice, or other services. The calculation changes once strangers are invited to buy shares. Investors want to know that money leaving the company is being spent on the best available terms, not simply routed to insiders.
Between the lines: Ending the contracts makes Quickmart easier to scrutinise as a public company, but it does not mean the entire KES 638 million ($4.9 million) suddenly becomes profit. The retailer may still need some of those services and could pay outside advisers or build the work in-house. The more important change is who gets to decide what those services cost.
Some links to the founders remain. Eighteen Quickmart stores are still leased from businesses connected to founders or directors, though the retailer said those leases are on normal commercial terms.
Zoom out: Governance matters more here because Quickmart itself is not raising money. Its owner, Sokoni Retail Kenya, is selling two billion existing shares for KES 15 billion ($116 million), and will collect the proceeds from the public offer in a much-needed listing for Kenya’s capital market. Quickmart has already opened the offer, with full trading expected by November 12.

True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. Join us on October 28 & 29, 2026. Get your ticket.
E-mobility
Eskom opens its first public EV chargers in Durban, South Africa
Eskom has spent decades keeping South Africa’s lights on, mostly by burning coal. Now, it wants to help keep the country’s electric cars moving, too.
What happened? The state-owned electricity company has opened its first public electric vehicle (EV) charging stations at the Gateway Theatre of Shopping in Umhlanga and The Pavilion Shopping Centre in Durban, South Africa. Eskom’s two new charging stations each have two fast direct-current (DC) charging ports capable of delivering up to 120 kilowatts (kW), plus one alternating-current (AC) port offering up to 22kW.
Explain like I’m new here: Eskom may be best known for generating electricity, but charging electric cars can be a natural extension of that business, using its operating experience with electricity infrastructure to support the growth of electric transport. E.ON, one of Europe’s largest investor-owned electric utility service providers, operates a network of public and home electric vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure across Europe and the UK.
Eskom has been trying its hand at clean business for a while. In August 2024, the company, in partnership with GridCars, a South African charging-network operator, launched a pilot with 10 charging stations across five of its properties, but kept it closed to the general public. In September 2025, it introduced 20 electric vehicles (EVs) and said it wanted to transition its entire fleet to electric by 2035. It also announced plans to roll out 55 public charging stations over two years. Eskom also signed an agreement with BYD, the Chinese car-maker, to support electric mobility and expand public charging infrastructure in South Africa.
From generating power to selling a charge: Eskom is entering the EV charging business, giving it an advantage because it already runs South Africa’s electricity system. Charging operators make money by selling power to drivers, but they also pay for equipment, maintenance, grid connections and demand fees.
Some industry players have raised concerns that Eskom may have offered certain sites lower demand charges, which could let them price charging more cheaply than rivals. Eskom says its pilot pricing follows existing tariffs and regulations.
What does this mean for drivers? Eskom’s new DC chargers cost R5.88 ($0.045) per kilowatt-hour (kWh), compared with R7.35 ($0.057) at GridCars’ public stations, making Eskom’s rates 20% cheaper. For a driver buying 50 kWh of electricity, that means paying R294 ($2.27) at an Eskom station instead of R367.5 ($2.83) at GridCars, the country’s largest EV charging station operator, helping them save about R73.50 ($0.57) on a single charge. Eskom’s lower prices offer drivers a cheaper alternative to existing charging networks, although its ability to compete with established operators will depend on how widely it expands its public charging stations.
South Africa recorded sales of over 16,000 new-energy vehicles in 2025, but expanding its public charging network remains important to making electric driving more practical, especially for drivers who cannot charge at home or travel frequently between cities.
Capital Markets
Investors get a two-week extension to buy into Dangote Refinery shares
The Dangote Refinery initial public offering (IPO), originally scheduled to close on October 13, has been extended by two weeks, Bloomberg reported on Monday. The extension gives retail investors more time to buy shares in the company, amid growing interest from investors in other African countries.
What happened? Dangote Refinery says it has received strong interest from eligible investors across Africa and other markets. The IPO, which opened on September 14, will now remain open until October 27.
Explain like I’m new here: Dangote is giving everyday investors a chance to own a piece of its refinery. Each share costs ₦525 ($0.40), and the company plans to sell 4.1 billion shares to raise ₦2.15 trillion ($1.6 billion). The extra two weeks will allow it to bring in investors from more African countries and complete the arrangements needed for them to buy shares across borders.
Many people want in: In Kenya, Renaissance Capital, a Kenyan investment bank, worked on a new vehicle that would allow Kenyan investors to participate in the IPO through Kenya’s stock exchange, for KES 49 ($0.38) per share. In Zimbabwe, asset manager Bard Santner Investors is facilitating local participation by securing the required approvals and moving clients’ money from Ecobank Zimbabwe to Ecobank Nigeria.
More time, more shares? Not necessarily. The extension gives more investors time to participate; it does not automatically increase the number of shares on offer. Dangote has regulatory approval to sell additional equity if demand warrants it, potentially raising to $2.1 billion, but the company has not said that the extension itself will trigger a larger offer.
What does this mean? The extension gives Dangote more time to increase participation and benefit from the possible cross-border demand in its refinery. Dangote’s IPO has become a major test of how easily investors can buy shares across African borders. Kenya’s route and Zimbabwe’s bank-transfer arrangement show that investors are finding ways in, and Dangote wants a pan-African shareholder base.

articles.title: Laplace Intelligence red-teams robots and self-driving cars before they hit the real world | TechCrunch
articles.text:
If there’s one lesson the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident taught us, it’s that AI agents can be unpredictable.
“Imagine if something like that happened in the physical world,” Howie Sun, CEO and co-founder of Laplace Intelligence, told TechCrunch. “AI agents are moving from computers into the real world, and we don’t really want physical AI to fail in the real world.”
Ann Arbor-based Laplace is building automated red-teaming — essentially, stress-testing a system by deliberately trying to make it fail — for robotics and physical AI. The company is betting that the only way to make sure physical AI is safe is to have AI test it.
“Our goal is to help companies discover and fix problems before deployment — and, over time, build a shared foundation of evidence that customers, insurers, and regulators can trust,” Sun said.
Laplace is one of 20 startups competing in Startup Battlefield 200, the startup pitch competition taking place at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco this week, October 13-15. It will present on the Disrupt Stage Tuesday afternoon, October 13.
Sun, alongside his co-founder and chief scientist Henry Liu, founded Laplace a year ago out of the University of Michigan. Sun has spent the last eight years in academia researching how to challenge autonomous driving AI in simulation. In 2023, he and Liu — his then-PhD adviser — published a paper on the subject that made it onto the cover of the top scientific journal Nature. That’s when the calls started coming in from autonomous vehicle companies interested in implementing their ideas.
“I realized that I wanted to build this and take it from purely academic research into a product that’s useful in the real world,” Sun said.
Using their academic research as a base, Sun and Liu built Laplace, so named for “Laplace’s demon,” an 1814 thought experiment by French scholar Pierre-Simon Laplace, who imagined that if you knew the exact state of everything in the universe, you could predict the future with total precision.
“We are essentially using simulation to predict the real world’s future,” Sun said.
At the startup’s core is a high-fidelity simulation reconstructed from the real world, paired with an AI agent that constantly probes for weaknesses and failure points. The goal is to ensure that any physical AI — be it a robot, autonomous vehicle, or smart city solution — is safe in simulation before it’s deployed in the real world.
The simulation environment is a post-trained version of Nvidia’s Cosmos, an AI world simulation platform, which is grounded in the real world, allowing Laplace to reconstruct anything from an Arizona highway to a Paris pedestrian crossing. Simulations are generated by blending a mesh of different real-world information. A Google Street View image could serve as a reference from which an entire street is generated. But rather than generating something random, the simulator combines real-world map data to re-create an environment that’s true to scale.
Developers can then use language prompts to change the setting in real time, like adding in afternoon traffic. Sun says Laplace pulls real-time traffic and congestion information from navigation providers like TomTom.
Within Laplace’s simulations, not only is the environment simulated, but also the behavior of other actors. For example, during a demo, Sun directed the test agent vehicle to swerve into oncoming traffic. The car it would have hit — or driven through, as is common among some generative world models — moved out of its way to avoid a collision.
“It’s truly an interactive simulation environment,” Sun said. “Everyone is reacting to everything … This is more like a world model with interactive participants.”
While the simulated environment is an important part of Laplace’s product, the real unique selling point is the AI agents the startup is developing to automatically design corner cases (tricky, rare scenarios that could trip up an AI system), moving the human further out of the loop.
“They can design from the news, from police reports on collisions — all kinds of information to actively challenge the autonomous vehicles and other physical AI agents,” Sun said.
Today, autonomous vehicle developers mostly train an AI to handle edge cases using recorded footage that they then turn into a simulation, or by relying on humans to come up with new ideas and design them. While many AV companies have done what Laplace is pitching and started embracing AI to create edge cases for training — self-driving truck company Waabi comes to mind — the need for this kind of technology will really become apparent when we start placing generalized robots in the real world.
“There’s less data on generalized robotics,” Sun said. “No one knows what the edge cases will be in the real world.”
Despite Sun and Liu coming from academia, with no shiny Silicon Valley tech company pedigrees, the two have managed to start generating revenue and even turn a modest profit. Most of the money is coming from autonomous driving use cases, with customers including Japanese trucking manufacturer Isuzu and Texas-based autonomous trucking firm Bot Auto.
Nvidia is also a customer, says Sun. The two companies, alongside T-Mobile, are working together on a free smart city pilot for San Jose, California, to provide high-level traffic operations. Laplace is also in the early stages of working with partners building humanoid robotics for warehouses.
Most of Laplace’s customer contracts are project-based today, and the company is working toward turning that into recurring revenue. The startup’s near-term goal — which it hopes will be aided by competing at Disrupt — is to raise funds and scale so it can compete with its rivals.
Chief among its rivals is Applied Intuition, a buzzy late-stage startup that’s raised $1.2 billion to date at a $15 billion post-money valuation. Isuzu is also one of Applied’s customers.
Sun isn’t too worried. He believes Laplace’s core methodology of using AI to test AI is a “new paradigm that changes the testing of physical AI entirely,” turning it into a “dynamic interactive testing process.”
“That will be the biggest moat,” he said.

articles.title: From Enterprise to Earthshot: UK’s Ecosystem Moves From Ambition to Application With NVIDIA
articles.text:
Across industries, the U.K. is putting the full stack to work — and the scale of deployment is growing fast, from enterprises transforming their businesses to startups solving some of the planet’s hardest problems.
NVIDIA is putting that principle into practice, including through a five-year, $250 million compute commitment to strengthen the U.K.’s agentic safety and security research, providing $50 million in accelerated computing access annually through BOLD at the University of Oxford, SOFAIR at UCL and Imperial College London.
In addition, NVIDIA is partnering with the Earthshot Prize, joining as a Global Alliance Founding Partner to bring compute and technical expertise to innovators working on solutions for the world’s greatest climate and sustainability challenges.
Technology Leaders Pioneer Intelligent Solutions Across the UK
In energy, Fuse Energy is moving its customer AI onto its own in-house infrastructure, built on NVIDIA B300 Blackwell Ultra, delivering faster, more responsive support to over 450,000 U.K. households.
Meanwhile, sovereign AI company Locai Labs released Nemotron-Personas-UK — an open source dataset of one million synthetic personas representing the UK’s demographic, regional and cultural diversity — helping developers build fairer, more representative AI systems.
Healthcare
In healthcare, OneAdvanced is deploying what it calls the U.K.’s first and most advanced fine-tuned LLM for Primary Care AI-triage — built with NVIDIA Agent Toolkit software and open models — supporting millions of National Health Service patients.
Heidi has now integrated NVIDIA Nemotron open models to give clinicians faster access to trusted medical evidence.
Speechmatics is deploying Oak, a multilingual medical speech recognition model, using NVIDIA Triton Inference — giving healthcare organizations control over where sensitive patient audio is processed.
Apian, SYNLAB and NVIDIA are teaming up to use advanced computing and digital simulations using NVIDIA Cosmos to help hospital robots handle the heavy lifting of moving lab samples, freeing up medical staff to focus on patient care.
Danaher and NVIDIA are collaborating to advance autonomous science and help accelerate the pace of discovery by bringing accelerated computing, scientific and physical AI into laboratory workflows and instruments. Danaher’s recently announced AI-powered autonomous lab — designed to deliver up to 8x faster discovery of affinity reagents — is using NVIDIA BioNeMo open models within its AI-driven protein design workflows, data and automation technologies that connect design with experimental feedback.
Smart Cities
On the civic side, Liverpool City Region is building an NVIDIA-powered “City Brain” — a sovereign AI strategy designed as a blueprint for dozens of Unitary Authorities across the U.K.
Digital Jersey, Innovation City Belfast and Tees Valley Combined Authority are each exploring how trusted AI compute can serve communities and public services.
Financial Services
In financial services, LSEG and NVIDIA are bringing GPU-accelerated market analytics to global institutions.
Revolut introduced PRAGMA earlier in the year — a foundation model for banking event sequences, pre-trained on 26 million anonymised user histories. PRAGMA has moved from research to real-time scaling.
Lloyds Banking Group built ATUM, a transaction foundation model that converts billions of banking transactions into reusable AI. And Starling is developing a banking foundation model trained on Civo’s U.K. sovereign cloud infrastructure.
NatWest is collaborating with NVIDIA on Nemotron Voice to better understand how banking customers across the U.K. speak, while Modulr is deploying a network of agents using Nemotron for distinct parts of payment operations.
Quantum
Quantum is moving from research to systems deployable alongside classical AI, and the U.K. is at the heart of this shift.
Riverlane has shown how GPUs can accelerate decoder recalibration workflows used in quantum error correction, helping decoder performance keep pace with real-time changes in quantum hardware behaviour. The work forms part of a broader collaboration exploring how AI, accelerated computing and quantum error-correction technologies can work together to support future quantum systems.
Together, these announcements showcase how enterprises, organizations and startups in the U.K. are fostering innovation across the nation. This includes more than 3,100 U.K. companies that are a part of the NVIDIA Inception program for cutting-edge startups.
Tune in to NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang’s GTC Berlin keynote on Wednesday, Oct. 21, at 11 a.m. CEST.

articles.title: Natural language security queries at Orca Security using Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Natural language security queries at Orca Security using Amazon Bedrock
Security analysts need fast answers about their cloud infrastructure without deep familiarity with domain-specific query languages. Orca Security’s tool covers over 900 cloud models (the resource types Sonar tracks, such as an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance or an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket). Querying that data required precise model names, nested relationship navigation, and selection from 18 operators (comparison functions like equals or contains used to filter results).
To solve this, Orca Security partnered with AWS to build Discovery AI, a natural language query agent on Amazon Bedrock. Orca provides context-aware security for cloud, code, and AI, and Sonar is its domain-specific query system where users search, filter, and explore across the entire data graph.
In this post, we share the architecture and results of Discovery AI, which converts a natural language question into a Sonar query. As a result, Orca reduced query costs by 90 percent, input tokens by 93 percent, and latency by 75 percent compared to the initial baseline.
Bridging natural language and structured queries
Orca Security’s Sonar query system supports 900+ cloud infrastructure and application models with complex relationships between them. To query this data, users construct JSON objects that specify exact model names, select from 18 operators, and navigate parent-child hierarchies across cloud providers. Doing this well requires deep familiarity with the Sonar schema.
To build this capability, the Orca team set out to build a natural language interface that can generate valid Sonar queries from plain text.
Their initial proof of concept loaded the full Sonar schema into a single prompt on the largest available model. This included over 900 model definitions, every relationship type, and a generous set of example queries. The output quality was strong (design partners and internal users responded positively) but three significant drawbacks emerged at production scale.
Token consumption was inefficient, at roughly 2 million input tokens per workload, which drove up cost. Latency was high, with end-to-end response times of around 60 seconds per workload. Accuracy on complex, multi-model queries was limited because nested relationships and multi-condition queries often required additional refinement.
The Orca team validated that the concept worked. The next challenge was making it cost-effective, fast, and accurate enough for production. To address this, the Orca team designed and deployed a solution that handles thousands of queries per day at 15-second response times using Amazon Bedrock.
Solution overview
Orca designed Discovery AI as a hybrid solution on Amazon Bedrock that combines Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) with schema-aware query construction. The system converts natural language questions into valid Discovery filters through a multi-stage pipeline, with each stage matched to the most appropriate Amazon Bedrock model.
Orca chose Amazon Bedrock because it provides multi-model access through a single API, letting the team allocate different foundation models to each pipeline stage without managing separate integrations. Amazon Bedrock also inherits AWS governance controls through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoints, and AWS CloudTrail, meeting Orca’s security requirements. The model-agnostic architecture meant the team could swap in newer model versions as they became available without rearchitecting the pipeline.
The following diagram illustrates the nine-stage pipeline architecture.
The Discovery AI pipeline converts a natural language request into a validated Discovery filter through nine steps.
- Request Entry and Context Setup: The pipeline starts by combining the user’s natural language request with relevant context, including the user’s organization, connected cloud providers, and request metadata. This context helps the pipeline interpret the request accurately and generate a Discovery filter that matches the customer’s environment.
- Quick Deterministic Matcher: The Quick Matcher identifies structured inputs such as IP addresses, Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs), ARNs, file hashes, Amazon Machine Image IDs, Oracle Cloud Identifiers, EC2 IDs, URLs, and alert IDs. It uses regex and rule-based matching to detect high-confidence patterns.When a match is found, the pipeline can return a predefined Discovery filter through a fast path, without using large language model (LLM) inference. When no match is found, the request continues to the next step.
- LLM Guardrail Screening: The Guardrail component checks whether the request is safe, relevant, technical, and supported. It blocks prompt injection attempts, off-topic requests, and unsupported inputs before they reach the rest of the pipeline. Requests that fail the guardrail checks are rejected with an appropriate error. Approved requests continue to example retrieval.
- Embedding-Based Semantic Candidate Recall: The pipeline searches for relevant previously validated query examples using Amazon Titan Text Embeddings. It retrieves the 20 nearest examples from the vector store based on semantic similarity. These candidates provide the pipeline with examples of how similar natural language requests were previously translated into Discovery filters.
- Neural Relevance Reranking: The retrieved candidates are reranked using Cohere Rerank 3.5 on Amazon Bedrock. It identifies the examples that are most relevant to the current request and selects the five highest-signal examples. When an exact or high-confidence match is found, the pipeline can reuse the known-good filter directly. Otherwise, the reranked examples are passed to the generative stages.
- LLM-Driven Relevant Model Selection: Model Selection narrows more than 900 Sonar models to the small set relevant to the request. It considers the user’s request, connected providers, and retrieved examples when selecting the appropriate models. The selected models are provided to the Generator using the appropriate schema level, ranging from compact micro schemas to more detailed mini schemas. This reduces unnecessary context and makes generation more efficient.
- Tool-Augmented Agentic Filter Generation: The Generator uses a tool-augmented agent to construct the final Discovery filter. It reasons over the selected model schemas, retrieved examples, user context, and available tools. The agent can iteratively refine the filter as it works toward a valid representation of the user’s request.
- Static and API-Backed Validation: The generated filter is checked for syntactic and semantic correctness. The pipeline first applies static validation and then verifies the filter against Orca’s Sonar API. When validation fails, the validation error is returned to the Generator so the agent can correct the filter and try again. If the maximum number of retries is reached without producing a valid filter, the pipeline returns an invalid-filter response. The Generator is constrained to the reranked examples and selected schemas. Static validation resolves every model, field, and operator back to those schema definitions. Each validation error goes back to the agent with the offending element identified, so retries re-ground rather than re-guess.
- Post-Processing and Response: After a valid filter is produced, whether through the Quick Matcher, reuse of a known-good example, or agentic generation, the pipeline prepares the final response.The team allocated different foundation models on Amazon Bedrock across components based on each stage’s requirements. Anthropic Claude Haiku 4.5 powers the Model Selector and Generator. These components require strong reasoning for accurate query construction. Amazon Nova 2 Lite handles the Guardrail and Validator, where fast inference at lower cost is prioritized. Amazon Titan provides embeddings for semantic search in the Example Retrieval component. Cohere Rerank 3.5 reranks retrieved candidates to maximize relevance. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Regional availability by models.
Maximizing relevance and diversity in example retrieval
Example retrieval emerged as the single biggest accuracy lever in the pipeline. Strong examples teach the Generator how to translate questions into Sonar queries more efficiently than schema alone, so the Orca team benchmarked several retrieval strategies on Amazon Bedrock. Each strategy traded off relevance, diversity, or speed in a different way, and comparing them directly showed which combination worked best.
Pure top-K semantic search on Amazon Titan embeddings performed quickly, but it tended to return near-duplicate examples that starved the Generator of diversity. Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) improved diversity, but it traded off relevance when the top candidate was actually the right answer. Retrieving a larger candidate set and then reranking it pulled in a broader pool and used a reranker to select the most relevant subset, which pointed toward the winning approach.
The winner was top-20 nearest-neighbor retrieval using Amazon Titan embeddings. Orca then reranked these results with Cohere Rerank 3.5 down to the top five. This approach gives the Generator a small, diverse, highly relevant set of examples without forcing a trade-off between coverage and precision at retrieval time.
Loading over 900 models into context
A core constraint shaped the architecture. It wasn’t feasible to include 900+ Sonar model schemas into every prompt. Even with long-context models, doing so degrades both cost and accuracy.
The Model Selector resolves this. Running on Anthropic Claude Haiku 4.5, it works against compact, semantically rich representations of each model (name, purpose, key fields, and key relationships). Given the user’s question, it returns only the models the Generator actually needs. The Generator then receives full schema detail only for those selected models plus the relationships that connect them.
Evaluation methodology
To iterate confidently, the Orca team built a continuous evaluation harness early in the project. The harness combines a curated dataset, an automated scoring layer, and a slice-based measurement approach so the team can trust every change before it ships. Together these elements turn evaluation into a routine step rather than an afterthought.
The curated evaluation dataset spans the question types, model families, and complexity tiers seen in production, so it reflects real usage. An LLM-as-judge scoring layer grades generated queries on correctness, completeness, and semantic equivalence to a reference query, which gives the team a consistent quality signal. The measurement methodology then breaks deltas down by slice, allowing the team to identify exactly where regressions occur and what to correct.
Every change to a prompt, a model, a retrieval parameter, or an example flows through the harness before it ships to production.
Domain-expert-in-the-loop labeling system for continuous improvement
Sustaining accuracy as customer environments evolve and new question patterns emerge required more than a strong initial deployment. The Orca team built an internal labeling tool for product managers, support engineers, and security researchers. With the tool, they can flag queries, correct outputs, and push corrections into the example bank in one action. Furthermore, the system automatically collects production queries with low-confidence matching examples and routes them to the appropriate domain expert for daily labeling. The next pipeline run retrieves the new example through Cohere Rerank 3.5, and accuracy on that class of question improves the same moment, with no deployment.
        “The labeling UI is the single most important investment we made for long-term quality. It turns Discovery AI from a static deployment into a living system, with our domain experts continuously improving it inside their normal workflow.”
— Or Gabay, Director of AI, Orca Security
Combined with end-to-end pipeline observability and shared dashboards spanning product, engineering, and customer-facing teams, this feedback loop is what keeps Discovery AI improving after initial launch.
Results
After deploying Discovery AI to production, the new solution outperformed the initial baseline across cost, latency, and accuracy. Input token usage fell by 93 percent, from approximately 2 million tokens down to 140,000 per comparable workload. Overall cost fell by 90 percent, driven by that lower token consumption together with per-stage model allocation across Amazon Bedrock.
Latency also improved, with end-to-end response times dropping by 75 percent, from approximately 60 seconds to 15 seconds. Accuracy on complex, multi-model queries also improved, measured continuously through the team’s evaluation harness.
Discovery AI now handles thousands of queries per day in production since March 2026, with internal subject matter experts and customer feedback validating quality.
Conclusion
In this post, we shared how Orca Security built Discovery AI on Amazon Bedrock. The solution reduced query costs by 90 percent, input token usage by 93 percent, and latency by 75 percent compared to the initial baseline. The solution combines several key technologies. These include RAG-based example retrieval with Cohere Rerank 3.5, per-stage model allocation across Anthropic Claude Haiku 4.5 and Amazon Nova 2 Lite, and semantic search powered by Amazon Titan. Additionally, a continuous human-in-the-loop labeling system provides ongoing improvement. This combination allowed Orca to turn a working prototype into a production-grade solution that is both cheaper to run and more accurate.
To get started building similar solutions, explore Amazon Bedrock for foundation model (FM) access, Cohere Rerank on Amazon Bedrock for retrieval optimization, and Amazon Titan for embeddings. To learn more about Orca Security’s cloud security tool, visit orca.security.
To learn more about how Orca Security applies AI across its framework, see how Orca drives security outcomes with AI and how Orca secures AI adoption, including Amazon Bedrock.
For more on the techniques used in this post, read related posts on the AWS Machine Learning Blog.

articles.title: Estados Unidos autorizó a los camiones sin conductor a prescindir de los triángulos de advertencia
articles.text:
La Administración Federal de Seguridad de Transportistas de Carga por Carretera de Estados Unidos, la agencia que regula a los camiones de carga interestatales, otorgó una exención de cinco años a Aurora Innovation y Kodiak AI para que sus camiones sin conductor dejen de usar los triángulos reflectantes de advertencia en la ruta.
La exención rige desde el 7 de octubre de 2026 hasta el 7 de octubre de 2031 y resuelve un obstáculo que frenaba la operación comercial a gran escala de camiones autónomos en rutas estadounidenses.
La norma vigente hasta ahora obliga al conductor de un camión averiado a activar las balizas de emergencia y colocar triángulos reflectantes alrededor del vehículo dentro de los diez minutos posteriores a detenerse en la banquina. El problema es evidente para un camión que no lleva a nadie al volante: no hay quien baje a colocarlos.
Qué cambia con la nueva norma en Estados Unidos
Con la exención, los camiones autónomos de nivel 4, es decir aquellos que conducen todo el trayecto por sí solos dentro de condiciones predefinidas, podrán usar balizas color ámbar instaladas en la cabina, orientadas hacia adelante y hacia atrás.
Esas luces deberán activarse dentro de los cinco minutos posteriores a la detención del camión, un plazo más corto que los diez minutos permitidos para que un conductor humano coloque los triángulos. Deberán contar con una fuente de energía redundante y mantenerse encendidas junto con las balizas de emergencia estándar del vehículo.
La autorización no se limita a Aurora: cualquier otro operador de camiones de nivel 4 puede sumarse si notifica previamente a la agencia y certifica que cumple con todas las condiciones técnicas exigidas.
Cuál fue el camino judicial hasta la exención
Aurora había llevado a los reguladores a la Justicia después de que un primer pedido de exención fuera rechazado. Tras ese revés, la empresa escaló el reclamo ante la Corte de Apelaciones del Distrito de Columbia.
Mientras el litigio seguía su curso, la compañía operó bajo exenciones temporales sucesivas que la agencia fue renovando. Con esos permisos provisorios, Aurora recorrió más de 500.000 millas (unos 800.000 kilómetros) con 34 camiones entre octubre de 2025 y enero de 2026.
Durante ese período, las balizas estuvieron encendidas durante casi diez horas en total. La empresa no reportó fallas, mal funcionamiento ni problemas de energía, y la agencia confirmó que ninguno de esos camiones estuvo involucrado en choques mientras circulaba con las luces activadas.
La agencia revisó estudios que compararon el comportamiento de otros conductores frente a las balizas y frente a los triángulos tradicionales. Encontró que los automovilistas comenzaban a frenar o cambiar de carril más lejos del camión detenido cuando veían las balizas, y que de noche generaban frenados más tempranos y menor velocidad de paso.
Qué dicen las voces detrás de las empresas
Daniel Goff, vicepresidente de asuntos externos de Kodiak AI, dijo que la exención ayudará a la industria a “inaugurar una era autónoma del transporte de mercancías en las rutas de Estados Unidos, una que puede salvar vidas y mejorar la eficiencia de la entrega de bienes”.
Gerardo Interiano, responsable de relaciones gubernamentales y asuntos públicos de Aurora, coincidió en que la decisión refleja el reconocimiento del gobierno a los beneficios económicos y comunitarios del transporte autónomo.
Describió las balizas instaladas en la cabina como “una solución del siglo XXI que mejora la seguridad vial al alertar de inmediato a otros usuarios de la ruta, sin necesidad de poner nunca a una persona en riesgo”.
La agencia impuso obligaciones de control permanente: los operadores deberán reportar cualquier choque ocurrido mientras las balizas estaban o debían estar encendidas, y presentar informes anuales sobre fallas del sistema hasta que la exención expire en 2031.
Cuál es la visión en contra
La decisión no fue unánime. Durante el proceso, la agencia recibió 402 comentarios públicos antes de resolver el pedido de Aurora.
La Asociación Estadounidense de Transportistas de Carga y la Asociación de la Industria de Vehículos Autónomos apoyaron la exención, al igual que Waymo, que también había pedido en el pasado un alivio regulatorio similar junto a Aurora.
En contra se manifestaron la Asociación de Propietarios y Operadores Independientes, que representa a camioneros que son dueños de su propio vehículo, sumado a dos organizaciones dedicadas a la seguridad vial: Advocates for Highway and Auto Safety y Truck Safety Coalition.
La propia agencia reconoció en su resolución que no existe evidencia que demuestre que los triángulos reflectantes mejoren de forma sustancial el tiempo de reacción de otros conductores, lo que respaldó su decisión de aceptar una alternativa distinta para los camiones sin conductor.
Kodiak AI ya había comenzado a usar su tecnología en una ruta comercial de 435 millas (700 kilómetros) entre Dallas y Laredo, en Texas, donde transporta productos de consumo y mercadería refrigerada junto a la empresa de transporte Charger USA.
La exención federal no habilita una operación sin restricciones en cualquier ruta: cada camión debe mantenerse dentro del dominio operativo validado para su sistema autónomo, y quedan excluidas las cargas peligrosas y el transporte de pasajeros.

articles.title: Así es HomeView, la última pantalla inteligente de Apple para controlar los hogares con su nueva IA
articles.text: HomeView, el nuevo dispositivo inteligente de Apple estará disponible el 13 de noviembre en cuatro colores diferentes Apple ha llegado varios años tarde a la carrera de la IA generativa y pretende recuperar terreno donde flaquean sus rivales, que todavía no han sido capaces de lanzar dispositivos que lleven ChatGPT, Gemini o Claude más allá del móvil, la tableta o el ordenador. El gigante tecnológico ha presentado este martes HomeView, una nueva pantalla táctil diseñada específicamente para Siri AI —su asistente de inteligencia artificial de nueva generación—, con el objetivo de llevarla a los hogares y convertirla en el panel de control de todo tipo de dispositivos inteligentes. Además de esa función de central domótica, reconoce la cara de cada usuario de la casa para darle acceso, en pantalla y por voz, a la información personal de sus mensajes, calendarios o recordatorios. También sirve como un marco digital compartido por la familia y para poner música, podcasts, vídeos y programas de televisión. Seguir leyendo

articles.title: Nikolas Bullwinkel, Circus Group founder & CEO, joins the EU-Startups Summit 2027 | EU-Startups
articles.text:
We’re excited to announce that Nikolas Bullwinkel, Founder and CEO of Circus Group, will join us at the EU-Startups Summit 2027, taking place on May 13-14 in sunny Malta! Nikolas will deliver the keynote AI robotics and how Europe can scale DeepTech from lab to market.
Nikolas is a serial entrepreneur currently building at the intersection of artificial intelligence, robotics, and autonomous infrastructure. Through Munich-based Circus, he is working to automate one of the world’s most fundamental activities: producing meals.
The company develops AI-powered robotic systems designed to autonomously prepare food for enterprise customers across commercial, industrial, and defence environments.
Drawing on his experience building both Flink and Circus, he’ll explore what it takes to turn ambitious European technology into commercially viable products, move from prototypes to industrial production, and compete globally in the emerging field of Physical AI.
His Story
Before founding Circus, Nikolas was one of the co-founders of Flink, the Berlin-based quick-commerce company that became one of Europe’s fastest-growing delivery startups. During its rapid expansion, Flink grew to around 12,000 employees and more than 140 locations, while a €669 million ($750 million) funding round in December 2021 valued the company at €2.5 billion ($2.85 billion) post-money.
Nikolas subsequently turned his attention towards AI and robotics.
He founded Circus in 2021 alongside Carsten Wille, Helge Plehn, and Fabio Haebel. The company initially set out to rethink food production and delivery through technology, automation, and its own micro-kitchen infrastructure.
By 2022, EU-Startups reported that Circus had secured €11 million in investment and expanded its services across several German cities.
A major step in its evolution came with the acquisition of Berlin-based culinary robotics startup Aitme in 2023, bringing robotics expertise and automated cooking technology directly into Circus. The following year, Circus completed its Xetra listing and began trading on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange, marking its transition into a publicly listed European DeepTech company.
Today, Circus is focused on its CA-1 autonomous food-production robot, combining robotics, proprietary AI, software, and automation into a system capable of producing meals with minimal human intervention. Its technology is being developed for a range of civilian and defence applications, with Nikolas continuing to lead the company as CEO.
EU-Startups Summit
On May 13-14, 2027, we’ll be bringing the European startup ecosystem together once again for the EU-Startups Summit in sunny Malta. We’re expecting around 2,500 founders, investors, startup enthusiasts, and ecosystem players for two packed days of networking, inspiration, and learning.
The event will showcase many of Europe’s hottest startups and bring attendees face-to-face with some of the most successful entrepreneurs and innovators of our time. With inspiring keynotes, fireside chats, workshops, a buzzing exhibition hall, and plenty of opportunities to make valuable connections, it is set to be another unmissable edition.
Ready to join us?: Secure your ticket to the EU-Startups Summit 2027 today!

articles.title: Apple presenta HomeView, su nueva apuesta para adueñarse del hogar inteligente
articles.text:
Apple acaba de presentar HomeView, su nuevo hub para controlar el hogar inteligente. Los de Cupertino no solo se meten en una nueva categoría de producto, sino que aspiran a darle batalla a propuestas ya establecidas como el Amazon Echo Show o el Google Nest Hub. Para ello sacan a relucir todas las capacidades de su ecosistema de software y hardware.
El HomeView de Apple equipa una pantalla táctil de 7 pulgadas y llega en dos variantes. Por un lado, una versión que se puede colgar en la pared; por el otro, con el panel acoplado a una base metálica que funciona como altavoz y que le permite residir sobre una mesa o cualquier otro mueble. Esta última cuenta con un brazo que permite ajustar la inclinación de la pantalla.
El nuevo dispositivo de la manzana puede llevar a cabo una gran cantidad de tareas y no se limita a ser el centro de control del hogar inteligente. Si bien el HomeView podrá controlar otros dispositivos conectados como termostatos, luces, persianas, timbres, etc., también servirá para ver fotos y vídeos, hacer videollamadas, escuchar música, pódcast y audiolibros, y más. Además, sacará provecho de la integración con Siri AI para aprovecharlo como asistente personal.
Quienes tengan una suscripción a iCloud+ podrán acceder a la función de reconocimiento de personas conocidas, paquetes, vehículos y mascotas al conectar HomeView con una cámara compatible. De acuerdo con Apple, esta característica funciona con cifrado de extremo a extremo para proteger la privacidad de los individuos y los datos procesados.
HomeView, el primer hub para el hogar inteligente de Apple
Un detalle interesante de HomeView es que puede reconocer hasta 6 usuarios diferentes y cambiar la apariencia de la pantalla de inicio, así como los widgets y las aplicaciones disponibles. Si bien el nuevo dispositivo de Apple no cuenta con acceso a la App Store, sí llega con algunas de las apps más importantes de la compañía (Mensajes, Apple Music, FaceTime, Calendar, etc.).
Apple menciona que al usar HomeView emparejado con un dispositivo compatible con Apple Intelligence, puede acceder al contexto personal del usuario. Vale aclarar que ese contexto personal no está disponible para todas las personas que utilizan el hub inteligente, sino que se mantendrá en privado solo para quien corresponda.
Apple ha dotado al HomeView de un chip A18 con Enclave Seguro. Esto significa que la información que ingresa por el micrófono y/o la cámara se procesan por separado del resto del sistema. Este sistema dividido en compartimientos ayuda a garantizar la privacidad de esos datos, impidiendo su acceso a terceros (incluyendo Apple).
Respecto del uso de Siri AI, algunas de las solicitudes de los usuarios se procesan de modo 100 % local, con modelos de inteligencia artificial que se ejecutan dentro del dispositivo. Sin embargo, para las tareas o consultas que requieren de mayor poder de procesamiento, HomeView se conecta con Private Cloud Compute, la red de servidores de Apple, pero sin poner en riesgo la privacidad de la información.
Una interfaz conocida
El software del HomeView de Apple llega con muchos elementos ya conocidos de las demás plataformas de la compañía. Si alguna vez usaste un iPhone o un Apple Watch, verás que la interfaz del nuevo dispositivo tiene varios puntos en común con la de dichos productos. El hub inteligente incluso permite seleccionar entre diferentes diseños, algunos similares a la pantalla de bloqueo del iPhone y otros más parecidos a una esfera del Apple Watch.
La idea de Apple es que HomeView sea fácil de usar, tanto con la voz como con los comandos táctiles. Y la posibilidad de utilizar el dispositivo apoyado sobre la mesa como montado en una pared, le brinda a los usuarios una versatilidad interesante pensando en la posibilidad de tener varios en la casa. Tengamos en cuenta que incluso es posible usar el aparato como intercomunicador entre las diferentes habitaciones del hogar.
Tal y como se rumoreaba, Apple también ha aprovechado para lanzar una línea de dispositivos para el hogar inteligente en colaboración con LG y Schneider Electric. Los productos en cuestión incluyen varios modelos de timbres con cámara, termostatos y cerraduras electrónicas. Todos estos, compatibles con el nuevo HomeView, por supuesto.
Disponibilidad y precio del Apple HomeView, con malas noticias para Europa
La disponibilidad inicial del HomeView será limitada, pues Apple lo lanzará primero en seis países: Estados Unidos, Reino Unido, Canadá, Australia, Nueva Zelanda e India. En dichos mercados se pueden reservar desde hoy, con las entregas comenzando el próximo 13 de noviembre. El dispositivo también llegará a Singapur y Sudáfrica. Sin embargo, hay malas noticias para quienes viven en la Unión Europea.
En la letra pequeña del anuncio, Apple ha informado que HomeView no se pondrá a la venta en la UE debido a la ausencia de Siri AI en el iPhone en la región. Así que si estás en España o cualquiera de los demás países que conforman el bloque, son muy malas noticias. Es lógico pensar que el nuevo hub inteligente llegará eventualmente a la Unión Europea, pero todavía es imposible saber cuándo. "Apple está trabajando constructivamente con la UE en un intento de encontrar una solución", indican los de Cupertino.
Respecto del preci0, tanto el HomeView con base como la versión para colgar tienen un precio de 299 dólares en Estados Unidos. La segunda opción necesita una montura para la pared que se vende por separado, con opciones que inician en los 59,95 dólares. Pero esto no es todo.
Ninguno de los modelos HomeView tienen batería integrada, así que funcionan enchufados. El modelo con base incluye el adaptador de corriente en la caja, pero la variante para colgar no. De modo que si eliges esta última tendrás que comprar el adaptador USB-C por separado o utilizar algún otro que ya tengas disponible en tu casa.
El HomeView con base se encuentra disponible en cuatro colores: plata, blanco estrella, rose pink y gris espacial. La opción para montar en la pared solo se consigue en gris espacial y plata.

articles.title: Jackery's Explorer 1000 V2 is our top pick for power outages at $519
articles.text:
'One of the best portable power stations': The Jackery Explorer 1000 V2 is our top pick for power outage prep at $519
This reliable off-grid unit has a 1070Wh capacity, 1500W output, and fast charging
The Jackery Explorer 1000 V2 is one of our favorite off-grid power units. Combining a 1070Wh battery, 1500W output, and fast charging, we called it "one of the best portable power stations around, a solid choice and one of the most robust and reliable options available," after testing this one out.
That 1070Wh capacity means it can run a range of everyday electronics, while the unit delivers 1500W of continuous AC output, with a 3000W surge rating for devices that require more power when starting.
• Best for: Homeowners preparing for power outages, campers, RV owners, and anyone needing portable electricity for laptops, phones, small appliances, and other compatible devices.
• The deal: The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 Portable Power Station in Dune White is now $519 (was $589) at Jackery. Don't want white? The black model is also on sale at $499 (was $559).
Today's top Jackery portable power station deal
This Dune White version of the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 features a 1070Wh LiFePO4 battery, 1500W AC output, three AC outlets, dual USB-C ports, USB-A charging, optional solar input, and a five-year warranty for buyers.
Black model: now $499 (was $559).
Why we recommend it
In his 4.5-star review, our expert Alastair said the Jackery Explorer 1000 V2's "feature set makes it an ideal choice for anyone needing mains-style power away from the home or office and will run most domestic appliances up to 1500W without issue. What's more, the added features make it a durable choice when working off-site, as well as packing in features that make it a great choice for home power backup with UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply) technology."
There are three AC outlets, two USB-C ports, a USB-A port, and a 12V car outlet. One USB-C port supports up to 100W output, the second offers up to 30W, and the USB-A port provides up to 18W.
Emergency Super Charge mode can top up the battery from 0% to 100% in an hour, and the power station uses LiFePO4 battery chemistry, with the cells rated for 4000 charging cycles before capacity falls to 70% of the original level. Its ChargeShield 2.0 protection system is designed to manage charging and battery safety, and you get a five-year warranty.
You can recharge the power station using compatible solar panels, including Jackery's bifacial 200W panels, making it useful for longer outdoor trips.
Price context & historical value
The Dune White Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 has dropped from $589 to $519, giving you a $70 saving (approximately 12%). There's also a Black version of the power station with the same features. This sells for $559 and is currently priced at $499, a $60 saving.
This isn't an all-time low though, as the Explorer 1000 v2 was available for $449 last year. For more options, take a look at our roundup of the best portable power stations we've tested.
Should you buy it?
✅ Buy the Dune White Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 if...
You want a portable backup power source for essential electronics during outages, camping trips, or other situations where mains electricity isn't guaranteed. The 1070Wh battery and 1500W output can power a wide range of compatible devices.
❌ Skip the Dune White Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 if...
You need to run high-power appliances such as large electric heaters that exceed the 1500W continuous output limit. For occasional smartphone or laptop charging, a smaller and less expensive portable power station would be better.

articles.title: AI Turns Familiar Cyberattacks Into a Race Against Time
articles.text:
In the AI era, phishing remains the top attack vector in both use (17% of breaches) and breach costs (averaging at $5.29 per breach) according to the IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report 2026. AI creates more personalized content for phishing with higher success rates. At the same time, AI can identify vulnerabilities, use the phished entry point and elevate privileges for lateral movement at greater speed.
None of this is new – cyberattacks haven’t changed with AI. “It just allows attackers to do the same familiar things much faster and at greater scale than ever before. The pressure comes from minimizing the time for defenders to respond,” says Steve Wallin, director of core integration and R&D labs leader at IBM UK.
For now, AI-generated attacks are still in the minority – little more than 20% of all attacks. But the writing (written by AI) is on the wall, and it is incumbent on enterprises to improve their security defenses now before the tsunami arrives in full.
SecurityWeek talked to Wallin on how enterprises should respond to this growing AI threat. Again, it is nothing new – it must just be done better.
It starts with a basic maxim that is as old as the ancient Delphic Oracle: ‘know thyself’. “Organizations must understand their existing security posture. The key to defending against this increasing volume of attacks and decreasing time to respond is again nothing new. It means focusing on proactive rather than reactive defense. It is security by design from the ground up rather than a bolt-on reaction,” said Wallin.
Proactive cyberdefense is a combination of understanding how attacks work, understanding the enterprise infrastructure and business, and being prepared for all possibilities.
“Zero trust is fundamental to stay in control of credentials, access, and enterprise data. You can no longer build a moat or wall around the infrastructure, so zero trust security by design must be built into the infrastructure, the applications, the API entry points, and the data management,” said Wallin. “This can only be achieved with a full understanding of what is important to the business.”
Interestingly, the father of zero trust, John Kindervag, has published a new book titled Cyber Resilience at Machine Speed: The Zero Trust Model for the AI Era. “Any AI-generated packet still has to move across the same network that attackers have always had to traverse – and correctly implemented zero trust can still halt it,” he told SecurityWeek. He echoes Wallin’s view: the principles of cybersecurity have not been altered by the arrival of AI-driven cyberattacks.
The only thing that has really changed is the statistical likelihood of a breach. This likelihood increases the need for resilience. But if defense starts from the position of ‘know thyself’, the enterprise will understand its key areas. Defensive use of AI can help here. “It is increasingly difficult for everything to be completely free of all unknown vulnerabilities. We can use AI to help us with prioritization, and risk management. We can use it to automate, to discover and to understand, so that we can continuously improve the environments that we’re running as an organization.”
This still doesn’t guarantee that a catastrophic breach won’t happen, so resilience must also include recovery of damaged data to ensure business continuity. This isn’t new, just more pressing – a cyber vault backup facility is necessary. This can be built internally using air-gapping and WORM technology; or acquired externally. The IBM Z mainframe, for example, offers a cyber vault designed for high-end workloads such as banking and core financial services, using automated validation, forensic tools, and immutable backups to test and recover corrupted data rapidly.
AI hasn’t changed the fundamentals of cybersecurity, it has simply made good cybersecurity by design, resilience and recovery more important.
