articles.title: Pluto Security raises $42M as AI gives enterprise security teams a new headache | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The problem with giving everyone in a company access to AI tools is that people will use them in unexpected ways. And that fact is steadily seeding fears that companies now have new, gaping security holes in their systems or, at least, will soon.
Illustrating the pace of AI tool adoption within enterprises driving such fears, Shahar Bahat, CEO and co-founder of Pluto Security, says a newly announced AI tool can show up inside companies’ environment within a mere two hours of its release. And about 60% of the risks her company detects across its customer base are in tools vibe-coded by non-developers: Finance departments are the biggest source of such risks, she told TechCrunch, followed by marketing and legal teams. Developers rank fourth, she said.
Her startup’s tools apparently found a vibe-coded app made by a finance employee at a Fortune 500 company to manage customer information and churn, but the app was left exposed to the internet.
Pluto, fresh out of stealth with $42 million in funding, is the latest in a new crop of security startups that have quickly sprung up to help companies address those fears gaps, and all of them are raising big money from investors on the back of the conviction that only using existing security software to monitor and control AI tools, connectors, and usage is a square-peg-round-hole approach.
Bahat tells TechCrunch her startup started selling only in April and has already found some takers for its tech, which helps companies gain context, risk analysis, visibility, and control over how their employees use AI tools. She said Pluto began selling in April and has already crossed $2 million in annual recurring revenue, with more than 30 enterprise customers, including Oscar Health, Workato, Sixt, and AlphaSense.
Pluto’s funding spans an $8.5 million seed round led by TLV Partners, with cybersecurity firm Armis’ founders also investing. The company recently raised a Series A of $34 million led by Jump Capital, with Skinos (Check Point co-founder Shlomo Kramer’s venture firm), Ansa Capital, and other angel investors participating.
That’s decent traction for a young startup, though not unique in this AI era. But it may be because the breadth of the risk isn’t isolated to large tech companies that lead the AI adoption charts.
When I asked Bahat where she’s seeing the biggest risks, she said the issues are differentiated by the mindset of the CISO and how willing the organization is to adopt AI, but there were risks to be found anyway.
“In general, I’ll say there was not one POC in which we entered and didn’t find malicious stuff,” she said. “Whether those are extension packages or skills — some of them had active live attacks while we did the POC. Which again, for me, product-wise is amazing. For the companies, it’s not very good.”
Pluto’s entire bet is that securing such environments will require security tools to pay attention to what AI agents are doing in real time, in addition to keeping track of what and how employees are building and deploying.
“We’re moving from user behavior to agent behavior,” Bahat said.
In line with that vision, the startup’s software monitors the AI tools employees use, the skills, extensions, MCP servers, and other components those tools rely on, as well as the apps and agents being created. The company says it can identify risky components, spot potentially dangerous agent activity, and enforce security policies without stopping employees from using or making AI tools.
To do all that, Pluto connects to endpoint security and device management systems and can deploy its own sensors through them or directly onto devices. It gathers information, including prompts, commands, running processes, permissions, and users’ previous activity, and uses its own “lightweight” models on endpoints to help assess what an agent is trying to do.
What stood out is that Pluto’s system can intervene while an agent is working, Bahat said. If an agent tries to gain permissions beyond what a user intended, for example, the system can stop the action or add instructions into the session that prompt the agent to ask for confirmation.
“We can inject context back to the session, and this way I can change how the agent is working,” Bahat explained.
The startup also takes an unusual approach to finding customers. In April, it launched Plutonium, a free platform that lets anyone check risks associated with publicly available AI skills, connectors, and add-ons. There’s also an MCP scanner and a catalog of verified components. Bahat claims thousands of security professionals use Plutonium and that the community around it has become an important source of feedback and prospective customers.
She said 70% of Pluto’s sales pipeline now comes from inbound interest, although she didn’t break down how much of that comes directly through Plutonium.
Pluto said it plans to invest the new capital in developing its product, expanding its security research efforts, and growing its presence in the U.S. It has 40 employees in the U.S. and Israel.

articles.title: Lightspeed lays off staff as part of “organizational changes” | BetaKit
articles.text:
Lightspeed Commerce has laid off staff and closed vacant roles at the company, impacting a total of 250 roles.
The news: Last week, multiple former Lightspeed employees across content and sales roles announced on LinkedIn that they had been laid off. When reached for comment by BetaKit, the Montréal-based e-commerce and point-of-sale company confirmed the “organizational changes” and said that 250 roles across the company were impacted, including “vacant roles that are being closed.” The company did not break down how many of those jobs were cut compared to how many roles were no longer open.
From the source: “These decisions support Lightspeed’s long-term objective of growing responsibly and profitably so we can continue to invest in our business, our products, and the customers we serve,” a Lightspeed spokesperson wrote to BetaKit in an email on Friday.
The context: Founded in 2005, Lightspeed sells point-of-sale and commerce software and hardware to restaurants, retailers, and hospitality providers. Since last year, the company has been executing a transformation plan to focus on two key markets: North American retail and European hospitality.
The company has tried to balance growth and profitability in part to raise its share price, which never regained its 2021 zero-interest-rate period high. It dropped from a peak of $159 CAD on the Toronto Stock Exchange in September 2021 to a third of its value in three months, and now hovers around $15 CAD.
Final thought: Lightspeed also made roughly 100 job cuts earlier this year, across a team of about 2,000 people, to find further efficiencies in the business, CEO Dax Dasilva told BetaKit in July. In March, the company divested a US hospitality business unit and has told The Globe and Mail that it’s open to more divestitures. A Lightspeed spokesperson said the company would share more details about its organizational changes on Nov. 5 when it reports its fiscal second-quarter earnings.

articles.title: Russian bot farms are still trolling, even after Ukraine’s drone strikes on Yandex
articles.text:
Days after Ukrainian military drones took down several Russian data centers, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed that the campaign had hurt Russia’s disinformation efforts. “It suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social platforms,” Zelenskyy said Monday. “There was less hate, less division, and fewer provocations.”
Russian bot farms are still trolling, even after Ukraine’s drone strikes on Yandex
Zelenskyy celebrated ‘less division’ on social media after the strikes but the data isn’t backing that up yet.
Zelenskyy isn’t the first to assert that the drone operation, which targeted data centers belonging to the Russian technology company Yandex, has cut down on spam and disinformation campaigns fomented by Russian bot farms. Social media users have claimed they’ve noticed less traffic on posts by MAGA-affiliated accounts, as well as those associated with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party. Some have even said they’ve noticed a steep drop in spam calls and messages.
But these people are wrong. The drone strikes appear to have affected Yandex’s web crawlers, not any disinformation or political operations.
In fact, the account antibot4navalny, which tracks state-sponsored troll farms, reports that bot traffic is steady as ever. On Monday, the same day Zelenskyy claimed that disinformation had died down, antibot4navalny reported that several Kremlin-aligned accounts posted videos falsely claiming that experts are demanding the European Union lift the ongoing sanctions on Russia. Danish analyst Valdemar Osted said interactions on MAGA and AfD accounts have actually increased since the strikes. And the charts purportedly showing a decline in bot activity appear to be AI-generated.
Ironically, claims that the drone strikes hindered Russian disinformation campaigns appears to be a form of disinformation itself, no matter what Zelenskyy says.

articles.title: Rivian partner Mind Robotics hires Doug Field as president
articles.text:
Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe’s startup Mind Robotics announced the appointment of Doug Field as president in a major coup for the CEO’s secretive robotics project.
Rivian partner Mind Robotics hires Doug Field as president
Ford’s former EV and software chief will run Rivian’s robotics startup at a time of maximum hype for physical AI.
Field was a VP of special projects at Apple, where he was the de facto head of the company’s ultimately unsuccessful Project Titan effort to make an autonomous electric car. He had a previous stint at Apple as VP of Mac hardware engineering, but he left the company in 2013 to become Tesla’s chief vehicle engineer, where he helped oversee the Model 3 sedan. He left Tesla in 2018 and rejoined Apple. In 2021, Field was hired by Ford to run the automaker’s electric vehicle and software division, a position he held until earlier this year.
Mind Robotics said Field will oversee its effort to build “universally capable robots” for the purpose of working in Rivian’s factories, as well as other applications. The startup was founded by Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe in 2025, and has since raised over $1 billion in financing. While the company has yet to show off any of its robots in public, the startup says its robots are being designed with “dexterity and physical reasoning” that’s required for industrial work.
“Doug is a remarkable leader with a track record of delivering new technologies in successful products, and I couldn’t be more excited to be building Mind with him,” Scaringe said in a statement. “He has an incredible ability to foster great teams that take on big, complex ideas and deliver products that reset expectations. That’s exactly what Mind needs as we deploy robots into real factories and beyond.”
Field joins Mind Robotics at a major turning point for the field of robotics, with rapid advances in physical AI colliding with major hurdles in hardware and software development. Several companies, like Tesla and Hyundai, are pursuing humanoid robots for factory and warehouse work — even as experts note that making a robot act like a human is easier than scaling the technology for practical work. Mind Robotics hasn’t confirmed whether it’s working on a humanoid design or something else entirely. The company has been on a hiring spree and currently has 32 open positions.
Scaringe, who serves as acting CEO and chair of Mind Robotics, has said he wants to keep the companies separate, rather than try to combine the work like Tesla. That said, the companies are certainly linked in several ways. Mind Robotics is using AI training data from Rivian, and the robots will be initially tested in Rivian’s factories. Rivian also owns equity in Mind Robotics and will be the first customer for its robots.
Field said he is excited for the challenge in running the new startup.
“Integrating AI and robotics is one of the most important—and difficult—engineering challenges of our time,” he said in a statement. “Mind has assembled an exceptional team and has a unique advantage: the ability to deploy and learn inside a real, high-volume factory from day one. I’m thrilled to join RJ in building a team, culture, and technology that will redefine what we can make in America.”
Correction October 13th: Mind Robotics is a partner of Rivian, but not a spinoff. A previous version of this story misstated the relationship between the companies.

articles.title: NVIDIA Run:ai Is Now Open Source as Part of NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
NVIDIA is making the full NVIDIA Run:ai platform available as open source software, giving customers, developers, and ecosystem partners access to production-grade AI workload and GPU orchestration capabilities. This release expands the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform by establishing NVIDIA Run:ai as an open foundation that enables the broader ecosystem to bring differentiated solutions to market faster in response to evolving customer needs.
Over the past several years, NVIDIA Run:ai has helped organizations run AI workloads on Kubernetes at scale by dynamically allocating GPU resources and managing workloads across the full lifecycle, from data processing and training to inference.
By open sourcing NVIDIA Run:ai platform capabilities as part of NVIDIA DSX AI Factory, it is now possible for every NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partner and AI cloud to increase workload throughput, improve GPU utilization, and operate shared AI infrastructure more efficiently and effectively.
This post details the open source release, which includes the complete NVIDIA Run:ai platform and four components that can also be adopted independently: KAI Scheduler, GPU Fractioning Operator, KAI Resource Management, Workload Map. Together with additional platform code, these components form the integrated NVIDIA Run:ai platform. Platform teams and ecosystem partners can adopt NVIDIA Run:ai as an integrated whole, build on it for their own products and services, or integrate individual components based on their requirements.
How to adopt open source NVIDIA Run:ai
NVIDIA Run:ai can be adopted directly as open-source software or through NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partner offerings.
Deploy the open source platform directly
The complete source code for NVIDIA Run:ai is available in the NVIDIA Run:ai repository within the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory GitHub organization. Teams can inspect the code, contribute to its development, build on top of the platform or adopt its modular components independently.
The complete open source NVIDIA Run:ai platform is also available on NVIDIA NGC as a Community Product, with a Helm chart for installing the integrated stack.
Note: The NVIDIA Run:ai source code is governed by its applicable open source licenses. Downloading the Community Product from NGC requires acceptance of the applicable NVIDIA Software License Agreement and Product-Specific Terms for NVIDIA AI Products. No paid NVIDIA Run:ai subscription or NVIDIA support entitlement is required for the Community Product, and NVIDIA enterprise support is not included.
Adopt open source NVIDIA Run:ai through NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partners
Open source NVIDIA Run:ai gives NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partners direct access to AI workload and GPU orchestration innovations they can use in their own NVIDIA DSX AI factory solutions. By adopting the complete platform or integrating individual components, partners can bring those innovations to market faster and respond more quickly to evolving customer and operational requirements.
- Crusoe integrates NVIDIA Run:ai with Crusoe Managed Kubernetes, combining GPU workload orchestration with managed Kubernetes and GPU infrastructure.
- Mirantis extends k0rdent AI with NVIDIA Run:ai to deliver a lifecycle-managed, Metal-to-Model AI factory stack that automates infrastructure provisioning and maximizes GPU utilization.
- Nebius offers NVIDIA Run:ai as a one-click application deployment in Nebius AI Cloud, giving customers a streamlined way to deploy and operate the complete platform on Nebius Managed Service for Kubernetes.
- OpenNebula Systems integrates NVIDIA Run:ai with the OpenNebula AI Cloud Platform through OneKS, combining GPU workload orchestration with infrastructure provisioning and lifecycle management for open and sovereign AI clouds.
- Rafay is expanding its NVIDIA Run:ai integration to deliver it as a fully managed service. Rafay automates the entire stack, from GPU infrastructure and clusters to the NVIDIA Run:ai control plane and tenants, so AI cloud providers and enterprises can offer it through their own self-service catalogs.
- Saturn Cloud integrates NVIDIA Run:ai to help AI cloud operators launch white-label AI inference services through its Token Factory platform, combining GPU orchestration with dedicated and multi-tenant model serving, per-token metering, and automated billing.
- Spectro Cloud integrates NVIDIA Run:ai into PaletteAI, enabling customers to deploy it through PaletteAI Studio and manage it with the same lifecycle automation used across their AI infrastructure.
- vCluster provides NVIDIA Run:ai through pre-validated deployment templates that stand up a complete environment per tenant, allowing operators to strengthen tenant boundaries while NVIDIA Run:ai continues to schedule across one GPU fleet.
For NVIDIA Enterprise AI Factory deployments, NVIDIA Run:ai continues to be available through NVIDIA-supported commercial offerings including as a standalone product, through NVIDIA Mission Control and NVIDIA AI Enterprise, and select cloud marketplaces. Availability, licensing, and support terms vary by offering.
For teams that already have a platform and need to fill a specific capability gap, the following sections describe when and how to use each modular component independently.
Modular open source components of the NVIDIA Run:ai platform
This section details the four components included in the open source release: KAI Scheduler, GPU Fractioning Operator, KAI Resource Management, and Workload Map. With additional platform code, these components form the integrated NVIDIA Run:ai platform. You can adopt NVIDIA Run:ai as an integrated whole or integrate individual components based on your unique requirements.
KAI Scheduler: The scheduling engine behind NVIDIA Run:ai
KAI Scheduler is the Kubernetes-native scheduler that powers the NVIDIA Run:ai platform. NVIDIA released KAI Scheduler as open source software under the Apache 2.0 license and contributed it to CNCF as a Sandbox project. KAI remains the upstream engine behind NVIDIA Run:ai, and all scheduler development happens in the community repository, so every improvement flows through the same codebase. NVIDIA continues to support the project’s maintainers and work with the broader ecosystem to advance AI workload scheduling at scale.
KAI Scheduler is purpose-built for GPU workloads at scale, coordinating:
- Gang scheduling with prescheduling in-memory simulation, so multipod jobs are placed all-or-nothing and aren’t evicted needlessly
- Fair-share (including time-based fair-share) and quota allocation that keeps resource shares balanced across teams
- Topology awareness and bin-packing at the scheduling-decision level
- GPU sharing, which allows multiple workloads to share single or multiple GPUs (MIG, MPS, time sharing, HaMi, CUDA 13.4 MPS fractioning)
- Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) support
To learn more about key features, visit the kai-scheduler/KAI-Scheduler GitHub repo.
Use KAI Scheduler for diverse AI workloads that require fair access to cluster resources and topology-aware placement. It can be deployed in an existing cluster alongside the current software stack without requiring the complete NVIDIA Run:ai platform.
Follow the project, ask questions in the #kai-scheduler channel on CNCF Slack, and contribute on the kai-scheduler/KAI-Scheduler GitHub repo.
GPU Fractioning: An operator for GPU fractions on Kubernetes
The NVIDIA Run:ai platform has long supported fractional GPU allocation, enabling multiple workloads to share a GPU with hard memory isolation. Fractions can be requested on demand and set up on the fly, with no per-node setup from an administrator in advance. It is one of the most widely used capabilities among ML teams running workloads that do not require the full memory of a GPU, including interactive notebooks and inference for smaller models. NVIDIA Run:ai pioneered that experience with a proprietary implementation.
GPU Fractioning Operator brings CUDA-native GPU fractioning to Kubernetes and the proprietary implementation has been retired in favor of the native capability available in CUDA 13.4. The CUDA driver enforces a hard limit on GPU memory for each workload, and each workload sees only the GPU memory allocated to its fraction. What is still needed is a clean way to consume it on Kubernetes. This is what GPU Fractioning Operator provides: an operator that enables CUDA GPU fractions on a cluster, along with a metrics exporter for per-pod visibility into fractions in use. It is a Kubernetes integration layer that allows workloads to use CUDA-native fractioning, and it is scheduler-agnostic.
Use the GPU Fractioning Operator for workloads that can share underutilized GPU capacity, including notebooks, development sessions, and smaller models. GPU Fractioning Operator integrates with KAI Scheduler to translate available GPU capacity into an actual placement decision, while remaining compatible with other schedulers.
GPU Fractioning Operator brings CUDA 13.4-native GPU fractioning to Kubernetes and integrates with KAI Scheduler. To get started, refer to the GPU Fractioning Operator documentation.
KAI Resource Management: The organizational layer
While the scheduler decides how work is placed, KAI Resource Management governs who gets what:
- Projects and departments: The organizational structure, or “org layer,” that maps resources to the teams and initiatives that consume them.
- Resource management with an organizational hierarchy: The ability to allocate, guarantee, and share GPU capacity across that org structure, with fair-share and quota semantics.
- Node pools: Grouping and targeting of heterogeneous hardware so workloads land on the right resources.
Together, these let platform teams move beyond raw Kubernetes scheduling and manage GPUs the way organizations actually operate: by team, by department, by initiative, and by resource guarantee.
Use KAI Resource Management for heterogeneous clusters shared by multiple teams that require defined shares of capacity. For example, a platform team could guarantee 50% of the cluster to research while preventing any one team from monopolizing the remaining capacity. If you are already tracking quota entitlements in a spreadsheet or hand-maintaining namespaces per team, this is the layer that replaces it. It can be combined with KAI Scheduler in your clusters.
Read more about how these concepts map to real deployments in the KAI Resource Management documentation.
Workload Map: A workload-management contract for Kubernetes
Workload Map is the contract NVIDIA Run:ai uses to support any workload type. KAI Scheduler uses it for scheduling and gang semantics; the rest of the platform uses it for workload discovery, monitoring and lifecycle management.
In Kubernetes, an AI workload is almost never a bare Deployment or Job. It is a PyTorchJob, a RayCluster, a JobSet, a KServe InferenceService, a Dynamo graph deployment, or a company’s own custom resource. Each type has its own internal structure, components with different roles (driver and workers, head and workers, prefill and decode), its own scaling and gang semantics, and its own way of reporting status.
Workload Map provides a consistent way to treat these workloads as first-class objects throughout their lifecycle:
- Describing pods, components, and roles
- Submitting and configuring
- Scheduling with gang and topology awareness
- Observing status and health consistently
- Applying policy at admission or runtime
This workload-management layer sits between Kubernetes primitives and the schedulers, dashboards, SRE and troubleshooting tools, cost tools, backup tools, and ML platforms that serve users. Instead of each tool building a private, partial integration for every CRD, Workload Map defines each workload type once so any platform or tool can schedule, observe, act on, and govern it consistently without hardcoding each CRD.
Use Workload Map for platforms and tools that must understand and manage multiple Kubernetes workload types without hardcoding each CRD. It ships as a Go library that works offline on unstructured objects, so you can adopt it without adding anything to your cluster. It is deliberately narrow: Workload Map describes workload structure and does not schedule, queue, autoscale, or propagate across clusters.
Learn more in the dsx-ai-factory/workload-map GitHub repo and check out the adopter projects.
Related open source platform software
The following open source projects address complementary AI infrastructure challenges. They can be adopted independently or incorporated into broader solutions that include the complete NVIDIA Run:ai platform or selected components.
Model Streamer: Reducing cold-start latency
Cold-starting an inference workload on Kubernetes can take several minutes, during which time GPUs are allocated but idle for a single step: loading model weights from storage onto the GPU. Model Streamer reads weights concurrently and streams them directly into GPU memory, cutting load time for large models.
Since its release, Model Streamer has been adopted across the inference stack, including by inference engines, cloud providers and storage platform vendors.
Inference engines
Model Streamer is integrated upstream in vLLM and SGLang, where it can be enabled with the --load-format runai_streamer flag, as well as in ModelExpress. Support covers local filesystems, S3-compatible stores, and network file shares alongside several cloud backends detailed below.
Clouds
Major cloud providers now document Model Streamer in their own guidance.
- AWS: Model Streamer ships in the vLLM Deep Learning Container and is the recommended fast path in the official EKS documentation for running AI/ML inference, with tuned concurrency and chunk sizing for S3.
- Google Cloud: Native Cloud Storage support built in collaboration with NVIDIA, including GKE documentation for streaming straight from a bucket into accelerator memory.
- Microsoft Azure: Azure Blob Storage integration, jointly developed by Microsoft and NVIDIA Run:ai to provide first-class model streaming for Azure customers. Published benchmarks on eight NVIDIA H100 VMs shows 3x-6x faster loading than the default loader and a steady 80 Gbps, compared with approximately 40 Gbps for the default path.
Storage platforms
Several AI data infrastructure partners have independently benchmarked Model Streamer and published their results:
- WEKA loaded into GPU memory in just 3.5 seconds, roughly 40% faster than loading from local NVMe—enabling organizations to build petabyte-scale shared model repositories that accelerate model readiness without the time, effort, and capacity required to maintain duplicate model copies across the inference environment.
- VAST Data measured measured 1.7 seconds, a 60% improvement over loading from local NVMe
- DDN streamed the 65.5 GB Qwen3-32B across 8 GPUs in under four seconds, and translated it into cost: saving up to 10% of daily GPU runtime compared to using local storage.
Use Model Streamer when starting new replicas and loading model weights is the primary bottleneck.
Grove: One API, any inference architecture
Emerging workload patterns—including agentic pipelines, disaggregated serving and mixture-of-experts training—consist of multiple connected components that must scale together. Grove provides a Kubernetes API for orchestrating these workloads, from a single pod to deployments spanning tens of thousands of GPUs.
Grove provides topology-aware autoscaling and hierarchical gang scheduling, allowing components such as prefill and decode to start as all-or-nothing units. On NVIDIA GB200 NVL72, it also manages ComputeDomain resources automatically, enabling multinode NVLink performance through a single annotation instead of hand-authored YAML.
Grove is a modular part of NVIDIA Dynamo that can be used independently, and it already powers training and inference pipelines at scale across a range of companies. Recent work includes support for llm-d and Volcano as a scheduler backend, with Kueue support in progress.
Use Grove for graph-based workloads with distinct roles and coupled scaling requirements.
Get started with open source NVIDIA Run:ai
NVIDIA Run:ai is available now as open source software in the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory GitHub organization. To learn more and get started, check out these resources:
- NVIDIA Run:ai full platform
- KAI Scheduler scheduling engine
- KAI Resource Management for projects, departments, quotas, and node pools
- GPU Fractioning Operator for CUDA GPU fractions on Kubernetes, with per-pod metrics
- Workload Map workload-management contract
Related open source projects include:
- Model Streamer for fast model weight loading
- Grove for multicomponent inference orchestration
We’re excited to bring this work to the community and to build the next generation of AI workload and GPU orchestration in the open. We welcome your contributions, issues, and feedback.

articles.title: Netflix compra los derechos exclusivos del Mundial 2030 y emitirá todo el torneo en España
articles.text:
Netflix acaba de anunciar que ha adquirido los derechos exclusivos de la Copa Mundial de la FIFA 2030. La plataforma de streaming redobla una vez más su apuesta por el contenido deportivo y emitirá el evento más importante del mundo del fútbol en España y Andorra. Así, el servicio ofrecerá en directo a sus suscriptores los 104 partidos de la mayor competición deportiva del planeta.
La Copa Mundial de la FIFA 2030 conmemorará el centenario de la competición. Curiosamente España, vigente campeona del mundo, será uno de sus tres países anfitriones. El país compartirá la organización con Portugal y Marruecos. Además, con motivo de ese centenario, Argentina, Paraguay y Uruguay acogerán algunos de los primeros partidos de la fase de grupos.
Todos esos encuentros del Mundial 2030 se podrán ver en Netflix tanto en España como en Andorra. Además, como parte del acuerdo, en España podrá verse gratis un partido de cada jornada. Y también se ofrecerá a una cadena nacional de televisión en abierto (todavía por determinar cuál) un paquete de partidos que incluirá todos los de España, las dos semifinales y la final.
Como parte de su estrategia de emisión del Mundial 2030, Netflix tiene previsto también ofrecer la cobertura íntegra y en directo del torneo, con emisión de programas —con un planteamiento genuinamente español— antes de cada partido, durante el descanso y después del encuentro, además de un programa resumen diario los días de partido y otros contenidos destinados a generar expectación en la antesala del torneo.
Netflix emitirá el Mundial 2030
El acuerdo se suma a la creciente oferta de deportes en directo de primer nivel de Netflix en todo el mundo, que abarca las ediciones del 2027 y 2031 de la Copa Mundial Femenina de la FIFA, partidos y eventos de la NFL, la MLB, WWE y algunos de los principales combates de boxeo y de artes marciales mixtas (MMA).
"Pocos acontecimientos unen tanto a la gente como un Mundial. Este año, yo estaba en el estadio cuando España levantó el trofeo y viví de primera mano la pasión, el orgullo y las historias que acaban formando parte de la cultura de un país y perduran en la memoria durante generaciones. Ahora que España va a ser uno de los países anfitriones en 2030, nos hace muchísima ilusión ofrecer en Netflix todos los partidos a los aficionados de España y Andorra", confiesa Bela Bajaria, directora jefe de Contenidos de Netflix, en un comunicado remitido a la prensa.
"Para los aficionados españoles al fútbol, recibir al mundo como vigentes campeones y poder seguir todos los partidos en Netflix hará que esta ocasión sea única. Además, nuestra creciente colaboración con la FIFA, que incluye las ediciones del 2027 y 2031 de la Copa Mundial Femenina de la FIFA en Estados Unidos y Canadá, refleja nuestro compromiso constante por acercar a los aficionados a los grandes momentos del deporte mundial", añade.

articles.title: AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
articles.text:
AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München
- Summary:
- A new study reveals that people draw a surprisingly sharp line between human consciousness and artificial intelligence, even when both behave identically. Researchers found that participants considered even the most responsive AI less conscious than the least responsive human. Yet when asked about "awareness" instead, people judged humans and AI much more similarly.
- Share:
Even when artificial intelligence behaves exactly like a human, people are reluctant to consider it conscious, according to a new study from Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU).
As artificial intelligence becomes more advanced, reports of AI systems misleading users, working together, or appearing to pursue independent goals are becoming increasingly common. These behaviors often lead people to describe AI as though it can think, feel, or make decisions for itself. But does behaving like a human actually convince people that a machine has consciousness?
New research from LMU suggests that people make a clear distinction between displaying intelligent behavior and possessing a conscious mind, even when humans and AI act in precisely the same way.
How Scientists Tested Perceptions of AI Consciousness
Published in the journal Cognition, the study was led by Dr. Louis Longin of LMU's Chair of Philosophy of Mind, working alongside Dr. Bahador Bahrami, Professor Ophelia Deroy, and other researchers.
"Whereas previous studies have typically asked general questions about whether AI actually has mental states, our study is the first to directly compare how people attribute the same mental states to AI and humans behaving in exactly the same way, under identical circumstances," says Longin.
"We may be using mental terms to refer to AI, but this may only be because we lack better words," says Ophelia Deroy, philosopher and a senior author of the study. "After all, AI is trained to act and speak like a human, so these descriptions seem natural."
To investigate how people judge consciousness, the researchers conducted experiments involving nearly 1,100 participants. One group read brief descriptions of artificial agents that showed different levels of responsiveness to their environments. For example, some agents reacted to sounds or recognized the emotional states of others.
Another group encountered the same situations, except the characters were described as humans rather than AI systems. Participants then evaluated how conscious or aware each character seemed to be of its surroundings.
A Surprising Gap Between Human and AI Consciousness
The experiments revealed that responsiveness influenced how participants judged both humans and artificial intelligence. Characters that reacted more actively to their surroundings were generally considered more conscious and more aware.
However, a striking difference emerged when participants evaluated consciousness specifically. Even the most responsive AI was rated as less conscious than the least responsive human. In other words, identical behavior did not lead people to assign the same level of consciousness to humans and machines.
The results changed considerably when participants were asked about awareness instead. For this characteristic, judgments of humans and AI followed largely similar patterns, suggesting that people interpret awareness and consciousness in fundamentally different ways.
"There is a growing worry in public discussion that people will see AI behaving in a human-like way and start treating these systems as if they had human-like mental states," says Longin, lead author of the study. "We found something much more nuanced: People are quite willing to say that an AI notices things and is aware of its surroundings. But they clearly draw a line when it comes to the term 'consciousness'. People consistently attribute less consciousness to AI than humans -- even when their behavior is identical."
Although people sometimes describe AI as conscious when discussing its actions, the findings indicate that they still distinguish between artificial systems and human minds.
Why One Word Changes How We Perceive AI
The researchers believe the difference between consciousness and awareness offers an important insight into how people understand artificial intelligence.
Awareness is a relatively neutral term that can describe an agent's ability to detect and respond to information in its environment. Consciousness, however, carries deeper implications about subjective experience and what it means to have an inner mental life.
Because awareness focuses more directly on observable behavior, people appear comfortable applying it to both humans and AI. Consciousness carries a different meaning, leading people to judge the two much less similarly.
The findings also highlight why the language used to discuss artificial intelligence matters, particularly as AI systems become increasingly capable of producing convincing human behavior.
"Our study teaches us lessons for how we communicate about AI," says Bahador Bahrami, who is also a senior author of the study and an expert in social neuroscience. "Companies and journalists often reach for hyped descriptions of AI models, and credit them with intentions, plans, or even moral conscience and hesitation. What our study shows is that everyday judgments are much more discriminating: People do not simply put AI and humans on the same mental scale. But the boundary also depends on which terms we use. For more neutral descriptors such as 'awareness', the distinction can largely disappear. That makes our choice of language important."
Story Source:
Materials provided by Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Louis Longin, Jurgis Karpus, Nadine Meertens, Bahador Bahrami, Ophelia Deroy. AI is not as conscious as humans: Essentialism in mental state attributions to artificial systems. Cognition, 2027; 278: 106733 DOI: 10.1016/j.cognition.2026.106733

articles.title: Steam: Warum eine Gratis-Demo einen Entwickler 1.000 Dollar am Tag kostet
articles.text:
Dieses KI-Spiel auf Steam begeistert Gamer – und zwingt die Entwickler, einen Kredit aufzunehmen
Normalerweise sorgen Steam-Spiele, die KI nutzen, eher für negative Schlagzeilen und Kritik von Spieler:innen. So ist es etwa bei einem Entwickler passiert, der sein Game gelöscht hat, weil ihm die KI-Nutzung von der Community vorgehalten wurde. Bei Teach My Little Sister How to Drive ist das anders. Obwohl hier KI essenziell zum Spiel gehört, wird das Steam-Game aktuell von vielen gefeiert.
Hype um Steam-Spiel: Wenn die KI fahren lernt
Wie der Name schon verrät, musst du in Teach My Little Sister How to Drive (oder BF17 gescheitert: Meine kleine Schwester am Steuer, wie der deutsche Titel lautet) der kleinen Schwester deiner Spielfigur das Autofahren näherbringen. Dafür nutzt du Sprachanweisungen, die von einer KI im Hintergrund verarbeitet und im Spiel umgesetzt werden. In der Simulation, die zunächst als Demo erschienen ist, müssen zahlreiche Herausforderungen bestanden werden – primär, heil am Ziel anzukommen.
Die Demo des KI-Spiels hat im Laufe der Zeit eine Menge Spieler:innen auf Steam angezogen. Während nach der Veröffentlichung maximal 30 Gamer:innen gleichzeitig das Spiel ausprobierten, stieg die Zahl in den kommenden Wochen schnell auf 400 Steam-User:innen an, wie Steam Charts zeigt. Der Zuwachs in den vergangenen 30 Tagen liegt bei über 130 Prozent.
So schön das für die Entwickler:innen ist, so problematisch ist der rasante Anstieg der Spielerzahlen auch, wie sie in einem Steam-Post betonen. Darin heißt es, dass sie normalerweise Google Gemini als primäres KI-Modell für die Antworten der Fahrschülerin nutzen. Da aber immer wieder die Nutzungslimits ausgereizt wurden, mussten sie auf mehrere Fallback-KI-Modelle zurückgreifen.
Laut dem Beitrag geben die Entwickler:innen aktuell jeden Tag mehr als 1.000 US-Dollar für die entstandenen KI-Kosten aus. Sie haben sogar einen Bankkredit aufgenommen, um die Demo noch längere Zeit am Laufen zu halten. Allerdings könnte es sein, dass die Testversion frühzeitig beendet werden muss, sollten die Kosten noch weiter ansteigen.
Damit das nicht zum Problem beim Release des Steam-Spiels wird, haben die Macher:innen angekündigt, die anfallenden KI-Kosten mit in den Verkaufspreis einzurechnen. Dadurch könnte der Preis also etwas höher ausfallen, aber Steam-Spieler:innen werden nicht für ihren jeweiligen Token-Verbrauch zur Kasse gebeten. Zudem arbeiten die Entwickler:innen daran, auch lokale Modelle nutzbar zu machen. So können Gamer:innen eine KI ihrer Wahl nutzen und sparen den Verantwortlichen dabei sogar noch Geld.

articles.title: The new Apple TV 4K finally brings two features I’ve wanted for years — but it now costs $299
articles.text:
New Apple TV 4K finally brings HomePod Dolby Atmos surround sound and a Siri Remote you can’t lose — but its price has been hiked to $299
The price you pay
- The new Apple TV 4K is official and starts at $299 / £299 / AU$449
- It has microphones built-in for hands-free Siri control and supports HomePod surrounds
- The updated Siri Remote can chirp to help you find it, supports Precision Finding, and works with older Apple TV models
I fondly remember when Apple brought the price down on the Apple TV 4K box, and then I also remember the unfortunate price hikes from earlier in 2026. That pushed the Apple TV 4K without Ethernet to $199 / £199 / AU$299 and the one with Ethernet to $249 / £249 / AU$399.
Now, alongside the HomeView and the second-generation HomePod mini, Apple is ushering in the new Apple TV 4K and sunsetting the previous models. It keeps a similar shape — it's still a black square with curved edges and a logo up top — but there are some new tricks here.
It also carries a new price point: the Apple TV 4K (2026) comes in one version and costs $299 / £299 / AU$449. That’s a big jump, especially when compared with competing Roku players and Fire TV Sticks. It’s actually the same price as the new Apple HomeView, which includes a screen and speakers. Still, it's up for preorder now — beginning October 13, 2026 — and ships on November 13, 2026.
I’ve spent a bit of time with the refreshed Apple TV 4K, seeing it work through some Siri AI tasks and hearing its new audio capabilities, which include the ability to work with up to four HomePod speakers in a surround setup.
That could mean two second-generation HomePods up front and two HomePod mini second-generation as rear speakers, four full-sized HomePod 2 units, or four HomePod mini 2 units.
By far the most meaningful upgrade, and the one that shows Apple’s listening to customers, is the new Siri Remote. Now in its fourth generation, it can finally chirp and emit a sound when you can’t find it. So you can ask, “Hey Siri, where’s my remote?” to no one in particular (the Apple TV 4K box's microphones will hear you) and the remote will emit a sound.
It’s pretty loud, though Apple isn’t sharing the exact decibel level, and it should be very audible even if the remote is stuck deep between couch cushions, in a pile on the floor, or somewhere else entirely.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
If you also have an iPhone 17 or newer, iPhone Air, or iPhone Duo, you can open Find My, tap Devices, and then use Precision Finding to help you locate the remote. These are both super-helpful features, and you don’t need the new Apple TV 4K to take advantage of them, as this remote is backwards compatible with the Apple TV HD and previous Apple TV 4K models. I’m still waiting for price confirmation, but for reference, the current Siri Remote is $59 / £59 / AU$89.
As someone who’s bought into the sound quality of the HomePods since the first generation, which sadly isn’t supported here, this is a welcome upgrade. But you do need a lot of new hardware.
Theoretically, that’s $895 / £895 / AU$1,365 for an Apple TV 4K and four HomePod mini 2 units, or $1,695 / £1,695 / AU$2,645 for four second-generation HomePods and the Apple TV 4K, or $1,295 / £1,295 / AU$2,005 for two HomePod mini 2s, two second-generation HomePods, and an Apple TV 4K.
I heard a brief snippet of Widow’s Bay, which streams on Apple TV, with the latter setup: two full-sized HomePods next to a TV and two HomePod mini 2s a bit farther back behind a couch. It sounded really good, and compared with just two HomePods, the full setup offered a much wider experience that excelled at showing off both the low and high ends, from a quieter scene that ramped into a more vibrant one. This combo packs a punch.
There's no doubt that $299 / £299 / AU$449 for a streaming box, even with that audio capability, is a lot. But the Apple TV 4K does pack in a few other bells and whistles. Under the hood, it should be speedier, with quicker app launches and more runway into the future thanks to the A19 processor.
The new Apple TV 4K also supports Siri AI at launch in Australia, Canada, India, New Zealand, the UK, the US, Singapore, and South Africa.
This lets you ask questions with personal context, like, “Hey Siri, what was the episode of Star Wars Rebels I was talking about with Max?” or “What was that show that Benjie recommended a few months back in the group chat?”
Leaning on personal context from a connected iPhone, it can deliver those results, and it worked quickly in a demo, pulling up an episode of Ted Lasso in short order.
That about wraps up the new Apple TV 4K — it replaces the previous-generation models, though if those get discounted, they’re definitely worth a look. It’s available to order now ahead of its November 13, 2026 launch.
It’s a sizable price increase, and I wish Apple still offered the previous generation as a more affordable option, something like an entry-level iPad equivalent or an “e” option, similar to the iPhone 17e.
It’s clear that this is a higher-end, premium streaming box, but we’ll need to spend some time with it to see how it compares and whether the $299 / £299 / AU$449 price point is worth it. Let me know what you think in the comments below, particularly your thoughts on that higher price and feature set.
Follow TechRadar on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our expert news, reviews, and opinion in your feeds. Make sure to click the Follow button!
Jacob Krol is the US Managing Editor, News for TechRadar. He’s been writing about technology since he was 14 when he started his own tech blog. Since then Jacob has worked for a plethora of publications including CNN Underscored, TheStreet, Parade, Men’s Journal, Mashable, CNET, and CNBC among others.
He specializes in covering companies like Apple, Samsung, and Google and going hands-on with mobile devices, smart home gadgets, TVs, and wearables. In his spare time, you can find Jacob listening to Bruce Springsteen, building a Lego set, or binge-watching the latest from Disney, Marvel, or Star Wars.

articles.title: Apollyon Dynamics quits building drones to make defencetech for the military
articles.text:
Apollyon Dynamics quits building drones to make defencetech for the military
Hyderabad-based student startup Apollyon Dynamics sold drones worth over Rs 1.5 crore last year. It has now moved to a jet-powered target drone, a multirotor interceptor, and a marine unmanned system.
When Jayant Khatri and Sourya Choudhury started in May 2025, the focus of the Hyderabad-based defencetech startup was building drones. Its early portfolio included trainer, endurance, multirole, and FPV systems, with the company selling drones worth more than Rs 1.5 crore last year.
But foresight prevails over immediate success. Anticipating saturation in the market, Apollyon has now pivoted.
“We have stopped building regular drones. Instead, we have completely shifted towards making higher value products,” says Khatri, Co-founder and CEO of Apollyon Dynamics.
The founder says the conventional drone market had become too crowded, with limited room for differentiation. “It’s basically a race to the bottom now. People are just assembling stuff. That included us as well. There’s not a lot of value addition,” he says.
The startup’s current portfolio has been rebuilt around three core products: Nightshade, Ahuti Mk II, and Project Piranha.
Apollyon now has around 20 full-time employees, two manufacturing labs, and an office in Hyderabad.
The new defencetech portfolio
Khatri says Nightshade is a jet-powered platform that can be configured as a target drone, decoy, or loitering munition. The company has already conducted multiple tests. “We were the first company in India to launch it from top of a car, a jet-powered system,” he says.
The startup plans to begin supplying pilot batches of the target-drone variant to the Indian Army by December, while trials of the loitering-munition version are expected to begin next year.
Nightshade's three configurations are designed for different battlefield roles. The target-drone variant is intended to simulate threats during air-defence training, while its decoys can help identify enemy radar positions. The loitering-munition variant combines a jet-powered platform with components typically associated with more expensive missile systems.
Khatri says that Apollyon has also repurposed Ahuti, its earlier flagship drone, into an interceptor.
“After several iterations, it has reached a top speed of 498 kmph, making it the fastest multirotor drone in India. The India Book of Records has certified this,” shares the CEO, adding that the platform is part of a Make II programme (a special system used by the Indian army to build military hardware) and is being developed with defence partners.
Project Piranha expands Apollyon's ambitions beyond aerial systems. The company hasn’t revealed much about it, only that it is a marine-based unmanned system.
“We wanted to make a family of products, a family of unmanned systems, and we don’t want to be just known as a UAV-making company,” Khatri says. “We want to be a proper defencetech company with multiple products in our portfolio.”
The evolving industry of military tech
Apollyon has also stopped selling its mobile drone lab and is instead integrating its systems into command-centre products with companies like the Noida-based Raphe mPhibr and Hyderabad-based Dhruva Space in a collaborative effort. Raphe and Dhruva Space are also customers of Apollyon; they buy Ahuti interceptors.
In June 2026, the startup had conducted a pre-seed round raising $480,000 led by Naandi Ventures. The startup is now looking to raise $5 million through a seed round within the next six months.
Started as a drone-making student startup, Apollyon’s ambition is now considerably larger: developing cruise-missile-class systems capable of carrying thousands of kilograms and travelling at least Mach 1 by 2030. M R M Babu, who led DRDO’s Agni-V missile programme, has joined as an advisor to help with hiring, programme planning and fund allocation.
For 21-year-old Khatri, collaboration will be important as Indian defence companies become larger. “If we want to survive, we can’t do it alone,” he says. “Others have realised that too and have become a lot more collaborative. It’s a good thing for the long term.”
Apollyon Dynamics is part of YourStory’s Tech30 cohort—a showcase of India’s most promising startups of 2026, unveiled at TechSparks Bengaluru.
Edited by Teja Lele

articles.title: Plus légère et ultra-précise, la Razer Basilisk V4 Pro veut détrôner Logitech et SteelSeries
articles.text:
| Catégorie | Gaming | 
| Sans fil | Oui | 
| Technologie sans-fil | Dongle USB (2,4 GHz), Bluetooth | 
| Poids | 100 g | 
| Capteur | Optique | 
| Nombre de boutons | 14 | 
| Résolution max | 50000 dpi | 
| Vitesse de transmission | 8000 Hz | 
Après trois ans d'absence, la souris la plus célèbre de la marque nord-américaine Razer fait son retour dans une version 2026. La Basilisk V4 Pro conserve la forme de ses aînées, mais embarque le dernier capteur optique Razer Focus Pro 50K et la connectivité radio HyperSpeed Gen-2.
Voilà bien longtemps que nous n’avions pas évoqué la Basilisk de Razer, certainement la gamme de souris la plus célèbre de la marque aux trois serpents. Hormis une itération mobile qui nous avait néanmoins convaincus en 2024, la souris ergonomique pour droitier n'a pas connu de cure de jouvence majeure depuis la sortie de son modèle V3 Pro en... 2023, lui-même une évolution timide de la V3 standard de 2021. Trois ans d'absence, donc, corrigés aujourd'hui avec l'arrivée surprise de la V4 Pro dans une période automnale certainement chargée en sorties sur le marché des périphériques.
Entre la rentrée des Suisses de Logitech et des Danois de SteelSeries, les Étasuniens de Razer auront-ils assez d'arguments pour justifier le positionnement très premium de leur mulot ? À 180 € toutes taxes comprises, voilà un investissement qui mérite considération . Et cela tombe bien, puisque la Basilisk V4 Pro arrive justement sur notre banc de test.
Pas de surprise pour les aficionados encore accrochés à leur Basilisk V3 Pro après toutes ces années : la forme de cette version V4 est quasi identique à celle de sa devancière avec des dimensions dont les différences se mesurent à quelques millimètres de longueur en moins (127,5 x 75,8 x 42,7 mm).
La nuance est beaucoup plus marquée au niveau du poids, puisque la V4 Pro pèse 100 g pile sur la balance contre 112 g pour la V3 Pro ; une cure d'amaigrissement bienvenue. On reste toutefois loin de la légèreté des gammes DeathAdder et Viper, toujours chez Razer, conçues avant tout pour les sessions de FPS.
La Basilisk V4 Pro fait ainsi le pont entre ces poids plumes et la Naga V3 Pro, qui affiche non seulement un embonpoint remarqué (117 g), mais aussi une forme rectangulaire beaucoup plus explicite au niveau de son clic gauche. Et c’est sans compter un flanc gauche dénué de repose-pouce pour pouvoir y coller le plus de boutons possible, souris pour MMO oblige. Ainsi, la Basilisk V4 Pro se veut surtout polyvalente pour satisfaire toutes les occasions de jeu, ce qui explique aussi une prise en main qui convient à (presque) tous les profils de paume (à condition, évidemment, d'être droitier).
Le plastique sollicité sur la souris est par ailleurs peu ou prou identique à celui de la Naga susmentionnée, soit légèrement plus imperméable aux traces de doigts par rapport à la Viper, bien que son revêtement mat laisse toujours apparaître quelques marques après plusieurs jours d’utilisation.
Les deux côtés profitent d'un revêtement caoutchouteux texturé qui offre une meilleure préhension. Sa résistance dans le temps reste toutefois un facteur important qu'il nous est impossible d'évaluer pour le moment. Notre dizaine de jours d'utilisation s'avère néanmoins encourageante quant à la non-accumulation de saleté dans ses aspérités.
Sans surprise, les deux clics principaux ont des courses de pré-activation distinctes l'une de l’autre, le clic gauche étant résolument plus court que celui de droite. Plus généralement, ces deux clics sont plus courts que sur d'autres souris gaming récemment passées dans notre comparatif, notamment la Rival Pro de SteelSeries.
Côté bruit, la Basilisk V4 Pro s'aligne une nouvelle fois sur la Naga V3 Pro avec un son aigu qui n'est pas aussi irritant que celui, très creux et métallique, du duo Viper/DeathAdder. Pour le silence total sur une souris gaming, il faudra une nouvelle fois se tourner vers la Dark Perk de Be quiet!
Le côté gauche de la souris se pare de quatre boutons différents. La première rangée de trois, qui a fait ses débuts sur la Basilisk mobile, assigne les actions classiques de retour arrière et avant sur les deux éléments les plus proches du pouce. Le bouton le plus éloigné (et proche de la face avant de la souris) ouvre le chatbot Razer AI Prompt Master, si tant est que l'application Razer Synapse soit installée. Une option totalement dispensable comme on en a rarement vue sur le marché des périphériques. Il est heureusement possible de désactiver cette fonction, ce qui est vivement conseillé.
L'habituel bouton destiné à être déclenché du bout du pouce, autrefois surnommé “sniper clutch”, est moins prononcé que sur la V3. Par défaut, il permet de basculer sur la couche de commande secondaire HyperShift, caractéristique de l'écosystème Razer. On regrette que sa forme oblique oblige à le déclencher via sa pointe intérieure au lieu d'une forme plus rectangulaire, façon “pédale”, comme c'était le cas sur les précédentes générations. Du reste, sa course est généreuse pour éviter les clics accidentels, mais le retour est bien senti et légèrement moins bruyant que sur les clics principaux. À noter que le bouton placé dans la pointe gauche du clic gauche est par défaut assigné au changement de profil mémoire.
Après avoir fait ses débuts sur la Naga V3 Pro, la molette optique HyperScroll Gen-2 de Razer fait son retour sur la Basilisk et reste toujours parmi les meilleures molettes utilisées dans les souris de notre comparatif. Débrayable ou crantée sur 24 ou 48 niveaux d'une simple pression sur le bouton assigné, elle se montre précise et efficace, si ce n'est un peu trop sensible lors d'une utilisation en défilement libre. On apprécie toujours les clics horizontaux qui en font une excellente alliée pour les tâches bureautiques, comme les tableurs à rallonge.
Le dessous de la Basilisk V4 Pro cache cinq patins dispersés de part et d'autre de la souris, notamment un plus large situé sur l'excroissance du repose-pouce. La glisse est très prononcée, et il faudra s'en accommoder en l'absence de patins de rechange. On remarque l'inclusion du palet de charge sans fil, compatible avec le tapis de recharge officiel de la marque, qui permet en l'état d'abriter le dongle USB-A. Autour du capteur se placent l'habituel interrupteur de mise en marche et le bouton de bascule entre la connectivité 2,4 GHz et le Bluetooth 6.2, la souris étant appairable avec trois machines différentes en plus de sa connexion filaire en USB-C, également dédiée à la recharge.
Sur ce dernier point, difficile d'être définitif : Razer promet 200 h d'autonomie via la connectivité 2,4 GHz (1000 Hz) et 275 h en Bluetooth. D'après notre expérience étalée sur une dizaine de jours avec une batterie initialement chargée à 50 % (1000 Hz et rétroéclairage RGB activés), nous n'avons dû recharger qu'une seule fois le périphérique. À noter que l'activation de l'éclairage et le passage à une fréquence d'interrogation supérieure à 1000 Hz ont un impact direct sur la consommation d'énergie.
Pas vraiment grande ni particulièrement petite, la Basilisk V4 Pro tombe entre toutes les mains, des plus modestes comme celles de votre humble serviteur jusqu'aux paluches plus imposantes du chef de rubrique informatique. La butte est placée vers la partie arrière de la souris plutôt qu'en son milieu. L'inclinaison, elle, est subtile, mais notable. Le repose-pouce sur la partie latérale gauche est aussi bienvenu. En résumé, qu'importent les styles de prises, cette souris de Razer devrait contenter tous les profils.
Pas de doute sur les performances de la Basilisk, qui embarque le capteur optique Focus Pro 50K Gen-3, le même que dans la Viper V4 Pro et la Naga V3 Pro de la marque. Le module est capable d'une résolution maximale de 50 000 DPI (dots per inch), d'une vitesse de suivi de 930 IPS (inches per second) et d'une accélération de 50 g ; les deux dernières valeurs étant nécessaires à la bonne reconnaissance des mouvements rapides et brusques.
L'intégration logicielle de la Basilisk V4 Pro apporte une nouveauté dans l'écosystème Razer : Perfect 180. Il s’agit d’une fonctionnalité optionnelle qui peut être assignée à un bouton pour tourner à 180° immédiatement dans un FPS, à condition d'avoir bien ajusté les DPI à partir du logiciel Synapse.
En pratique, Perfect 180 nous a permis de viser quasi instantanément derrière nous sur Quake 2 et CS2. L’option prend surtout du sens sur les jeux où les DPI sont réglés bas pour une visée précise (pensez Rainbow Six Siege)… Et elle pourrait bien faire du bruit, d'une façon analogue au fameux SOCD Cleaner des claviers, devenu la norme sur bien des périphériques, mais interdit sur certains jeux car considéré comme une forme de tricherie, notamment sur le shooter de Valve.
Du reste, il faudra inévitablement passer par le logiciel Razer Synapse pour exploiter au maximum la Basilisk, à commencer par l'assignation des commandes sur les 14 boutons programmables et le paramétrage des niveaux de DPI. On retrouve aussi les marronniers de la marque, comme l'ajustement de la distance verticale de détection pour ceux qui ont le coude léger, ou l'angle d'utilisation pour les avant-bras à tendance diagonale. Autant de features qui font partie intégrante de la communication de Razer, dont la pertinence reste à la discrétion des gamers parmi nos lecteurs. Enfin, aucun problême de connectivité vis-à-vis du dongle USB-A HyperSpeed, avec son plafond de 8000 Hz et sa moyenne de 0,125ms respectée.
Avec cette V4 Pro, la Basilisk de Razer fait un retour plus que réussi. La souris gaming est toujours aussi polyvalente, capable d'assurer lors des sessions de jeu comme sur des travaux de tableur de manière intensive, et se pare même de quelques nouveautés intéressantes pour qui adopte l'écosystème de la marque. Pour celles et ceux qui n'accrochent pas aux modèles ultra-légers qui semblent dominer le marché, la Basilisk V4 Pro constitue une très bonne alternative.

articles.title: Pour refroidir l’iPhone Duo pliant, Apple fait passer un conduit de graphite dans sa charnière
articles.text:
Pour évacuer la chaleur de l’A20 Pro dans un appareil qui double d’épaisseur une fois plié, Apple a fait passer un conduit de graphite flexible à travers la charnière de l’iPhone Duo. Les ingénieurs de la marque détaillent cette pièce, qui relie les deux moitiés du pliant.
L’iPhone Duo, premier pliant d’Apple, doit gérer la chaleur d’une puce gravée en 2 nm dans un châssis en deux parties. Selon un entretien accordé par Apple à PCMag, la charnière joue ici un rôle thermique inattendu : elle sert de pont pour répartir la chaleur sur une plus grande surface.
Un conduit de graphite flexible traverse la charnière
Banafsheh Barabadi, responsable senior de la conception thermique chez Apple, qualifie ce point de « l’un des aspects techniquement les plus difficiles » du design. Le conduit transfère la chaleur d’une moitié de l’appareil à l’autre, ce qui augmente la surface disponible pour la dissiper. Sur un pliant, l’épaisseur double une fois l'appareil refermé, d’où l’intérêt de mettre les deux moitiés à contribution.
La pièce a dû être conçue conjointement par les équipes thermique et mécanique. Il s’agit d’un matériau flexible qui doit encaisser de très nombreux cycles d’ouverture tout en conservant sa conductivité thermique et son intégrité structurelle sur toute la vie du produit. Autrement dit, la même pièce doit être un bon conducteur et un bon ressort, deux qualités qui s’accordent rarement.
Une puce A20 Pro légèrement adaptée au pliant
Cette puce équipe les iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max et iPhone Duo. C’est la première puce d’iPhone d’Apple gravée en 2 nm, après les débuts de cette finesse avec la M6 du Mac mini en août. La version du Duo diffère un peu, Dan Murray, vice-président de l’ingénierie silicium, explique qu’Apple a ajouté un second moteur d’affichage pour faire fonctionner simultanément l’écran intérieur et l'écran extérieur.
Le circuit prend aussi en charge une caméra FaceTime placée sous l’écran intérieur. Le refroidissement général repose par ailleurs sur une chambre à vapeur et sur un matériau baptisé « metal over foam », que l’iFixit a également examiné lors de son démontage de l’iPhone 18 Pro. Barabadi le décrit comme un couplage thermique et mécanique direct entre la puce et la chambre à vapeur, dont la mise au point a demandé des mois.
Deux écrans à alimenter, une seule enveloppe thermique
Le second moteur d’affichage a un coût : deux dalles pouvant s’activer ensemble, c’est davantage de chaleur à évacuer dans un châssis qui ne se dilate pas. Le conduit de graphite apporte la réponse côté dissipation, là où une chambre à vapeur classique ne peut pas franchir une charnière.
L’iPhone Duo arrive en magasin le 23 octobre. Les ingénieurs ne donnent à ce stade aucun chiffre de température ou de performance soutenue : c’est à l’usage, sous charge prolongée, que ce conduit fera ses preuves.

articles.title: « Équipé comme un véhicule à 200 000 € » : le spectaculaire Xpeng G9L débarque en France à moitié prix
articles.text:
Avouons que les gros SUV chinois que nous vous faisons régulièrement découvrir dans nos colonnes n’existent pas réellement en France. Ils ne sont pourtant pas très chers, ultra équipés, hyper autonomes et super rapides à recharger. Beaucoup expriment alors à juste titre leur frustration dans les commentaires… Bonne nouvelle, Xpeng semble aujourd’hui les avoir entendus en parachutant l’immense G9L sur notre marché.
Avec ses 5,12 mètres de long, l’engin parvient à surpasser le déjà très obèse G9. Et contrairement à ce que son nom peut suggérer, le G9L n’est pas une vulgaire version rallongée du G9. Il s’agit d’un modèle inédit de la tête aux pieds se plaçant au sommet de la gamme Xpeng. Pour justifier un tel statut, ce porte-drapeau promet un équipement de pointe drapé dans un confort bluffant.
Écran pliant au toit et frigo intégré : la vie de château aux places arrière
Car ce n’est pas au niveau du style qu’il se distinguera des autres. Le G9L est massif avec des éléments esthétiques vus et revus. C’est plutôt à bord que les choses deviennent véritablement intéressantes avec des configurations en 6 et 7 places. Bien vu pour le confort avec des assises zéro gravité massantes sur 16 points installées sous une climatisation centrale innovante. Un vrai réfrigérateur électrique est également à disposition des gourmands.
Plus impressionnant, l’écran multimédia intégré au toit se déploie devant les passagers arrière pour une expérience numérique haut de gamme. La qualité de finition est d’ailleurs du même acabit, avec des matériaux très soignés y compris en partie basse. Cette atmosphère premium se prolonge naturellement sur la liste des équipements. Le G9L embarque ainsi une suspension pneumatique double chambre optimisant le toucher de route.
Suspension pneumatique et feux projecteurs : la débauche technologique
Ses quatre roues directrices améliorent la maniabilité, tandis que les feux matriciels à LED sont une première chez Xpeng. Ils permettent en outre de projeter des guides lumineux au sol. Les cinq ouvrants sont également électriques, même s’ils manquent parfois de finesse dans leur fonctionnement. En configuration 6 places comme ici, l’accès au troisième rang est plutôt aisé. La modularité sera à confirmer en version 7 places avec une banquette au deuxième rang.
Au dernier rang, les attentions ne manquent en tout cas pas avec des sièges chauffants au dossier électrique. L’espace aux jambes est par ailleurs excellent, quelle que soit la place retenue. Côté conduite, le G9L est bien entendu semi-autonome avec ses 3 puces Turing permettant une puissance de calcul ultra élevée. Sa batterie nickel manganèse cobalt en architecture 800 V garde une capacité encore inconnue.
Dès 74 990 € : des prestations de luxe à prix « cassé » ?
Xpeng promet en tout cas jusqu’à 591 km d’autonomie et un 10 à 80 % de charge en seulement 12 minutes. Cela nous amène alors aux trois versions proposées à la vente. L’entrée de gamme Autonomie Étendue Propulsion s’échange contre 74 990 € avec 367 ch et un rayon d’action de 591 km sur le cycle WLTP. Le niveau supérieur Performance Intégrale attaque à 79 990 €, voit sa puissance grimper à 585 ch et son autonomie freinée à 553 km.
Ces deux modèles peuvent accueillir 7 personnes. Ce n’est pas le cas du haut de gamme Performance Intégrale avec ses 6 places facturé 85 990 €. Oui, c’est bien loin des prix pratiqués en Chine qui sont à minima deux fois inférieurs. Mais il faut rappeler que l’industrie automobile chinoise est massivement subventionnée et que l’Europe taxe lourdement les véhicules provenant de l’Empire du Milieu.
Audi, BMW et Volvo dans le collimateur : le pari audacieux de Xpeng
Cela ne suffit de toute manière pas à effacer l’argument prix brandi sans cesse par les constructeurs chinois. Xpeng explique ainsi que « le G9L offre le niveau d’équipements, la technologie et la norme de confort des marques de luxe traditionnelles dont le prix est supérieur à 200 000 € ». La marque vise en priorité les familles roulant en Audi Q7, Volvo XC90 et BMW X5 avec pour principal argument la garantie et le rapport qualité/prix.
