articles.title: How ShipStation Global built an AI IT help desk on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How ShipStation Global built an AI IT help desk on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
This post is co-written with Kenneth Salmon, Edward Boswell, Jack Armstrong, Robert Bahn, and Nick Ciubotariu from ShipStation Global.
Answering the same IT questions and clearing routine tickets drains time that IT teams could spend elsewhere. To reclaim it, the ShipStation Global Engineering team built Deckhand, an AI-powered IT help desk agent for Slack, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
ShipStation Global is the leading intelligent shipping and logistics platform for small and mid-sized shippers, and it operates on a simple belief: the more efficient its teams are, the better it delivers for customers. Deckhand puts that belief to work. It answers routine IT and company questions from a curated knowledge base, reads error-message screenshots, and creates and updates Jira Service Management tickets.
In this post, we discuss how ShipStation architected Deckhand, which resulted in resolving 97.5 percent of incoming channel queries while earning a 96 percent positive feedback rating by employees (Figure 1).
Business challenge
The problem Deckhand solves is the one every IT team will recognize: the same questions are routinely asked, error messages are posted after business hours, and information needs to be gathered from different teams. At ShipStation Global, those conversations lived in a busy help desk Slack channel, where employees asked, and IT answered, one thread at a time. The answers usually already existed in a Confluence how-to article, on a company intranet page, or in a thread from eight months earlier. Finding them was the hard part.
The channel data made the scale concrete. In the 12 months before launch:
- Employees posted more than 1,500 threads, and volume kept growing.
- With employees in the US, UK, Spain, Poland, Australia, and the Philippines, more than a fifth of questions arrived outside US business hours.
- Answers were split across different places: Confluence articles, intranet pages and PDFs, IT-maintained guides, and the channel’s own history.
- Repetitive questions consumed time that structured self-service steps could have handled.
        “We created Deckhand because getting help should be as simple as asking a question in Slack, not deciphering a ticket form or sending an email into the void. We believe that tickets are an indication of operational friction not productivity. Deckhand resolves common questions on the spot and, when it can’t, converts the conversation into a fully contextualized ticket with one click, improving the employee experience and freeing our team from endlessly repeating the phrase: ‘Please file a ticket.’”
— Chris Collins, Senior Director IT at ShipStation Global
Solution overview
Deckhand works in Slack like any teammate—joining channels, reading the conversation, and drawing context from Slack profiles to answer IT questions in place. We run it on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, hosts the agent in isolated sessions, so we run no servers or containers.
The solution has four main components, shown in Figure 2:
- Slack service: A FastAPI and Slack Bolt application, hosted on AWS App Runner. It receives Slack events, decides whether the bot should respond, and builds a user-context payload from the requester’s Slack profile, including name, email, time zone, and manager.
- Agent service: A Strands agent, deployed as a container on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, manages the multi-turn tool agent loop using Anthropic’s Claude in Amazon Bedrock.
- Tools and knowledge: A single AWS Lambda function, exposed as Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, classifies requests, creates and updates Jira tickets, and analyzes images. An Amazon Bedrock knowledge base indexes content from Confluence, the company intranet, Slack, and marketing pages, storing it in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3).
- Operations and feedback. Amazon DynamoDB stores feedback, AWS X-Ray traces request paths using OpenTelemetry, and the services log to Amazon CloudWatch.
When an employee posts in a channel where Deckhand is a member, the Slack service assembles the full thread history and user context. It then invokes the agent through the AgentCore runtime API. The agent searches the knowledge base and calls tools as needed. When it finds an answer, it returns a final response (Figure 3). When it doesn’t, it asks a clarifying question or offers to create a ticket (Figure 4).
Deckhand workflow
This section walks through how Deckhand is implemented, from prerequisites to a working deployment.
Prerequisites
To implement this pattern, you need the following:
- An AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock, AgentCore runtime, and AgentCore Gateway.
- A Slack app with event subscriptions, a signing secret, and a bot token scoped to your use case.
- A container image registry such as Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR).
- An Amazon S3 bucket and an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base.
- AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles scoped to each runtime and tool, and AWS Secrets Manager entries for third-party credentials.
Building the agent with Strands Agents and AgentCore
The agent is intentionally lightweight. Using the open source Strands Agents SDK, an agent consists of a model, a set of tools, and a system prompt. The SDK manages the reasoning loop, allowing the model to select tools, process results, and iterate until it produces an answer. Deckhand’s agent service is implemented in a few lines of Python.
The model ID is set through an environment variable, which allows switching models without modifying application code.
Tools are integrated with the agent in two ways. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases retrieval is a native Strands tool that supports knowledge base search with a single import. Other functions, including classification, ticket management, user resolution, and image analysis, are handled by a Lambda function registered on AgentCore Gateway. The Gateway exposes these as MCP tools, and the Lambda routes each invocation by tool name. This separation allows tool logic to be updated independently, and the agent can access new tools from the Gateway without requiring a rebuild.
AgentCore runtime hosts the agent as a container, avoiding the need for server or session management. The Slack service calls the agent synchronously for each message, providing the thread transcript and user context, and posts the final response. Since context, including the employee’s profile, is included with every request, the agent can complete ticket details automatically.
Knowledge base design and answer routing
Deckhand answers from a single Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with core S3-backed data sources:
- Articles synced from Confluence.
- Internal pages, PDFs, and events synced from the company intranet.
- Resolved support threads mined from Slack (covered in the next section).
Each document includes metadata such as title, source URL, content type, and event dates. This allows the agent to filter content, for example, when users ask about upcoming events or weekly lunch menus in the Austin office.
Mining Slack history with Recursive Language Models (RLMs)
The most valuable data source is the archive of resolved support threads. Before Deckhand existed, Slack was where problems got solved: years of employees describing issues and IT walking them through fixes. That history is an organic knowledge base, validated by the best possible reviewer: the person whose problem got fixed. It’s also noisy: a raw export mixes banter, automated alerts, and threads that never actually got resolved. Indexing an unverified fix or a garbled summary means the knowledge base surfaces an incorrect answer with the same confidence as a correct one, so extraction needs to be precise.
The mining process follows a three-stage pipeline (Figure 5):
- A script exports the channel’s full history via the Slack API, retrieving complete replies for every thread and writing a structured dump that includes thread markers, timestamps, and reply counts.
- DSPy’s Recursive Language Model (RLM), running Claude on Amazon Bedrock, treats that export as a navigable memory space inside a sandboxed Python read-eval-print loop (REPL) rather than a single prompt. Working iteratively over the data, it classifies each thread as resolved, unresolved, or escalated and filters out announcements and non-questions. Strict criteria keep quality high: a thread counts as resolved only when the full, workable fix is visible in the thread itself.
- For each resolved thread, the RLM orchestrates recursive sub-LLM (large language model) calls to extract structured fields, each validated against a Pydantic model. The fields include an issue summary, the original question, and the resolution. They also capture whether the fix is self-service or needs a ticket, the self-service steps, the application and system involved, error messages, and tags. When a sub-LLM call returns something that fails the schema, the RLM’s code-based loop catches the validation error in the interpreter and retries. The results are written as a markdown document organized by issue. The pipeline uploads it to Amazon S3 for the knowledge base to index.
We chose RLM because it maintains the entire Slack history in a persistent sandbox variable space, allowing iterative reasoning over the export and consistent output structure. As a result, when an employee encounters a problem previously solved by a colleague, Deckhand provides the proven solution, often as actionable, numbered steps.
Knowing when not to answer
An AI bot in a shared channel fails socially before it fails technically. Deckhand’s most refined logic decides when to stay quiet:
- The agent’s first decision on every message is whether it’s an announcement, a social message, or a conversation between people. If so, it outputs “SKIP,” and the Slack service suppresses the reply.
- In threads, it replies only to the original poster.
- If the last reply came from another human helper, it stays silent, because a person has taken over.
- If a reply starts by @naming a person, the message isn’t for the bot.
Collecting feedback
Each answer includes feedback buttons. A thumbs-up is recorded directly, while a thumbs-down prompts a brief “what went wrong” field. Ratings are stored in DynamoDB with the original question and the bot’s response.
Negative feedback is a valuable dataset used to improve the system prompt and agent behavior, and to update incorrect knowledge base information.
Security and validation
Prompt rules enhance behavior but do not replace access controls. Enforcement is managed through code and infrastructure:
- Ticket creation requires explicit confirmation. When Deckhand offers to create a ticket, the Slack service adds a Create Ticket button, and selecting it sends confirmation through the agent. Ticket updates only accept valid keys matching the helpdesk project pattern and reject empty comments.
- Classification is validated before it acts. Request classification runs as a separate Amazon Bedrock Converse API call that returns structured ticket fields, validated with Pydantic before anything reaches Jira.
- The image tool is restricted to downloading only from Slack’s file host. It authenticates with the bot token, limits each request to five images of up to 5 MB each, and sends the files to a vision model using the Converse API.
- Credentials stay out of code. Slack tokens, the signing secret, and Jira credentials live in AWS Secrets Manager, and each service and tool runs under its own scoped IAM role.
- The prompt enforces behavioral safeguards: never request passwords or multi-factor authentication (MFA) codes, never write credentials in ticket comments, and never expose profile metadata used for ticket fields.
Outcome
Deckhand launched in April 2026. It started at about 30 messages a day and reached as many as 100 by early summer. In its first three months it handled 1,935 messages, started 1,221 agent conversations, and opened 409 Jira tickets. It replied to 97.5 percent of messages. A third of the questions came in after hours, when no one on the IT team was working, and Deckhand answered 94 percent of those. People who would have waited until the next morning got an answer that night.
Feedback improved as the team worked on it. Positive ratings went from 82 percent in April to 96 percent in June, after they revised the system prompt and knowledge base to fix what people complained about.
The clearest win was ticket deflection. An agent conversation is a question that would otherwise have become a Jira ticket. Of the 1,221 conversations, only 409 turned into tickets. The other 812 were handled in chat. Filing a ticket and then working and closing it runs about 30 minutes. Those 812 conversations add up to roughly 406 hours over three months, or around 1,600 hours a year. Employees kept that time for their own work, and IT never spent it on intake.
Conclusion
Deckhand took repetitive IT questions off people’s plates and gave the time back to employees and the IT team. It works because each part of the stack has one job and runs as a managed service: AgentCore runtime hosts the agent, AgentCore Gateway turns a Lambda function into MCP tools the agent can call, and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases handles retrieval. The team shipped it without standing up servers or maintaining orchestration code.
To build a similar solution, begin with a well-maintained knowledge source and a clearly defined action. Refer to the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation and Strands Agents SDK for agent development, and the Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases documentation for connecting content sources.
To discuss an agentic AI use case for your organization, contact your AWS account team.

articles.title: Le nouveau jeu du créateur de Dragon Quest a été conçu avec l’IA en 30 minutes
articles.text:
Avant de parler de sa nouvelle création, le co-créateur de la saga Dragon Quest a évoqué, dans un message publié sur X le 11 octobre 2026, la manière dont il a conçu l’un de ses premiers jeux, The Portopia Serial Murder Case, sorti en 1983 et publié par Enix. Il avait tout fait seul : l’histoire, les images et la programmation.
Une époque en partie révolue, si l’on en croit la suite de son message : « Aujourd’hui, grâce à l’IA, même sans savoir dessiner ou programmer, il me suffit de donner des instructions à l’intelligence artificielle pour créer tout seul un jeu tout à fait correct. C’est vraiment stupéfiant », écrit Yuji Horii.
Son nouveau jeu, Komiya en salle d’interrogatoire, a été créé avec Claude, l’IA d’Anthropic, et il en partage le lien. C’est une enquête en forme de visual novel, un genre de jeu narratif où l’histoire avance surtout par des dialogues, du texte et des illustrations, avec parfois des choix qui influencent le récit. Selon lui, il ne lui a fallu qu’une trentaine de minutes pour le créer.
Le joueur incarne un policier qui interroge Komiya, un ancien serrurier de 72 ans soupçonné d’avoir vidé le coffre d’un prêteur sur gages. Il ment, et il faut confronter ses déclarations aux preuves pour faire tomber son histoire. Deux jauges, « agitation » et « résistance », évoluent au fil des questions : si la résistance atteint 100, le suspect se mure dans le silence. Le jeu est gratuit et se joue directement dans le navigateur.
L’IA impressionne les vétérans japonais de l’industrie
Yuji Horii, qui travaille actuellement sur Dragon Quest XII: Beyond Dreams (l’ancien The Flames of Fate, renommé en mai 2026 après un redémarrage complet du développement), défend ouvertement l’intelligence artificielle. Le MMO Dragon Quest X a ainsi intégré Gemini, l’IA de Google, à un chatbot incarné par un PNJ. Dans une interview accordée à Famitsu et traduite par GamesRadar en août 2026, le développeur s’était montré enthousiaste sur le sujet : « L’IA actuelle est vraiment intelligente, c’est amusant. »
Yuji Horii n’est pas le seul vétéran de l’industrie japonaise à afficher son intérêt pour cette technologie. En mai 2026, Hironobu Sakaguchi, le créateur de Final Fantasy, avait lui aussi fait réagir en saluant la qualité d’une vidéo de Final Fantasy VI générée par IA.
Pour ces vétérans du jeu vidéo japonais, qui n’ont plus rien à prouver, l’IA devient un terrain d’expérimentation. Toujours est-il que Komiya en salle d’interrogatoire divise. Certains y voient une forme de mépris envers l’industrie et les développeurs qui consacrent leur carrière à créer des jeux, tandis que d’autres invitent ces vétérans à profiter de cette nouvelle technologie, après des décennies passées à faire leurs preuves.
Paradoxalement, Yuji Horii supervise en parallèle, comme directeur exécutif, Next: The Portopia Serial Murder Case, un remake complet de son jeu de 1983 annoncé en septembre lors d’un Nintendo Direct. Le développement est confié aux équipes des studios room6 et Game Studio, pour une sortie prévue en 2027 au Japon, sur Switch, Switch 2 et PC.

articles.title: Vienna-based reebuild raises €3 million to build the AI operating system for construction and real estate | EU-Startups
articles.text:
reebuild, the Vienna-based AI-native back-office automation platform for construction and real estate, has raised a €3 million Seed round.
The round was led by Fortino Ventures, a Ghent-based VC firm backing B2B AI and software companies across Europe from its third-generation VC fund. Other investors in the round include Rise PropTech and CuriosityVC, and existing backer Hansmann Family Office also participated.
“We know the problems of this industry firsthand, and we build reebuild together with our customers, extremely close to the day-to-day reality on site. The software many construction companies and developers still work with today has barely evolved in decades and has fallen behind rising expectations. We’re convinced that we can shake up this market with a team that combines deep construction and technology know-how. Not with another tool, but with a solution that truly understands how construction sites and projects are handled on the commercial side,” said Alexander Kornell, CEO and founder of reebuild.
Founded in 2022 by Alexander Kornell (CEO), Matteo Cimadom (CRO) and Luca Papay (CTO) joined as co-founders, reebuild operates as a vertical AI platform that reads every incoming document line by line, whether a PDF, photo, scan, or e-invoice, and converts it into structured data and automates invoice review, cost management, and material tracking.
On its platform, delivery notes, invoices, and order confirmations are matched automatically, and the software progressively learns from the decisions of commercial managers, reducing repetitive administrative workload over time. On site, a foreman can photograph a delivery note with the mobile app and have it instantly embedded in the system.
With cost administration between departments still largely managed in spreadsheets and paper folders, invoices matched by hand, approvals lacking transparency and early-payment discounts routinely unclaimed, reebuild wants to fix this gap with AI agents preparing work, flagging repetitive tasks and recommending next actions, while keeping human teams in charge of final approvals.
The company says its platform has processed more than €530 million in invoice volume across over 120 construction companies and property developers, spanning more than 8,200 construction sites and projects. It has automatically handled more than 345k documents, counts more than 2,350 active users across its customer base, and includes Pittel+Brausewetter, 3SI Immogroup, Rödl & Herdegen, and Kratzert Gruppe. It also reports that invoice handling time has been cut from over 20 minutes to approximately three minutes, while customers have indicated a reduction in procurement costs by up to 20%.
“We believe now is the time for construction companies to digitise and automate their back-office processes with SaaS and AI. reebuild is the right team to execute on this, with the founding team having their family roots in the construction sector,” said Wouter Goossens, Partner at Fortino Ventures.
The funding will be deployed across three areas: geographic expansion beyond reebuild’s established markets in Austria and Germany, the development of new AI-native modules that fully automate contractors’ workflows from calculation to accounting; and team growth at its Vienna headquarters, where the company currently employs around 25 people.
For reebuild, AI-native modules are the first step, but the company intends to become the agentic back office for the construction industry, where AI agents independently handle routine tasks such as invoicing, on-site documentation, and project estimation, covering a contractor’s entire commercial workflow from calculation to accounting.

articles.title: I don’t miss the camera on the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses
articles.text:
The other day I whizzed past several people while running in the park, my playlist blasting at full volume. The next morning, I smiled at a barista while ordering a caramel apple-flavored matcha latte. Afterward, I sat on a park bench reading a book, called up a pal to chat about her recent trip to Prague, and then asked my Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses what meetings were coming up on my calendar. The chipper AI voice said I hadn’t connected my Google Calendar yet (I had) and asked if I would like help connecting. I sighed and then asked it to play an upbeat song. It picked Kendrick Lamar’s “Not Like Us.”
I don’t miss the camera on the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses
It’s harder to be a perv in these audio-only glasses, but removing the ick does make them less ‘useful.’
These past few days, dozens of people have seen or interacted with me while wearing smart glasses. Not a single person noticed. Probably because these audio-only versions look just like normal glasses. They come in a retro Clubmaster look — like the ones pictured in this review — or a more Wayfarer-esque Burbank style. Honestly, people usually don’t notice when I wear camera glasses either. But for once, I didn’t feel like a creep.
The Good
- I don’t feel like a creep wearing these
- Long battery life
- Lightweight
- Stylish
- Good for open-ear audio
The Bad
- Expensive for what they are
- Still not convinced AI is the killer app for these
The audio-only Ray-Bans aren’t a novel concept. Seven years ago, I strutted around Manhattan taking calls and listening to tunes in the Bose Frames, which also combined Bluetooth audio with stylish sunglasses. Nobody noticed me in the Bose back then, either. What makes this pair notable is that it’s 2026, they’re made by Meta, and, well, there’s been vigorous discourse about whether smart glasses are a form of spyware.
Let’s get privacy out of the way. During setup, all the privacy and data opt-out disclosures were much more prominent than when I’ve previously tested Meta glasses. A screen explained how visual data from AI experiences is handled. (You can opt out of Meta using that data to improve AI; voice data, however, is still used.) There’s no visual data from these glasses — this is simply the new messaging for any pair of Meta glasses. You can also opt out of sharing “additional data” with Meta as well, which is enumerated in a separate document online. This is a good thing, though it doesn’t address what makes people uncomfortable about smart glasses: the uneasy feeling that someone else is recording you.
You know what sort of does, though? Removing the camera. The Bose Frames never triggered the same level of distrust because they were “just” sunglasses-shaped headphones. That applies here too. Frankly, I felt much lighter wearing these out into the world precisely because I couldn’t record footage of anyone. (Even if I feel lame saying “Hey Meta” in public.)
I can imagine people still distrusting these Ray-Bans because they have always-listening capabilities for waking up the AI assistant. However, you can disable the wake word in settings and use a customizable button on the right temple arm instead. (This automatically feels 10 percent less silly if you “must” talk to AI assistants outside the home.) There’s no native way to record a conversation directly from the glasses. Any other audio-based feature, like live translation, has to be manually started.
I’m not saying these can’t be modded or used for evil out of the box. Where there’s a perverse mind and ill will, there’s a way. I’m saying it’d take more effort because these glasses simply don’t do very much.
At least, not yet.
Meta’s Muse AI is eventually coming to the glasses, but it’s not available right now. Right now, the glasses ship with the less powerful Muse Spark model. It’s better than what was on the Ray-Bans in 2023, but it’s still meh unless you’re using it for accessibility reasons. In which case, these glasses may not be the best use of $350. A camera-equipped model is more helpful for low-vision and blind users. For hard-of-hearing users, the FDA-cleared hearing assistance feature isn’t available yet, and for deaf users, the Meta Ray-Ban Display may be more useful because they support live captioning.
For everyone else, Muse Spark is nerfed without the camera but can still come in handy. For example, granting access to your messaging apps, Google Calendar, and email lets it do some light scheduling and correspondence on your behalf. If you enable location sharing, you can send where you are to the group chat. It’s fine for these tasks, but not great. It’s adept at short queries like “What’s my next calendar event?” or “Set a reminder to update my editors at 12PM.” With more complex asks, I’ve found Muse Spark gets confused, and it’s faster to whip out my phone. I ended up mostly asking it to set reminders for to-dos I remembered while in the middle of something else.
Muse Spark can also give you local recommendations and turn-by-turn audio directions while walking. As I’ve written before, that’s great if you’re traveling. Less so if you’re familiar with your local haunts. In my neighborhood, I already know which coffee shops have the best Wi-Fi and snacks — and it wasn’t the one Muse Spark suggested. As for walking directions, they’re not something I need that often. When I did, I found using Google Maps on my phone more helpful for getting my bearings.
I’m sure Muse will open up more possibilities when it arrives later this year. Then again, I’ve seen demos, and I’m still skeptical that agentic AI will be the thing that convinces people to buy smart glasses.
So what do I like about these? They’re simply a good pair of open-ear headphones.
I said good, not great. Sound quality is decent, but you’re still dealing with all the tradeoffs that come with this form factor. They struggle at louder volumes. The trebles start to get tinny, and bass can sound distorted. There’s inevitably sound leakage. My spouse frequently reminded me that they could hear everything I was listening to, all of the AI’s responses, and my phone calls. Conversely, even at top volume, ambient noise can still drown out your content. These won’t cut it on a loud subway, for instance.
Still, it’s nice to listen to audiobooks around the house without jumping out of my skin anytime my spouse or cats want my attention. On my daily walks, I’m less afraid of my maniac neighbors mowing me down in their murder mobiles. (New Jersey drivers, man.) It’s not mind-blowing, but it’s a meaningful improvement to my day-to-day routine. And I don’t have to think too hard about it.
At 43 to 47g, these are also much comfier than every other pair of Meta glasses I’ve tried. So far, I’ve worn them for two full days, including a 30-minute run and multiple walks, with zero issues. My Clubmaster review unit also has nose pads — huzzah for anyone with a low nose bridge. That also made for a huge improvement in call quality since the mic for calls wasn’t smushed up against my schnoz. The temple tips can also be adjusted for a better fit.
I usually ding smart glasses for not supporting my -10 prescription and severe astigmatism. These support a range of -12 to +6 — I’m still waiting on a prescription pair, but at least my garbage eyeballs don’t preclude me from wearing these as my daily glasses. All in all, these glasses will fit a much broader range of faces and vision needs.
Battery life is also phenomenal. I was able to eke out two full workdays without sticking the glasses back into the case.
Okay, I lied — one more gripe. These feel expensive for headphone glasses that don’t do much yet. The Meta Glasses, for example, now start at $250 and technically do more. These are $100 more for what, exactly? The Ray-Ban branding? The privilege of not worrying about freaking out other people? If these were $150 or $200, I’d say these would be a no-brainer. Starting at $350 without prescription lenses, without the hearing assistance features, without Muse? That feels off.
But pricing complaints aside, I didn’t miss the camera. (I only ever use it to take cat videos anyway.) Muse Spark isn’t what I’d call the most compelling AI model, but it’s useful now and then. For the casual user, the headphones are the most useful part of smart glasses.
I wish I could just thrust these into the air and declare that nixing the camera solves the privacy problem. I can’t. Yes, I’m relieved that I don’t have to worry about people punching me in the face if I wear these out and about. I don’t think most people want more than this right now. Still, I’d be lying if I said I didn’t personally know several people who would miss the camera. Not because they’re perverts, but because they find them to be genuinely useful tools for candid home videos, content creation, accessibility, or multimodal AI. For those people, this type of smart glasses isn’t a real option.
Besides, who’s to say Meta won’t add more ambient listening features down the line? Then what? The lack of a camera is only a comfort for now. It doesn’t negate the need for continued, thoughtful discussion about AI wearables, the definition of recording, and what role these gadgets ought to play in our lives.
Photography by Victoria Song / The Verge
Agree to Continue: Ray-Ban Meta Audio
Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate.
To use the Ray-Ban Meta Audio smart glasses, you’ll need a Meta account and the Meta AI app downloaded onto your phone. A Meta account works across platforms like Meta, Instagram, and Quest and comes with its own terms of service and privacy policy. Should you decide to integrate with services like WhatsApp, Messenger, Instagram, Apple Music, Apple Health, Garmin, Strava, Amazon Music, and Spotify, you also agree to those terms and privacy policies. You may also be asked to give permissions related to Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, location services, and voice data. If you choose to get a pair of prescription lenses, you may also be asked to share that information with Ray-Ban and/or LensCrafters.
If you are concerned about privacy, you can access the Glasses Privacy menu in the glasses’ settings. There you can view the voice activity log as well as the “Share additional data” toggle. To access the visual data opt-out toggle, go to the glasses’ settings and navigate to the Meta AI menu.
The smart glasses also come with supplemental terms of service and privacy policies / notices, including:
Final tally: Two mandatory agreements, eight supplemental agreements and notices, and several optional agreements.

articles.title: New USFP Pluggable Optics Form Factor for Higher Speeds from Cisco and NVIDIA
articles.text:
Ahead of the OCP Global Summit, Cisco briefed analysts on AI-infrastructure announcements spanning optics, silicon, systems, and software. For us, the headline is clearly the ultra-dense small form factor, or USFP, a pluggable module Cisco developed with NVIDIA for 400G SerDes lanes, which it says enabling higher-density 1.6Tbps fabrics. Cisco also detailed the Silicon One G300 in first systems, a G302 front-end top-of-rack switch coming in Q4 2026, and the Silicon One A100L aimed at lower-cost 10G/1G out-of-band management switches. USFP will be a big one with both Cisco and NVIDIA behind it and because next-generation pluggable optics are a key part of the 1.6Tbps Ethernet generation. To me, the A100L stood out on the briefing call since Cisco’s custom silicon applied to cost-sensitive switching rather than only the high-performance fabric.
Cisco OCP AI Networking Announcements
Cisco and NVIDIA are designing a new pluggable form factor for 400G SerDes lanes rather than today’s common 200G lanes. We will say “common” because there is still a lot of 56G PAM4 SerDes and 112G gear being sold today. Moving to 400G means 1.6Tbps networking can happen on four lanes, scaling to 6.4T aggregate across 16 lanes and 12.8T across 32. Cisco and NVIDIA are jointly drafting the multi-source specification so other vendors can build to it.
It is interesting that QSFP/ OSFP were not sufficient for the next-gen speeds. Pairing that optics work with switch silicon produces the ethernet-to-optical architecture on the next figure, which places the Silicon One G300 in first-shipped Cisco 8000 and N9000 systems at 102.4T of capacity across 1.6T ports. Now, the new G302 drives a 51.2T front-end top-of-rack switch using 200G SerDes.
The Silcon One A100L made me ask a question at the analyst pre-brief. Custom AI silicon usually appears in high-performance fabric switches since that is where the value from doing something custom often can be captured. Lower-end silicon found in management boxes running the 1G/10G networks in racks tends to be mostly just a volume play. Cisco said it was proof the architecture scales and hyperscale clients wanted to run SONiC on everything. I asked what the licensing model would be, more perpetual like a C1300 or more like the Nexus 9K series but did not get a clear answer on that one so I am going to call it a TBD. The reason I asked is that if you are doing custom silicon versus like a Marvell Prestera and not capturing software revenue, that feels like a tough road to take.
Live Protect for Cisco SONiC on Nexus One adds runtime vulnerability shielding to N9000 switches, applying policy to a running system so operators can protect it before scheduling a conventional patch and reboot. Cisco SONiC is set to be available in 2027, but that feels like a big move for Cisco as well.
Cisco positions Live Protect to shrink the exploit window, with availability slated for Q2 2027 in Cisco-validated SONiC environments. Customers will also be able to choose between community or custom SONiC and a Cisco-validated distribution, as the final operating-model figure shows.
Rounding out the software story is how Cisco intends customers to run SONiC. An operating-model figure lays out two tracks. A community or custom path offers full customization and source access for maximum control, while a turnkey Cisco-validated path provides a defined upgrade path and professional services. Notably, Cisco’s use of NVIDIA Spectrum-X is an option we have covered before, but aside from supporting the open-source SONiC, Cisco is also supporting switching platforms from NVIDIA.
Final Words
With Cisco and NVIDIA behind USFP, it will become an industry standard. Hopefully we will get to see some module shells on the OCP show floor this week. Silicon One G302 is a meaningful milestone on its own, but A100L sliding into out-of-band management feels almost crazy to me, since the sub-1Tbps switch space was widely assumed to be largely commoditized.

articles.title: El ex de Hayden Panettiere pide al tribunal que actúe como representante de su hija para proteger la herencia
articles.text:
Wladimir Klitschko ya tiene la custodia de su hija Kaya, pero eso no le da ningún poder sobre lo que la niña hereda de su madre. Por eso ha ido al tribunal de sucesiones del condado de Los Ángeles: pide que lo nombren tutor temporal de su patrimonio. El escrito se presentó el jueves 24 de septiembre y la vista está señalada para hoy.
Hayden Panettiere murió el 16 de agosto, a los 36 años, en un apartamento de Greenville, en Carolina del Sur. El forense del condado habló de una sobredosis accidental de varias sustancias, entre ellas fentanilo; la policía de la ciudad investiga y, según lo publicado, la DEA se habría sumado a la investigación. Kaya es, según el escrito, su única heredera.
Tiene la custodia, ¿para qué quiere una tutela?
Son dos cosas distintas. Por un lado, la custodia decide dónde vive la niña y quién la cuida. Lo que es la tutela del patrimonio decide quién firma por ella cuando hay dinero de por medio, porque, como es normal, una menor no puede administrarlos.
En el primer caso, Klitschko decide el colegio; para firmar en su nombre un papel del banco, necesita otro tipo de autorización.
Por eso mismo, Klitschko pide ser tutor temporal, no definitivo, y el escrito define la medida como “urgent and essential”. Lo que dice buscar es proteger lo que hereda Kaya hasta que el tribunal designe a alguien que administre el patrimonio de la actriz, y según la petición, también quiere estar legitimado para impulsar ese nombramiento.
Todo esto viene porque, según varias informaciones de la prensa del corazón, Panettiere no dejó testamento.
Joyas, correos y cerraduras: lo que dice el escrito
En toda esta historia se ha dado una situación que puede resultar especialmente preocupante. Según parece, una persona sin identificar habría entrado sin permiso en la propiedad de Los Ángeles antes de la muerte de la actriz; por eso, contrataron seguridad. Según parece, faltaban joyas y otras pertenencias.
Pero eso no es todo; se dice que personas ajenas a la familia habrían accedido a correos electrónicos de la actriz y los habrían borrado. Tras su muerte, se habrían cambiado las cerraduras y trasladado ropa y accesorios a unidades de almacenamiento.
Nada de esto está verificado de forma independiente. Lo único comprobado: hay una petición, está en un tribunal de Los Ángeles y tiene vista. El escrito no dice quién es la persona que preocupa a Klitschko y, según uno de los resúmenes que se han publicado, parte de lo que dice le ha llegado de oídas.
Una casa de empeño, 26.800 euros y una petición a la policía
Poco después de conocerse la petición, salió a la luz una ampliación: Klitschko quiere que su nombramiento incluya la autoridad de pedir una investigación policial sobre los bienes.
Lo que parece es que piensa que una persona no familiar vinculada a la actriz pudo vender joyas en una casa de empeño (no se sabe si de las desaparecidas o no), aunque la tienda, dice, no da datos sin intervención policial.
El 7 de octubre se conoció otro argumento. Klitschko dice que adelantará de su bolsillo unos 30.000 dólares (unos 26.800 euros) por los impuestos de 2025 de la actriz, que vencen el 15 de octubre. Eso sí, seguidamente pedirá a la herencia que se los devuelva.
¿Quién puede leer los correos de alguien que ha muerto?
Este tipo de nombramiento provisional existe en California. El artículo 2250 del Código de Sucesiones pide que se presenten hechos que acrediten una causa justificada y, mientras tanto, deja al tutor temporal en funciones hasta que se resuelva la petición.
En el caso del patrimonio de la fallecida, hay otra figura relevante, la del administrador especial del artículo 8540, con poderes limitados a conservar los bienes.
Respecto a los correos. La ley californiana separa dos cosas. Según el artículo 876, el proveedor solo entrega al representante del patrimonio el contenido de los mensajes si el difunto lo consintió o lo ordena un tribunal.
En este caso se desconoce qué proveedor está implicado ni que alguien haya pedido nada. A nivel práctico, lo mejor es dejarlo preparado en vida: Google permite designar hasta diez contactos de confianza en su administrador de cuentas inactivas, y Apple da a su contacto de legado tres años de acceso una vez aprobada la solicitud.

articles.title: La nouvelle Samsung Galaxy Tab S12+ est déjà vendue en pack avec près de 200 € de remise — Frandroid
articles.text:
La Samsung Galaxy Tab S12+ est sur le marché depuis le 7 octobre 2026 seulement, autant dire que c’est tout récent. Il s’agit, comme son nom l’indique, de la 12e génération de tablette tactile de Samsung, avec notamment une toute nouvelle puce malgré un design qui peine à se renouveler. Mais l’ergonomie reste au top avec une finesse de 5,3 mm et un poids contenu de 553 grammes, ce qui facilite son transport et son utilisation. Pour célébrer sa sortie, Boulanger fait une petite réduction de 40 euros et propose 150 euros de bonus au rachat de votre ancien matériel, ce qui fait ce pack avec un étui à au moins 1 169 euros au lieu de 1 359 euros.
Ce qui plaît chez la Samsung Galaxy Tab S12+
- L’intégration de la puce Dimensity 9500 capable de monter jusqu’à 4,21 GHz
- Son design fin avec 5,3 mm d’épaisseur pour 553 grammes
- Elle intègre nativement un stylet S Pen et le pack propose un étui de protection, toujours pratique
Le pack avec la Samsung Galaxy Tab S12+ et l’étui de protection coûte normalement 1 359 euros mais est affiché à 1 319 euros sur Boulanger. En plus, vous avez un bonus reprise de 150 euros qui s’ajoute si vous avez du matériel à faire reprendre. Ce qui met le tout à 1 169 euros, sans compter le prix de reprise de votre matériel.
Un design inchangé mais des mensurations impressionnantes
Avec la Samsung Galaxy Tab S12+, la marque ne tente pas de réinventer la roue, mais plutôt de recycler ce qui fonctionnait déjà bien pour pouvoir se concentrer sur l’essentiel : la puissance. On l’a déjà dit, la tablette fait 5,3 mm d’épaisseur pour 553 grammes, ce qui permet de l’emmener partout facilement. En plus, la tablette profite d’un bel écran confortable de 12,6 pouces qui affiche 2 800 x 1 752 pixels. Donc que ce soit pour travailler, regarder une vidéo ou même jouer un peu, ça reste tout à fait jouable. Et elle est certifiée IP68, donc elle résiste à l’eau et à la poussière.
En plus, elle est livrée avec un stylet S Pen, ce qui permet de naviguer dessus avec plus de finesse, sans laisser de traces de doigts. Si vous faites du dessin ou de la prise de notes, c’est aussi un réel avantage. Parce que vous pouvez en plus compter sur des fonctions novatrices avec Galaxy AI et l’application Studio Création, qui renforcent la polyvalence de cette tablette. Mais tout ça est rendu possible par la véritable vedette de cette nouvelle tablette Samsung, la puce Mediatek Dimensity 9500.
Samsung et le pari audacieux de Mediatek
Pour la première fois sur la famille Galaxy Tab S, Samsung délaisse ses fournisseurs habituels pour intégrer un processeur Mediatek Dimensity 9500. Un composant avec huit cœurs qui peut afficher une cadence maximale de 4,21 GHz, ce qui promet des performances de haut vol. Sur smartphone, le Dimensity 9500 a prouvé sa valeur dans des modèles comme le Xiaomi X17T Pro ou encore le Oppo Find X9 et sa déclinaison Pro. La puce est épaulée par 12 Go de RAM et 256 Go sur le modèle qui nous concerne ici.
L’autonomie n’est pas en reste avec une batterie de 10 600 mAh qui promet jusqu’à 21h en lecture vidéo, avec en plus une charge rapide 45 W, à condition d’avoir le chargeur compatible. Tout n’est pas parfait toutefois, avec notamment la perte d’une caméra arrière par rapport à la génération précédente. Il ne reste que deux capteurs, dont un objectif principal de 13 Mpx. Quand on prend un appareil pareil, ce n’est pas pour faire de la photo, mais quand on voit le prix, on aurait aimé quand même quelque chose d’un peu plus avancé.
Vous pouvez consulter notre guide sur les meilleures tablettes tactiles si vous souhaitez comparer cette nouvelle Samsung Galaxy Tab S12+ avec d’autres modèles déjà passés entre nos mains.

articles.title: El CNI busca 17 perfiles técnicos para anticiparse a las amenazas de la IA y la cuántica: lo que piden dice mucho de cómo se prepara
articles.text:
El Centro Nacional de Inteligencia ha abierto una campaña para incorporar ingenieros y analistas técnicos. Son 17 perfiles, desde el análisis de malware hasta el despliegue de modelos de IA, para los que el CNI está recibiendo currículums durante este mes de octubre.
Qué está ocurriendo. El CNI se prepara para un escenario de amenazas dirigidas por máquinas. En ese sentido está trabajando sobre dos cuestiones: la IA y lo que la computación cuántica puede hacer con el cifrado de las comunicaciones.
Su brazo de ciberseguridad, el Centro Criptológico Nacional, llevará esos temas a las Jornadas STIC, que se celebran del 24 al 27 de noviembre en Madrid. Y las contrataciones van en la misma línea: formar ahora a quienes tendrán que estar preparados cuando esas amenazas maduren.
La amenaza. Un ordenador cuántico lo bastante potente podrá romper el cifrado de clave pública que protege casi cualquier comunicación, del RSA a las curvas elípticas. Ese ordenador todavía no existe, pero un adversario puede guardar hoy tráfico cifrado y esperar a tenerlo.
- Lo que viaja protegido en 2026 tal vez pueda leerse en 2035.
- Para quien maneja información clasificada con una vigencia de décadas, el plazo para prepararse ya ha empezado.
Migrar a criptografía poscuántica exige gente que sepa dónde vive cada clave dentro de cada sistema. Es un trabajo que encaja con perfiles como los de consultoría de ciberseguridad, acreditación de sistemas clasificados o comunicaciones.
Entre líneas. Las fichas dan pistas de cómo trabaja el CNI:
- Pone a prueba sus propias defensas. Uno de los puestos incluye desarrollar pruebas de concepto de malware para sus propios equipos de pentesting. La idea es atacarse primero para saber por dónde entraría otro.
- Quiere la IA en casa. El perfil de Data Science pide desplegar modelos on-premise, ajustarlos y conocer el hardware necesario para ejecutar modelos grandes. Un servicio de inteligencia no puede ir subiendo documentos clasificados a un chatbot comercial. Necesita su propio LLM funcionando en sus propias máquinas.
- Analiza la tecnología. Otro puesto se dedica a buscar vulnerabilidades en Bluetooth, Zigbee, Matter o Thread, los protocolos domóticos que gobiernan enchufes inteligentes o timbres con cámara.
El contraste. En la misma lista que los modelos de IA aparece un ingeniero TEMPEST. Su trabajo es certificar que un equipo no filtra, a través de su radiación electromagnética, lo que muestra su pantalla.
Es una disciplina nacida en la Guerra Fría que sigue haciendo falta hoy. Para las amenazas nuevas no sobra ninguna de las viejas.
En detalle. Los requisitos comunes son bastante terrenales: un grado o una ingeniería superior (Telecomunicaciones, Informática, Matemáticas, Física o Ciencia de Datos, según el puesto), carné B y un nivel B2 de inglés.
Hay un detalle en ese último requisito: el B2 se puede acreditar durante los dos primeros años. Así, un buen ingeniero no se queda fuera por el idioma. El CNI dice además que impulsa activamente el equilibrio entre hombres y mujeres, algo que considera necesario para cumplir sus objetivos en un sector técnico todavía mayoritariamente masculino.
Entre bambalinas. Quienes superen la primera criba irán a un encuentro presencial y restringido en Madrid a principios de 2027. Allí no solo les entrevistará el departamento de selección, que valorará el perfil personal. También lo harán sus futuros jefes y compañeros de despacho, que evaluarán los conocimientos técnicos. El propio CNI lo presenta como algo nuevo entre los servicios de inteligencia.
En una empresa privada, un candidato puede preguntar a un conocido o mirar en LinkedIn quién hace exactamente qué. Aquí nada de eso es posible, y ese encuentro es la única ventana. Funciona en las dos direcciones: el equipo puede comprobar de primera mano los conocimientos técnicos del candidato, y el candidato verá con quién pasará los próximos años en un trabajo del que sentirse orgulloso.
Los currículums se envían a través de la web del CNI.

articles.title: $86 Million Crypto Heist Linked to Ledger Signer Hardware Implant
articles.text:
A hardware implant in Ledger signers is blamed for the theft of at least $86 million in cryptocurrency from multiple users.
Ledger provides users with a secure cryptocurrency wallet that is backed by a signer, an offline hardware device used to securely authorize blockchain transactions.
Ledger signers sold via Southeast Asia reseller CryptoBilis were found to include an unauthorized hardware implant designed to intercept user data and send it to the attackers.
The cryptocurrency theft was disclosed on October 9 and was immediately pinned on devices sold through CryptoBilis. Ledger asked the company to stop selling its devices and instructed customers to stop using them.
“We recommend Ledger users who purchased from this reseller in the last 90 days to not initiate set up if you have not done so yet. If you have set up your Ledger device, consider moving assets to a new Ledger signer (with new seed),” the company said.
On October 13, Ledger confirmed that all confirmed fund losses linked to the incident involved a signer sold through CryptoBilis.
It appears that someone along the distribution chain modified the signers to manually solder the hardware implant to the device’s circuit boards.
“The implant sits inside the enclosure and reads the data shown on the screen. During setup, the signer displays the 24-word recovery phrase. When the implant detects these screens, its microcontroller decodes the words and transmits them over LTE using a provisioned eSIM,” Ledger said.
The implant was designed only for information interception and does not modify the device’s OS, transactions, or signatures.
According to on-chain investigator Specter, the total losses associated with the supply chain attack may top $86 million.
Ledger, on the other hand, says it has not confirmed the number of impacted users or the total stolen.

articles.title: Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
articles.text:
Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of Oxford
- Summary:
- Oxford physicists have recreated a bizarre quantum effect in which a particle responds to a magnetic field without ever traveling through it. Using a hybrid quantum computer, they demonstrated how introducing a simulated magnetic flux could completely halt a particle's movement through quantum interference. The experiment brings a decades-old prediction into a new setting where matter and quantum fields influence one another.
- Share:
A particle does not have to pass through a magnetic field to be influenced by it. That surprising feature of quantum physics has now been recreated by researchers at the University of Oxford, who used a hybrid quantum computer to demonstrate how an invisible magnetic influence can bring a simulated particle's movement to a complete stop.
The experiment reproduced a phenomenon known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect, in which a charged particle traveling around a region containing magnetic flux experiences a measurable change in its quantum state, even though its path never takes it through the magnetic field itself.
The Oxford team achieved this using a quantum system that combines qubits, the basic units of quantum information, with quantum oscillators, which represent vibrating motion. Their findings, published in Nature Physics, demonstrate how this combination could help scientists investigate fundamental interactions between matter and fields that are increasingly difficult to simulate using conventional computers.
A Strange Quantum Effect Predicted in 1959
In everyday physics, a charged particle responds to the electric and magnetic fields it encounters. Quantum mechanics, however, reveals that particles can behave in ways that have no straightforward counterpart in our ordinary experience.
In 1959, physicists Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm predicted that a charged particle could be affected by magnetic flux even if it traveled entirely outside the region containing the magnetic field. Rather than experiencing a conventional magnetic force along its path, the particle would undergo a change in its quantum phase.
Quantum phase describes an aspect of a particle's wave behavior that influences how different possible paths interfere with one another. Although the phase itself is not directly visible, differences in phase can produce measurable effects.
The prediction became known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect and was eventually verified in experiments involving real electrons. It remains one of the clearest demonstrations that the quantum world operates according to rules that go beyond the familiar laws of classical physics.
Researchers are now exploring how this phenomenon behaves in more complex theoretical systems known as lattice gauge theories.
These theories describe how matter interacts with fields associated with fundamental forces. They represent space as a grid, with matter located at individual points and fields associated with the connections between them. Such models are particularly important in particle physics and high-energy physics, where scientists study the basic particles and interactions that make up the universe.
The challenge is that the mathematics becomes extraordinarily demanding as these systems grow more complicated. Even powerful conventional computers can struggle to calculate how all the interacting components evolve.
Quantum computers offer a different approach. Instead of attempting to calculate every aspect of a quantum system using classical computing methods, scientists can construct another quantum system that follows the same underlying rules. They can then observe its behavior directly, an approach known as quantum simulation.
How Scientists Built the Quantum Experiment
The Oxford project began in 2022, when lead author Dr. Sebastian Saner, Dr. Oana Bazavan, and their colleagues started developing a way to simulate lattice gauge theories using a hybrid quantum system. They collaborated with Dr. Alejandro Bermudez of the Instituto de Física Teórica in Madrid.
Their experimental design relied on two different quantum components that performed separate functions.
The first consisted of qubits encoded in the internal states of trapped ions, which are electrically charged atoms held in place using electromagnetic fields. These qubits represented the gauge fields in the theoretical model.
The second component used quantum oscillators, created by the vibrations of those same trapped ions. These oscillators represented matter.
By combining the two, the researchers constructed a simple loop that served as a basic building block of a lattice gauge theory. Two oscillators represented matter at two different locations, while two qubits represented the fields connecting those locations.
Although the arrangement was small, it was sufficient to reproduce an important interaction between matter and magnetic flux.
Quantum Entanglement Creates a Surprising Solution
The researchers next placed the two qubits into an entangled quantum state. Entanglement is a phenomenon in which quantum systems become linked in ways that cannot be fully explained by classical physics.
Within the team's simulated lattice gauge theory, this entangled state represented magnetic flux passing through the center of the loop.
Initially, the researchers had planned to introduce the magnetic flux as a fixed background condition. However, creating the necessary interaction would have required capabilities that their quantum hardware did not possess.
Encoding the flux directly into the qubits provided a practical alternative. More importantly, it allowed the magnetic flux to become part of the evolving quantum system rather than remaining an unchanging external influence.
"For us, the exciting step was to encode the magnetic flux in a gauge field that was itself dynamical," says Dr. Saner. "Rather than having matter evolve in a fixed background, the matter and gauge field become part of the same quantum dynamics."
What began as a technical workaround ultimately enabled the researchers to explore a more interesting version of the phenomenon, one in which matter and the field could participate together in the quantum dynamics.
A Quantum Effect That Stops Particle Motion
With their simulated loop in place, the scientists examined how a matter particle moved between locations through a process known as quantum tunneling.
Quantum tunneling allows particles to move between states in ways that would not be possible under ordinary classical rules.
When the researchers ran their simulation without magnetic flux, the particle could tunnel freely around the loop.
Introducing the simulated flux produced a strikingly different result.
The particle had two possible paths around the loop, but the magnetic flux changed their relative quantum phases. As a result, the two paths interfered destructively, meaning their quantum contributions canceled each other out.
This interference completely suppressed the tunneling, leaving the simulated particle frozen in its original state.
The outcome demonstrated the Aharonov-Bohm effect within a lattice gauge theory containing a dynamical field. Rather than simply reproducing the familiar behavior of a particle moving around a fixed magnetic influence, the experiment showed how the phenomenon can emerge when matter and the field are both represented by interacting quantum components.
A New Tool for Exploring Fundamental Physics
The Oxford findings were published alongside a related study by researchers at the University of Maryland, led by Professor Norbert Linke.
The Maryland team also used a hybrid quantum system, but their experiment focused on simulating the Yukawa potential, a mathematical description of an interaction relevant to nuclear and particle physics.
Although the two research groups developed their methods independently, they later coordinated the submission of their studies to Nature Physics.
Together, the experiments demonstrate how hybrid quantum computers could become valuable tools for investigating fundamental interactions that are difficult to reproduce using classical simulations.
By combining different types of quantum components, researchers can build systems in which matter and fields are represented in ways that more closely reflect the physics they want to study.
The Oxford experiment provides an example of that potential. A phenomenon first predicted in 1959 and later observed with electrons has now been recreated in a quantum simulator where the field itself participates in the dynamics, offering scientists another way to explore the unusual rules governing the quantum world.

articles.title: Los datos de casi nueve millones de daneses, ¿expuestos por usar la contraseña 123456?
articles.text: Ilustración de miniaturas de personas con ordenadores frente a códigos binarios. La contraseña 123456 es poco recomendable para una cuenta de Netflix o de banco, pero aún menos cuando es la clave para acceder a una base de datos de todos los ciudadanos de un país. Ha sido el caso de Dinamarca. Unos ciberdelincuentes descargaron en septiembre los nombres, direcciones y números de seguridad social de casi nueve millones de daneses, un número superior incluso a la población, que es de seis millones, porque incluye también a personas ya fallecidas o habitantes en el extranjero, en la mayor filtración de datos de la historia del país. El supuesto pirata informático afirma ahora en una entrevista con el diario danés Politiken que accedió al Registro Central de Población (CPR, por sus siglas en inglés) tras probar la combinación 123456 como credencial de una empresa privada que tenía acceso legal a la base de datos. Seguir leyendo

articles.title: European Cities Deploy NVIDIA-Powered AI Agents to Run Smarter Urban Operations
articles.text:
Keeping a city running means making decisions that affect residents every day — from when to repair a road to how to use energy more efficiently.
Across the EMEA region, cities and local software, infrastructure and integration partners are using NVIDIA accelerated computing to build physical AI agents and digital twins that help teams make those decisions. These applications can anticipate maintenance needs, guide urban planning and make public services more responsive.
Software partners including ABA Technology, Akila, Galene AI, Honeywell Technologies, K2K, Linker Vision, Milestone, Onetera, ThinkDeep and Younite are using NVIDIA physical and agentic AI to develop solutions for city operations and public services.
Video courtesy of Linker Vision.
NVIDIA Cosmos open models and the NVIDIA Metropolis Blueprint for video search and summarization (VSS) help agents interpret video and identify conditions, such as traffic congestion, equipment condition, underused spaces and safety hazards, that need attention. NVIDIA Nemotron open models enable developers to build agents that reason over information, respond in natural language and deploy digital twins with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries.
Projects span Belgium, Finland, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Poland, Sweden, the U.K. and elsewhere.
In the U.K., the Liverpool City Region, K2K is exploring how to build AI factories using NVIDIA accelerated computing, Cosmos and the VSS blueprint that can support urban planning and public services — testing applications for mobility and safety. The Island of Jersey is working with K2K to strengthen decision-making, mobility and urban planning while advancing clean energy and public services. Innovation City Belfast is exploring a pilot with K2K focused on smart mobility, transport systems, citizen safety and event and response management.
Video courtesy of K2K.
In France, the Department of Côte-d’Or, Akila and ThinkDeep built operations agents that combine sensor, infrastructure and historical data in a sovereign digital twin using NVIDIA Nemotron, Omniverse and accelerated computing, with Cosmos adoption planned for video data. Across more than 500 public buildings, the agents support energy, compliance, safety and climate resilience, and cut document search time from weeks to minutes and reduce total operating costs by 10%, targeting 30% at scale.
Video courtesy of Akila.
In addition, Port Sud de France in Sète is working with ThinkDeep’s agentic platform that uses Cosmos and Nemotron to analyze cargo and safety data, coordinate operations and guide secure handling of hazardous materials.
In Italy’s Milan region, Galene.AI, Dell Technologies and TD Synnex are deploying an NVIDIA-powered, locally operated AI factory, starting with Cinisello Balsamo and planning expansion to four additional municipalities. Services include real-time translation, citizen chatbots and assistance with procurement and funding. These applications aim to simplify administrative work and help people get access to municipal data in seconds versus hours, while keeping local governance of data.
At Belgium’s Port of Antwerp-Bruges, Milestone and Dell Technologies are testing how agentic vision AI technologies, using NVIDIA Cosmos and the VSS blueprint, could support complex use cases such as oil-spill warnings by training models with synthetic data to prepare for incidents where real-world data is scarce.
In the Nordics, Younite is developing a digital twin experience with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for Gothenburg in Sweden as a part of the EU’s Citiverse initiative, focused on helping cities simulate changes and improve accessibility by providing event entrance previews, seating and crowd conditions before arrival.
These cities point toward a broader ambition: adapting agentic applications to local needs and extending them across departments and neighboring municipalities and countries such as Poland’s city of Wroclaw.
Elsewhere in the region, Honeywell Technologies is deploying Forge Cognition, powered by NVIDIA Nemotron, Cosmos, Omniverse and the VSS blueprint, at the Dubai Fairmont Hotel to connect AI agents with building systems and improve reliability, energy efficiency and operations.
Video courtesy of Honeywell Technologies.
Building the AI Infrastructure for European Cities
For European cities, scaling from pilots to everyday operations requires infrastructure that can process local data, customize models and run AI agents.
System builders and infrastructure partners including Cisco, Dell Technologies, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro are packaging NVIDIA accelerated computing, networking and storage into locally operated AI factories. These systems let cities customize and run intelligent applications locally while retaining control of their data, models and operations.
Nebius and Net Zero Compute are part of the broader ecosystem building AI factories designed to accelerate deployment and reduce costs for agentic services. EY and Accenture provide the integration and operational expertise to connect applications with city systems. Their work helps cities build repeatable deployment blueprints that they can adapt across departments and expand as local needs grow.
Learn how NVIDIA and its ecosystem are bringing physical AI, agentic AI and local AI factories to cities worldwide at Smart City Expo World Congress, running Nov. 3-5 in Barcelona.

articles.title: MIT startup says it can turn diesel trucks into cheaper hydrogen haulers — see it at Disrupt | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Diesel fuel powers everything from shipping to agriculture, and with prices hitting record highs in recent weeks, governments around the world are scrambling to contain the fallout.
For now, that’s meant releasing fuel from stockpiles, but in the coming years, the answer might be a new technology from an MIT startup called LNK Energies.
LNK has created a way to convert existing heavy-duty trucks from diesel to hydrogen, slashing pollution and costs while shielding operators from the price spikes that result from geopolitical instability like the war in Iran. “If you look at total cost of ownership of a Class 8 truck, it’s 13% cheaper than diesel,” Alexis Huynh, chief technology officer at LNK Energies, told TechCrunch. (Class 8 is the heaviest category of trucks, including big rigs.)
Automotive companies have been exploring the use of hydrogen in long-haul trucking in part because refilling a hydrogen tank is faster than recharging the massive batteries those trucks require. But hydrogen is challenging to move to refilling stations, and the pressure tanks required to store it on the truck are large and costly.
LNK’s approach is to carry hydrogen chemically attached to another compound. Liquid organic hydrogen carriers, or LOHCs, are liquids that can absorb and later release hydrogen, and they have been widely studied, but mostly for moving large quantities of hydrogen from refineries to fueling stations. The equipment needed to separate hydrogen from the LOHC, known as a reactor, has been too big to fit onto a truck.
“A lot of the reactors that LOHC companies have today are really large. They’re about the size of a shipping container,” Huynh said. “We have shrunk that basically to the size of a mini fridge.”
Moving the reactor onto the truck saves a surprising amount of energy. When hydrogen is stored on a truck, it must be pressurized to more than 11,000 psi (800 bar), roughly 800 times normal air pressure, and squeezing it that hard takes a lot of power. Because LNK’s fuel carries the hydrogen in liquid form and releases it on board as needed, that step goes away. “We’re eliminating the expensive compression step,” Sayandeep Biswas, co-founder and CEO of LNK Energies, told TechCrunch.
In LNK’s system, once the hydrogen is released on the truck, it can be burned in a conventional internal combustion engine, the kind in today’s diesel trucks, with just a few modifications. The company uses waste heat from the engine to help power the on-board reactor. Or, if the trucking company wants to fully eliminate combustion emissions, it can use fuel cells instead, which convert hydrogen into electricity to power electric motors.
The LOHC can be stored in a traditional fuel tank and dispensed using pumps, just like diesel. “The entire hydrogen infrastructure doesn’t need to exist,” Biswas said. “It’s just a standard diesel station.”
Biswas and Huynh have a demonstration reactor working in the lab that can power an engine from a lawnmower. In 18 months, they plan to install a larger version in a commercial truck.
The trucks will cost more up front, but promise to be cheaper to operate. The duo are confident that they can undercut diesel at a price of $6.50 per gallon after they’ve made just 50 to 100 trucks. None of their projections include government subsidies. “The idea isn’t to have a technology that is cheaper at scale, but one that is cheaper even during that adoption period,” Biswas said.
LNK will present live onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt, taking place October 13-15 in San Francisco, as part of our Startup Battlefield pitch competition. Come join us in San Francisco and take part in the action.

articles.title: Steam regala cuatro juegos para PC: terror, misterio, ciudades y realidad virtual
articles.text:
Steam regala cuatro juegos para PC este martes 13 de octubre, con una selección que reúne terror, misterio, construcción de ciudades y realidad virtual. Los títulos pueden añadirse sin coste a la biblioteca, mientras que una de las propuestas requiere un visor compatible con Steam Frame. La oferta permite incorporar experiencias distintas sin pagar y suma un juego que antes tenía precio para los usuarios de la plataforma.
La selección ofrece alternativas de géneros diferentes, además uno de los títulos obsequiados pasó de ser un producto de pago a distribuirse gratis de forma permanente. Junto con ese título, Steam incluye una historia corta de terror, una aplicación inmersiva y un simulador de gestión urbana con nueve etapas históricas. Antes de instalar cualquier descarga, conviene revisar sus requisitos técnicos y las funciones que ofrece cada ficha.
Cuáles son los cuatro juegos gratuitos para ampliar la biblioteca de Steam
La lista reúne propuestas que se alejan de los lanzamientos de gran presupuesto. Huckleberry Fields Forever propone investigación y plataformas; Whistling at Night sitúa al jugador en un bosque nocturno; Arcturus Vision Gaussian XR utiliza tecnología de realidad virtual; y Keepshore plantea el crecimiento de una ciudad desde sus primeras viviendas.
Las cuatro descargas están disponibles sin coste y no tienen una fecha límite anunciada por sus responsables.
Huckleberry Fields Forever pasó de ser de pago a gratuito
Huckleberry Fields Forever es una aventura bidimensional donde el jugador persigue a un ladrón por más de 50 localizaciones. Para avanzar, debe entrevistar testigos, recoger pistas y superar niveles que combinan exploración con saltos y obstáculos.
El juego incorpora escenarios generados de forma procedural, de modo que algunos recorridos pueden cambiar entre partidas. También admite cooperativo local para cuatro personas desde un mismo ordenador y cuenta con cientos de niveles para jugar.
El elemento diferencial de este título está en su modelo de distribución. Sus creadores lo ofrecieron inicialmente como juego de pago durante el acceso anticipado, pero retiraron ese precio al concluir la etapa.
Huckleberry Fields Forever puede reclamarse de forma permanente sin depender de una campaña limitada. La decisión permite instalarlo más adelante y conservarlo vinculado a la cuenta una vez que se complete el proceso de adquisición en Steam.
Whistling at Night apuesta por el terror y la tensión
Whistling at Night presenta una experiencia breve de terror inspirada en el folclore indígena. Su historia sigue a un joven que recorre solo un bosque oscuro con una linterna, después de ignorar las advertencias de sus mayores. La propuesta no se basa en combates ni en una campaña larga. Su recorrido se apoya en los sonidos del entorno, la falta de visibilidad y la incertidumbre del paso nocturno.
Arcturus Vision Gaussian XR requiere un visor compatible
Arcturus Vision Gaussian XR es la descarga más específica de la selección, porque no funciona como un videojuego convencional para ordenador. La aplicación permite recorrer entornos tridimensionales reconstruidos mediante Gaussian Splatting, una técnica que representa espacios digitales a partir de puntos visuales.
Incluye ocho escenas de ejemplo, herramientas para desplazarse y opciones para visualizar archivos compatibles. Para utilizarla es necesario disponer de Steam Frame y comprobar la compatibilidad del equipo.
Keepshore permite construir una ciudad a través de nueve épocas
Keepshore completa la lista con un simulador de construcción de ciudades en tres dimensiones. La partida empieza en una isla con viviendas y avanza hasta formar asentamientos a través de nueve épocas históricas.
El juego incluye más de 600 edificios, cadenas de producción y una economía dinámica que obliga a administrar recursos y planificar el crecimiento. La versión principal es gratuita, aunque ofrece contenidos adicionales opcionales de pago.
Cómo añadir los cuatro juegos gratuitos a Steam
- Iniciar sesión
- Buscar cada título
- Confirmar precio 0,00
- Seleccionar “Obtener”
- Validar la operación en la cuenta Steam personal

articles.title: What’s old is new: Lightwell discovers novel zero-day vulnerability in core Java framework
articles.text:
Enterprise IT runs on decades-old foundational code. The prevailing assumption around these mature components is that if code has been sitting untouched in production for ten years without breaking, it must be safe. Libraries like the Eclipse Implementation of Jakarta XML Binding (JAXB) quietly power enterprise applications in the background. Embedded deep into middleware stacks and application servers, they carry heavy workloads without drawing attention.
Advanced AI security tooling doesn’t ignore these deep-stack layers, however. It finds zero-day flaws hidden in structural parsing logic that standard static analysis tools miss entirely. And discovery is only part of the story. Any new vulnerabilities impacting these load-bearing pillars need to be discovered, analyzed, and swiftly addressed by the community. This is exactly what Lightwell did with a novel vulnerability within JAXB, identified as CVE-2026-92877.
Addressing novel flaws across the software lifecycle
When a vulnerability is discovered in a new framework, communities and maintainers respond quickly. The code is fresh, developers are actively tweaking it, and patches roll out quickly. Legacy components face a different reality. Unaddressed flaws in fundamental XML binding logic can compromise every application server, middleware pipeline, and cloud service that relies on it.
Left unaddressed, a flaw like this could create severe operational consequences:
- Chained exploits: Isolated parsing bugs can be chained with other system vulnerabilities to escalate privileges, bypass access controls, or even execute arbitrary code.
- Unplanned downtime: Malformed payloads can trigger unhandled exceptions or resource exhaustion deep within key services, bringing critical business workflows to a sudden halt.
- Supply-chain amplification: Because JAXB is buried deep within thousands of enterprise software packages, downstream vendors and IT teams often don't realize they are exposed until an exploit hits production.
Discovering and addressing a novel vulnerability in a legacy codebase in real-time is key, not simply finding the problem and passing the hard work to the community. Lightwell’s work with JAXB shows the value that a collaborative, responsible, and technically innovative security practice brings to global IT infrastructure, as well as the health of upstream open source communities.
True security is upstream security
Scanning a container image and flagging a potential common vulnerability and exploit (CVE) is relatively easy with modern off-the-shelf tooling. Finding a zero-day flaw in a decade-old upstream project, engineering a fix, and contributing that patch back to the open source community is hard.
That is the core value proposition of Lightwell.
Lightwell centers on active engineering at the source and deep-level stewardship. When the Lightwell team uncovers a novel vulnerability or one is brought to our attention by a customer, our mission is to fix it upstream at the source.
By contributing this fix directly to the eclipse-ee4j community, Lightwell helps protect the broader open source ecosystem before downstream enterprise runtimes face exposure. These upstream contributions, however, are only part of the equation.
In many enterprise environments, critical infrastructure runs on older software versions that upstream communities no longer actively patch or maintain. Upstream maintainers eventually move on to new major releases. When a flaw impacts legacy versions, downstream systems are left exposed.
Lightwell steps in during those exact scenarios. Whether fixing current code upstream or backporting security patches to older releases that organizations still rely on, Lightwell helps protect critical workloads without forcing disruptive, unplanned upgrades. 
Durability is an active commitment
Durable enterprise software, the kind that allows critical infrastructure to run reliably for decades, isn’t easy to deliver. It requires continuous, active maintenance and rigorous upstream security engineering. Red Hat delivered this work for the better part of 30 years across Linux, Java, Kubernetes, and supporting projects.
The discovery and upstream acceptance of this patch to JAXB is a major milestone for Lightwell and further validates our core commitment to open source security. Protecting critical enterprise applications starts deep in the software stack, and Lightwell provides the engineering required to keep those foundations resilient.
