articles.title: SpaceX and Google both said no. Now his software is riding a SpaceX rocket next to Google’s | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The way Rama Afullo tells it, he saw orbital data centers coming.
The Kenyan American engineer previously worked in Google’s cloud computing business before a brief stint at SpaceX’s Starlink communications network in 2024. His experiences convinced him that there was untapped potential for computers in space.
“When I was at SpaceX, I tried to pitch this internally. They said no. When I was at Google, I tried to pitch this internally. They said no,” he tells TechCrunch.
So he left SpaceX and co-founded Satlyt, a new company with headquarters in Sunnyvale, California, and Nairobi, to build software for satellites that he hopes will let many satellites share the work of large computing jobs in space. The company has raised an $8 million seed round, Afullo exclusively told TechCrunch.
The timing looks good for him. SpaceX has since gone all-in on orbital data centers, and Satlyt’s software is set to launch Thursday on a SpaceX rocket alongside the first prototype for Google’s space data center effort, Project Suncatcher.
Unlike SpaceX, Google, or startups like Starcloud and Cowboy Space Company, Satlyt isn’t planning to build its own spacecraft. Afullo’s team is building the software to operate AI models on satellites, comparing his approach to VMware and Snowflake — companies whose platforms let users run complex software without worrying about the underlying infrastructure.
“The folks like SpaceX who are doing orbital data centers — if they are the iPhone, we’ll build Android as a horizontally integrated, open ecosystem,” he said. In other words, Satlyt wants to offer software that works across many companies’ satellites.
Satlyt has already flown its software on two demonstration missions. The initial focus is finding operational efficiencies for spacecraft, which typically depend on flight controllers on the ground to solve any problems that arise. Sending data back to Earth, known as downlink, is expensive and often slow, so using AI to make decisions on the spacecraft can mean real savings, either when resolving anomalies or by processing sensor readings on the spacecraft instead of on the ground.
Earlier this year, Satlyt deployed Google DeepMind’s Gemma AI model onboard a spacecraft operated by Momentus. The model cut the size of a transmission about onboard software errors by more than 60%, the kind of efficiency that Afullo says can save hundreds of thousands of dollars per satellite each year.
A launch will put Satlyt’s software to work onboard a spacecraft built by TakeMe2Space, an Indian startup that builds computing hardware for satellites. The mission involves three customers: NASA, which is paying the company to test protocols for cloud computing in space; Stellerian, a startup focused on space surveillance (tracking objects in orbit) that wants to test image processing workloads; and TakeMe2Space itself, to show the satellite can host other companies’ software.
Right now, few high-powered GPUs are in orbit. For now, the most likely opportunity lies in the kinds of workloads Satlyt is working on. But the company’s next project is to show that it can create a shared computing system — a cloud — spanning two different satellites, which it expects to attempt next year. If successful, it will allow the company to build a true compute cloud in orbit as a third-party provider to spacecraft builders.
The way to think about it is that we turn your satellite into a revenue-generating managed service,” Afullo said.
Satlyt’s seed round was led by Houston-based Non Sibi Ventures, where partner Bernard Harris, who served as a NASA astronaut for more than 20 years, helped ground the firm’s conviction in a novel, space-based business.
One reason the firm invested was that Satlyt doesn’t depend on a highest-octane vision of space data centers, which faces uncertain economics and a launch bottleneck. “We don’t need data centers in space for Rama to be wildly successful, right?” Non Sibi partner Kent Lucas told TechCrunch. “It can just be driven by the number of satellites going up.”
Afullo’s hope is to be live on 20% of satellites by the end of the decade, when he expects virtually every spacecraft builder to be putting GPUs and similar advanced processors in their satellites.
“If you’re putting up a satellite without putting up a GPU on it, at the very least, you’re doing yourself a disservice, right?” he says.
This story was originally published on October 1. Satlyt is among dozens of other startups vetted by TechCrunch and appearing at Disrupt as part of our broader Battlefield competition happening this week in downtown San Francisco. It all kicks off on Tuesday. Learn more here.

articles.title: The UAE embraces AI for kindergartners
articles.text:
In September, Henry Price observed a classroom of 7- to 8-year-olds learn about the Stone Age. They discussed and wrote about cave paintings, then put on virtual reality headsets to explore them.
The founding principal of Rugby School Dubai hopes his students will soon study ancient Egypt the same way — reading about it, creating artwork, and then stepping inside a virtual pyramid, or using artificial intelligence to “interview” a pharaoh.
“AI does not replace reading, writing, discussion, or creativity. It enhances them and opens new doors,” Price told Rest of World. “We want our students to be excited by AI, but never [be] passive users. We want children who use AI to ask better questions, not children who rely on it to give them all the answers.”
The United Arab Emirates recently became the first country to make AI a required K-12 subject.
That puts the country on one side of a growing global debate over what children should learn about AI and when they should encounter it. While the UAE and China are treating early AI literacy as a national priority, some Western governments are moving in the opposite direction. New York City introduced a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI in public schools from preschool through grade eight, citing concerns about children’s mental health. Norway has also enacted a similar near-ban for primary school children.
“On one side is the wish to protect childhood, to guard against the addictive pull of some technology, and to raise happy, well-rounded children,” Prince said. “On the other is the fear that those same children could be left behind in a world changing at extraordinary speed.”
The UAE’s approach is not to give young children unrestricted access to AI. Instead, schools teach them how the technology works, where it fails, and when humans should use it.
Teaching kids AI
At Dubai Schools Al Khawaneej, a joint initiative between the Dubai government and K-12 education provider Taaleem Education, students in grades one through three are not expected to use generative AI independently, elementary principal James Efford told Rest of World. Instead, teachers use discussions, stories, and role-play to teach them about AI.
In one activity, a teacher might show children something an AI system got wrong, and ask them to identify what is incorrect or unfair. In another, the teacher pretends to be a robot and asks children to give increasingly precise instructions, teaching them how machines respond to the information they receive.
Most UAE schools are treating AI as a form of literacy rather than technical training.
Dubai’s Knowledge and Human Development Authority is developing a broader policy framework for digital technology and AI in education. It has a 10-year roadmap to prepare students for rapid technological change with personalized learning.
“Our goal remains to ensure that any integration of technology is developmentally appropriate and supports meaningful learning without replacing the essential non-digital experiences that contribute to children’s growth, well-being and development,” Saeed Kharbash, CEO of policies, research and programmes at KHDA, told Rest of World.
Abu Dhabi’s Department of Education and Knowledge, which is developing the AI education framework for more than 170 private schools in the emirate, did not respond to Rest of World’s request for comment.
AI is also being used to make classrooms more accessible. Jayda Keer, an inclusion and neurodiversity consultant and former head of inclusion at Dubai International Academy, said schools have used AI to simplify texts for students who struggle with complex vocabulary, translate material for students learning English, and create word banks.
Schools are still cautious
The UAE’s embrace of AI does not mean children are being handed ChatGPT and left alone.
Schools monitor apps and use firewalls. Younger children rarely use AI directly, while older students have restricted access to school-approved apps such as Padlet, Toddle, Canva, Mathletics, Times Tables Rock Stars, ClassDojo, Edmentum, and Epic. At least two schools told Rest of World they use MagicSchool for teacher-directed activities, while one uses Microsoft Copilot.
“We do not currently allow students to use public ChatGPT etc. accounts in school. Nor do we define the programme around a particular AI model or specialist hardware platform,” Efford said.
The government plans to train 22,000 teachers to use AI for teaching, assessment, curriculum analysis, and lesson planning.
22,000 teachers will be trained to use AI for teaching, assessment, curriculum analysis, and lesson planning under the UAE government’s plans.
“Teacher training and support is paramount,” Victor R. Lee, who leads the AI + Education program at the Stanford Accelerator for Learning, told Rest of World. “This is new territory for teachers, and they have their own unique considerations for how they use it and introduce it to students.” At Dubai Schools Al Khawaneej, teachers receive initial training, weekly briefings, lesson guides, and prompt banks, as well as support from colleagues. School leaders evaluate how AI is being used through classroom observations, student work, and teacher feedback.
“The emphasis is on developing teachers’ pedagogical confidence as much as their technical knowledge,” Efford said. “When should AI be used, when should it not be used, and how do we make sure it deepens rather than replaces thinking.”
Most countries are yet to commit as deeply. A U.K. primary school trained staff before introducing an AI chatbot to pupils, but there’s no national mandate yet. Estonia has started teacher and student training but for older ages.
China is perhaps the only major exception. Its National Workshop on AI-driven Teacher Capacity Building has reached 103 cities over eight years, and trained 2.97 million teachers, according to the country’s education ministry.
Parents want transparency
Several parents who spoke to Rest of World said they weren’t consulted about the introduction of AI in their children’s curricula, but they all supported it. Still, they raised concerns about transparency and accountability.
“I work in IT, so I see firsthand how fundamentally AI is going to change the workplace and society,” said Gigi Thomas, whose son is enrolled in Year 7 at Cambridge High School. “I would actually be more concerned if schools weren’t teaching children about it.”
Thomas and other parents would rather AI support and complement learning than replace it. “I am also mindful of screen time, online safety, and making sure teachers and parents understand the tools children are using,” said Amna Al Almarri, a homemaker whose 8-year-old son is enrolled at Al Mawakeb school.
Bedour Almarri, who works with the Dubai Land Department, has three children between the ages of six and 12 attending Dubai Schools Al Khawaneej. He called for a clear breakdown of the exact tools being used, how much classroom time is spent interacting with AI versus interacting with teachers and peers, and the guidelines teachers enforce regarding academic integrity.
“While I trust that the school uses educational-grade software with privacy filters, I remain cautious about data privacy, how prompts are stored, and whether children can accidentally bypass safety restrictions,” he said.
Edward Tsoi, CEO and co-founder of AI Safety Asia, a nonprofit focused on governance, public policy, and risk mitigation, said children need to struggle with a difficult sentence, sit with a math problem, and write a clumsy first draft to build the reasoning capacity they would need later in life, including to evaluate AI critically.
“If we let AI shortcut that struggle before the underlying skill exists, students get fluency with the tool and no muscle underneath it,” he said. “That’s why we’d draw a hard line between teaching AI and handing children an AI tool, which is commonly treated as the same policy when they’re not.”
Can the UAE’s model travel?
The UAE is not the only place where children are already using AI. Schools in India and Singapore have experimented with AI in classrooms, while South Korea introduced and later withdrew AI textbooks. In Colombia, Meta’s AI tools have interfered with learning rather than improving it.
A recent UNICEF report found that children as young as nine in Congo and Mozambique use AI for homework and want more guidance on how to use it safely.
The UAE has advantages many countries lack. Kenya and Pakistan, for example, are using AI partly to address teacher shortages in schools with much larger classes. Kenya has as many as 68 students per teacher, versus the UAE’s two. That makes the UAE’s approach difficult to replicate.
“Different governments have different value bets, and they’re operating under very different structural constraints,” Tsoi said. “The UAE has a comparatively small, centralized, well-resourced public school system with the political will and budget to back a national mandate. Other large, decentralized systems in the U.S. and much of Southeast Asia, for instance, don’t have that, and a mandate that’s achievable in the UAE’s system could not be implemented as effectively elsewhere.”
Additional reporting by Aarti Jhurani in Dubai.

articles.title: Mixture-of-Experts kernel engineering on Amazon SageMaker AI | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Mixture-of-Experts kernel engineering on Amazon SageMaker AI
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a sparsely-activated architecture that scales large language model (LLM) capacity while keeping per-token compute low. Because its operations account for a large share of total compute time, inefficiencies there directly raise request latency and cost. Therefore, optimizing MoE operations through kernel engineering offers the largest opportunity for performance gains.
Fused MoE is a key optimization technique for the MoE architecture. A fused MoE system merges token routing, data shuffling, and specialized network calculations into a single batched operation on the GPU. This replaces executing those routing and expert computations as separate, sequential loop operations. While this provides latency advantages, it also brings complexity in kernel implementations and debugging capability. High GPU utilization for this architecture requires hardware-specific optimizations.
In this post, we describe the different kernel optimizations we implemented for fused MoE models and show you how you can benefit from this work. We used a representative MoE model as our primary example.
Swap-AB for WGMMA utilization
To maximize tensor processing throughput, the NVIDIA Hopper architecture relies on the Warp Group Matrix Multiply Accumulate (WGMMA) instruction protocol, which executes collectively across a cooperative warpgroup of 128 threads. This operand asymmetry is fundamentally an instruction set architecture (ISA)-level property. In the underlying wgmma.mma_async assembly definition, the hardware fixes the matrix row dimension (M) at a constant scale of 64 to define its parallel thread-mapping topology. The column dimension (N) remains highly variable. Operand A strictly maps across this fixed M dimension (using registers or shared memory), and Operand B maps across the variable N dimension (through a shared memory descriptor). These operand slots are therefore structurally non-interchangeable. Consequently, peak hardware tile utilization is governed by these rigid shape encodings, requiring that the M dimension equals or exceeds 64 to prevent compute execution lanes from sitting idle.
This structural preference stems from how Hopper Tensor Cores partition memory blocks. The hardware enforces a fixed minimum layout shape for the leading dimension of the first operand, locking the block height to exactly 64 (M=64). When a mathematical matrix possesses a large, continuous leading dimension in this primary slot, Hopper’s internal hardware schedulers can cleanly map and distribute data across the physical computing grid.
This structural asymmetry becomes a severe performance bottleneck during the decode phase of MoE networks. In a standard MoE layer, the linear algebra governing expert computation is formulated using traditional matrix notation:
A[M,K] x B[K,N] —> C[M,N]
Where (M) represents the token row count (or batch size), (K) represents the hidden feature dimension, and (N) represents the expansive expert output dimension.
During the decode phase, the system processes only one token per user sequence at a time. Consequently, the batch space or token row size is profoundly thin, regularly dropping to a profile where (M < 64), and frequently down to a single row (M = 1). Under this standard structural layout:
Matrix (A) transforms into a thin, fragmented horizontal vector (for example, 1 x 4096).
Matrix (B) (the core expert weights) remains in a large, dense vertical block (for example, 4096 x 8192).
Because the row count (M) is tiny, Matrix (A) is physically incapable of filling the hardware’s fixed (64)-row layout bucket for Operand A. When the WGMMA instruction executes over this layout, it leaves a vast portion of the physical Tensor Core capacity completely starved. The silicon spends clock cycles processing empty spatial slots, leading to poor hardware utilization.
In a standard dense LLM layer, weight matrices are static, unified, and perfectly contiguous. In an MoE layer, however, the workload is fractured across a fleet of independent subnetworks (experts). This creates unique memory and layout bottlenecks that make it hypersensitive to the WGMMA constraints of the Hopper GPU. In a standard dense layer, matrix multiplication multiplies a token vector by a single layer weight matrix. The output dimension (N) is the model’s hidden size (for example, 4096).
In a Fused MoE kernel, the GPU isn’t only multiplying against one expert. It’s grouping and running math for all active experts simultaneously to avoid launching individual kernels for each expert. For a standard dense layer, N is the hidden size (4,096). For a fused MoE layer, N is the number of experts chosen multiplied by the expert intermediate size. For a model running a topk=8 routine, the effective N dimension inside the fused kernel explodes into tens or hundreds of thousands of parameters. Because the N dimension is so disproportionately large compared to the tiny decode token size (M=1), the layout asymmetry becomes extreme. Transposing the matrices moves this large, combined MoE dimension into the primary slot, unlocking hardware prefetching at a scale that standard dense layers cannot match.
To resolve this hardware misalignment without altering the underlying mathematical integrity of the model, we exploit the algebraic property of matrix transposition:
BT[N,K] x AT[K,M] —> CT[N,M]
By programmatically flipping the matrix multiplication before it reaches the PTX assembly layer, we realigned the software to match the exact topography of the Hopper silicon. This transposition triggers two immediate architectural advantages on the GPU. First, it saturates the physical layout. The expansive expert dimension (N = 8192) is promoted to the first operand position (BT), and because (N) is large it easily floods the hardware’s mandatory (64)-row threshold. The Tensor Cores then operate at maximum local density with no wasted execution cycles. Second, it activates asynchronous prefetching. Hopper’s dedicated hardware copy engines can prefetch memory addresses asynchronously from shared memory straight into registers before the math execution block fires. Placing the continuous, large weight blocks (BT) in the leading slot lets these engines trace the data layout smoothly and keep the compute pipeline saturated without CPU intervention. This produced a 2–4 percent end-to-end output throughput improvement across large-scale MoE models on H200. We upstreamed this optimization to vLLM, and it is available in version 0.24.0 or later.
Backend routing for FP8 tensor quantization
Beyond kernel internals, the choice of which backend executes the MoE computation has a large effect on performance. The vLLM MoE oracle routes different quantization schemes to Triton, FlashInfer+CUTLASS, or other backends. Profiling revealed that for FP8 tensor-quantized models on Hopper, the Triton backend consistently outperforms the default FLASHINFER_CUTLASS path.
The Triton backend outperforms CUTLASS in low-concurrency MoE workloads primarily because it replaces rigid, framework-level matrix math configurations with custom, operator-level register fusion. CUTLASS relies on standard C++ template structures that treat FP8 tensor scaling, matrix multiplication, and expert aggregation as discrete mathematical operations. The Triton backend instead consolidates this entire pipeline into a single hardware pass. Data is pulled from global high-bandwidth memory (HBM) exactly once and processed entirely within the GPU’s ultra-fast local SRAM registers and compute execution files. It’s then streamed back to the final matrix destination. This removes the slow global VRAM read/write roundtrips that compromise CUTLASS when it is forced to constantly step through intermediate tensor scaling steps.
Furthermore, this register-level fusion is specifically paired with dynamic scheduling layouts designed around variable token bucketing, resolving a severe structural flaw in traditional compilation templates. CUTLASS is natively optimized for dense, large, and predictable matrix dimensions. When it encounters the fluid, ultra-thin batch profiles (M < 64 or M = 1) typical of the live decode generation phase, its default block-tiling and thread-mapping structures become profoundly inefficient. The result is heavy warp under-utilization or expensive memory padding overhead. Conversely, the Triton MoE backend excels at dynamically mapping these small, fragmented token arrays across the physical boundaries of the active expert weights. This keeps the hardware’s internal prefetch streams and Tensor Core pipelines fully saturated even when processing highly unstable workloads at very low batch sizes.
Updating the routing policy is a pure configuration change with no kernel code modified. Still, it yielded a 10 percent end-to-end throughput improvement for FP8 quantized fused MoE models on H200. This improvement is available in the AWS Large Model Inference (LMI) v28 container.
Triton JIT recompilation elimination
One of the most impactful performance pathologies in GPU inference is also one of the least obvious: unnecessary kernel recompilation. Triton, the compiler framework underlying many of vLLM’s custom kernels, specializes integer arguments by default. Every time a kernel is invoked with a previously unseen value for a specialized parameter, Triton triggers a fresh just-in-time (JIT) compilation. In serving workloads where sequence lengths and batch sizes vary continuously, this creates a steady stream of compilation overhead that inflates latency, particularly Time to First Token (TTFT).
In MoE model serving, the _fused_inv_rope_fp8_quant_per_head kernel (responsible for fused rotary position embedding and FP8 quantization) was recompiling on every new num_tokens value. Adding do_not_specialize annotations to the variable-length parameters removed these recompilations entirely, improving TTFT by 9 percent on H200 at 8-way tensor parallelism (PR #42849).
In a multi-GPU cluster, all 8 GPUs must execute their kernels in perfect, microsecond-level synchronization. If even one GPU must stop to recompile its local _fused_inv_rope_fp8_quant_per_head kernel because its local token batch count changed, the other seven GPUs sit idle and wait for it. By eliminating recompilations across the entire cluster, we smoothed out the multi-GPU coordination overhead, delivering a 9 percent speedup for the user’s initial response latency. The principle here is to treat the compiler as a first-class optimization surface. Understanding how Triton specializes semantics and recognizing when parameters are dead or variable unlocks latency improvements with minimal code change.
We upstreamed this optimization to vLLM, and it is available in version 0.22.0 or later.
Conclusion
Through our collaboration with the vLLM community, we implemented and open sourced multiple kernel optimizations for fused MoE models. We apply these optimizations in the LMI Deep Learning Container on Amazon SageMaker AI. Together, these optimizations have delivered up to 10 percent higher throughput and up to 9 percent faster TTFT. To get started with custom model hosting, see the Amazon SageMaker AI hosting documentation.

articles.title: Promise Robotics strikes deal to supply largest US homebuilder DR Horton
articles.text:
Toronto-based construction tech startup Promise Robotics is ready to grow south of the border after landing its first United States (US) customer: DR Horton, the nation’s largest homebuilder in terms of volume.
Through the multi-year commercial agreement, DR Horton will leverage Promise’s tech and “factory-as-a-service” capabilities to support the production of more than 1,250 largely single-story, single-family homes for buyers in the Phoenix, Arizona area.
Promise CEO Ramtin Attar said a deal like this “requires quite a bit of trust.”
Promise co-founder and CEO Ramtin Attar told BetaKit in an interview that a deal like this “requires quite a bit of trust.” He said the deal emphasizes the power of the startup’s platform, which aims to help developers build homes faster and more cheaply than traditional construction methods.
“That a company at that scale is able to look at what we have done and say, ‘We’re ready to work with you,’ that, to me, is very significant,” Attar added.
Promise announced the deal today, also revealing it intends to open a 16,000-square-foot factory in Phoenix. There, its AI-powered robots will assemble the components necessary to construct these houses in what marks the start of its broader US expansion. “This is our go-to-market facility in [the] US,” Attar said.
The hub, which will be Promise’s first outside of Canada and the company’s third of its kind after Calgary and Edmonton, is expected to begin manufacturing in early 2027.
“I was actually talking to an investor the other day who said, ‘I really love your odds. If you can build in the frost in Calgary, Phoenix is going to be pretty darn simple,’ and that’s exactly the case,” Attar said.
While the US housing market is very different from Canada’s, Attar said it faces similar challenges, from labour shortages to rising costs, and pressure to build more homes faster.
RELATED: Canada’s housing supply is in crisis. Can robots help?
Promise uses AI to interpret existing home designs, generate production plans and robotic instructions, orchestrate manufacturing, and connect that production with site installation as part of one integrated platform. The company equips off-the-shelf robots with its own tooling and software to produce everything from repeatable modular housing to custom builds.
“We are continuously focused on improving cycle times, increasing production capacity, and bringing greater consistency and predictability to our operations,” DR Horton senior vice president of strategic innovation Brad Conlon said in a statement. “Promise Robotics’ integrated platform gives us a new capability to support those goals.”
Attar claimed Promise, which is now contracted to build just over 2,500 homes for several different homebuilders, has completed over 200 builds to date for a group that includes Brookfield, Hopewell, and Mattamy.
“These are real market homes that people are living in,” the Autodesk alumnus said.
Promise’s factories are currently capable of producing many of the core components that make a house, from the interior and exterior walls to the flooring, stairs, and roof.
The 80-person startup is working to add heating, ventilation, and air conditioning, and plumbing, followed by drywall, insulation, and more over time as it looks to grow to 100 employees by the end of 2026.
Feature image courtesy Promise Robotics.

articles.title: Introducing Firefox Enterprise | The Mozilla Blog
articles.text:
Mozilla introduces Firefox Enterprise
Institutions are recalculating who controls the technology they rely on. Mozilla has an independent option to offer.
For years, organizations consolidated technology around a small number of providers to make things simpler. Fewer systems. Tighter integrations. More economies of scale. But that consolidation went well beyond technology. It consolidated dependency, too. The resulting risks have been debated, studied, and challenged along the way, but concentration continued. More work, data and critical infrastructure kept moving to the same few providers, while credible alternatives narrowed.
The deeper that dependency runs, the harder and more costly it becomes to change course. When something fails, changes or falls outside an institution’s control, that dependency becomes a risk for CIOs and CISOs to manage.
Nowhere are these stakes more visible than in Europe. Now institutions are re-assessing. Governments are pushing for greater digital autonomy, while regulated industries face growing pressure to find and manage their dependencies.
There’s a name for much of this debate about technological control: “sovereignty.”
What digital sovereignty means in practice varies. Across Europe, governments are investing in the security and resilience of critical IT infrastructure, reducing strategic dependencies and putting technological autonomy higher on national agendas. Different approaches, same underlying concern. Strip away the regional policy definitions and industry distinctions and a pretty practical, universal question emerges: how much technological dependency should we risk?
And a very specific, very important layer has been largely missing from that conversation: the browser.
The overlooked layer of modern business
The browser. Applications run there. Employees authenticate in it. Sensitive data transits through it. Files are uploaded and downloaded and AI tools are increasingly used through it. That raises the same questions of dependency and control: whose browser technology are you relying on, and who controls the infrastructure used to manage it?
Introducing Firefox Enterprise
Firefox Enterprise is built for organizations with strict security, governance, and compliance requirements. It pairs the Firefox browser, built on Mozilla’s independent Gecko engine, with a management console organizations can run on their own infrastructure. From that console, IT teams can centrally manage browser policy and access, govern how data moves through the browser and set controls around AI use.
IT and security teams get more control over their data, IT infrastructure and browser environment — helping strengthen technological independence and operational resilience.
“If all your options are built with the same technology underneath, ‘choice’ is a lie. So is control,” said Anthony Enzor-DeMeo, CEO of Mozilla. “We built Firefox differently. And we’re bringing its independent architecture to institutions that are ready to rethink their dependencies and risk.”
Bringing the browser under control
We’re starting with the browser because we see it as a key, but under-governed, layer. Firefox Enterprise gives institutions more control over the browser and the infrastructure managing it.
And because Firefox runs on Gecko, the only major browser engine developed outside Google and Apple, institutions have another path towards reducing dependence on a single architecture.
Finally, Firefox Enterprise is built to live alongside the systems that IT operations already use. Keep your identity provider. Keep your SIEM. Keep your MDM. Just add a browser whose management infrastructure you operate, so you decide where data lives and have greater visibility into how it moves.
For us, supporting the goal of technological sovereignty comes down to four things: More control. More transparency. More choice. More resilience.
Learn more about Firefox Enterprise.
A big bet on familiar ground
We know this territory. Independence isn’t a new direction for Mozilla. We’ve spent more than 25 years building and securing browser technology that intentionally works outside of the dominant architecture of the day. Firefox is used by roughly 200 million people every month and is already deployed across thousands of organizations.
That independence has always mattered to the web. Now it has practical value for institutions looking to reduce technological concentration — and dependency — in their own environments. 
This is the beginning
Our ambition is big but simple: make technology independence practical.
That means putting institutions in real control of the infrastructure and data they depend on, without asking them to rebuild or start over. Closing blind spots. Defining where policies, access and data live. Keeping core management within the institution’s environment. And bringing an overlooked layer — the browser — under institutional control.
Firefox Enterprise is unveiling across Europe with an initial sales focus on France, Germany, Austria and Switzerland, with more markets to follow. Thunderbird Enterprise is also in development, extending this customer-controlled approach to email and communications. We’ll have more to share as that work progresses.
If your organization wants greater control over its browser infrastructure, we’d like to work with you.
This post is also available in: Deutsch (German) Français (French)

articles.title: Should Carney give Canadian tech a (tax) break?
articles.text:
Two years ago, Canada’s then-governing Liberal Party proposed a capital gains tax inclusion rate hike, and much of the country’s tech sector freaked out. While this plan was scrapped after Mark Carney replaced Justin Trudeau as party leader, the surprise decision and the message it conveyed had severely hurt the Liberals’ relationship with Canadian tech. As Roadmunk co-founder Latif Nanji told me last year, “The damage [was] done.”
Today, many of the same industry leaders have penned an open letter asking Carney’s Liberals for a capital gains rollover and a US QSBS-style tax incentive in the upcoming federal budget to better retain Canada’s entrepreneurs, talent, and capital. The key difference this time around is that both parties seem more receptive to working together.
As NACO CEO Claudio Rojas told BetaKit, “We want to see Canadian companies succeed, we want to control our own destiny, and that aligns quite well with the signals that we’re seeing from this government that they’re willing to take action.”
Hundreds of Canadian CEOs, investors, and other business leaders have signed the open letter. Its authors frame these measures as a means of derisking investments in domestic firms and incentivizing the reinvestment of associated profits in Canada.
As CVCA CEO Ben Bergen noted, it will take more than a single investment summit, budget, or prime minister swap to transform Canada. Others say it will also require more than just tax reform. Community builder Jesse Rodgers singled out removing personal guarantees on business loans and leases as another logical step.
These calls to do more signal how much has changed since 2024, when a large portion of Canadian tech was ready to run the Liberals out of town. Now, instead of regime change, Canadian tech feels emboldened to ask the new(ish) Liberals for sizeable tax breaks. With Canada’s latest budget expected to drop next month, BetaKit will be watching to see whether Carney heeds them.
Josh Scott, 
Reporter
